An excellent representation of a brilliant card game full of interesting gameplay mechanics and wonderful in-character comic book flavour.  Looking forward very much to the release of the expansions as DLC.  The base set has huge replayability, but adding the expansions will bring replayability off the charts.

Having played more than enough of the physical card game, Sentinels is the closest thing you can get to making your own epic comic book battles we all know and love without working at Marvel/DC/etc.  Choose your team of 3-5 heroes, each with their own playstyles such as buffing/protecting Legacy, drawing/using mass cards as Bunker, and sacrificing health for major powers from Fanatic/Absolute Zero.  Next pick a supervillain, each with its own set of rules and a "flipped" state that changes things further.  Finally select an environment that plays by its own rules and may hurt or help both sides, and have at it.
The magic of Sentinels is that no two encounters will be the same.  Cards may come up at just the right time for your band of heroes to pull together impressive comboes.  Legacy's "Heroic Sacrifice", preventing the damage taken by all other heroes until his next turn, would allow Fanatic, whom most of her abilities include self damage, to go ham for a turn with no drawbacks.  However this luck of the draw can work in favor of the villains, especially when some have special conditions that cause an instant loss for the heroes, such as when Baron Blade exhausts his entire deck.
Think on your toes, prepare for anything that the villain might pull on you, and you are ready to join the ranks of the Sentinels.
Also to those who might be complaining about not enough [insert aspect here], this was the contents of the starter box for the physical card game and more heroes/villains/environments are on their way.  I eagerly wait the time where I can recreate dealing over 200 damage in a single turn with Unity against Akash'bhuta.  Good times.

Some impressions for those who are both familiar and unfamiliar with the tabletop card game, and a couple suggestions regarding UI.
It comes with an in-game manual and also a tutorial playthrough. Those of us who are familiar with the tabletop game can skip the tutorial playthrough, but I skimmed through the manual just to make sure I understood the UI.
There is a lot of cards to keep track of but that's no different than the original. Fortunately you don't have to jockey the life & modifier counters in this, which takes up some extra time when you're playing the actual card game.
But the digital version has a shortcoming in this area; it doesn't mark temporary damage type immunities on the cards. So, for example, you must remember the last damage type you did to Omnitron when it has that Adaptive shield-type thing in play. I played against it with four characters and by the time I came back around on next turn, I had often forgot and ended up wasting an attack of the same type. I'd like to see some graphic indicator, such as a colored version of the min-card symbols, temporarily added while under such effects.
The indicator thing isn't a total loss. You can actually use a rather extensive "Go Back/Undo" feature that gives you a few options on how far back you want to replay. So if you mess up like this, you can just start your turn over from a few recent save points corresponding to the beginning of a character turn. This should also come in pretty handy when you miss or forget a good synergistic play between a couple characters on the same round, and for those new to the game.
I also wish that we could rt-click on the "mini-cards" to get the full text version to pop up, instead of having to use a double left click. Just personal preference, but the right mouse button isn't in use anyway so it would make sense.
Despite some qualms about the UI, it definitely remains the same SotM card game that gushes theme, has unique character powers/styles, and forces you to make tough strategic decisions. My favorite solitaire card game. I'm happy to finally get it on the PC.
I would recommend this for anyone into sophisticated tabletop games with a lot of theme, or anyone who thinks a superhero themed card game brawl would be fun.  One warning - it can be a difficult struggle to win.  But that's a plus in my opinion.

We’ve all played our fair share of zombie games, but imagine a game like left 4 dead; instead this time when you get bitten… it’s all over.
No More Room in Hell is a co-operative realistic first person survival horror mod (quite a mouthful) for the Source Engine. Originally made as a Half Life 2 mod, No More Room in Hell has now progressed into a full standalone title which has just recently been released on Steam as a Free to Play game.
No More Room in Hell is not like most other cliché zombie survival games, its main features include:
Co-op play with up to 8 players
Dynamic Objective Maps: Each time you play a map, it could be different from last time, with different objectives placed in different locations.
Realism: No crosshairs, No HUD. (Protip: Conserve your ammo, you’ll need it)
Infection: Now this part is what really makes the game fun. Unlike all the other games, when you get bitten by a zombie on NMRiH, you have the chance of becoming infected. When infected you only have a certain amount of time before you die and come back as a faster, stronger zombie than the rest. You can use this time to tell your friends to get ready… or you can keep quiet and hope to find a cure…
This game is without a doubt one of the best free to play games I have encountered, especially when playing with friends, granted the game is near impossible to play solo. (THERE’S SO MANY OF THEM!)
The gameplay is fast, fluent and fun. Swinging axes at zombies’ heads and watching multiple heads explode from a 12 gauge is just so satisfying, how can you not love it?
Graphics wise, NMRiH hit’s average to high standards, it’s not made for looks, it’s made for fun, and I can’t see anything wrong with the looks.
I recommend this game if you like zombies, gore and teamwork, what could be better?

(This review contains minor spoilers.)
When a man, a finely tailored suit and a well tuned and deadly pair of piano strings come together there is only one person that comes to mind: Agent 47. The hitman, the legend, the approaching shadow that you don't seem to see but never cease to fear. This is the very essence which makes Hitman games unique, remarkable and an unmistakeable mark of excellence that comes out of developer studio that is IO Interactive.
Where Hitman Absolution went a separate approach to the franchise's signature game design,
, on the other hand, has returned to its roots and comes close and even outshines titles prior to Hitman Absolution convincingly.
So what makes this game outstanding? Below you might find the answer.
Welcome to a world of assassination. Your next target is a world class dealer of classified government information in the guise of a fashion mogul in the eye of the public. Your client wants you to take care of this matter, no matter how. Approach it discreetly, make it look like an accident or leave bodies? You decide.
At the beginning of each Destination you get to choose your starting gear, a variation between the signature Agent 47 suit or apparel tailored to complement the scenery of the Destination more closely. Each Destination is filled with lots of opportunities to approach your targets, lure them out and to get the job done.
Ultimately, the cleaner the kill, the smaller the casualty and witness list, the higher the payout and the more points you gain in your Mastery stat, unlocking new weapons, gadgets and spawning locations for a more varied approach in later attempts. The more variation and creativity you achieve in your attempts the higher your Mastery and the better the unlocks.
The Destinations in this game are just gigantic. Every stage or part of a Destination feels alive and beautifully detailed. Many ways lead to success and in this vein there are multiple access points and opportunities to reach your targets. At times, though, this game design decision of having huge maps comes with the disadvantage of feeling maze-like but after you spend a good hour or two into a Destination you will quickly grasp the map's layout.
It's fairly calm in this regard.. until the situation goes south of course! The music cues in this game are reactive so whenever you eliminate a target/complete an objective, eavesdrop on an important discussion, complete all objectives or are spotted the music alters to enhance the immersion into a situation.
Thus far I had a hard time finding much of a flaw with this game, it certainly blew my expectations out of the water!... but unfortunately there are two topics that I had in mind after completing the game.
This is one of the major complaints by the community. In order to have your Mastery progress saved you must be online on Steam, which is then also linked to the "SE Link" online mode service by Square Enix. Although, admittedly, IO Interactive has done quite a bit regarding slowly removing this "Always Online" requirement, I sincerely hope they will take note when developing Season 2.
As much as I like this game and would recommend it to whoever that asks, I'd have a hard time defending the $ 59.99 price tag. It feels like a dilemma when buying it on a sale where it'd be criminally low and full price being too much. I feel around 45 to 50 it would have been ideal but maybe that is just me.
Overall I feel this game deserves the GOTY 2016 stamp, it's unfortunate it did not receive the amount of attention it deserves due to the Online Mode problems in the beginning, the lack of marketing done for the game and that it's a fairly niche game, but one that has been mastered by IO Interactive with an incredible amount of creativity and care for detail. If elegantly making your way to bad guys and delivering swift justice to their illdoings is your forte, try out the first episode of the game and decide.

Spec Ops: The Line is a cover-based third person shooter set in a ruined Dubai.  The gameplay is fun, but nothing revolutionary.  It's a little difficult, but it makes the combat feel more desperate.  The desperation makes good set dressing for the events of the plot.
The big selling point of this game is the narrative.  I don't want to spoil it too much.
Let's talk about the concept of choice in games for a minute, because that's one of the heavy themes of this game.  In Mass Effect, you're made to make lots of choices in dialogue.  Most of it resolves the same way no matter what you pick.  It tricks you into beleiving that the choices you make matter, but the truth is that Mass Effect 3 happens, and nothing you do even matters.  So, you make choices based on what abilities you want to use.  Maybe you make some choices so that you can fill a red bar instead of a blue one or bang a specific alien chick.  The writers of Mass Effect, and Fable, and InFamous, and any number of games that deal with morality fail to understand that choices made unconsciously during gameplay can add another layer to the story if the player is made to face the consequences.  Do you flank left or right?  Do you cast a healing spell, or press the offensive?  Do you jump on that goomba or over it?  What if you faced a penalty at the end of Super Mario Brothers for breaking all those blocks who were, at one point, ordinary citizens of the Mushroom Kingdom?
Spec Ops: The Line does this to great effect.  By the end of the game, you'll want to curl up into the fetal position and cry.
It felt like whoever wrote this story had respect enough for the gamers to deal with mature subject matter in a way that games seldom do.
My one major gripe is that the bad guy you're supposed to be looking for in this game is named John Konrad.  It's a too-on-the-nose reference to author Joseph Conrad who wrote Heart of Darkness, the story from which this game takes a lot of inspiration.  It's like how that one goth kid you went to high school with wrote poetry about how they wanted Charles Baudelaire to turn them into a vampire.  It's just a little cringey.  It also lets anybody with any knowledge of literature know early that things aren't going to end well.
TL;DR: If you're tired of your average modern military shooter, then Spec Ops: The Line is the game for you.  Definitely not for your twelve year old who wants a break from Call of Duty.   (9/10)

Batman; Arkham Origins is the third installment in the now legendary Arkham series, but it is the first chronologically. The story pits a fairly new Batman, with only a couple of years of crusading under his belt, against some of his most powerful adversaries, many of whom he will encounter for the first time. This game features a gripping story line, amazing graphics, and the revolutionary combat interface that makes this series a must have.
I own this game on WiiU and PC, and I am happier with the PC version. The WiiU version had a number of glitches and problems that made it difficult to play at certain points of the story. The game is fantastic on either platform, however, and I would certainly recommend it for WiiU owners.
The absence of the voice talents of Mark Hamill (Joker) and Kevin Conroy (Batman) may have diminished this title, but only slightly.  Roger Craig Smith and Troy Baker fill in for the roles respectively, and do a very nice job. I will always prefer the former couple, but the latter don't spoil the fun. I can't help but believe that this change, as well as the fact that Rocksteady didn't develop the game, is what earned this game a generally lower score from most critics. Personally I find the tighter battle elements that were introduced, particularly in some of the boss fights, has only pushed the series forward. The boss battles are varied and engaging, and the I Am The Night mode gives the title enormous replay value. There is also an online mode for PC which allows the player to conrol either a hero or a villain's cronie in a fight for control of a map.

This is perfect for anyone who even remotely enjoys 2D platformers, trust me, since I count myself as somewhat hesitant to the genre. But Ori and the Blind Forest hit all the right spots for it to be a vastly enjoyable, tear-shedding, awesome and beautiful experience for me.
First off - The art style. WOW is it beautiful, and neither screens nor video does it justice. Fluid animations, hand-drawn and incredibly detailed environments, and beautiful lighting. This game is a moving canvas of painterly atmosphere.
The gameplay is also really, really good - responsive input, clear and unobstrusive UI, good range of abilities and character progression. This is what really makes the game so accessible - on lower difficulties, players can enjoy the game without dying all the time. Higher difficulties provide challenges for those seeking it, and overall I feel as if there aren't any severe difficulty spikes, the pacing of the game is really smooth and natural. The game isn't too long, I went for a 100% completion on all treasures and secrets and still beat the game fairly fast, but for the price - I'm more than satisfied. It also depends on what you're looking for, so if you wanna play it for the story you may consider it a bit on the short side. But if you wanna play it for the challenge, you may get quite a bit more replay value out of it.
I would commit a crime if I didn't mention the music - I may never have experienced a game where the music is allowed so much space, and still manages to convey the atmosphere and story of the game in such an emotionally tangible way. And in the Definitive Edition you get the OST - 100% worth!
Storywise, the game is narrated well, and it sure as heck succeeded in making my manly man eyes shed some ounces of manly man tears - but don't expect anything overwhelming. It's reallly good for a 2D platformer game, let's put it that way.
Overall, I can't do anything but recommend this game, wholeheartedly. It's a gem of a game that no one should miss.
TL;DR - Game made me cry, 10/10, would cry again.

Digital version of an incredibly addicting tabletop game with tons of replay value. The UI is smooth and easy to use, and all the cards are very readable at different resolutions. The ability to active/use cards without having to double-click each one is very handy once you get used to the game and learn the cards by heart - which will happen if you use a hero long enough. The music is great as well, which was a pleasant surprise, and fits the superhero theme wonderfully. The inclusion of unlockable variant promo cards is a great addition, because each varant changes up the base power of the hero, or in the villain's case can really change the way the villain plays. This adds even more variety and combinations to a game already full of hundreds of hero/villain/environment combinations. And with the expansions inevitably on their way, there'll be even more. The tutorial is also really well done so you don't have to worry about being familiar with the tabletop rules before hand. It really walked through everything you could possibly need to know about how the game works, which is nice for those who've never played before.
On the flipside, the only thing I don't really like about this digital version is the lack of online multiplayer, although it is coming in a future update. The game does, however, lend itself really well to playing multiplayer locally by simply sharing the computer. And of course being able to play the game solo when you're craving a Sentinels fix is really where this game shines. Controller support would also be nice for playing on a TV, but that is also coming down the pipe eventually. Handleabra games is really doing a nice job of making the transition from physical boardgame to digital version.
As for the gameplay itself, it plays exactly like the tabletop version. Each player takes control of a superhero and teams up to take down a villain. Each hero has it's own unique deck of cards with wildly varying playstyles between each hero. Legacy, for example, is the paragon of justice who uses his cards and abilities to buff and defend his team of heroes, while someone like Tachyon uses her super-speed to burn through her deck drawing and discarding cards, many of which do more damage based on how many specific cards are in her discard pile. Each hero's deck of cards fits the hero's theme and superpower wonderfully, making for a different experience and strategy with each hero.
However, the villains also have a deck of cards full of minions and nasty super-powered attacks to take down the heroes. At some point during the game the villain's card will trigger an effect that causes it to flip over, which changes up the mechanics of how the villain plays - and sometimes changes the max HP the villain has. Plus each villain has a nemesis (or multiple ones) attached to it, which means the villain does extra damage to his nemesis, and vice-versa. And you can't forget about the environment you're playing on. After the villain has had his turn and all the heroes have gone, the environment itself gets a turn and draws a card from it's deck. Sometimes the environment deck helps the heroes out in someway, most of the time it does horrible, horrible things to the players like having pterodactyls steal all of your equipment. Each enviroment has it's own gimmicks to it's deck. Megalopolis has lots of city hazards like a speeding train that can damage both heroes and villains, or cops that show up to aid the heroes. Meanwhile something like Wagner Mars Base has a self-destruct timer, which if it reaches the end kills both the heroes and the villain and everyone on the Mars base ending in a draw.
The game has hundreds of combinations, as each time you play you pick a villain, and environment, and anywhere between 3-5 heroes. Everytime you play even just changing one of those from the previous game can really affect the outcome of the game and change the strategy you'll be using. The game has so much variety, and the rules are so simple to pick it up, that it makes itself very addicting. You can play dozens of times and still be surprised when something crazy happens that flips the current game on it's head. I really can't recommend this enough.

Divine Divinity is a fantastic old-school RPG.  There's a little bit of everything here in one aspect or another: Ultima VII, Sacred, and the great Infinity Engine games with some Diablo hack-n-slash action thrown in--though most things not done quite as well.  The graphics (again, like the Infinity Engine games) have held up amazingly well and the game is still beautiful, boasting a soundtrack just as much so.
There's a vast, incredibly detailed above-ground and subterranian world packed full of secrets, quests and treasure for you to discover.  The skill system is filled with useful abilities, very little filler and doesn't restrict you to your class skills; even if you start as a mage you can pick up some thief skills along the way if you desire, and chances are you'll want to.  Combat is satisfying and the difficulty seems just right.
Not much point in playing as multiple characters due to the open skill system, but the game already packs dozens of hours.  Same price as GOG, so don't hesitate to buy it if you don't have hangups about playing older games.

Borderlands 2 I give it a 6 out of 10.
Just finished borderlands 2 for the first time. What it does right it does amazing. What it does wrong it falls utterly flat.
It's a great game. Don't get me wrong. Every character is memorable. The style is outstanding. The dialog rarely falls flat. But the actual gameplay is actually rather boring. Play it once through for the story and characters. They're worth the price of the game. If it wasn't for them I'd have dropped this game before the half way point.
It's very grindy. The mission set ups and stories are fun but the actual execution is "shoot the same enemies you've been shooting for the past three hours". You out level your weapons requiring you to constantly replace them. Find a good weapon? Get into a groove using it? Well it's not doing crap now. Gotta find a new one! This aspect of the game is fine when you're max level, I'm sure. But when you're leveling it's a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ There's no real cover system. So unless the enemy has a massively telegraphed or slow moving attack there's no reason to ever budge from one spot. And the one ability each character gets just doesn't shake up the game play enough for it not to be a "Stand there and keep shooting" afair. Like a point and click game but the only puzzle is solved by "Use gun on man."
The after game is all about grinding to get the insane weapons. As if you haven't had enough of that by the point of beating the game. The end game is all that grinding x10. Hey everyone let's go back and fight the same boss 100 times to get that one weapon we want. Ah, but only one of us can grab it. So if you're with friends it's 100 times multiplied by how many people you have with you.
It needs more abilities, more enemy types, a gun crafting system would be nice, independent loot drops for each player, and a cover system.

I would like to start off by saying that I was first introduced to DMC when it first came out many years ago. To put it mildly games like DMC and Onimusha simply blew me away. I've been playing this for a short periof of time and I would put this up there with the Darksiders series (both great games in their own rights) and Dantes Inferno. They'd better make a sequel to this reboot effort. It would be a gaming crime if they didn't.

The game launched on Friday December 16th, and in four days I put in over 33 hours.  This is a great addition to the survival crafting genre, building upon established gameplay mechanics while introducing a few of its own.
Probably the most unique aspect of this game is its utter lack of any user interface.  You interact directly with each item in real time and your inventory is displayed right on your backpack (which you can zoom in on with "Q").  I really liked this approach to things.
Like most other crafting survival games, this one is all about collecting resources and progressively unlocking better tech.  In the progression department the game doesn't currently have a lot to offer, but I'm confident more content will be added as the game is developed.
In the end, if you like survival crafting games this one is a no-brainer.  Do yourself a favor and pick it up.

Mediocre but OK for the money while it's on sale and  the only reason I voted "recommended"is that you can't go wrong at that price. If I'd have bought this at full price when it was first released, I'd have felt cheated. After twelve hours I just finished the final mission and am none the wiser as to what it was all about. I didn't find the storyline very engrossing and there were very few times a moral decision needed to be taken contrary to what some of the reviews had led me to believe. I always play the ruthless type in any rpg game anyway so i just shoot anyone slowing me down. I don't know whether it would have made a fundamental dirfference to the outcome of the game if I'd have made different choices but I suspect not and don't intend to play it through again to find out.
It's an OK shooter though. Combat is fairly good. It can be quite difficult to fight through multiple waves of enemies at times. I normally play games on medium difficulty but did have to switch to the easiest setting a couple of times when I was really stuck. The game helpfully suggest you do so when you die multiple times in the same area. It has the usual array of weapons to loot and swap around and that is very important as you'll find yourself running out of ammunition quite often and only by switching to a different weapon type can you carry on.
My main gripes are that it plays on rails. You can only follow a very narrow predefined path. You can't vault over a knee high wall unless the game invites you to do so and for some reason the default controls include some very peculiar presets. Just about every PC game I've played for the past twenty years has used the space bar as the jump key and yet this one is set  by default to the shift key and the interaction key, which is E or F in most games is ther space bar here. Fortunately, you can reassign the keys so that's the first thing I recommend you do.
So, if you just want something new to play for a few days or so, go for it if it's still on sale.

The game's flaws started popping up at around the 2 hour mark - Ori had always been controlling a bit floaty, which I was fine with since it worked with the aesthetic beautifully and hadn't been interfering with the platforming thus far, but I was beginning to notice that the hazard placement was becoming a bit too precise for that to work. The enemies, meanwhile, were starting to increase their damage and health much faster than I could deal with, leaving me to either rush past them and hope I avoided damage or stop for 15-30 seconds per opponent.
When I reached the second dungeon, I was beginning to get worried. The game introduced floors that cause instant death unless you hold an item that inhibits your movement, and was putting moving instant-death floor platforms on top of instant death spike pits topped off with an enemy that. Then the instant death lasers showed up and I had to repeatedly slog through about a minute's worth of laser gauntlet without being allowed to create any save points during any of it, since the only spot that wasn't covered in spikes or lava floor was arbitrarily unsafe for saving even though the rotating laser nearby only ever grazed the corner opposite of where I was trying to save.
I got though that dungeon, only to be trapped in an escape sequence that demanded I dodge falling spikes with minimal reaction time and even floatier controls than normal, reflect a curving projectile to hit a small target, and precognitively realize which spots were safe to stand in while giant instant death screen covering rocks fell periodically.
Immediately after that was one of the most infuriating plot developments I've seen in ages (
) followed immediately by a forced stealth segment that was hard to even start because the only hint as to what to do to get past the starting position was a patch of ice glowing slightly brighter than all the other glowing ice.
I then had to use updrafts to glide up a mountain...which turned out to be absolutely
in instant death spikes, to the point where the
had no safe spots to stand whatsoever other than the entrance, and expected me to pick up multiple items inside narrow, curving tunnels while dealing with the updraft physics the entire time. As soon as I got through that bit, of course, I had to do more of the same, except with enemies and instant death lasers this time.
I ended up throwing in the towel on the path to the volcano - the screen was half covered with instant death traps, enemies were firing projectiles that I was expected to use as my only means of transport while other identical-looking enemies were firing screen-crossing rotating instant death lasers without even being consistent as to what direction they'd rotate in, and I realized that there wasn't any chance of the game returning to what I considered to be fun.

Despite Arkham Origins' problems it is a title worth your time if you enjoyed the previous titles in the franchise. Good voice and character direction combined with a stellar performance by Troy Baker makes it a memorable addition. There are plenty of gadgets and upgrades, a plethora of collectables that help flesh out the world and even the boss battles are some of the better entries into the series.
It is not without its flaws. The game has crashed for me once or twice and even on beefy PC there can be minor graphical glitches. The combat feels less 'tight' in its execution and several cutscenes looke compressed and less pretty than they do on console. As I use a gamepad I cannot comment on the keyboard and mouse controls but gamepad support is excellent (not a surprise given this is a console port) and responsive.
If you enjoyed the other Arkham games this one has lots of content for you to enjoy, including the ability to play Deathstroke in challenge maps and several fun predator rooms. You will find some the gadgets make certain parts of the game trivially easy, which is my only real gripe.
If you  haven't played an Arkham game before than I suggest you spend your money on Asylum or City first and see how you enjoy them. All are complete and excellent experiences but the Rocksteady developed duo has tighter controls and an extra level of polish.

This game dresses to impress.  While I was was a big fan of Hitman: Absolution, I found it was completly possible to beat the game going guns blazing, Call of Duty style.  This game can be done like that, but it puts way more emphasis on the stealth hitman we all know and love.
The mechanics feel solid, the story is suprisingly good, and after I beat the first mission, I was quickly impressed by the wide range of activities that can be done outside of the 5 main missions.  While 5 missions seems like nothing, each can take 30-60 minutes to beat one way.  Each mission also has a plethera of sandbox ways to beat the game.
This is the Hitman game that we have been waiting for since Blood Money.  8/10

I have not finished the game yet, but I can already tell that I will be replaying all the episodes/chapters a bunch more times.
They have done a really good job with creating a Hitman game that is true to the old titles!
The game is a lot more challenging than in Absolution. In Absolution you could just use instinct mode to remain unnoticed and to not raise suspicion from guards, in this game thats no longer an option and thats a good thing.

The prologue part was a bit underwhelming and was basically nothing more than a 1 hour long mandatory tutorial level (like in Blood Money). I can understand why they have added it to the game, but I wanted to just skip it and get on with the real game.

The episodes I played so far (the first 3) have well designed maps that look really atmospheric. I especially like the Italy themed map. Walking through the narrow streets on that map looks almost exactly the same as walking around in real Italy. It almost felt like I was back on holyday in Toscane!

Only small negative points I have is that the colours looks a bit to washed out for my taste. It looks like as if they have reduced the contrast and colour intensity in the game.  And the performance is not optimal, but acceptable. I overall have a good fps, but some spots dips the fps just to much. At my end (@high/ultra settings) looking at a large crowd of people = 50 fps, looking at a fountain = 38 fps for some reason. Generally depending in what direction I look at the fps is good (enough) or dips by 10/20 fps.

The game also has a 'always online' DRM build in. I am personally not bothered by it, but some gamers really dislike that. I have read on the forum that they are going to remove that DRM, but I don't know if thats true.

If you are a fan of Hitman or even if you just like the genre I defenitely recommend to pick this '1st season' up during a sale. Also at full price it is certainly worth it.

Edit: They have removed the DRM!

Max Payne 2: The Fall of Max Payne, a sequel to the original Max Payne, keep the same great gameplay, suprisingly undated graphics and gripping story. An absolute must buy for anyone who has played the original!

Max Payne 2: The Fall of Max Payne is a direct sequel to Remedy Entertainment's critically acclaimed 2001 third-person shooter Max Payne and picks up after the events of its predecessor. The game could be best described as noir-style love story, in contrast to the first that was more of a film noir revenge tale.
NYPD detective Max Payne is once again the primary protagonist, although a few very interesting segments sees you play as his love interest, Mona Sax. Max Payne 2 borrows a lot from the original and there are enough hints and references to the previous game which helps keep the narrative interesting and fresh for old-timers.
Max Payne 2 is, in many ways, a huge improvement over Max Payne 1. Gone is that constipated look  replaced instead with full 3-D modeled faces. The game also sees an immense graphical upgrade with excellent usage of the Havok 2.0 physics engine. Game characters are more detailed while environment objects, including enemies, tumble and fall very realistically.
Gameplay is largely the same with a few refinements to combat. Bullet Time sees an upgrade allowing you to dodge bullets and reload quickly, with a cool whirling animation to go alongside it. This results in a higher body count but also makes gun-play segments a whole lot less challenging. Level designs are, once again, brilliant with mission locales ranging from warehouses, mansions, hospitals and clubs to constructions sites. And the enemy AI is, on a whole, pretty decent although in a few instances they end up killing themselves with their own grenade.
The plot is riveting with almost non-stop action throughout. The storyline unfolds in much the same fashion as the original. The usage of graphic novel comics complete with melodramatic over-the-top dialogue sucks you into the game's environment. If anything, the writing is more polished this time around with lots of witty and philosophical quotes thrown into the mix. The story focuses too much upon the love-story angle though which tends to get a bit jarring towards the end. In comparison, the original Max Payne's story, although slightly rough around the edges, was more dark, grittier and compelling than its sequel.
For a game that is over twelve years old, Max Payne 2 still holds remarkably well today. It overshadows the original in many aspects while also introducing a few cool mechanics of its own. Simplified mechanics make for interesting combat segments making Max Payne 2 one of the very best third-person shooters ever made.

Okay to get the game running on newer PC's you need to go to msconfig, to get there on Windows 8.1 you should first hold down the windows button usually found on most keyboards on the left side and then hold the R key until a program simply known as Run pops up. Once you complete that step you can simpy type msconfig and and from there enter the program. Once your in head to the boot tab and enter advanced options, then check the box that says number of processors and put it to 1 by clicking it in the box below, then you hit OK and apply and then OK again to exit msconfig. Then it will ask for you to restart your PC to limit the processor usage to 1. To get all of your processing power back in use go back to msconfig and uncheck the the number of processor usage box go through wth OK and apply and restart. Now after all that you can play Max Payne 2: The fall of Max Payne on your Windows 8.1 PC.

A continuation of the successful first game
attempts to take what made the campaign of the first game good, that is to say the story and characters, but instead offers very little in those aspects; instead we have better all around guns blazing action to compensate right? Well maybe...
So Black Ops was really good, the twists and turns of the story made up for the standard CoD formula you've come to experience
since the start of the franchise. Black Ops II picks up on the 'Mason' character but adds a nonsensical plot with the addition of
. He is as cliche as they come; a man swearing revenge against what he considers imperialists, after said enemy 'accidentally' killed a member of his family. Naturally he vows vengeance against the world, manipulating and plotting against entire governments and always staying a step ahead of the elite intelligence and military power of both US and China. The absurdity of the character is pretty evident from the notoriously weird mission where you play as him and you'll be finding your self eye rolling whenever he appears on screen. He has several aces in the hole which make up for very lazy plot writing and that's in my opinion a huge disappointment coming from the first game.
So the plot is tiring and the deviation from the original formula seems a little off since many of the characters you've come to know and respect in the first game, while present in the second, they're shadows of their former selves and not just because of the years past. The dialogue is predictable but forgettable, the plots carries on for far too long but as a saving grace the fun is still there for the most part.
What's to say about the gameplay? You have your shooting galleries, your awkward vehicle stages, basically your run of the mill CoD game is here. There are however some extra elements which are there to break the monotony.
These include the addition of 'strike force' missions, special missions which are a bit more strategic by design but turn out heavily flawed from a gameplay point of view. During these missions you can switch to an isometric RTS style camera and control troop movements towards completing an objective. You can actually play as the soldiers you command from a first person perspective and you'll soon find out that is actually the best way to do it. So the game becomes sort of an endurance and time trial match which while it is still fun to shoot things, you'll be left wondering why these type of missions where included as 'strike force' missions and not part of the original campaign.
Another major difference is the inclusion of different story paths. Make no mistake, the game is still linear but there are different routes you can take depending on your actions during the missions which will determine how the story will unfold. It is quite interesting for a CoD game to include this and I have to admit that it did actually help to break a little of the staleness that has befallen the franchise but only barely. If anything I didn't feel the need to play the game again and go for a different route because of my indifference in the characters and main story.
As I mentioned above, the saving grace of the game is the fun shooting enemies accompanied by the exceptionally good soundtrack of the game (I'd dare say even better OST than the first Black Ops) while having lots of futuristic weaponry and gadgets at your disposal. But again, if you've played a CoD before, you know what to expect.
Finally I'm giving this a very very reluctant thumbs up, solely due to the fact of the shootin'-tootin' fun gunplay and soundtrack through some of the nicer missions of the game. If you're a CoD fan, getting this
is probably the way to go and to add to your collection. If you're somehow new to genre/franchise, there are better games to start your journey.

Spec Ops: The Line is something... more than a game. Obviously it
a game, because it features gameplay--specifically, gameplay where you and two squad mates are sent into a war-torn Dubai on a recon mission that turns into something so much more. Spec Ops has the most basic, mundane third person shooting that one can wish for: you can hide behind cover, you shoot humans with guns, your health recovers by waiting, and there is a ton of sand.
But that's the point of Spec Ops. A mundane facade designed to undermine your expectations, because nothing can prepare you for what the game's story puts you through. There comes a point where you stop shooting the enemy and you question what you're even doing--you get so caught up in the gameplay that you don't even realize the decisions you're making, and furthermore, the decisions out of your control.
Spec Ops: The Line is, essentially, a deconstruction of the modern military shooter genre. It grabs hold of the likes of Call of Duty, Battlefield, and other contemporaries and asks them: why?

This is a game with a considerable level of morality to it, unlike the usual 'Gung-Ho' ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
Having said that, I found it most entertaining and highly enjoyable and for the price, I would most certainly recommend it.

Fun little survival on alien world/s early access game. Collect resources, build your base up, perform research and explore the surface and underground caverns (and then other planets/moons). Game is very much in alpha, but able to be enjoyed in single player currently, recognising that you will have some crashes and glitches. If you expect your games to be optimised, with polished controls and relatively bug free, then wait until release.
Multiplayer is enabled but I wouldn't recommend doing more than just taking a look. Sync issues are rampant and there appears to be no mechanism to routinely resync. When driving, lag can result in the non-host players getting ahead of landscape detail being rendered, causing physics issues when things pop in underneath or inside you. Falling through the terrain is a regular occurrence. Some messages e.g. research outcomes are only displayed to the host. Basically, the multiplayer allows others to jump into the hosts game and help them out. They don't have separate bases of their own and can't save their own progress - it simply saves to the host and non-host players rejoin from scratch, hoping to locate and raid their previous backpack (corpse). Potential to be an enjoyable co-op experience once the dev's get around to working on the multiplayer. They've apparently published a roadmap on their site/forum, but I've not taken a look at it yet to see where mp sits in their priority list.
As at the date of this review, only recommended if you plan on playing single player. Not recommended in its current state if you primarily want to play multiplayer - wait for some multiplayer specific patching to occur.
Reviewed based on 20 December 2016 version (four days day after release into early access and with a couple of patches).

Pills4Skills is a psychedelic precision puzzle-platformer that will test all of your reflexes. This is Petro Shoferystov’s first game on Steam but if you take a look on his YouTube channel he has posted gameplay videos of other games that he has designed as well (they’re also on his website). Some of them such as Project J look very interesting so I do hope that they make it past the concept and development stage and onto Steam at some point.
I tend to agree with ¡OOO67VH who despite only playing the game for about 35 minutes summed up how I feel about this one succinctly. It reminds me of VVVVVV if that game dropped acid. You need quite a bit of skill to be successful here although quite a lot of that comes from using your head as some of the levels are much easier than they appear to be.
There isn’t a lot that needs to be said for it. It pretty much explains itself – and better than words could put it – through the watching of the gameplay videos. You need to go through levels collecting pills – which causes the psychedelic distortion to take place every time – and a key before heading to the exit to advance to the next level.
The game has some nice Steamification in it with nine achievements and it is a part of the Steam Trading Card program which as you know I really appreciate. The game also has full controller support.
One brilliant note is that Petro even considered those of you that suffer from epilepsy and epilepsy-like symptoms when playing video games. You can turn the effects to low rather than a high setting and you should be able to play the game. Unfortunately because I am not a sufferer I cannot confirm whether it works but I am led to believe that it has been tested sufficiently – though your millage may vary.
At the $3 mark the game is an absolute bargain. If this type of game appeals to you from a gameplay and/or a visual perspective jump on it.

Borderlands 2 is a big game. The sprawling cooperative shooter has arrived, delivering long hours of shooting, looting, and butt jokes. Well, almost intact. Game design changes, like changing the enemy death animations, do a good job of cutting corners while preserving the core action. Technical shortcomings, however, leave little doubt that this is the lesser version of Gearbox's great sequel. Dialogue and sound effects frequently sound flat and occasionally disappear, while the frame rate often slows down in combat and makes the chaotic action feel unwieldy.
Combat in Borderlands 2 is naturally a bit floaty and loose, largely due to way player movement and enemy behavior are paced. As a result, it can accommodate the small degree of control imprecision added by the touchscreens and be none the worse for it. Likewise, the smaller range of motion of the analog sticks may cause some making the PC/console transition to balk a bit, and indeed, aiming can initially feel ungainly if you're used to the game on other platforms. After you adjust the aim sensitivity and spend some time wandering the wastelands, however, the mercenary satisfactions of long-range headshots and up-close bullet barrages are well within reach.

No More Room in Hell is an exhilarating experience guaranteed to give you hours of addicting gameplay, but that is not to say that it doesn't have its learning curve. If you are used to the gameplay physics of games like Call of Duty: Zombies or Killing Floor, you got some combat to get used to.

Think about traditional George Romero style zombies.
Why are they scary? They're dumb, slow, and a heavy blow to the head is all you need to put one down. Many zombie games stray from these standards resorting to turning all zombies into Olympic sprinters, making them extremely resilient to damage, or flooding the levels with zombies as far as you can see to make them feel imposing.
No More Room in Hell hugs the Romero formula that I've always loved consisting of a majority of slow zombies, infectious bites, and always reminding the player that letting their guard down for even a second could be the death of them or a friend. The scarce ammo supply forces players to use melee weapons and to be very mindful of their shots. If someone gets infected, they can delay their impending demise with medicine or they can be cured with a bullet to the head. Once turned, players lose control over their character and become an AI controlled running zombie, sabotaging all of the players' hard work.
Game modes are divided between objective based maps and wave-based, survival maps. Objective maps dynamically choose which objectives the survivors will need to complete to finish the map. Survival maps pit the survivors against wave after wave of zombies with the only objectives being defending the marked bases and not dying in the process. Players get supply drops from the military after surviving enough waves. I can't comment much more on this because I usually die or lose all my bases after 2 or 3 waves with my usual 3 person team.
This game on realism mode (1 headshot = kill) is quite possibly my favorite zombie game of all time. It's also 100% free. I highly recommend grabbing a friend or two and giving it a try.

Disclaimer: The game is still currently sitting at 20 bucks. If you're not ok with an extremely short campaign of about 5-6 hours at most and not interested in the MP mode, which apparently still has an active community, I would definitely wait for a deep sale of at least 50%.
Why? Because the game as it is is just another 3rd person cover shooter. In a realistic military setting. It's nothing special in terms of gameplay: take cover, aim, shoot, kill. The game swarms you with more and more enemies the further you advance in the story, which can be somewhat offputting. Why can your 3 man squad mow down entire armies? At least most enemies die with 1 headshot, so I would definitely recommend using mouse and keyboard. You, however, also die very quickly and I assume it only gets worse on the higher difficulty levels. At times I felt just without many options when you're pinned down, which is somewhat realistic, but doesn't make for great gameplay. So, on that front, the game is ok, but nothing special. And like I said, it's very short, but then again, since it doesn't introduce any new gameplay mechanics later on that is for the better. I couldn't stomach 10+ hours of this.
Now, the real gem here is the setting and story. You're tasked with establishing a link to a storm wracked Dubai, which lies pretty much completely in ruin. Of course♥♥♥♥♥♥goes south and you're forced to kill a lot of people. The interesting thing here is that...let's just say: not all is as it seems and you mostly don't have to deal with a lot of the typical American oora ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t ;) The story is more serious, sober, terrible, to be honest. Not talking about the story itself. That's great, but the overall message is...different than what CoD shows us. Consider this an anti-war game. During the story you will be "forced" to make several decisions that slightly alter the story. But these are more for your own sake than the game's. They are morally amigious decisions.
10 bucks for the SP campaign seems warranted. Not more though. Dubai, however, the setting in general, it has been beautifully realized.

Amidst the awkward controls, the dated 2012 graphics (even for their time), and the mostly run of the mill 3rd person cover-to-cover shooter, lies a gem of a game, mostly due it's superb storyline and unique narrative.
starts off a bit slow but once you picked up on the pace of the game, it quickly turns into a very entertaining and thought provoking experience.
I'm gonna start reviewing the game from a gameplay and technical point of view. The 2012 release looks barely OK in 2017. It's not horrendous and I'll admit certain parts of the game look really good for their time, but even 5 years ago there were prettier things. The gameplay is your typical 3rd person action cover-to-cover shooter. Nothing you haven't played before, nothing revolutionary, just OK. You're in control of your character and two squad mates who you can order to help you to take down the enemy and provide covering fire. They can use flashbangs and revive each other but that's just about it. You can carry only 2 weapons, from a variety of assault rifles, submachineguns, snipers, shotguns, pistols and heavy weaponry. You can also have up to 3 different types of grenades. Ammo is not as generous as you might expect and truth be told that adds a little bit of difficulty and immersion to the game but overall there's not gonna be an issue. The controls are little bit awkward and for me it was a sore spot for the overall enjoyment of the game. Running from cover-to-cover is weird and you might die as a result of poor mechanics since sprinting and taking cover is the same button. Really poor design choice but again, nothing too serious.
There's not really many types of enemies. Soldiers, snipers and heavies, very little
combat with turrets/vehicles but I'd be a liar if I didn't say it wasn't fun. Not the best fun you've ever had but enough for you to push on through the campaign. I have to be honest here and say that there's really not much else to talk about the gameplay. It is as generic as it comes, I can understand people liking or not but for me it was as uninspired as it comes. The maps and level design were interesting at times and the environment of Dubai looked pretty nice for most of it's part. But the game is not about the way you shoot and kill and people, but rather the
.
Spec Ops: The Line storyline remind me of the first Black Ops game. Kind of weird how both have the word
in their title right? I don't want to spoil too much of the story but I will try to provide context for the game. You're in control of Captain Martin Walker and his two squadmates, First Lieutenant Alphanso Adams and and Staff Sergeant John Lugo, part of the elite Delta Force, send to Dubai during one of the worst dust storm season the region has ever seen where
33rd Battalion of the U.S. Army is stranded after returning from Afghanistan. The 33rd is trying to help to evacuate the civilians out of the city but upon your arrival you notice that something else might be going on. The premise piqued my interest and the way the story unfolded over the course of the game had me at the edge of my seat. I wish I could divulge more information but sadly that would take away from the story. Naturally, the game's been out for over 5 years so really spoiler warnings might be unnecessary for some but if you're one of the lucky few who haven't experienced this yet, I feel it would be a shame if you didn't do so first hand.
The game explores a variety of themes directly from the nature of warfare. If there's an anti-war game, I guess Spec Ops: The Line would be it. Nowadays you can rightly claim that some of the tropes and themes of the story have been explored before in other visual and interactive mediums, but the game has a great narrative supported by brilliant dialogue and an otherwise excellent soundtrack, with polarizing characters who you will meet. You have choices in the matter too; it's not RPG level type of divergence, but certain actions in the game will have lead to different outcomes.
I have to add that I would love to see this game made into a movie or a miniseries even. If I could imagine
with a note of
, this would be it. The game has attracted a variety of theories regarding the meaning of its story, the characters and I think that is a sign of pretty good storytelling.
Spec Ops: The Line is not long, ~6 hours, but it's guaranteed to provoke some interesting feelings and thoughts upon completion. It's not the most difficult of games but there a few challenging situations especially on higher difficulties. I definitely recommend this game for everyone who enjoys action games and people who want a decent story and rich characters in their games as well. Do not be deterred by the mediocrity of its gameplay cause underneath all that game lies a great storyline and the feeling of completing the game will make you wonder about all that you experienced.

I finally played Max Payne 2 all the way through.
I did play the first game when it was released back in the day, but never really liked it.
Don't get me wrong, it's a entertaining game, but story wise, there's not much there.
I never really cared to try Max Payne 2 out for that simple reason.
But I recently played the first Max Payne again, and just like when I played it back in the day... I didn't think too much about it. Then I decided to give Max Payne 2 an honest try.
And boy is it soooo much better than the first game.
Even though the story is pretty predictable, it never gets boring.
The script is awesomely written (props to Sam Lake), especially if you like the film noir-genre.
I grew to love the characters, and just like Max, I ended up falling a bit for Mona Sax (who is modeled after the beautiful Kathy Tong).
If you, like me, have a soft spot for tragic love stories mixed with a heavy dose of awesome action, then this is the game for you.
Another game in the same vein (but without the film noir-influence) is The Darkness, and I love both these games equally as much.
Now it's finally time to give Max Payne 3 a try!

Super Meat Boy is a platformer of the hard and simple variety. You play as Meat Boy, trying to rescue your love, Bandage Girl, from the evil Dr. Fetus. Gameplay isn’t all that more complex than the story. You move left and right, and there’s a button to jump, and another button you hold to run (which also allows you jump further).
Speaking of the controls, they game is frankly awful to play with a keyboard. I highly recommend getting an X-Box 360 controller for Windows and using that instead.
Anyhow, let’s get back to the game itself. As mentioned, it’s not all too complicated. You run and jump, you can wall kick, and you try not to die. Which you will do anyway. A lot. See, this game likes to kill you in one hit. Fall off an edge? You die. Jump into a saw blade? Shredded to bits and dead. Lasers? Kiiiiill yooooou. Missiles? Kaboom! And your life is gone! Salt? One grain will ruin your cholesterol levels. You get the idea, everything will kill you. Once you manage to overcome death and beat the level you’re treated to a replay featuring all of your attempts to complete the bloody thing. These replays are quite enjoyable to watch, seeing your many meaty selves fall to the ground while only one manages to successful reach Bandage girl at the end of the stage.
For all the game’s difficulty, it never really seems unfair. You can plainly see what’s coming almost the entire time, and the occasional difficulty spike from a surprise is one that can be overcome quickly (discounting  of course the ensuing difficult from still beating the level once you do know what’s coming). Blind jumps are thankfully non-existent in the game, for the most part anyway. It wasn’t until I was well into the game on chapter 5 or 6 when I took a jump and though “gee, really don’t like that I have to take a blind jump here,” that I then realized this was a problem I had not encountered up to this point (and didn’t again that I can recall). So for all the times you die, it does seem fair, which helps the game not be as frustrating after several dozen or more deaths on a single stage.
In addition to the basics of the game, one can also collect bandages scattered throughout some of the levels. This serves as both an additional challenge and a way to unlock some bonus characters (which I’ve not really taken the time to try). Each level also has a par time for you to aim to complete, do so fast enough and you unlock the dark world version of the level (which serves as a hard mode for it). Scattered throughout the levels are also a small number of retro warp zones, which kick things a little more old school, and are again mostly there for a little extra challenge, though some also feature new characters that you unlock upon completion of them.
Special mention needs to be made of the music in this game, which is really, really great. It’s chip music reminiscent of the platformers of yore, and it’s fantastic.
Now, while the game starts off on a strong note in all the departments of its strengths, I think it’s worth noting that in chapter 4 everything takes a noticeable uptick for the better. This is where the difficulty gets kicked up a notch, and the hard-as-balls platforming is even more noteworthy for its difficulty. More importantly the level design itself becomes notably stronger, and it wasn’t slouching to begin with. The same is true for the soundtrack, which again, I’d like to impress upon you is really quite good.
The main game itself will probably take you around 10 hours to beat. I confess, while I’ve managed to finish the main game without issue, I’ve not been able to complete all of the bonus stages or dark world stages. Some of them are really, really hard. I do intend to play more of this game, but I’m not actually certain I’ll be able to finish every level. So I’m not sure how long it’d take to 100% this game, none-the-less, I’ve certainly got my money’s worth and had a blast with what I have done in the game.
Main criticism I have of the game is issues with frequent crashes. There’s really no good reason for this, while I’m not running a top of the line gaming rig, I do have a gaming computer that’s able to handle most any game on the current market without issue, so a low specs game like this can’t be tripping it up. This is an issue I’ve had on both 64-bit Windows 7 and 64-bit Windows 8, so it’s an issue that’s managed to persist on two different computers. Other than that, well, the keyboard really does suck for this game, and you are best off getting a 360 controller to play it.
In the end though, this game’s a must have for fans of platformers, especially those with an affinity for the super difficult ones. And since the game often goes on sale for pretty darn cheap, you really have no reason not to pick this up.

=== OUTDATED REVIEW ===
Please note, this review was posted 6 days after game launch. A lot has seemingly changed since then. This review focuses on what at the time, was a very big problem with the game and what many other players felt needed changing (see older forum threads).
The devs and the gaming community have since said that Koshey (a red card) is no longer imbalanced. As such, this review would no longer be relevant.
I'm leaving the review "as-is" until I play the game again, in which case I'll update the review accordingly. So until then, please take this review with a grain of salt.
========================
Perhaps the single most P2W game on Steam.
There is only 1 card you need to win this game: Koshey.  Period. He's a red card (epic). There are only a couple dozen different cards (there isn't much variation at all), but this one, single card dominates them all.
If you do not have Koshey, yet your oppoent does, exit the match. You'll be wasting time otherwise. Koshey takes very little damage from any other hero card in game, takes very little spell damage, has a big chance to rez when (if) he dies, and 1-2 hits any other hero in the match.
Koshey can be defeated by playing A LOT of other cards against it...each taking a quick death, but doing at least a small amount of damage to him. The problem with that however, is that if you have Koshey, you get him out asap...before the opponent can get more than 2-3 heroes out.
Koshey, by himself, will march down the lane, take out 2-3 heroes very easily (which is at max, how much can be created in the same time period), then destroy the gate.
It's an absurd card that makes the game completely unfun. But, everyone recognizes this to be true, so most people will spend money on packs until they get him.
There is only 1 meta in this game: Koshey.
Interested concept...but one of the worst deliveries possible.

if you can get around the obvious early access caveats, this game already has a lot to offer:
+ almost full diegetic UI: the strongest point in my opinion. every bit of crafting material/object is part of the 3d game world. your energy/oxygen bars are part of the player model and there is no classic HUD. the inventory is always visible in an immersive and unobstrusive way and crafting is not your usual watching of bars filling up.
+ artstyle and theme: it's low poly but very consistent. everything fits together, there's a positive dissonance between what you look like (cute cartoony lil astroneer) and what you do (exploit and destroy the environment)
+ terrain manipulation: the sculpting seems simple, but it just works and feels very satisfying
+ general survival gameplay: not countless hours of ressource collecting and continuous refilling of typical survival meters but rudimentary automation and relaxing exploration of beautiful environments.
+ great developement team so far. very responsive and open about the games future and current events.
that being said, there are aforementioned caveats:
- no real optimization: widely varying performance across all specifications. I run an old i5 2500K and gtx 960, but had no serious problems so far. some framerate dips after long sessions from 60 down to ~15 and the occasional CTD, but other people report more serious problems uup until unplayability.
- research and technology: needs to be fleshed out, more a proof of concept for now
- no real challenge: you have to try really hard to die and if you do, there are almost no repercussions.
TL;DR: great space exploration crafting game with ~15 hours of gameplay (til you have seen everything for now) and a solid base for expansive features to be added, but some flaws regarding performance. 7/10 if it was considered finished, 11/10 for being early access and already way more fun than another certain space exploration crafting game.

First things first: You have to pick your runes and masteries. Normally, cooldown reduction runes and perks that lead up to Thunderlord's will easily net you the seven killstreak required for the attack helicopter reward, which will inevitably win you the game through sheer brutality and a higher score count. Just a quick reminder, that you have to flame anyone in chat that uses the ACR since that gun is for nerds and weaboos. Pros always use the desert eagle as their primary weapon, despite the fact that you cannot equip it in the primary weapon slot in your create-a-class menu; you have to beat the game with legendary difficulty on at all times ever since you last left Helgen. If you manage to mine enough stone to make a pickaxe, you can start mining for the next tier of tools, which are iron tools.

An extremely impressive and worthwhile entry in the DMC series.
As someone whose played all the games (except for the infamously disappointing 2nd game), this definitely ranks amongst the best in the series.
I feel that the combat is more fluent, varied, and more open to experimentation than in any of the previous Capcom games.
It's understandable that people resented and were judgemental of this younger, dark haired version of Dante. Even I, as a fan of the series, was a little put off just because it was DIFFERENT. And gamers typically don't appreciate changes.
But developer Ninja Theory has given him more personality, depth, and emotion than any of the Capcom-developed entries.
You'll see his character grow as the plot moves on, and certain events happen which take a toll on him. Classic Dante (in the older games) has only two traits: style and badassery. This version of him gets pretty boring after you realize how two-dimensional he is.
But Ninja Theory has crafted a deeper, relatable version of the iconic protagonist. Yes, the style and badassery remains in abundance, but Dante is more than that in this game. I've never been so into a Devil May Cry story as I am with this game.
Character depth isn't limited to Dante; the game has a wealth of likable (or despicable) characters with a lot to them. The superb voice acting does well to compliment this.
Visually, the game is gorgeous. Colorful and vibrant, and plenty of incredible art and style also make this game stand out amongst the rest, particularly DMC 1 and 3, which sport dark, gothic color pallets, and generally have a depressing vibe (for me, at least).
I can't recommend this product enough. If you consider yourself a fan of the Devil May Cry games, you NEED to play this. Don't be put off just because Dante's freakin hair is a different color. Yes, its tone is wholly different than the previous games, but it's place is well-earned amongst them. In my own opinion, the combat and story have never been better.
Ninja Theory has crafted an excellent product, and a sequel is very much deserved. Look forward to DMC5 from Ninja Theory!

This latest update to the future of HITMAN is exactly the move needed to build fanbase loyalty and goodwill for people who had gripes with Season 1 from the newly established IO-Interactive. For a brilliant game marred mainly by the former publisher’s demands for always-online DRM, the Elusive Targets and the Episodic Model, which I found to be surprisingly beneficial, this franchise has taken the first steps to restore its name.
While not all the infamous issues are gone, such as level progression (not player progression) being unlocked by connecting online, IO-Interactive have taken great strides by removing Denuvo and including the two prologue missions as a demo. For a newcomer, it will probably take you around 5 – 7 hours to complete all challenges as you learn the intricacies of what makes HITMAN a different type of stealth game. Even if you’re still on the fence because of the online component as well as the idea of Elusive Targets, the demo is still worth experiencing to see how an episodic model can enrich an AAA game.
Unlike my other reviews on episodic games, I think this one warrants examining the levels individually for what they offer because of how infamous this game has become. This review will serve to talk about the overall experience of Season 1.
As someone who abstains from purchasing games with episodic releases until they’re complete as I don’t like to wait to finish my games nor do I enjoy incomplete storylines, I cannot help but think that outside of Square-Enix’s demands there were also good intentions with this design to make a true-to-form Hitman game for modern audiences. The reason I stress this point is because if this game was released as a complete season I don’t believe a lot of modern audiences would enjoy it.
When it comes to modern gamers’ tastes, the sad fact is that many people will not replay a game after their first experience, even less will replay a level to appreciate what the game offers. You could play through  Season 1 in under seven hours to experience all the content, but you would be experiencing the game at its worst when you’re unfamiliar to the levels, unsure of how the AI behavior works, and you end up fumbling your way to success. This is ultimately the most difficult hurdle to get into the series that it’s understandable why HITMAN has never been popular.
I believe this is why Absolution was such a departure; it emphasized more bite-sized open-areas in a linear progression with optional challenges for replayability that didn’t feel like a true HITMAN game. Season 1, however, is more tightly designed to reward replayability in the style of Blood Money by offering huge levels of stealth-sandboxes of timers for opportunities and items to create a meta-game progression. In terms of HITMAN, you don’t level up your Agent 47 to get better; you increase the number of variables you can influence as well as your overall understanding of every level with rewards to persuade you to try again.
It’s an experience that can undoubtfully feel intimidating to new players that are not accustomed to this playstyle. Unlike Metal Gear Solid V that also forced you to replay levels by changing area parameters, enemy placements and objectives in the same environments, Hitman has you replay the same levels for alternative objectives and challenges. The result is a system that rewards the player becoming more intimate with all 14 levels to truly master your knowledge, and this progression could take you up to 50+ hours with no filler.
This all leads into a question about the episodic model, “Was the model meant to force players to replay levels to truly appreciate how much depth there is?” Now whether the quality of Season 1 was the result of IO working around/with Square-Enix demands or if it was designed to encourage newcomers to enjoy the HITMAN experience I think the final product goes to show that AAA episodic releases could be beneficial if handled correctly.

For those who are unfamiliar with the series, the question that probably comes to mind is, “What makes HITMAN distinct from other stealth games?” In many ways, the archaic controls such as placing items on the ground, the odd AI behaviors, and the stealth gameplay are all rather simplistic that would be black marks in any other game. Its simplicity, however, is what makes it so rewarding to infiltrate as a caddy to set an explosive golf-ball on a target or to perform an act of irony by killing a target with a safety-inspection procedure.
HITMAN itself embodies the phrase there is an art in murder, and the gameplay runs with the idea to ludicrous, self-aware rewards for taking out horrible people in the enjoyment of the act. It’s not something you earn on your first runs, nor do you master the game on your third. In fact, it’s preferable to spend a good hour learning the ins-and-outs of a level as well as the locations of items, opportunities and disguises before you attempt it. There are some settings to help guide players to explore levels, but the satisfaction you earn by finding out the best route and quickest means to get through a level with only your suit and no traces behind is the ultimate test of your skills.

With this design that admittedly feels more like a stealth puzzle game or reminiscent of the abandoned house in Metal Gear Solid 3, there are shortcomings to the design of HITMAN that I hope are fleshed out in the future.
The first of which is the lack of storytelling in this game. It’s a concern I can ultimately live with as the act of replaying the level with new clues and more detail about your targets is a more enriching storytelling experience than the narrative between levels. Even though the story relies on piecing together pieces of cinematics and random mutterings of NPCs in the levels between hours apart from trial-and-error gameplay, the story itself is rather simple. None of this is to say the narrative is weak; it’s intriguing enough for what it is if a bit too subtle for most people to piece it together and too impersonal to invest interest long-term into what is offered.
The far greater issue, however, is the repetitious nature of all missions sharing the same objectives: Kill two targets and escape. I realize that with HITMAN it’s more important how you handle both targets that provides more variety along with the act of exploration and a few additional objectives, so the fact that all missions share the same structure is perhaps beneficial. Even with this design I think they could add modifiers like the Escalation challenges to add more variety in the core gameplay, but the fact that a mode already exists to fix that issue should make my point moot. However, I think for Season 2 there should be something new to shake up what feels very formulaic to a fault with Season 1.
The only thing about HITMAN that I don’t agree with are what are known as Elusive Targets, one-time opportunities for contracts in certain levels that are available only for 48 hours until they’re gone forever. While I can live without them as they are meant to be like matchmaking special tournaments or long-term reasons to replay HITMAN, I cannot deny they can make some feel like it punishes players who wait for the full season or for reviews and it creates an appearance of a product decaying with time.
For the moment, the future of HITMAN is brighter than ever with these few first steps and moving in a better direction that I can only help will benefit IO-Interactive if they continue to build upon what they have achieved so far. While I doubt that HITMAN will ever reach an audience beyond those who desire something different from modern games, what has been crafted is an experience as fine as wine and, hopefully, something that will age better once all the constraints on single-player are lifted.

I've been burned by Early Access titles many times, so I was nervous about a game that looked so promising right out of the gate. Now that I've played for a little while, my worries are gone. Astroneer is a ton of fun, with a unique mechanic that makes shaping the world and gathering resources fun again. While it may be a bit light on content at the moment, Astroneer has enough to keep players engaged. I can't wait to see what this game shapes into. As long as the developers keep the quality level as high as the initial release, this game has a bright future.

The game as it stands, has a ton of performance issues, most of which are to do with the game mechanics. Setting up a base or digging too much or creating huge stuff causes performance issues. Simulation is too detailed for a more adventure type game (the base's energy simulation could do with losing some detail and gaining performance instead). Overall, I wouldn't recommend this on any basis other than the fact that it's really ♥♥♥♥ing fun to play even though I get crashes and low FPS (only after building huge bases). Multiplayer (although further decreases FPS) multiplies the fun. Must buy.
