Now I'm here to give Call of Duty: Black Ops 2 my full and honest review for the PC, from the single player to the garbage multiplayer, and to the zombies mode. This review is not at all like the unintelligent and very short nonsense reviews you see when you scroll down on the store page for this game.    Let's begin.
surprisingly the campaign is rather fun. Our star characters return from the original Black Ops, Alex Mason and Frank Woods. I'm not going to spoil the story of the single player campaign, but after beginning of the game, your actions and decisions in certain missions will have an impact on certain characters and the overall ending of the game, in which, there are multiple endings. You have loadouts to customize with a fine amount of pieces you can unlock before you begin the next mission, you can even put a gold skin on your weapons late in the campaign.
'Strike Force' missions, which is a new single player concept for Call of Duty, is a mix of real time strategy and First person shooter combined into one. I have to say it's pretty satisfying to play on hardened difficulty. It's a shame the later Call of Duties don't have a feature like this.      All missions have around ten unique challenges to complete, which by the way, most of them are very difficult and just straight up ridiculous, along with achievements tied to these challenges, thay take hours and hours and hours to complete just for a couple missions.
But overall, the single player campaign is well done, and worth a playthrough.
Oh my God... Multiplayer on Call of Duty started going downhill since Black Ops 1. Peer to peer connections, terrible maps. Let me get to the point,
In this carbon copy shooter, everyone is their own little Rambo running around like chickens with their heads cut off trying to get the most kills.There is no semblance of strategy or teamwork-That's Call of Duty, that's what it's been for the longest time. Only here, it's gotten worse over time since Black Ops 1 and Modern Warfare 3. Why? It's because development of the multiplayer now has all of these ridiculous prestige levels in which you start your multiplayer rank ALL OVER once you reach the max level. Upon prestige, you are given a single permanent unlock token in which you can use to obviously permanently unlock any weapon, attatchment, or perk that you want, and smart players will use their tokens on an item you unlock near the final rank they achieve. Starting all over more than ten times.
Prestiges aren't the only reason why multiplayer is a missfire.

I'm going to get this out of the way. Dante looks like king of the♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥nozzles. I'm new to this series, but it seems like each iteration they make him more of a jerk. Every shot in this game portrays him like a snarky ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, and his smug face reaches record levels of punch-worthy. It's the face of the guy who cuts you off on the highway despite having three wide open lanes. That guy.
That being said, this game is really freakin' good. If you're a fan of the action-platformer genre (Darksiders, Castlevania: Lords of Shadow, that whole shebang), there's a ton of awesome, raw carnage here. The mechanics of battles are smooth like butter, slicing and leaping from baddie to baddie, and the kills are seriously gratifying. There's even a few secrets spread out among the levels, although their difficulty ranges from "really damn annoying" to "turn to your right and there it is."
In terms of sound and graphics, the game runs beautifully. No stuttering, sharp and crisp sounds, intense soundtrack, and really interesting environments. Seriously, the level designers for this game are brilliant. The story's alright, although most people can see some of the twists coming a mile away. Still, it did its job, and there were quite a few likable characters (aside from Dante, that prick).
All in all, I'd definitely recommend getting this game, even for folks who are new to the series. Pick it up with the DLC as well if it's on sale, adds a new campaign on that follows Dante's brother, Virgil.

I never played the other Devil May Cry games, so this obviously colors my perspective. However, the fanbase of DMC seems rather Japanophilic (and I'm a Silent Hill fan so I know what this affliction can do to fanbases). "IT ISN'T JAPANEEEZ THEREFORE IT SUCKS" is both terrible logic and the sign of someone trying to feign being educated and sophisticated.
That aside, the plot has some good ideas (the idea of "Limbo" and the like seems inspired by tabletop RPGs like Kult) although its social/political/economic commentary is about as deep as the kiddie pool. The cliche pseudo-Marxism has me rolling my eyes.
But what makes this game good?
The gameplay is FUN. Seriously, the combat is incredibly fun and fluid and fast. It has depth and variety and tactics yet manages to not be too arcane, the movements and animation are stylish and awesome, and stringing together combos and the like is just a blast. DmC just provides pure flowing hack-n-slash joy.
Also, the visual design is striking.
And the music. Oh man the music suits the game perfectly and totally indulges the rebellious spirit. Its awesome.
So, whether its a "good DMC game" is something I cannot comment on. Is it a good game? Oh hell yes.
PROS:
+ Awesome, fun fighting with a good balance of depth and accessibility
+ Stylish, striking visual design and art direction
+ Killer soundtack
CONS:
- The social commentary can come off as pseudointellectual trash that Fails Economics FOREVER
OVERALL:
Turn off the brain. This game is all about fun combat, fun music and awesome aesthetics. And it delivers in spades. And I'd REALLY like the developer to sell replicas of Virgil's coat.

This latest update to the future of HITMAN is exactly the move needed to build fanbase loyalty and goodwill for people who had gripes with Season 1 from the newly established IO-Interactive. For a brilliant game marred mainly by the former publisher’s demands for always-online DRM, the Elusive Targets and the Episodic Model, which I found to be surprisingly beneficial, this franchise has taken the first steps to restore its name.
While not all the infamous issues are gone, such as level progression (not player progression) being unlocked by connecting online, IO-Interactive have taken great strides by removing Denuvo and including the two prologue missions as a demo. For a newcomer, it will probably take you around 5 – 7 hours to complete all challenges as you learn the intricacies of what makes HITMAN a different type of stealth game. Even if you’re still on the fence because of the online component as well as the idea of Elusive Targets, the demo is still worth experiencing to see how an episodic model can enrich an AAA game.
Unlike my other reviews on episodic games, I think this one warrants examining the levels individually for what they offer because of how infamous this game has become. This review will serve to talk about the overall experience of Season 1.
As someone who abstains from purchasing games with episodic releases until they’re complete as I don’t like to wait to finish my games nor do I enjoy incomplete storylines, I cannot help but think that outside of Square-Enix’s demands there were also good intentions with this design to make a true-to-form Hitman game for modern audiences. The reason I stress this point is because if this game was released as a complete season I don’t believe a lot of modern audiences would enjoy it.
When it comes to modern gamers’ tastes, the sad fact is that many people will not replay a game after their first experience, even less will replay a level to appreciate what the game offers. You could play through  Season 1 in under seven hours to experience all the content, but you would be experiencing the game at its worst when you’re unfamiliar to the levels, unsure of how the AI behavior works, and you end up fumbling your way to success. This is ultimately the most difficult hurdle to get into the series that it’s understandable why HITMAN has never been popular.
I believe this is why Absolution was such a departure; it emphasized more bite-sized open-areas in a linear progression with optional challenges for replayability that didn’t feel like a true HITMAN game. Season 1, however, is more tightly designed to reward replayability in the style of Blood Money by offering huge levels of stealth-sandboxes of timers for opportunities and items to create a meta-game progression. In terms of HITMAN, you don’t level up your Agent 47 to get better; you increase the number of variables you can influence as well as your overall understanding of every level with rewards to persuade you to try again.
It’s an experience that can undoubtfully feel intimidating to new players that are not accustomed to this playstyle. Unlike Metal Gear Solid V that also forced you to replay levels by changing area parameters, enemy placements and objectives in the same environments, Hitman has you replay the same levels for alternative objectives and challenges. The result is a system that rewards the player becoming more intimate with all 14 levels to truly master your knowledge, and this progression could take you up to 50+ hours with no filler.
This all leads into a question about the episodic model, “Was the model meant to force players to replay levels to truly appreciate how much depth there is?” Now whether the quality of Season 1 was the result of IO working around/with Square-Enix demands or if it was designed to encourage newcomers to enjoy the HITMAN experience I think the final product goes to show that AAA episodic releases could be beneficial if handled correctly.

For those who are unfamiliar with the series, the question that probably comes to mind is, “What makes HITMAN distinct from other stealth games?” In many ways, the archaic controls such as placing items on the ground, the odd AI behaviors, and the stealth gameplay are all rather simplistic that would be black marks in any other game. Its simplicity, however, is what makes it so rewarding to infiltrate as a caddy to set an explosive golf-ball on a target or to perform an act of irony by killing a target with a safety-inspection procedure.
HITMAN itself embodies the phrase there is an art in murder, and the gameplay runs with the idea to ludicrous, self-aware rewards for taking out horrible people in the enjoyment of the act. It’s not something you earn on your first runs, nor do you master the game on your third. In fact, it’s preferable to spend a good hour learning the ins-and-outs of a level as well as the locations of items, opportunities and disguises before you attempt it. There are some settings to help guide players to explore levels, but the satisfaction you earn by finding out the best route and quickest means to get through a level with only your suit and no traces behind is the ultimate test of your skills.

With this design that admittedly feels more like a stealth puzzle game or reminiscent of the abandoned house in Metal Gear Solid 3, there are shortcomings to the design of HITMAN that I hope are fleshed out in the future.
The first of which is the lack of storytelling in this game. It’s a concern I can ultimately live with as the act of replaying the level with new clues and more detail about your targets is a more enriching storytelling experience than the narrative between levels. Even though the story relies on piecing together pieces of cinematics and random mutterings of NPCs in the levels between hours apart from trial-and-error gameplay, the story itself is rather simple. None of this is to say the narrative is weak; it’s intriguing enough for what it is if a bit too subtle for most people to piece it together and too impersonal to invest interest long-term into what is offered.
The far greater issue, however, is the repetitious nature of all missions sharing the same objectives: Kill two targets and escape. I realize that with HITMAN it’s more important how you handle both targets that provides more variety along with the act of exploration and a few additional objectives, so the fact that all missions share the same structure is perhaps beneficial. Even with this design I think they could add modifiers like the Escalation challenges to add more variety in the core gameplay, but the fact that a mode already exists to fix that issue should make my point moot. However, I think for Season 2 there should be something new to shake up what feels very formulaic to a fault with Season 1.
The only thing about HITMAN that I don’t agree with are what are known as Elusive Targets, one-time opportunities for contracts in certain levels that are available only for 48 hours until they’re gone forever. While I can live without them as they are meant to be like matchmaking special tournaments or long-term reasons to replay HITMAN, I cannot deny they can make some feel like it punishes players who wait for the full season or for reviews and it creates an appearance of a product decaying with time.
For the moment, the future of HITMAN is brighter than ever with these few first steps and moving in a better direction that I can only help will benefit IO-Interactive if they continue to build upon what they have achieved so far. While I doubt that HITMAN will ever reach an audience beyond those who desire something different from modern games, what has been crafted is an experience as fine as wine and, hopefully, something that will age better once all the constraints on single-player are lifted.

Okay, full disclosure, I bought this game randomly and super late at night. The previews were kinda cool, and I'm a sucker for platformers, so I went for it. And I'm happy I did, because this game is maximally fun, to the point where I was actually surprised at how fun it is (don't you love when that happens?). The effortless way that new special powers are integrated into the game gives it just the right mix of learning curve and instant utility, and there's something incredibly satisfying about watching Ori cavort and fly and spin across the screen smoking baddies with slow-motion camera angles interspersed throughout. Even though the game is a platformer, the highly imaginative art makes it seem to have the freedom of a sandbox, and the environment will look amazing even on lower-end machines. Easy to get lost in, so much fun to play, and filled with thinking-man's challenges and puzzles to boot, my only real complaint is that you need certain power-ups to save your game, so if you don't have them, you can lose a lot of progress to an accidental death. Max Payne 2 is a third-person action game that follows the events of Max Payne 1. It depicts a broken Max seeking redemption and he gets this through the game's other main character, a femme fatale known as Mona Sax.
Story: The game is basically a tragic love story between Max Payne and Mona Sax. Over the course of the game, Mona Sax is constantly on the run (for reasons you will find out in the game) and Max Payne, now an NYPD cop must pursue her. The more Max encounters Mona, the more he becomes infatuated with her and this creates an interesting dynamic between them. The story is well-told and interesting but not as poetic and dark as the original Max Payne.
Graphics: I can't say much about the graphics given that it came out more than 10 years ago (in 2003). What I can say that the visuals are still servicable and okay for today's standards and I would imagine that the graphics at the time were ground-breaking. Not so much nowadays.
Gameplay: The movement, gunplay and overall responsiveness in MP2 is much improved over Max Payne 1. Now you can equip an item like a grenade to another button, instead of needing to switch to it. Bullet time is back and it feels as good as ever. It is a lot of fun to activate Bullet Time and take out 3 to 4 enemies , and this really makes you feel like a badass. There is much less frustration to the controls this time round.
Overall, Max Payne 2 is a great action game that I believe has stood the test of time and is still better than some action games of today.
I'd give the game an 8.5/10.

There are few games that I'd say they are a master of their genre. May Payne 2: The Fall of Max Payne is definitely one of them. I'd say it's the last of the good old games. Max Payne 2 is a strange specimen because it's between two periods, the old and the new. It has the charm of oldschool games while feeling modern and polished. The action is one of the best I've ever seen. The gameplay feels very cinematic, inspired by John Woo's motion pictures. But the best thing they've introduced since the first Max Payne is the physics engine. Enemies fall spectacularly when they die, especially in slow motion, and you can even jump into them and drive them to the floor.
The visual novel style cutscenes are back from the first game along with the heavy noir atmosphere. This time I fell like they've put a bit more emphasis on the detective aspects of the story which I personally love, and it's still every bit as thrilling as the first game (if not more). The music is great and strengthens the tension in the atmosphere, but the guns sound a little off to me. The main problem with the game is that it's too short in my opinion, but with the challenge modes making a return, and given the exquisite gameplay, I think you'll find yourself playing this game over and over again.
I can't recommend this enough. Go buy it! 10/10

This is my personal review of the game. I try to keep it as unbiased as possible, and that's rather easy considering I'm not a game developer fanboy. Keep in mind that this game is in Early Access at the time of the posting of this review and that things are most certainly subject to change. So, let's start out with the big bad wolf. The chief complaint people seem to have in this game. Pay to Win.
So, without further ado, let's go
in this game.
Everybody in the review section seems to be up and arms about how this game is Pay to Win. I decided, soley based on that theory, to download the game and play with it for a little while. Lo' and behold I came across my own pesonal decision on whether or not Heroes of Scene is P2W afterall. But I won't just give you what I think on the matter. I'm going to
you properly with why I think what I do. So let's take a look at the business model, shall we?
Is there a cash shop? Yes, there is. Is this the devil? No, it's not. This is what you can buy in the cash shop. A premium membership with premium currency (buttons) for whatever time you select. This gives you double experience and money accumulation. You can buy some light cosmetics. This is just for your portrait. There's no way to get that with the earned currency, either. You can buy a random hero card or random spell card with premium currency. You can buy a new deck slot with premium currency, but also earned currency. You can also level up your hero and spell cards with both currencies however those cards still need to have the required experience before you can do so. You can also buy a new card slot (to fit more cards into your decks) for premium and earned currency, but must reach a certain level before you can even see the prices of that.
So, now that we know all (unless I missed something) of what you can buy in this game with real money / premium currency we can begin to answer the question "Is Heroes of Scene Pay to Win?".
My answer is no, it's not pay to win. Admittedly there is one thing that does at least seem to be pay to win - and that's the ability to buy a random card. It's pay to advance more quickly, and that's it. While a good deck will usually beat a noob's deck, that's to be expected. People who buy into the game will keep winning until they get to the ranking that is within their skill group. If you lose to some crazy "Over Powered" heroes or spells that you've never seen before it's because you don't know how to counter that card, have nothing to counter it (due to your ♥♥♥♥♥♥ noob deck kekekekek), and/or matchmaking ♥♥♥♥ed you. However I find that matchmaking is done fairly well and most of my games aren't complete roflstomps either way.
Graphically and artfully this game is very well done and very polished. It's a very pleasing, light hearted style that's easy on the eyes. I enjoy the visuals greatly. The HUDs, GUIs, and Menu's are all done very, very well. To me it looks as if they would have texture, which is a pleasant thing to look at. While it's leaning towards a slightly more cartoony artstyle, that takes nothing away and only adds onto the theme of the game - which is toy/puppet battles. Furthermore, the Robot looks like bender. Easter Egg anyone?
Overall, no complaints about the graphics in the slightest. My computer runs these visuals just fine and there's no stuttering even when I've spammed two dozen hedgehogs on my enemies. Heheh...poor ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s...
The game sounds great. There are sound effects for everything in the game that needs sound effects and none of them get tiring over a long play period or are annoying in the first place. Sometimes I can be a little confused by some of the sound cues happening in a different part of the map I'm in, but other than that they're wonderful.
The music is light hearted and well composed. I never found myself needing to turn it down or off. It's nice to listen to as you set up your base and send your hoards of hedgehogs to destroy your enemies. It's a nice backing sound with different highs and lows here and there.
There is one problem where when a track ends there's a pause for a few seconds or so before it starts again which is annoying however I believe that's simply a bug.
The gameplay is superb. Everything feels responsive, as it should. The matchmaking works similarly to clash of clans, where it operates on a "Win a match get some rank points, lose one you lose rank points!" and it works well for it's purposes. The building is mostly instantaneous. You aren't often waiting for somethign to happen as you always have something to do. Build your base up, build your army, raid with hedgehogs, whatever floats your boat. You can build two buildings that offer upgrades to various buildings and stats and none of them feel useless. This adds to the strategies you can go with in a game. The matches are fast paced, as advertised. Most don't pass 15 minutes in length.
Your heroes and spell cards gain experience as you use them in matches. Once the experience bar fills up you can, outside of a match, upgrade them with either premium or earned currency. Trying to figure out a deck after you get a few more cards is fairly entertaining and engaging. Testing them out is also fun. Set up your peices and knock your opponents down, or snort as your trash-tier set up gets rofl-stomped by the enemy and say "Well that was♥♥♥♥♥♥"
Furthermore, the gameplay is easy to navigate. You only really need your mouse to play this game. So the controls are simple as can be.
There isn't a whole lot to say about the community. I haven't tried going to the forums as of yet, so this is just referring to the community in game. There's a global chat in the main screen which people use. Most of the people who speak in that chat seem to only speak russian. Some English speakers do speak there but it's usually to ask for help or to answer questions.
I'd really like to see the ability to chat to your opponent in match or at least in the lobby. This is supposed to be a multiplayer game and it makes it feel like the opponent is just a computer. That's not the case, though, considering you get some really skilled players and then you get the "Lol what are you doing noob?" players who don't know what's going on and are probably high off their♥♥♥♥♥or something.
So, like I said, there isn't a whole lot to say about the community.
This game is casual friendly as well as hardcore. There are ways to be skilled in this game. People will be encouraged to think of strategies to beat their opponents. You don't get angry when you lose since you only poured at most 15 minutes of your life into any given match in most cases, so the sting of losing is dull at worst and I find is usually nonexistent.
I definitely recommend this game. It doesn't take a lot of time, but I think you'll spend a fair amount of it playing anyway. It's fast paced, interesting, unique, and most importantly fun!
Also, Bender is in this game. I'm almost certain the Robot hero is a reference to Bender from Futurama. Hats off to the Devs on that one. Bender will forever be in my deck.
And yes, I would definitely go
into this game again. A solid 9/10 inches.

A game that has the potential to be fun, but ultimately is not.
1. Infection is ridiculous. It is difficult to tell if you're infected unless you stare at the edges of the screen, which often confuses new players and does little to notify the rest of the team. The player should have some visible sign of infection (or if it does, it should be more obvious, because I've played quite a few rounds and I've yet to see anything).
Also, once infected, it is -impossible- to remove without simply dying and hoping that people don't grab your supplies. The one method of reducing infection (pills) simply delays the inevitable. I get the message here, but there's a line between "semi-authentic zombie experience" and "absolutely annoying game mechanic". Infection should be -removed- on ONE pill usage. It detracts from the game experience when players are turning left and right because they are offered no ability to remove their liability to the team.
2. Hit detection can be really screwy. There are times when zombies die from one headshot, yet the same zombie type can later eat five shots to the head without dying.
3. Fast zombies are too difficult to kill a majority of the time, and often appear in tightly knit groups. They should have a weakness of some sort, as it is -very- easy to be overwhelmed if there are too many fast zombies. I know people will cry out that I'm a ♥♥♥♥♥ or something, but I'm tired of performing well in a game only to die easily because the fast zombie was impossible to kill.
4. Melee weapons feel rather useless UNLESS you're using a fireaxe or a sledgehammer. It feels like a zombie can hit you far too easily if not, and it's easy to be overwhelmed when using a lighter melee weapon. It doesn't help that hit detection is bad, making the 3-4 hits into 8-10 in some situations.
As such, people using the lighter weapons are often easily killed, which results in people ignoring the smaller weapons. Again, I get the intentions here, but sometimes the game requires something fairer. I'd suggest making the overhead, charged attacks all equal to an instant kill. Trust me, it won't make the game too easy.
5. The game needs some sort of method that encourages users not to squander supplies. Perhaps offering a point system that measures how many items someone picks up, giving more points for less items/less bullets fired? Maybe even making supply drops inaccessible to someone with too little points, with a message like "the rest of the survivors push you away due to your frivolous item usage'.
I mean, okay, that idea is silly, but the point is I've yet to see ONE successful game due to the constant item squandering. Perhaps the game can take a leaf out of Killing Floor's book and offer a traveling shop of sorts that allows users to purchase supplies based on how many points they've earned?
Idunno. Something needs to be done about it, that's all I'm saying.
6. The learning curve is far too steep, and the game requires a great deal of coordination. It's a plus, but new users often start with NO CLUE how to proceed, and it's because the game doesn't tell you much outside of the necessities. Some maps have multiple zones that players aren't even aware of. This problem lies in the UI, I think: A minimap with the zones marked would be a start. Another good change would be informing the players just how many waves they're expected to survive, and what benefits they can expect per wave. Stuff like that.
At any rate, the game is fun. Worth a shot, I suppose. But I'm not recommending a game this tedious. It has a lot of potential, but there's a lot that just makes the game a giant and rather boring chore.

I wasn't going to write a review until I finished the game, but considering the influx of interest and IO Interactive becoming independent, I figurednow was a better time than never.
In short, this was the best game released in 2016.
Since I've gotten into PC gaming I've been a fan of stealth games. Heck, I basically played Wolfenstien: The New order like a Sam Fisher game. But what sets HITMAN apart from the rest of the Genre is that it is a stealth game that somehow also combines the genre with the shenanagins of a Grand Theft Auto game.
There's a silly (not overly silly, they balence this tone quite well) tone to HITMAN that makes it feel so different from other games in the genre. Sure, it's a very DARK kind of silly in spots, requiering you to choke someone out in order to dress up as a fashion icon for example, but overall it has a playful mood that really makes it nicer to spend more time in this game than other stealth games out there.
As much as I like Deus Ex and Dishonored, or even Shadwen and Aragami, the worlds they inhabit are very dour overall, filled with monolithic buildings that tour over the player in a way that is exciting, but also sometimes oppresive. In those games, every sky is dark (less so dishonored) and every environment has a tinge of sadness or danger that while cool, kind of gets old. Meanwhile, HITMAN 2016 has three different missions (one main and two side missions) that take place in basically the world's nicest Italian beach town ever. You also get to go to a fashion party, and a pretty hotel turned recording studio. The fact that a large part of HTIMAN involves walking through large crowds and blending in means that you will get to go to some places where people will actually want to be, and it is a refreshing twist for the stealth genre where I am used to being only military bases and coporate headquarters. Don't get me wrong, you will go to those places too, but they are not the only locations offered.
Another element that adds to the silly tone of HITMAN is the impressive amount of ways you can pull off an assasination. You can always just shoot the dude, or choke them out, but HITMAN will also provide you with tools and scenarios to pull off the hits with much more whimsey and style. You can disguise as a statue and commit the hit while they are watching family videos in the same room. You can dress up as a golf teacher and persuade the hit to meet you in a bedroom. There are chances where you can kill the hit with a giant robot on a movie set. The clever scenarios that IO has made are really special and so different from the ways you can complete objectives in other games.
Overall, HITMAN is special because it is so different from other games in the genre. It has a way of embracing fun along with the traditional tension felt while playing a stealth game. So for now, I am going to leave Dishonored 2 and Deus Ex: Mankind Divided as unfinished games in my library because I have more HITMAN to play. In fact, I'm going to play some right now.
Do yourself a favor and at least try out the demo. I spent 10ish hours in the first two tutorial areas and I feel like a lot of people could get the same milelage out of it. I hope to God there is a season two of this game.

A relatively simple idea to grasp, EPOCH works on the system of a one sided combat arena with three different areas and two different 'positions'. You are either standin' and shootin' or crouching to reload. With a small selection of robots types used in many different lethal ways you will not fall prey to forgetting what the robot does as its weapon- rather to the selection of covering fire and synergy of the different weapons.
While the game is not based around 'strategy' as such is certainly rewards you for use of stun grenades to remove covering fire, or decoys to provide a moment to reload and focus on the main threat.
While the content is not exactly 100 hours worth, considering it was originally a phone game it is quite a lot. A bonus is the fact that when the difficulty increases the robots stats dont go up- they come in more numbers, and more combinations.
Overall EPOCH is a fun, simplistic, family friendly 3rd person shooter which will keep you entertained (and frustrated) for hours.

How does an arcade-ish shooter that lasts under an hour or two from start to finish wear out its welcome? Epoch will show you how.
It's a light-gun style cover shooter where most enemies take over a clip to take down, so each encounter feels exceedingly long and drawn out. Combine that with leveling AND a shop weapon upgrade system and you got the usual unevenness that comes with variable stats figuring into gameplay. All the best classic arcade lightgun games moved you along at a brisk pace. Epoch slows it down quite a bit, which is not necessarily a bad thing but Epoch just takes it too slow. The gunplay feels like you're blasting health bars rather than scrapheads and as a result, the thing you're doing all game, shooting, just feels like a giant chore.
The initial difficulty is almost insultingly easy and the game expects you to play through it multiple times to unlock the higher difficulties (Along with payouts orders of magnitude greater to give you stat-appropriate weapons for that difficulty level.), and, to its credit, the game does open up a bit on that second playthrough where you can occasionally pick out a weapon that beats the HP bar curve, but nothing new can really be introduced by this point. They had enough content for the first run and that's really it. Everything else now is just a retread that plays slightly faster.
And that's the problem, the developers can't just go back and patch open all the difficulties from the get go as they are balanced around you having accrued the requisite grind beforehand so there is just no damn good way for them to fix that oversight. Once again, stats and grind attached to a game add negative value.
I will admit the final boss is good fun but I cannot bring myself to go through the game enough times to get to see what he's like on higher difficulties.

Spec Ops: The Line is a decent third person action shooter with an amazing single player campaign story! You play as captain walker, a delta squad leader who thinks that he is helping the survivors in dubai with his actions but not everything is as it seems... During several moments in the campaign, you are given moral choices and what you choose would affect the narrative of the story in a small extent. There are also plot twists in the story which might surprise you and would also entice you to play more to find out more of the story.
The gunplay is pretty standard but decent. It is basically a cover based third person shooter with a good variety of guns. The game is also really challenging on a higher difficulty as you can die in around two shots and that would encourage you to make use of the cover system more if you do not want to die. The character models looks really dated at the time of this review, however the environment (e.g Buildings, shops, desert, etc ) looks really detailed and beautiful.
The multiplayer and co-op of this game is basically dead at the point of this review as I could not find anyone in matchmaking. However, you can still play the co-op mode alone or with a friend. There are only 4 missions in the co-op mode and they are really short and is also not replayable as the same mission would play out the same way everytime.
In conclusion, the single player campaign has a great story with a serviceable third person shooter gunplay mechanic. The multiplayer and co-op matchmaking are dead and not worth checking out. If I were to rate this game, I would give it a 6/10!

First of all, this is a great game. It does away with the Left 4 Dead (and other similar games) method of "I'm going to tear through this zombie horde with my guns and run to the exit". In No More Room in Hell, you will be hard pressed to find two clips for a pistol much less an AK-47 with ~500 rounds (cough L4D cough). This makes the zombie apocalypse seem much more real, and it really reminds me of the TV show “The Walking Dead”. By the same coin, survival time is greatly lengthened with more people playing together, just like it would be in a real life zombie outbreak. If you are having trouble finishing a level, find or make some friends and try to go through the level together.
There is no reason why you shouldn't try this game. It doesn't require Half Life 2, and it runs on the freely available Source SDK Base. If you are tired of playing Left 4 Dead or love “The Walking Dead”, you will probably like this game. At the very least, give it a try.
Verdict: 9.8/10 Because the ammo is unbelievably scarce (you can pick up two boxes of ammo and sometimes get fewer than five bullets) [-0.1] and that you realistically cannot do an objective map by yourself since the zombies respawn [-0.1]. Otherwise, it is a very good game that accurately simulates a zombie apocalypse.

EPOCH is an arcade shooter that harkens back to the days when Guncon games were in plentiful supply. As a title that began its life on a mobile platform, it’s all the more impressive that it remains as fun and entertaining as it is, and while it certainly suffers from a few slight impediments due to its original use of a smaller screen, EPOCH shines as a wonderful example of a regrettably dying and nearly gone genre.
EPOCH is a lightgun game, make no mistake, and a decade ago, this title would have eaten up quarters in arcades. But where titles like Time Crisis would limit you to ducking in and out of static cover, EPOCH allows relatively free movement along a designated 2D plane, made up of three to four points the player can position themselves, depending on the level. And you will utilize every point, because while you may be able to hide behind cover from standard bullets, other enemies face no qualms about launching timed explosives at your position or firing lasers that can cut right through whatever you’ve chosen to hide behind.
In order to combat the insurmountable odds that you’ll face in the short (but wholly replayable) campaign, you will have to earn (or buy) the use of several varying weapon types and abilities. There are only around a half dozen weapon types, but each is unique and requires a different style of play to succeed with. Abilities you can earn through play or purchase in the store add a little more flair to combat, as they may serve to slow time or increase weapon speed and the like. You are also allowed counter measures in the forms of multi-target rockets and hand-held grenades, both of which can hold perks of their own, like acidic or electrical damage. You will need to learn to properly utilize all of the abilities and weapons at your disposal, as some levels will all but require a specific loadout to give you the upper edge in later difficulties.
In addition to the hour long campaign, Arena mode allows for never ending waves of increasingly difficult robotic adversaries, and provides a chance at leaderboard glory. In this mode, you can complete mini-missions that reward increasing amounts of credits, such as killing a number of enemies before getting hit or not using cover. Unfortunately, the rewards for simply playing and surviving are far from ideal, and considerably less than that of simply replaying story missions on hard difficulty. It’s a shame that there’s no form of co-op play, online or off, as this mode would benefit greatly from such an arrangement.
Here, I’d like to make a note regarding general difficulty in this title, as I begin to speak more to the negative aspects present in the game. When you first begin EPOCH, you’re limited to the easy difficulty level, and to unlock the subsequent normal, hard and ultra difficulties, you will have to beat the roughly hour-and-half long campaign in each. The difficulty you’re originally relegated to, easy mode, is exactly that: way too easy. My first impressions of the game were constricted to this mode, and it almost caused me to quit early and write EPOCH off as a lame mobile shooter whose anemic difficulty simply couldn’t match up with the speed and precision of a mouse pointer. Quitting at this stage would have been a mistake, as upon reaching normal and hard difficulties, the game truly comes into its own, providing a challenging experience worthy of its arcade roots. So, while playing EPOCH, try and hold your bourgeoning opinions until
you’ve beaten the glorified tutorial/training mode that is the default difficulty.
As little as I enjoyed the default difficulty, it does serve a purpose beyond training you. Every time you beat a mission, you earn credits, experience points, weaponry, and snippets of dialogue from members of the world’s citizenry, all of which reveal the story of EPOCH’s world, and what led to the events of the campaign. Having read a healthy portion, I’ve enjoyed what bits of story I’ve pieced together. Collecting these snippets has become a driving force for replaying missions, beyond the leveling and credit farming. The simple fact is, forcing you to play through each difficulty allows you to earn story pieces and the necessary credits to buy the more expensive weaponry, thereby reducing any potential need to grind at later difficulties.
For the obvious question,
, the answer is,
. The store menu that you navigate has clearly been tailored to smaller screens, and the in-game symbols for your various recharging abilities hang out way up in the upper right corner of your screen, just outside of your peripheral vision, and in the heat of things, this can be a slight hindrance until you memorize cool-down times. It could be argued, too, that slight movement quirks could be attributed to the game’s original format. Moving to and from cover can feel stiff and slow, making it difficult to find a solid opening from which to return fire. This may of course be a design choice, but it bugs me nonetheless.
On very rare occasion, upon entering a new grid in any one of the dozen or so missions, my character will either initially ignore my input commands completely, or be firing his weapon without my say so. This issue has never gotten me outright killed, but it has caused me to lose several hit points in more than one instance.
My final thoughts, after having just reached the aptly named and truly brutal
difficulty, is that EPOCH is an exceptionally commendable mobile-to-PC port, whose gameplay transfers beautifully to a mouse and keyboard. It looks great, and with so few of the issues that typically plague mobile ports, and gameplay that could have satisifed lightgun fanatics even in a modern arcade, EPOCH stands as one of the finer of the few remaining shooting galleries available in a home setting.

Genre: Action-Adventure Platformer / Hack and Slash
Sub-Genre: Hardcore Hack and Slash
Atmosphere: 10/10 - The scenery in this game is absolutely breathtaking with art visuals you could chew on for hours. Due to the nature of the gameplay, the background is consistently changing as you progress. This was no lazy task, my friend. The atmosphere immediately immerses you into the world of DMC the second you turn it on.
Sound: 10/10 - Every slice, every shot, every dodge, & every grapple have their own unique sounds. I did not find one recycled sound track throughout the entire game. They are all loud, pronounced, and crisp.
Gameplay: 11/10 - You have five weapons to play with and upgrade: A sword, an axe, a scythe, two guns, and a gauntlet. You have the power to switch these out seamlessly, connecting different weapons for different combos to decimate your enemies. It is fun and easy to get innovative. This game has new game plus, as well as seven difficulty settings to play through. On top of that, there is another game mode called Bloody Palace Mode where you fight hordes of enemies as long as you can, eventually facing each boss as long as you can survive. Points earned in that mode carry over to the normal campaign.
You can compare this game to it's Eastern counterpart if you want to, but why butt heads just for the sake of butting heads?
Ninja Theory took an already developed franchise - some argue not yet fully developed - and rebooted it.
They changed the look, they changed the feel, they changed Dante - they changed Devil May Cry.
Does that automatically make it bad? To some it does, and for those people they can negate it's existence all they want. But for the other curious brains out there I can tell you that whether you're a fan of the original or not, this is one solid hardcore hack and slash.

No More Room in Hell, at its simplest, is a brutal, "Romero-On-Steroids" take on the zombie apocalypse sub-genre. Intent on creating as realistic (or, in the words of the developer, "Romero-style") an experience as possible, nearly everything is accounted for in this game, outside of the usual "stamina" and "limited HUD" features. Each individual item has its own weight, and is allocated to an inventory wheel, which the player can access at any time. A shotgun, for example, will weigh more than a machete (and consequently, take up more space than that machete on the wheel). Even your total ammount of ammunition is accounted for, and thusly limits your inventory space. Don't take this to be an inhibiting feature, though. If anything, this system adds to the terrifying immersion of the game. Certain items that are normally a "given", such as the flashlight, must be picked up manually to be used at all (but can be accessed quicker than other items by the usual 'F' key once it's picked up). The zombies themselves, as they always have in Romero's movies, are generally slow, and do not pose any threat if they're alone. As you progress through the waves, however, this "lone target" situation becomes decreasingly common, and replaced with crowds of zombies, often numbered in the tens to even twenties. Unlike other horror (or even generalized co-op) games that permit cooperation but do not enforce it, No More Room in Hell sternly (but not forcefully) nudges players into a peacefully-woven experience, complete with suppressing and covering fire, shared supplies, and coordinated strategy.

I'll preface this by saying Rust is an awesome game, and in no way is that hyperbole. Built well, intuitive, and a great experience all together. From the moment you start, the game draws you in and before you know it, 3 hours have passed and you're loving learning how much the game has to offer. From base-building to crafting, using weapons and tools to your advantage, the gameplay balances almost perfectly. That is until you encounter other people.
I've been playing this game since the beginning (stolen account) and have seen the development it has undergone. I also see that many of the reviews praising the game are from those with a lot pf experience. Often with a record of above 1000 hours played, while a ton of other reviews are from players with less than 10 hours. I've noticed that novice players love the sense of adventure and creativity the game offers, and review before they have the opportunity to truly add an informative experience.
That's why it get awry. If you have over 1000 hours on the game, then your experience drawrfs a new player's astronomically. Almost like dividing by 0. These are the players that will make your Rust experience absolutely miserable. Why? Because now that they've done all there is to do, their main focus becomes to excercise their power with experience and troll you in every way possible. That means, camping beach spawn points, killing you in your house and then waiting for you to come back just to kill you again. They'll put new doors on your base so you can't get it back.
Ah well, start a new base and eat the salt you might say? Okay let me just grab some woo- dead again. KoS. Again and again, over and over. I wish I was exaggerating but unless there at at least 4 of you, you won't garner enough pace to build your base into anything worth defending.
This cycle seems to continue invariably until you hate the game enough to stop playing it. It seems that the devs have catered toward experienced players, meaning that this game holds no longevity for anyone starting out and wanting to play more. You either fall under a frequent player, or the player who enjoys the game for the first 10 hours and never picks it up again.
I read another review saying "if you get salty eveytime you die, then this game isn't for you." No mate, this game is for everyone, because it's beautifully put together. It's the community that is not for you, it is not for most people.
So if you enjoy being miserable while you're trying to kick back on your evening after school/work, go for it, for everyone else with a shred of human dignity, rather spend your time doing something that makes you want more, pass on this game and spend your money elsewhere, because you're not finding a lasting experience here.

An amazing story initially wrapped up in a CoD-like presentation, but the more you delve deeper into the game, the more sinister you realise the story becomes. The less you know going in, the better it will be.
This game takes the "all-American action-hero" cliche and flips it on its head, demonstrating how mentally devastating a warzone can be to even the most hardened of soldiers.
My first playthrough took me 8 hours to finish on Normal difficulty, so it's pretty short, but it's an excellent experience nonetheless. If you buy this game, be prepared for a wild ride.

CONS:
- Graphics (let's be honest, they're old and outdated, even for 2012)
- Gameplay (it's pretty boring and repetetive, lame, unrealistic)
- Hordes of enemies will fly at you, even a special knife-soldier from the side and so called "heavys", and this will continue until a random moment when it stops because you apparently killed all the reinforcements.
- It's sorta too long
- Bullet-speed is ridiculously slow. Bullets hit a target almost instantly, but in this game, bullets are slow.
- Killing people is lame. Headshots is all that matters
- AI (which is a big thing in this game because of all the people you will kill) is very stupid
- You can take a sniper hit, and then regenerate up to full health in a few seconds
- Your 2 soldiers can be controlled, but the controls of this are very clunky (HL2 does this way better, and it's a much older game)
- Sensitivity is way too high in game. If you turn it down using Windows' mouse sensitivity settings, the sensitivity of the menu is too low.
- If you come up to a ledge, you can hit space for your character to jump down. If you don't do this, you character is locked upstairs still. (Cheap, non-functional engine)
- If you hit left-shift, you will do a melee attack with your weapon. If you are next to a short wall, left-shift will make you go over it.
- If you hit space while moving, you will run until you let go of W. If you hit space next to a wall, you will use it as a shield.
- There is no way of choosing how to get into a situation, like say going from the sides, stealthing etc. You will just appear somewhere, the enemy will give an alarm to each other even if they don't see you, and then start shooting.
- There are 2 or 3 stealth scenarios towards the end. These are the only situations in the game where the enemy isn't entirely mega-prepared to shoot you before they see you. If you are then noticed, it will go back to the mode of horde after horde coming to kill you. Except if you are meant to progress, in which case  they will be waiting here and there along your route.
PROS:
- The story. You might like the story, you might not. To me, it was not enough to balance out for all these cons of the game.

I can only recommend this game if you get it at a good discount. On the up side, the game has good graphics, sound, and the cover shooter gameplay is solid and enjoyable, if not particularly innovative. On the down side, the game is short (< 8 hours), the story makes little sense, the "choices" don't matter at all (except the very last, which determines whether you "live" or die), and the delivery is ham-fisted. It seems like they wanted to pull off a Bioshock ending, but they missed the mark because the big reveal is too unrealistic and unbelievable for a shooter with a realistic setting. Supposedly you can control a squad of three guys, but the control is very limited - basically just "kill that guy", and in the time it takes to mark the target I could have shot them myself - and I didn't use it much. I noticed a few minor control problems, where my character wouldn't get into cover, but overall the controls were okay.
In short, it's a solid but short cover shooter good for a rainy day, with decent gameplay but not much of a story. It's not worth $30 in my opinion, but it's worth playing if you can get it on sale.

Two things always come to mind when you have a Free-to-Play game.
#1) How Pay to Win is it?
#2) Is it any good anyways?
Being you can get the cards just by playing matches pretty much means the pay to win aspect isn't really there.  It seems it would be more "Pay to get Ahead Faster".  And that is up to the user I guess.
As far as is it any good?  I like it actually.  It has a tower defense sort of feel, and reminds me of a side scroller Tower Wars in some ways.  Except you aren't placing any towers, but the phase where you send out waves to attack the enemy aspect is here.  I would say matchmaking is a mixed bag, as you might play against players that have more experience, but you still would get a new random player.
Being this review is on launch day, there were a few issues with the server.  A couple restarts here and there, and currently the match making server is down.  But there is the ability to play against the AI.  So if you want to practice, that is possible, and when the servers are working, the match making is fun, depending on if you learn fast.
Part of how the game works, is there is strategy and it seems the more you play you can refine your build orders and unit launch timings and support spells in a manner that compliments your play style.  As for me, I found 5 cards that I have a strategy for that I won't reveal here, I might post a guide later.  But being the game is free to play, it's worth at least checking out.  But remember it's new so the match making server COULD be down, but if its up you will be having fun.  Don't be afraid to play against the AI for a dozen games to get the hang of everything. In general:
This game has nice ideas and nice death moments, which can easily triggered by chosing wrong dialogue option.
Some are hilarious, some are simply annoying.
Fighting:
The guards will sometimes attack you even if you've put away your weapon (just happened to me, and I noticed it when I had already saved my game...) and they're so tough you probably won't beat them.
Well, when it comes to fighting the whole fighting system is a huge mess it feels so clunky it ruined the gaming experience for me.
It feels like you want to hit a fruit fly, you'll hit with a chance of say...10% maybe. And there aren't enough interesting drops (see items) to motivate you, and no motivating quests...
It often is the basic thing : Kill x monsters and return, bring me this and that...
Items:
There are lots of clothes to find but they don't have any interesting stats only amour and an attitude rating which I've never experienced influencing anything, they just look different.
And there isn't much of an interesting weapon choice, neither.
I found ranged weapons to be even more useless than melee weapons at least most of them.
Characters:
They all seem very dump, dialogues are a bit funny and often pointless. You'll sometimes have different group members, but they have nearly no personality and they react not too intelligent.
There are a lot of unimportant nameless people running around always doing the same thing (dancing, cleaning)
Graphics:
Is o.k. but won't keep you exploring, small square-like maps which are all very similar to each other.
---> I wouldn't recommend the game, but for that low price, or better, on sale, you can try it, there are some funny sequences in it, but the gameplay is very annoying ( I often found me rather forcing me to play it any further than actually wanting it)

I can only recommend this game if you get it at a good discount. On the up side, the game has good graphics, sound, and the cover shooter gameplay is solid and enjoyable, if not particularly innovative. On the down side, the game is short (< 8 hours), the story makes little sense, the "choices" don't matter at all (except the very last, which determines whether you "live" or die), and the delivery is ham-fisted. It seems like they wanted to pull off a Bioshock ending, but they missed the mark because the big reveal is too unrealistic and unbelievable for a shooter with a realistic setting. Supposedly you can control a squad of three guys, but the control is very limited - basically just "kill that guy", and in the time it takes to mark the target I could have shot them myself - and I didn't use it much. I noticed a few minor control problems, where my character wouldn't get into cover, but overall the controls were okay.
In short, it's a solid but short cover shooter good for a rainy day, with decent gameplay but not much of a story. It's not worth $30 in my opinion, but it's worth playing if you can get it on sale.

I usually don't write reviews, much less a "not recommended" one, but this one has been eating at me a long time.  I know people generally read the first couple of lines and move on, but I wanted to do this, if only for me because I'm just another opinionated ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on the internet.
Before I begin, let me clarify:
Max Payne 1 was the best
Max Payne 3 was alright, but not as good as MP1
also: SPOILER WARNINGS
Okay, where to begin?  When I first played MP2, it was a Max Payne marathon session, so I had just finished the first game (again) and wanted to finish the second one (which I had not yet played) before I played Max Payne 3.
Now, when people talk about the series, MP3 especially, they always mention how the story was mediocre especially when compared to the first two games.  Granted, it wasn't much, the lack of noire was sorely missed and when compared to the FIRST game, yes, it is particularly weak.  However, I am completely baffled when people say how good MP2's story was and how it was better than MP3.  No.  Just ... no.
The flimsy story for this game (spoiler warning) is simply thus:
Take every character who didn't die in the first game and kill them off.
There you go.  That's it.  That's the whole 3-4 hour game right there, and the story abruptly ends when the bad guy, former "friend" Vlad who decides to kill you because they couldn't think of anybody else to do it and because he's Russian so why not, is killed.  The entire story, in a nutshell, is: "... and everybody died, the end."  If anything, this game is what paved the way for MP3 to have no connection to the first game's grim, atmosphereic noir setting simply by destroying any way to connect a third game to the first or second game.  And to anyone who wants to talk about how "gritty and noir" the story is, let me remind you that Vinnie Cogniti (or however it's spelled) puts on a ♥♥♥♥ing mascot outfit his arch rival gave him only to find out it's a bomb.  You're then tasked with saving his defenseless♥♥♥♥♥for a level so that in the next cutscene (an actual cutscene, not a graphic novel panel like in the first) he can get blown up anyway.  Whoop-dee-♥♥♥♥ing-doo.
So what do you do in this game?  Well, you run around and shoot people with a screwy version of bullet-time (when you activate it, time doesn't really slow down and only does the more people you kill, so if you've got a sliver of health and want to have those extra split seconds to take out a big group, like in the first game, you're in for a surprise.) occasionally triggering a graphic novel scene like in the first game, but those only come like once a CHAPTER.  And while in first game you could watch all those bits and it would tell a semi-cohesive story, in this they only come around long enough to say "HEY LOOK, SEE?  THIS IS JUST LIKE THE FIRST GAME!  LOOK AT THI-Oop, nevermind, it's over, back to game."  That's really all the noir is in this game: a coating, something to fool you into thinking it's a noir story like in the first.  Oh, and there's the really "FUN" bit where you have to protect someone whil using a sniper rifle, because trying to keep an NPC alive from a mile away is always great.
In the four or so hours it will take to beat the game, you'll get to do such things as watch cutscenes, kill guys with goofy ragdoll physics (which is actually pretty fun, don't get me wrong), go to the Ragnarok again (how original), visit the same Fun-House level three ♥♥♥♥ing times (with slightly changed layout) based on Valkyr V (see guys? this is just like the first game!) and along the way, Max will meet a variety of characters from the first game before they are subsequently killed as well as a paltry handful of new characters who get killed off to.  Oh, and if you played the first game, Mona (who got kinda killed but possibly wasn't killed or whatever) apparently survived and will be your love interest through the game until she dies at the end.  And as I said, the big bad guy is Vlad, who it turns out, in a huge case of the devs going "What things can we take from the first game and cram into here and retcon the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of, used to be in the same group as Alfred Woden, who he kills, then he kills Mona (she undied so she could re-die), then you kill him, then Max has a tiny necrophilia scene and then it just ends.  Max Payne accomplishes nothing, rescues no one, learns nothing except that people near him usually end up dead pretty fast (which I kinda thought was also part of MP1's story).  Oh, and if you thought the characters in MP3 were pretty unlikeable and had no connection to Max, then I re-invite you to play this game again and really take a good, long hard thought about it.
If you hated Max Payne 3's departure from noire and the things that made the first game so incredible, you can give a big round of applause to this game right here.  After playing it, there really isn't any ground left move forward from.  The only thing a sequel could have done is go far, far away from where the first two games took place and do something "fresh" with the franchise and, basically, just find some completely new ground to tread on.
So, in short, it's a functional game that goes nowhere, has no point, brings nothing new to the table and only does the "Noir" bit because it has to (and believe me, they only begrudgingly come out every now and again because it's in their contract claus) and, having never played it before, I beat it in a couple of hours in one sitting.  This game offers nothing and delivers nothing.  You're better off just playing the first game because that one actually is a good story, or if you really have to have ragdolls flopping around, get the third because of dem physics.

This game is absolutely fantastic. Metroid-vania puzzle platformer with excellent gameplay and very tight and effective game design all beautifully wrapped up in one of the most stunning and vivid art styles I have ever witnessed in a game along with a beautiful, emotional and poignant soundtrack which work together to build an incredibly powerful and immersive atmosphere.
I initially disregarded the story as it initially seemed generic but as the game progressed I actually became very engrossed in its simple yet charming and emotional story. Each of the different zones is distinct and thematic and none overstay their welcome or feel stale. The game is also the perfect length of around 8-15 hours allowing you to get immersed and engrossed in its world without it feeling repetitive at any stage even including the large number of collectables which still felt fun and rewarding to collect even after I found the last ones.
One of the greatest achievements of Ori and the Blind Forest is its tight game and level design which takes the metroidvania formula of growing from weak to strong and instead starts you off feeling powerful and growing even more powerful, without removing and of the challenge or difficulty or making you feel overpowered. It goes without saying that Ori feels great and fun to control with some very precise controls which make you feel fast and nimble from your first hour to your tenth.
Overall I feel this is a magnificent achievement of a game and deserves to be recognised as such and I thoroughly and confidently recommend this to anyone, regardless of thier feelings towards the general genre as it is such a hard game to play and not have a blast with.

Claybook is a lovely, charming world where everything is made out of clay where everything you do uses real-time deformation physics.
In Claybook, you are dropped into worlds entirely made out of clay to fulfill a number of different challenges and objectives. For this, you use the amazing real-time clay deformation physics to carve, create and destroy your way through this 100% moldable world. You can possess different objects and different shapes, get on a clay rocket and fly around, possess a clay tap and spray "water" all over the level, create pathways, destroy others, duplicate your own form to creat platforms, make yourself bigger, change into all kinds of different shapes. The game currently has 16 levels that show you all of the crazy things you are able to do in this game and how to mold its world. While there are only sixteen levels currently, the later ones can be quite long and are filled with many objectives. Each level also has time leaderboards which increases replayability for speedrunners. The devs plan to continously add new levels as the Early Access continues. In addition to this, the game also has a sandbox/level creator mode that allows you to screw around on a world of your own creation, and even add different objectives and goals, levels you can then share with the rest of the community thanks to the wonderful Steam Workshop support.
The game also supports local multiplayer which is amazing fun especially in the sandbox mode.
The game is extremely satisfying and it's finally a great implementation of the crazy physics tech demos people have seen shown around in game in recent years, finally making use of them in a actual game to great effect. And runs pretty well on even modest computers.
This is a game I heartily recommend to everyone. At 9.99$ in the current sale, and with the full launch planned for early 2018, this is the time to jump in. An amazing price for something that will provide you with endless hours of entertainment thanks to sandbox, level creation and steam workshop, making sure there will always be someone in the community producing new content.

It's the 26th century. You're an imperial soldier sent as an undercover convict to a penal colony on Planet Alzatraz with a mission to sabotage a spacecraft the convicts are building to escape the planet. The landing pod crashes, you are separated from your teammates, get captured and thrown in a labor camp. Because of your excellent build and opportunistic tendencies, you quickly rise through the ranks and become the go-to person for many Planet Alcatraz inhabitants, who have 25 hours' worth of quests for you.
The RPG-style 3rd person game lets you build your skills, as well as those of the members from your old squad which you pick up along the way. Overall, the game offers 2 major mission campaigns with dozens of places to investigate and clear out, and a final push through 3 extremely difficult areas to reach a shuttle and escape Planet Alcatraz. At one point, you're required to find item F for person E who has unfinished business with person D who first wants person C dead, but they turn out to be dead, and the trail is found with person B last seen at location A but it turns out he's actually held captive at location Z... this is just an example.
Pros - Immersive storyline and missions which get you really enthused to level up in the right skills. Fair hit system, smooth gameplay (although the animations are quite wooden), generous XP and money rewards for quests.
Cons - The storyline is pretty linear. It gives you the illusion that you can play both sides, but in the end you're left with no choice with regards to your loyalty. The developers could have spent more time developing alternative endings. Graphics aren't the best since the game came out in 2009. There isn't really a big variety of weapons, most are absolutely worthless and there's only 2-3 ones worthwhile keeping. Not many places to go for XP. Enemies can be permanently elimiated, so once you clear out an area it stays clear after re-loading the area.

Oh, did that massive sandstorm get you turned around while exploring, and now that it has cleared up you're not entirely sure which way is home?... BTW your Oxygen tank just hit 25%... tick tock. The feeling that you get running across an old tether line as you explore a cave system only to realize that it is part of the same cave system you were exploring about an hour ago also lends itself to a true feeling of exploration, instead of the same sad craft, upgrade, jump to the next star system loop of NMS.
Long story short I feel bad even mentioning NMS in the same review for fear that it will somehow taint this superior game, but it's next to impossible not to draw a comparison. In my opinion if you wanted to casually explore space this is a stellar option. Oh, and it has multiplayer.

Fantastic game!
A lot of people will go on about the plot and the twists to it. And they're good. Really good. But it's been covered very well by others and I also highly recommend it if you want a gripping story that WILL make you question your own morality.
One thing not covered that I think really needs to be talked about more is this game is an incredible shooter. The controls are responsive. Moving to cover works well (usually). Swapping weapons feels right and not clunky like some other games. And squad commands make a LOT of sense without having context sensitivity. For instance, throw on a silencer and creep around to a location. Telling your squad to attack will lead to your character calling for a silent approach. You don't have to specify that they go silent or anything else. And you don't have to fiddle with telling them to take cover. The AI takes care of itself, except for a few instances where they'll jump ahead out of cover and fumble around before coming back. But I've never seen another shooter that handles it so well!
Overall combat is satisfying. At first the experience of a slight moment where time slows down on head shots is jarring, but it quickly becomes a mechanic that draws you in and a small bonus for a well aimed headshot (or maybe a lucky spray and pray). And with the rest of the plot, that ends up REALLY flowing well into the psyche of Captain Walker, the main character.
It bothers so much that I never noticed this game until it appeared on a top ten list on Youtube that I saw. It easily trumps the garbage CoD games and Battlefield just completely misses the human aspect that Spec Ops gets right, not to mention keeps combat feeling right and not ridiculously over the top. You still soak up bullets and instaheal with a few breaths, as per the industry standard, but I only once recall being annoyed about the controls when I simply forgot the button to crouch during a firefight.
I can't recommend it enough. With the wild plot, lots of little details you notice after your first play through, and polished system, this game needs to be the type that dethrones the popular shooters of today.
Watch 'Apocalypse Now!' instead. It saves you time and it's a better told story.

Spec Ops: The Line is probably the hardest game to play. Not so much because of its difficulty but because the theme it presents to the player.
While many games nowadays tries to dehumanise war, this one pulls no string to show you the consequences of your actions, without trying to do any sort of guilt- tripping. Even more depressing to think that while this may be just a game, in many countries this is an everyday reality.........
Taking control of a 3 man squadron, Capt. Walker, Lugo and Adams are sent into the deep end of Dubai, tasked to find the 33 squad. But the more they go further, the more they realise that the once luxurious city became a living hell, where its every man for himself. There are no heroes, there are are no good or bad choices you need to make: but to sometimes having to decide between the lesser evil.
The game breaks the fourth wall at many occasions and among other things asks one simple question to the player: "Do you feel like a hero yet?", which never felt as gutt-wrenching and tear-jerking as it did in this game.

This game has quite a lot to it, so I'm going to review the goods and the bads separately again.
On the good side, this game can be idiotically fun with a friend or two and against equally matched opponents. You get to pick a side - either the Enforcers (the cops) or the criminals, both with their own oppoturnities. This game also allows an incredible amount of customization - you can make your character, vehicles and such just the way you like them by coloring them and by applying decals that you can create with an in-game editor. There is a lot of stuff to unlock, and the missions are randomly generated to keep it refreshing. The game also looks good graphics-wise, and you just might find yourself exploring the open-world city for hours.
Unfortunately, in this game, the flaws far outnumber the perks.
You will meet the stupidest, most childish playerbase on the planet in this game. You can expect a LOT of whining, raging and griefing to interrupt your playing. To further reinforce that scenario, cheaters run rampant due to an outdated anticheat system - and to make it worse, 90% get away with it no matter how blatantly obvious it is due to an inactive support team.
Mission districts tend to be flooded with overly zealous tryhards. And then, there's the bi-weekly DDoS attack by some angry player...
Another extreme flaw in this game is how much it focuses on making profit than quality. Generally speaking, the best weapons and equipment are exclusively reserved for those that pay monthly for them - and as you might guess, those who don't tend to find themselves stomped by Premium players using intentionally poorly balanced weaponry only available for them. Aside from that, the matchmaking system further reinforces the balancing issue: because of the system attempting to match players almost solely based on a "Threat Level" (which is affected by winning and losing missions), high-level players can be matched against beginners as they can simply decrease their threat by intentionally losing missions.
Aside from the common DDoS attacks, the servers (districts) are further loaded with excessive player counts. A mission district typically has a maximum player count of 100 -50 Criminals and 50 Enforcers- while their hardware is often incapable of handling such amount of players. In short, their idea seems to be to have as many people crammed into as few servers as possible.
In lesser evils, the game often tries way too hard to be badass to be entertaining. This shows particularly much in NPCs and some of the new content. I recommend you to play Batman AO if you are a fan of the Batman Arkham series, and I FULLY recommend you to get the Cold - Cold Heart DLC since its got a really good and interesting story, as well as the bad*** new suit
,
TL,DR; I still quite enjoyed playing Batman AO, but I don't feel the solid gameplay that I got when I played the previous installments.
Pros:
+ GOOD gameplay, but somehow I felt that AO has an awkward feel and controls compared to its predecessor.
+ GOOD story.
+ GOOD fighting system. Free Flow Combat with this new feature (
) is a huge fun.
+ GOOD array of gadgets, allowing you to takedown enemies with your own style.
+ GOOD sound.
+ GOOD atmosphere.
+ GOOD graphics, better than the previous games.

+ Batwing drop system, allowing us to Fast Travel to certain points in Gotham City.
Cons:
- The controls feel a bit awkward and clunky.
- Most areas are just copied from Batman Arkham City maps.
- More collectibles, but less Riddles.
- Gotham City is a huge city, but the lack of any civilians feels weird to me. All I see are thugs. Is this Gotham City? or Arkham City, where all its inhabitants are criminals?
- Dark Knight System Challenges should be able to be done in ANY ORDER, to avoid any missable challenge(s).
- Missable predator challenge, because some of them can only be done in certain maps of the STORY mode. This is seriously annoying, especially because this game uses autosave system. Imagine if you forgot to do a 1 predator challenge, progress through the story, autosaving and BAM you just missed the opportunity because its the only area where you can do the challenge.
- Less polished, Batman AO still has many bugs, such as:
-> gliding achievement sometimes not triggered, it takes a few tries.
-> sometimes after the Riddler Informant was interrogated, NO new collectibles are marked on the map, and then you must run around to find ANOTHER Riddler Informant.
-> sometimes predator challenges are not counted when the conditions are met, but sometimes counted when the conditions are not met. I know, I am confused as well...
Overall: 80/100

Let me tell you the story of Chris...
Chris was about... maybe the 150th prisoner to happen to find his way on my doorstep. Chris was a wild one. Picking fights, killing, stealing... It turns out he wasn't just wild. He was LEGENDARY. I had only one choice to contain him: Put him in a whole other area of the prison all by himself. No communication with anyone besides the janitors, guards, and his parole lawyer. (And maybe even God if you're into that kind of thing.)
But on day...
Some prisoners got a bit rambunctious. They started tearing up the place. My guards were dropping like... well... a person when they get shanked in the back. A few low risks felt like they might have an actual chance if they pulled the big guy out of his cage. They busted up Chris' cell door. Only to have Chris kill both of them as he stepped out.
Chris continued his rampage, killing guards and fellow prisoners as he pleased. Eventually gaining a posse to raid the armory. Sure the guard had a good fight, for it was all for not. Chris loaded him and his boys with enough ammunition to make military ammo drops look like a box of rocks.
Chris' posse stormed through all of the prison, murdering as he went. But that's when the military stepped in. They breached the front doors ready to work. Gunning down every prisoner that didn't surrender. Upon reaching the main corridor the locked eyes with Chris and his posse. The bloodiest confrontation I've ever seen in all my time playing Prison Architect.
Though the posse was armed to the teeth, they eventually lost. Chris (being the last man standing) alone took out 2 squads of soldiers. Only to eventually be gunned down by a flanking pincer maneuver constructed by our boys in green camo.
Chris fell to the floor, gun in hand. Never to terrorize the world ever again.
10/10 would have all my prison staff slaughtered again.
