I bought this game because I had seen a let's play of it and loved the design and the story. This game is beautiful, and I will sing the plot's praises to the moon and back.
But while I'm going to finish the game, it's definitely one I would also say I enjoy watching more than I do playing.
I am not a gamer. I am not good at games. I'll be the first to admit that. I also don't own a platform, so I'm forced to play on my computer, which probably makes things more challenging. The vast majority of damage I end up taking is preventable, and I'll admit most deaths are indeed my fault. But when two hours into the game, I've died almost 100 times, on "Easy" mode, simply because jumps failed to work the way I needed them to and I landed into spikes and am at the point of wanting to tear my hair out, I'm not enjoying myself. I don't mind challenges, but this game feels more punishing than it does challenging, and that's not enjoyable for anyone.
That said, if you're better at games than I am, or simply enjoy a really hard game (or both), and want to experience a beautiful and moving story with stunning graphics, this isn't a game to pass over.

The soundtrack is memorable, the environments are gorgeous to behold, the platforming is tight, precise and very well fleshed out as time goes by through all the upgrades and abilities you pick up throughout the game, ...And the utterly adorable cat/rabbit/goat/spirit thing that is Ori has almost certainly been scientifically designed to be the most "d'awwwwww/SQUEEEEEE"-inducing creature ever created.
The only real fault I can think of is that some segments can be very trial-and-error, especially the endings of the "dungeon" portions of the game, and the story can feel kind of generic; the usual "restore the light, keep the dark at bay" plot that's been done a million times. Still, if you're willing to overlook that, you're in for a VERY good time.
Overall, OatBF is one of the best MetroidVania's I've ever had the pleasure of playing through.

You play as a nameless man, of little known past, known only by his number: 47. He is a high skilled assassin, who works for the mysterious agency ICA. The agency is hired by politicians and other high calliber figures in the global elite to eliminate people. The contact 47 has with the agency is mediated by  Diana Burnwood, who works as 47’s boss and some kind of “mother figure” to him.
Most levels in this game work like this: you are set loose into an open world environment with people doing their jobs and thing. Among those people there your targets, that you have to kill. If you want an easy mode, you can follow the tips and hints given by the game. If you like fo figure things by yourself, then turn off the notifications and try to kill the targets in your own sloppy way. Observing patterns of movement is key: each NPC usually has a routine of places he goes and things he does. If you need his outfit as disguise, you just need to wait for him in that dark alley and then…
Agent 47 follows some kind of “perfect assassination honor code” were you are supposed to try to kill your targets in what is consedered the “perfect way”. So, there are some rules you should try to follow, such as: only kill the targets and no one eles, not being see, destrying evidences and só one. Every time you violate one of these rules, you lose points, which reflects in losing potential unlockable stuff in the end of the mission.
Agent 47 is a “good guy”.
I just dislike how the game devs tried to make Hitman, Diana and their agency some kind of “good guys doing a dirty job”. I mean, it seems like in every mission you are doing some kind of humanitary job by “killing evil people”. I don’t like this approach, it would be better if they tried something more “neutral”, were Agent 47 works for whoever pays more or something. Anyways, this is kind of minor, because the game has actually very little story whatsoever. One of the major complaints about “Hitman: Absolution” was that it was too much story driven and thous wasn’t a typical Hitman game. So, in Hitman 2016, they try to fix it and go back to the origins and focus more on the gameplay and level design than in story elements.
Mentally exausting.
Also, another thing, and this is very personal to me, is that this game seems to demand a lot of my head and after completing a mission I feel very tired of all that mental work. Each mission felt like and extended chess match, were my brain and senses worked overtime to finally beat the mission. It’s not a game made to “play for fun” or “play for relaxation”, at least not for me…

ASTRONEER clearly has the potential to become something exceptional. Its an early access game and the feature list is limited, but this is understandable and what's available is enough to keep you occupied for at least 10 hours. As it stands you can build a base, build and use vehicles and explore the landscape including very deep and complex cave systems.
There are other features, including going to other planets and cooperative play with friends - but these are incredibly buggy and therefore don't really provide a satisfying addition to the game, yet.
For an early access game its impressive, but its currently too buggy to recommend purchasing at this time. There are serious bugs that inhibit long term enjoyment of the product in its' current form but are clearly the kinds of bugs that can and undoubtedly will be fixed soon. For example - an essential aspect of the game is to place tethers that allow you to venture further and further from your base - currently these tethers dramatically reduce your frame rate if too many are placed, but the number required to impact your frame rate really isn't a significant amount. Going off planet will see your home planet despawn, leaving only your original base components that are still present in the sky, along with their demand for hardware resources, leading to much reduced frames per second.
In conclusion - great potential, very buggy. When the most serious bugs are solved this is an easily recommended title - as it stands too broken to recommend.
::EDIT::
Having spent a fair bit of time testing the game after the latest updates I can safely say that the game breaking bugs SEEM to be fixed and all of the intended features to date appear to be working as designed. Still some niggling bugs, like vehicles vanishing and still getting choppy FPS from time to time, but nothing significant or game breaking.
You will get about 10-15 hours of entertainment before you run out of stuff to do, but the prospects for the future are bright and I look forward to seeing where they take this gem of a game.

If you ask me, this is the biggest disappointment when it comes to Walking Simulators. It is not terrible, but expectations were high. Dear Esther played with the building blocks of walking simulators: journey, exploration, mystery, blank spaces, dream-like slow motion, confused philosophy. As a result Dear Esther was a lovely, inexpensive, curious and only occasionally unsettling stroll in a place you couldn't visit yourself which left the player with the inevitable amount of frustration ingrained in a certain kind of dissolved storytelling. Picnic at Hanging Rock, House of Leaves, and many more.
Everybody's Gone to the Rapture introduces itself with less vagueness but with plenty of mystery, and tries all the tricks possible to entice a certain kind of relaxed, slow-moving inquisitive nerds (myself included) with numbers station, aliens, religion, the 80s, and that major nod to the legendary BBC show from the 70s, The Survivors. Unfortunately, things didn't work as planned. As a walking simulator the visuals are as pretty as you would expect and even if only for that the game-world deserves to be walked into. But then the story turns out to be way less interesting than its premises, the development of it is uneven as we are presented with a number of characters that are more or less charming and whose endeavours are sometimes hard to give a ♥♥♥♥ about, and the exploration itself is hurt by a confusion between the freedom to roam around we are led to believe we have, and the glowing suggestions of what we should or could do in order to either advance the plot or simply get more glimpses about what happened to this beautiful and now abandoned English village.
I am not gonna criticise the "gameplay", but more than in Edith Finch I felt the frustration of not being able to interact with the many objects and items laying around. While in Gone Home and Tacoma picking up everything and looking at it from every angle is part of the fun, tickling the antiques-seeker or the creepy neighborhood in all of us, in Edith Finch and Rapture (and Esther) you can't touch anything at all. You just wander and look, and while that worked in Esther because there wasn't much to pick up in the first place, or in Edith Finch because the pace of the story and the creativeness of the different chapters distract you from that, in Rapture you will find yourself more annoyed than anything at the absolute inconsistence of your own self, to the point that you'll often feel like you are just demoing a game world where you are nothing but a floating dev-camera.
[POTENTIAL SPOILERS FOLLOW]
I still enjoyed my 4 hours, but more than in many other games in the same genre I felt boredom growing while trying to get to the next "memory video-clip" hoping it will finally shed a bit more light over what happened. Eventually, what happened is pretty much what you would have imagined from the get go. There is no big revelation in the end, on the opposite it all concludes in what could have been some sort of a poetic ending but that didn't make me feel accomplished in playing the game at all.
As I said, this is not a bad walking simulator at all. The walking part can be a slog because you will need to back track sometimes and that's no fun at 1 mph, but the environment is absolutely stunning. The problem is that the plot does not deliver, the characters don't deliver, and the expectations created by the title itself (Wow, the ♥♥♥♥ing Rapture!) and the first 3 minutes in the game (those wonderful radio robotic voices!) are simply let down more and more with every slow step deeper into the heart of Yaughton village.
But is it fun? Not that much.

I loved it.  I feel like I just watched a good indie movie -- the kind that leaves you with all sorts of thoughts swirling in your head as the credits roll.  I thought the visuals, music, and voice were all outstanding.  By the time it reached the end, I felt I had an actual connection to the characters, even though they are never seen.
Just be aware it is indeed a walking simulator (no combat, no puzzles) and the so-called run command is just a barely slightly faster walk, but I didn't care.  When a world like this is so well-crafted, I love taking the time to soak it all in.

I had some hopes for this game, some of them were met, but all of those hopes were crushed by a few MASSIVE flaws. Without any spoilers, the games is beautiful with it's visuals. It looks stunning and photo realistic in places. Well... for a game at least. And the story and voice acting are excelllent.
However, and it's what destroys the game for me, the game is buggy as hell and it's in desparate need of optimisation! My system specs:
Ryzen 1700 at 3.9ghz (game only uses 1 WHOLE core. Although in the option menu it uses 2...)
PNY 1070 Founders
16GB RAM at 2666Mhz
250GB Samsung 640 SSD (game install here)
512GB M.2 SSD
2TB HDD.
So those are my specs and this game runs badly. And I do mean BADLY! It's THE worst running game I've ever played. On high settings the fps would drop from 50 to less than 20fps! I had to reduce settings to medium and disable all options I could such as temporal AA and cap the frame rate at 30 fps to get anything remotely smooth. And there's plenty of screen tearing even at those settings. Awfully optimised game.
The next thing that breaks the game for me is the forced walking speed. You cannot go faster than a glacial walking speed in the game! And at key moments or points in the game, it slows your speed down even more! I suppose for dramatic effect. But all it did for me was to make it incredibly frustrating. The only reason I can think of for them implementing this 'walking' mechanic, is to purposely drag out the game as it takes AGES to get from one point to another to listen to the narrations. Incredibly stupid and frustrating.
You also can't skip the credits. In other words, it's a really bad game and I don't recommend it to anyone. It's been made badly so not even the most powerful PC can probably run it decently and they've chosen to drag out the game by forcing a slow walking pace on the player.

It is 1984 and the world ended 37 minutes ago. You are in Shropshire, English countryside. So, if the world ended, what happened? Why are you still here? Where is everybody?
An open world with authentic 1980s look and feel awaits your exploration. Can't help but it feels nostalgic when you are old enough to remember those times. The presentation is excellent, the game has beautiful graphics and music. But the world is not really as open as it looks at first. There is no way around or through a half a meter high hedgerow. Some doors can be opened while others can't. That is quite okay, there won't be hidden stashes of ammo or health to collect anyway. Still feels a bit disappointing sometimes.
The game is also a walking simulator so you can expect to do quite a bit of walking. Therein lies the biggest issue for me - the walks can be quite long and there is just nothing to do while walking. Yes you can admire the pretty landscape and listen to the soundtrack, but if I wanted to do that, I'd rather stop doing whatever I was doing than being forced to do it.
There is something to guide you forward all the time. In many places you can interact with the world to discover what happened there. The game really shines in storytelling through short fragments of history. The voice acting is excellent, and really brings the characters alive with their sad, carefree, hopeless, excited or confused moods. There are many stories to follow in addition to the main storyline.
Like any proper science fiction story, many things are left open for interpretation or not revealed at all. The pace of the game is (intentionally) very slow, but still the end comes very soon. Sure, you could explore everything and go for the rather odd achievements, but that would mean even more slow, slow walking around.
Pros:
- Beautiful graphics
- Voice acting and music are well done
- Story has a lot of depth and rich, varied characters
Cons:
- Sluggishly walking around and listening to conversations is not really that exciting for long
- Short

I do enjoy the "walking simulator" genre. A good story at the cost of interactvity and freedom is something I can live with.
Everyone's Gone To The Rapture has great voice acting, believable characters, and the story at least through ther first half of the game is very engaging. The villages are created with a lot of detail that add a lot to the back story, finding clues, scars of what happened to everyone during the incident.
Unfortunately you move real slow. Even running is slow. It can be painstaking to travel between areas. The locations are quite open and you can spend most of your time wondering aimlessly hoping to find more information of what happened.  In fact, I would have to not recommened the game, simply on the basis you move like a slug. It's really not fun travelling between breaks in the story, Even worse if you think you might have missed a tibbit of information and have to backtrack.

As someone who loves walking simulator's, I was bored to death.
Everybody's Gone to Rapture takes walking simulator's to another level, with an interesting enough story and some really beautiful visuals but there's large swaths of nothing at most times and the player's movement has to be some of the slowest I've ever experienced in any game. It's dreadfully slow, almost painful. Crossing a street to moving to another house is a chore.
A lot of the visuals are also repeat elements without much interest to them other than their high fidelity, most of the houses have copy and paste environments and there's absolutely nothing to look at. There's no family photos or really anything that gives you a backstory of the people that lived there, but it's just generic bookshelves, tables and chairs arranged in no special fashion. There's a lack of character in every house and it makes exploring them unrewarding and dull, also, with the slow pace of your character's movement many of the houses end up being locked making the trek to them pointless.
The story is told by glowing orbs that gives you a lightshow of the figures in the scene and their voices. You have no clue where these all are and you're going to have to spend a LOT of time just walking to every nook and cranny of the game world to fish them all out and it just adds to the tedium.
This game feels like an exercise to test your patience, with the slow movement and the emphasis on "exploration" it feels like the developers tried to pad out a game with not much content at all. Take a look at the achievements and some are so ridiculously bad and time consuming it'll probably take you 7 hours to do it all in a game that's has maybe 2 to 3 hours of content and I only give it this estimate for the slow speed of movement.
It's a shame, I REALLY wanted to love this game, the setting is wonderful, along with the soundtrack and visuals but it's so dull to play I don't even think I'll be finishing it and I'm pretty sure I'm right at the end. It's just too boring.

I bought this game on a recommendation and am not normally into platformers. I took a chance.
This is one of the best games I've played in YEARS. The story is gorgeous, the mechanics are added as you play without official tutorials, but requiring mastery of new abilities to progress-- and it feels seamless. The difficulty level is there (even normal has some difficult parts), but it won't have you pulling your hair out like Boshy. Even being fairly unenthusiatic about the genre, I enjoyed every moment of the game.
If I had one criticism, it would be the length of the main story. There is some higher difficulties and 100% type stuff to extend things a little bit, but the main story for a casual player at a (self-defined) mediocre skill level was good for about 12 hours.
Overall would highly recommend-- even if you're not a fan of the genre.

I bought this game because I had seen a let's play of it and loved the design and the story. This game is beautiful, and I will sing the plot's praises to the moon and back.
But while I'm going to finish the game, it's definitely one I would also say I enjoy watching more than I do playing.
I am not a gamer. I am not good at games. I'll be the first to admit that. I also don't own a platform, so I'm forced to play on my computer, which probably makes things more challenging. The vast majority of damage I end up taking is preventable, and I'll admit most deaths are indeed my fault. But when two hours into the game, I've died almost 100 times, on "Easy" mode, simply because jumps failed to work the way I needed them to and I landed into spikes and am at the point of wanting to tear my hair out, I'm not enjoying myself. I don't mind challenges, but this game feels more punishing than it does challenging, and that's not enjoyable for anyone.
That said, if you're better at games than I am, or simply enjoy a really hard game (or both), and want to experience a beautiful and moving story with stunning graphics, this isn't a game to pass over.

The soundtrack is memorable, the environments are gorgeous to behold, the platforming is tight, precise and very well fleshed out as time goes by through all the upgrades and abilities you pick up throughout the game, ...And the utterly adorable cat/rabbit/goat/spirit thing that is Ori has almost certainly been scientifically designed to be the most "d'awwwwww/SQUEEEEEE"-inducing creature ever created.
The only real fault I can think of is that some segments can be very trial-and-error, especially the endings of the "dungeon" portions of the game, and the story can feel kind of generic; the usual "restore the light, keep the dark at bay" plot that's been done a million times. Still, if you're willing to overlook that, you're in for a VERY good time.
Overall, OatBF is one of the best MetroidVania's I've ever had the pleasure of playing through.

2x shorter and easier than its predecessor, you can cut through this game in 5-6 hours, as opposed to 12-13 hours for Death to Spies 1. It's a bit more graphically demanding. AI has decreased in quantity and increased in quality - there isn't that spamming of enemies and civvies on a tiny map that you got with DtS 1.
The fewer AI require more "fooling" though - you won't get by with just dressing up as an officer. You will have to dress up as several different character types throughout each level (civvie, worker, butler, soldier, officer, scientist, cop, FBI agent) and have the relevant paperwork in order to be granted access to various sections of the map. The levels and challenges are much more unique, so you won't be doing the same thing over and over again, but instead complete different tasks each mission (reconnaissance, assassination, kidnapping, sabotage, counterintelligence, intel theft).
Overall, DtS: MoT is a shorter, higher-quality version of DtS 1 and is definitely worth playing.

You play as a nameless man, of little known past, known only by his number: 47. He is a high skilled assassin, who works for the mysterious agency ICA. The agency is hired by politicians and other high calliber figures in the global elite to eliminate people. The contact 47 has with the agency is mediated by  Diana Burnwood, who works as 47’s boss and some kind of “mother figure” to him.
Most levels in this game work like this: you are set loose into an open world environment with people doing their jobs and thing. Among those people there your targets, that you have to kill. If you want an easy mode, you can follow the tips and hints given by the game. If you like fo figure things by yourself, then turn off the notifications and try to kill the targets in your own sloppy way. Observing patterns of movement is key: each NPC usually has a routine of places he goes and things he does. If you need his outfit as disguise, you just need to wait for him in that dark alley and then…
Agent 47 follows some kind of “perfect assassination honor code” were you are supposed to try to kill your targets in what is consedered the “perfect way”. So, there are some rules you should try to follow, such as: only kill the targets and no one eles, not being see, destrying evidences and só one. Every time you violate one of these rules, you lose points, which reflects in losing potential unlockable stuff in the end of the mission.
Agent 47 is a “good guy”.
I just dislike how the game devs tried to make Hitman, Diana and their agency some kind of “good guys doing a dirty job”. I mean, it seems like in every mission you are doing some kind of humanitary job by “killing evil people”. I don’t like this approach, it would be better if they tried something more “neutral”, were Agent 47 works for whoever pays more or something. Anyways, this is kind of minor, because the game has actually very little story whatsoever. One of the major complaints about “Hitman: Absolution” was that it was too much story driven and thous wasn’t a typical Hitman game. So, in Hitman 2016, they try to fix it and go back to the origins and focus more on the gameplay and level design than in story elements.
Mentally exausting.
Also, another thing, and this is very personal to me, is that this game seems to demand a lot of my head and after completing a mission I feel very tired of all that mental work. Each mission felt like and extended chess match, were my brain and senses worked overtime to finally beat the mission. It’s not a game made to “play for fun” or “play for relaxation”, at least not for me…

I can't understand why so many seem to be giving this game a negative review, because I can't say enough good things about it. Most of the negative reviews seem like the unqualified musing of impatient teenagers looking to blow things up. I wouldn't take their criticism with anything more than a grain of salt, but do know that this is a walking simulator style of game.
The game is beautiful, the story is interesting (akin to the tv show Lost), the characters are complicated and realistic, and I can't deny that I had to fight back tears several times while playing. I played through it three times, once on my own terms, a second in a rushed effort to knock off a few achievements, and a third to complete the remaining achievements. With each play through, I felt I understood the nuances of the world and its characters even better. I enjoyed just roaming around and taking beautiful screenshots when I wasn't moving towards the next story event or achievement. For all the fancy guns and bombs other games have to offer, rarely do shooters or other action-based games make me feel as emotionally connected to a game as this one did. Have some patience, allow yourself to become immersed in the world, pause for thought about what's happening with the story and the characters, and it certainly will not disappoint.
The kids can have their CS:Go, the adults can get out of this game what they might out of a well-written novel, but with lots of pretty pictures. Bravo, development team! An underappreciated work of entertaining art. I can't wait to play more of their games.

Ori and the Blind Forest is one of few games that recieves very little negative attention (only notable negativity come from those complaining about the Definite Edition release). There is very little wrong with the game itself in terms of gameplay, glitches, and music. The story itself is known for making even the toughest of men cry as well. Everything in the game itself seems to come together and forge a masterpiece.
The main gameplay of Ori and the Blind Forest is the platforming. It features a unique respawn system I have not seen in any other game (though someone else may be able to name one), utilizing an ability to create a respawn point anywhere at the cost of energy. This energy can also be used for a blast charge that can break some walls. Respawning by itself needs strategy, deciding whether the energy could be used for a better cause or not. Platforming itself isn't frame perfect like many say, the game was very responsive with the jumping and was never frustrating at any time. This is one of few games where I had not one issue with the movement and controls.
As for glitches in Ori and the Blind Forest, they are so few that you are highly unlikely to experience any in the entire thing. You aren't going to be coming across a Spore: Galactic Adventures experience here, where you have to be purposefully avoiding things in order to prevent glitches. The lack of game-breaking glitches is actually rather impressive. Yes, there are some, though it appeared to me you have to be purposefully trying to cause them to occur.
The art and music in Ori and the Blind Forest is the most notable thing in the whole game. The music score by Gareth is incredible. Once you hear the songs, with how emotional and fitting they are for the game, you could easily see as to why they recieved such praise. The art design is incredibly unique compared to similar games as well. It is a 2D game that looks and feels as gorgeous as a 3D game. The backgrounds and foregrounds are utilized to their greatest potential, being able to see the antagonist, Kuro, flying at you from a distance to Gumo hiding in the foreground behind tall grass. The two combined, art and music, end up creating a visual masterpiece that is incredibly pleasing to look at. Despite how simple Ori's sprite appears to be, it is at the same time very detailed with the animation and look. Everything in the game looks and moves like something that is alive.
The final part of the game, the story, is known to make grown men cry. While it isn't the most unique story when you first start, with Naru perishing and Ori going on a quest for 3 elements, it ends up becoming apparent as to why it is unique later on. Gumo, Kuro, and even Naru end up making the story incredibly unique for many, many reasons. Each character has a lot of backstory, and it is incredible how it is told without words. Gumo, Naru, and Kuro are incredibly detailed and interesting to learn about despite how simplistic they appear to be. We learn all about Ori throught the whole game, similar to Kuro. Every character, even the dead ones, have so much thought and effort put into them that it shows what Moon Studios is capable of.
Gameplay: 8/10 - It could do with better combat, but since the platforming was nailed incredibly well with the platforming being the main focus as well, the combat can easily be looked over.
Soundtrack: 10/10 - This is the only soundtrack I can say I have never enjoyed more in my entire life. Every song fits the scenario and changes the mood drastically. Without the work Gareth did, Ori and the Blind Forest would not be so amazing.
Art Design: 9/10 - The game looks and feels exactly like you are playing a painting. The characters move and look like they are alive as well. There is very little I could say bad about the art of Ori and the Blind Forest.
Story: 8/10 - Every single character has a massive amount of thought put into them and has their entire story told without the need of text. Even the least interesting character, Sein, is still incredibly interesting to think of. Every character in the game has incredible amounts of story put into them and the game tells it without saying it directly. What happens to Kuro, you have to piece together. Why the ending is sad, you have to tell yourself as to why. The character's stories are incredible, and the game might have been even better if it was even more focused on them as opposed to the elements Ori and Sein were searching for.
Bugs/Glitches: 9/10 - While there will always be bugs, I did not experience a single one during my entire time playing the game. I thought this was incredible, considering how buggy many games are today. The game still has some glitches as expected, but the lack of any glitches that occur during the playthrough of it is astonishing. They seemingly have to be activated purposefully.
Amazing control, nice level design, loved the abilities, the story was great, it was just amazing

The game is coded well, the physics are pristine and the controls are fluid.
Everything you'd want in a metroid-vania except... something is missing. Combat feels flat, especially compared to a Castlevania. Now, I get that it's more of a puzzle platformer than an action game, but with it's long gameplay time it needs some oomph in the combat to keep it exciting. The exploration is great, the graphics are unbeatable. Definitely could use more unique enemies.
My biggest gripe lies with the escape sequences. They force too much trial and error, as you do not know and can't really anticipate what the next killing you obstacle is until you've died from it. It was a neat mechanic the first time. After the second and third "temples" it was just awful having to restart at the beginning every time you fail, especially when you get to the point in the fire one where there is barely an indication of what you need to do next if it's been a few days since you played and don't catch the visual cue.
The story is weak and gets really lame when you find out the antagonist's motive and your spirit guide waxes sympathetic.
All in all, this is a visual masterpiece but is only pretending to be Metroid.
Or who knows? Maybe I just don't like video games anymore.
It's worth playing if you like exploration games, and the graphics truly are stellar.

I'll write two versions, short and detailed one.
Moon Studios created a perfect platformer. It is not only beautiful, charming but it also has strong gameplay foundation. It is not a mere shell, it is not a weak attempt at being "Artsy". Ori and the Blind Forest is an experience one of a kind. It is a beautifully told story and a challenging journey with interesting mechanics and engaging storyline. Great gameplay, great graphics and music.
Keep in mind one thing though. You need to have a somewhat beefy PC for this game. Make sure Your hardware meets the requirements. If it happens that Your computer is struggling, the audio can go out of sync at the cutscenes. Just a thing worth mentioning.
Story is pretty simple, it's really nothing groundbraking or innovative, but it is still insanely captivating because of one reason. The way this story is told makes all the difference. Almost all characters are mute. Spirit Tree serves a role of the narrator in the first minutes of the game and there is also another character, a companion who explains more crucial parts of the journey, but the rest does not pronounce a single word, including the main hero Ori. They don't have to, all they are doing is showing emotions through simple yet perfectly understandable noises and body language. And it was the best narrative choice for this game. I think I'm not that much emotional but this game manages to squeeze the tears out of me right in the prologue, every time. Every. Single. Time. You're attached to the characters immediately. Snap of the fingers and You love them, just like that. It is also worth noting, the main antagonist of the story, Kuro, isn't a flat character, she have a reason why she's doing all these things to hunt You and hurt You. But, that's as far as I am going to describe it, the rest is for You to discover. ;) Definitive Edition also adds the backstory of one of the characters, Naru, although honestly I expected something more out of it. Still it is a nice addition to the lore.
The presentation of this game is perfect. Ori and the Blind Forest was (as far as I know) entirely hand-drawn in the span of 4 years. I don't know what else I can tell You to convince You that it's brilliant. Just... look at the screenshots. And the music? It's gorgeous. It fits the situations currently happening on screen perfectly. Same goes for sound effects. I think I'm going to skip this part of my review because I can't find anything constructive in my words. Only superlatives. To put it simple... the atmosphere is unforgettable. It's a feast for Your senses, it is an experience one of a kind.
Now, this is where it gets interesting. So, this game is an Indie, and probably the thought processes of some people was something like this: "Indie + 2D fancy graphics = artsy fartsy walking simulator, no real gameplay" etc. If for a second You thought about Ori this way then... oh boy You are so wrong. Don't be fooled by its cover. This game will snap Your neck without warning if You aren't prepared. It has solid gameplay mechanics that will test Your platforming skills and reflexes. It is brutal if You aren't familiar with the genre, and even if You are, it still serves a serious challenge. And I'm not talking about tougher achievements, I am talking about base game. After completing the game 100% my death count shows 380~ deaths so... It is a Metroidvania so You uncover chunks of the map after gaining new skills. Definitive Edition comes with two new very cool skills, and You can also teleport between "Spirit wells" and it's a very big time saver. I played with keyboard and a mouse and I didn't have any problems with controls whatsoever. In a game like this, it's a big deal. Controls are A+. Skills are interesting and meaningful. Like I said, it may be an Indie game, it may have beautiful graphics and music but it also has enourmous amounts of gameplay at its core.
Ori and the Blind Forest is aesthetically beautiful, it is emotional, it is challenging and fun to play. It is everything I ever want from a game. I love Ori, I will buy the sequel, and if ever will there be a third game I will buy it too.

One of the best 3rd person games to have emerged out of the 2000s.  The plot, acting, characters, voice acting and gameplay mechanics are amazing to play even a decade later.
The flim noir feel to this game coupled with the hammy lines and gritty New York scene make the plot memorable and enjoyable. The landscapes, sounds, soundtrack, layout and even odd and slightly macabre portraits of the cut outs in the game make for an overally gloomy, moody and atmospheric game.
The bullet-time mechanics make this a pleasure to play as you hammer away with your twin deagles in bullet-time mode.
What's also really enjoyable are the game's idiosyncrasies: the Lords and Ladies television show that everyone watches with its overly hammy and campy acting; the strung out junkies and hookers who decide to join you only to last several minutes; or the old ladies who toss you a spare shotgun from their living room closet.
The soundtrack is absolutely beautiful and haunting with that repeating cello and accompanying orchestra.
The first Max Payne introduced the gamer to bullet-time mechanics along with an equally gritty plot copuled with Max's foray into his drug-addled dreamscapes while looking for his family's killers.
In the sequel, the graphics have been updated along with a continuation of the plot. I love what Remedy has done with both games.
With the third Max Payne, you are granted access to way better graphics, thanks to Rockstar, but frankly the plot paled in comparison with the previous two releases.

Max Payne 2: Fall of Max Payne is the sequel to the critically acclaimed and award winning 2001 game, Max Payne. Max Payne 2 is a Third-Person action shooter developed by Remedy Entertainment which was acquired by Rockstar Games whose notable works include the popular Grand Theft Auto (GTA) franchise.
Once again the player steps into the shoes of Max Payne, a New York City Detective who, after the events of the first game, went on a downward spiral both in career and personal life, struggling with the death of his family and his newly formed Pain Killer addiction (the direct result of the pain killers taken by the player in the first game to regenerate lost health). While Max is investigating a series of murders and assassinations, Max encounters Mona Sax, a textbook femme fatale who was presumed dead from the first game. Follow Max and Mona's adventure through New York City and discover a conspiracy behind a Mob War between two rival Mafia groups and a deadly team of hitmen called 'The Cleaners' in this film noir love story.
+ Significant and highly noticeable improvements on the graphics, animation and texture quality from the first title
+ Better sounds, voice acting and sound track
+ Improvements on the innovative Bullet Time game mechanic
+ Great locations and level design which goes well with the better graphical fidelity
+ Graphic Novel style cutscenes are back and with better delivery
+ Expanded weapon variety
+ Mission variety
+ Challenging Difficulty levels (the game provides a good challenge on any difficulty setting)
+ Adaptive difficulty if the player is on Easy Mode. (AI gets toned down and pain killers heal more if the player dies too much on Easy Mode.)
+
story that surpasses even the first game
+ World is ALIVE and more immersive.
- VERY Short (I personally completed it within 5-6 hours)
- Replayability: - Linear storytelling is FINE, its a good way to tell a narrative story in a directed pace but Linearity does sacrifice replayability at degree because, after finishing the story, there is little reason to play through it a second time around. Like a good action movie, it's best to be played again after some time has passed. (Copy Pasted from my Max Payne 1 Review)
I rarely call something a 'MASTERPIECE' but after playing through the whole game, twice (once on my Xbox back in 2005, once again on my PC 2013), and sitting here writing this review, I cannot find any more CONs aside from the short story. Contrast this to the PROS I listed, I can easily say we have an almost perfect action game. Max Payne 2 blends perfectly the immersive storytelling of a good action movie, and the dynamic adrenaline pumping gameplay of a video game.
MUST BUY and HIGHLY RECOMMENDED for both new and old fans a like. I do, however, not recommend you buy this game solo but instead, BUY the MAX PAYNE BUNDLE which includes the Original Max Payne and Max Payne 2. At $15, this is a game worth your time and money.

This is one of those games that you should find on many people's "What single game would you take to a desert island?" answers.
+ Easy to learn, hard to master.
+ A lot to do: Make people happy, optimize your prison layout, upgrade security. There's always more to do and improve.
+ Massive replayability: Spend 10+ hours on a prison, sell it, start again with more cash, repeat until you remember you haven't had a meal in 3 days.
+ Optimize your buildings: There are always ways to make your prison function better. Figure it out.
+ Deal with your prisoners: Watch their needs, keep them calm, and at the same time, punish them.
+ Random events: The generator caught fire, power is out, automated doors don't work, people can't go to the yard, there's a riot now.
+ Manage everything: Adjust timetables, assign laundry distribution, adjust prisoner punishments, adjust meal quality and quantity, etc...
+ It's an ant farm: Build a prison and watch people use it. No super-micro control. I like it...
- Is this a bug?: Sometimes people freak out, you're not sure why and the game doesn't do a great job of explaining.
It's a fantastic management game with all the right details in all the right places, awesome replayability and it's very addicting. It's like Dungeon Keeper, but better.

I loved ths game. The storyline is absolutely fantastic, the music is atmospheric and haunting, and the graphics are probably some of the best I've ever seen in any game.
But before buying it, bear in mind that it's in *no way* an action game. It's very slow, and more like (to use a '90s term) an interactive movie. It's not a game you can dip into, but if you want to invest the time in it and be prepared for a slow-moving but apocalyptic storyline, give this one a try.
BTW, there were a couple of things which I had to look up because they weren't clear. I've stuck them behind a spoiler tag in case you want to work it out for yourself :)
About game saves:

First off, it's very important one knows what he/she is getting into with this game--the term "walking simulator" is not used loosely here.  The map is pretty expansive for a game of this sort, and you're going to be dragging yourself around a rather large portion of it if you've got plans to watch the whole story unfold.  If the first few minutes of gameplay don't pique your curiosity, then this is probably not for you.  If it does, however, you will likely not be disappointed.
I came into this one having just played Dear Esther and enjoying it, though being a bit let down by just how loosely woven the story was, and the lack of interactivity.  I was very pleased to see improvements on both of those elements in Everybody's Gone to the Rapture.  Interaction is still minimal and story still leaves a bit of room for interpretation, but both are still satisfying and fit with the style of the game.  As to the story: I have never done so myself I can only make assumptions, but I imagine it's quite challenging to put together a story that is immersive and actually develop a number of characters with nothing but snippets of dialogue, radio messages, and still-frames of what was once these people's lives.  Here it is done amazingly well, and the voice acting enhances it substantially.  Eagerness to learn more about these unseen denizens will carry you across the beautiful and tragic terrain as the story slowly unfolds before you.  Music is stirring and delighfully atmospheric.  The attention to detail throughout the world leaves little to be desired.
In the negative column: save system (or lack thereof) can be somewhat troublesome.  Sometimes I want to explore and don't really have an hour plus to wait for the game to autosave.  Don't really have that option here, especially since autosave points can only be triggered once.  Considering how much time one can spend wandering around this world just taking it all in, this is a bit of a drawback.  Visuals seemed choppy at first, but turning off motion blur made a sizeable difference for me.  If you're looking for a game that is relaxing but still has meaning, check this one out.  It will tug at the heartstrings a bit.

- I picked up Everybody's Gone to the Rapture ("EGTTR") for $4.99 during the Autumn Sale.
- I played the game with the Cheat Engine movement speed modifier enabled (more on this in a moment).
- I don't recommend this game at $19.99, but I
recommend it for $4.99
As other reviewers have mentioned, this is a game that really makes me wish there was something between Steam's "Thumbs Up" and "Thumbs Down" review system. Portions of this game were awesome, and I find myself with a much heavier screenshot folder after playing it. However, other portions of the game were pretty dismal, and unfortunately, I find myself not recommending the game at full price - which is what this review is based off of since it's full price as I write this.
I'm no stranger to "walking simulators" (I take issue with that term, but as it’s widely acknowledged at this point, I'll use it for simplicity's sake). In fact, there are a few walking simulators that I rank as some of the best games I've ever played. Unfortunately EGTTR is not one of those games, and it's not even close to them. EGTTR struck me as way too full of itself, not only from a story perspective, but from a game design perspective. Not only do you move far too slowly, the game itself "doesn't recommend" using the abysmal built-in running function because you "might miss something" (check the control screen, if you've played the game already and missed this tidbit). I'm one to meticulously explore an environment, that's what I like to do. However, if I want to move quickly to retrace my steps because there is nothing more to be seen, then allow me to do that. The choice to keep the player at a snail's pace for the sake of well... honestly it seems like for the sake of just bloating the game's length to me... regardless it's a bad mechanic. If you want to go through the world slowly, then do so, but if you want to move quickly, well that should be allowed. Now, lest you think I'm just a "run-and-gun" transferee who can't deal with this kind of system, smaller worlds are
with slower movement, but EGTTR is simply too large for the arbitrarily slow speed the developers have shackled you into.
I ended up using Cheat Engine (for the first time ever) simply to gain control over
experience in the game, and I enjoyed EGTTR more-so because of it (yet still don’t recommend it, which is telling). Perhaps I didn't get the "true" EGTTR experience, but the fact of the matter is that I don't think I would have bothered to continue through the game absent the movement speed modifier. That I still spent ~5 hours in the world
the increased movement speed, should showcase that I spent
of time exploring, and thus didn't hurriedly move through the game and miss important elements. Really, had I not used the speed modification, I can't imagine me progressing very far into the game as it would have taken too long to move across otherwise pointless sections, which is a shame, because the world itself is gorgeous.
Which brings me to my next point, as with Dear Esther (especially the 2012 recreation), the world is brilliantly pretty. I've got a few screenshots that are almost photorealistic. The level of detail is incredible - at least on the surface. You quickly find a
suspicious number of locked doors and invisible walls. The invisible walls, somewhat shockingly, seem less lazy than the locked doors. At least I can mentally accept the invisible walls as a limitation of the game's parameters, but the locked doors? Those just seem lazy in a game that wants to sell you on its environment. Am I really to believe that 90+ percent of the doors - including doors that often
- were locked up while all the events of the game were unfolding? Sure the game offers a placid explanation for
of the doors (
), but this explains... at
1/3 of the locked doors, and that's being quite generous.
The result is that while the world is large (for these kinds of games), and is gorgeous, it feels shallow. The good news is that the (former) residents of the town weave some very interesting side-stories. In fact, I dare say that the ancillary cast of characters is
more interesting than the two characters who are central to the "story." Indeed, by the end I found myself completely apathetic towards the two main characters - and heck, I'd go so far as to say that I was outright annoyed each time one of their "scenes" popped up as I simply didn't care anymore. I cared
more about the "secondary" residents of the area than I did the people who were supposed to carry the central story. As such, by the time the game draws near its conclusion - and the story narrows to almost exclusively these two characters, I found myself just hoping it would end.
In short, I found the primary storyline to be very unengaging, predictable, and far too reliant on bland protagonists who fit way too uniformly into the tropes I was expecting. The side-cast, so to speak, isn't particularly novel - but they have a softness and emotion to them that pulled me into their story, and I felt moved by their experiences during the "Rapture" - whereas the protagonists I just wanted to shut up.
EGTTR is a visually wonderful game, with a wonderful "backdrop" of its secondary cast. Beyond that, it isn't much else. The central story is basic, unfulfilling, and made quite monotonous due to some really, in my opinion, poor game design (movement and saving). Within Steam's binary review system, I wholly do not recommend this game at $19.99 and only recommend it at $4.99 if you are ok with horrendously slow movement (or are ok using Cheat Engine) and enjoy exploring ambient environments without any expectations of the central storyline beyond those snippets that involve the far-more-interesting supporting cast.

Playing Super Meat Boy is like learning a language.
If you're familiar with other platformers or languages, the beginner parts will be relatively easy.
There will be a point where you know nothing, and have to concentrate to acheive success.
Some parts you simply won't get at all, and you will become frustrated.
It will get progressively harder as you learn more and more.
You will sometimes know what to do, but not how to do it.
There is always something to improve on.
You will eventually succeed. Eventually.
And perhaps the most important thing to know: know when to walk away. As long as you feel like you've gotten at least your money's worth and the difficulty is too high, just stop playing. It's ok to not get 100% completion...uh, I mean, know every word of a language.
Remember: you can always revisit it at a later point to learn even more.

1. The concept is a interesting idea where it's based on Batman's early years, before he and Gordan saw eye-to-eye and with various villains who start coming out of the woodwork, even some who weren't even referenced in the past games.
2. There is also a cool moment where you get to enter Joker's Psyche and some very inventive looking environments when under the Mad Hatter's spell.
3. There's a awesome bit where you get energised gloves that charge as you beat people, leading to a unstoppable combos that affect those armed with weapons, shields or are just brutes.
Negatives and boy are there a lot!:
1. First, they somehow messed up the combat. At first it seems ok, but later as you fight many more people you find the camra stars to zoom into walls or environment gets in the way of anyone attacking you, meaning you get hit when not knowing where the attack is coming from.
2. The villains, more so on the side villains are ALL very dissappointing. I was very interested in Copperhead as it looked like they turned him into a sexy male (which is a nice difference as we have too many sexy females) but turns out they turned Copperhead into a female, stating there must be somekind of syndicate with the name all being assassins from South America and involved in Drug ring. This sound really cool and I would've loved to have seen more about this and maybe digging up stuff about this group, but that never happens. She poisons you, you beat her down, lock her up and leave her in a container for the police.
However, this was not the worst. The very worst was when you face the first one, The Executioner and defeat him be jumping over him and punching him ONCE leading to a single KO. Big bad mini-boss, punked out with a single blow. TRUELY WORTHY OF BATMAN'S TIME!
3. Despite being several years old the game is RIDDLED with glitches and bugs. None gamebreaking, but still irritating like Killer Crok turning invisible and flicking out of exsistance, people getting stuck in walls and people not talking to you when they should be. I also hardcrashed.
4. The designs of them are CRAP. I don't know what they did to Killer Crok but his design is rubbish! He looks like one of Michael Bay's Turtles. Most of the designs are just terrible and really don't work.
I'd suggest avoid this game unless you REALLY want to complete the series and don't bother with the season pass unless you REALLY want ot play endless challenge maps.

A Solid Stealth Game for only the Most Diehard Stealth Fans
Death to Spies 2 is much like the original game nothing has been drastically changed, only minor tweaks, the game is still extremely hard and the focus is on disguising yourself as the enemy. There as several tweaks incuding the ability to carry a disguise in your backpack, the addition of yellow enemies whom get suspicious only if you get close.
The biggest change is the disguise system where its more about getting the right disguise for the task as opposed to going straight for the officer disguise, for example in the second mission the officer disguise is good for the 3rd floor however in the shipyard most enemies are suspicious towards the officer. However most of the time getting the officer disguise will do the job.
Some negatives about the game are its length, there are only seven missions, a lack of tutorial, leaving players confused and struggling unless they played the first game, there is a visiual filter that gives the game a sepia filter, which looks extremely ugly in my opinion however you can get rid of it by disabling depth of feild also vehicles are not well utilised, they can be used in 3 missions only and are not too useful.
The biggest flaw was that the game didn't give you as much help as it should, sometimes I would get stuck and have to go to a guide to work out what to do. For example in one mission I needed to kick a bucket of water on my target to get him to a secluded location, however the bucket looked just like a normal prop and the map didn't highlight the location of the bucket leading to frustration.
Overall if you liked the first game or enjoyed the brutal difficulty of Hitman 2 and Contracts you will enjoy this one, the game is just as unforgiving. Your freedom to choose how to acheive your objectives is less than the extent in hitman but more or less the same as the first game.
Pros:
-Graphics are better.
-You have some freedom to choose how to acheive your objectives.
-Unique Disguise gameplay is excellent, this and hitman are the only games that utilise this feature effectively.
Cons:
-Can be confusing
-Quite short
-No Tutorial

Death to Spies: Moment of Truth is a WWII-era stealth game in which you play as a Russian agent named Semion Strogov, a man tasked with eliminating espionage-related threats to the Soviet Union. The missions that you must accomplish range anywhere from gathering intel to assassination, with the locations in which you will be inserted range from German military camps to an English hospital. The areas are varied, and you never feel like the developers ran out of ideas.
The gameplay of Death to Spies is very similar to the Hitman games, with most of the stealth revolving around disguises. While crawling through bushes and vents are a viable way to play the game, using the game's disguise system is the most reliable way to play. The disguise system in this game is usually pretty realistic, and the AI is consistent when it comes to detecting you (I'm looking at you, Hitman 2 Japan levels), so you always know why your disguise did not work, and what you can do to improve it. Certain disguises don't work in certain areas, and if you take the clothes of a high-ranking officer, the guards will recognize that you aren't the person you claim to be. Adding to that, in the higher difficulty settings, blood-stained clothes and clothes with bullet holes are unusable, so stabbing and shooting is a no-no. Much more reliable weapons are the garrotte and chloroform if you prefer a non-lethal approach. The game doesn't seem to punish you for taking the lethal approach (as long as you are merciful to civilians), unlike many other stealth games out there.
I can't speak much for the graphics of the game, since it doesn't seem to like my graphics card, washing out all the colors. This made the game look like an old movie, which in my opinion added to the atmosphere. The animations are nothing special, but they do their job and you can always tell what's going on. The music was mostly forgettable, but it always fits what's going on.
One thing I did not mention earlier is that this game is very difficult, and the poor shooting mechanics don't do anything to help it. Unfortunately, there's no tutorial in this game, so some of the more nuanced parts of the game must be learned through experience. I personally enjoy when games give me a challenge and didn't mind the lack of a tutorial that much. As for the shooting mechanics, this is a stealth game, so you shouldn't be shooting much anways. This game really shines when you're walking down the corridor of a German military base, doing your best to remain inconspicuous.
The thing that really sets this game apart from other games in this genre, and indeed, from other games period, is the amount of realism in this game. As I said earlier, if you stab people or shoot people, it renders their disguise useless, and people may recognize you if you take a unique disguise anyways. One of the options in the game is to make everyone speak their native language, adding to the atmosphere. Being a German speaker really helped me here, as most of the enemies in this game are German, and certain small hints can be drawn from their chatter. Strogov himself is, obviously, a Russian speaker, making all of the briefings and cutscenes in Russian with English subtitles. Death to Spies itself was a Soviet anti-espionage program during WWII, which I did not know originally.
Overall, I really enjoyed Death to Spies: Moment of Truth. People calling it a rip-off of Hitman obviously didn't see the game for what it is: a realistic spy game set during WWII. A disguise system and assassination missions don't make a game a Hitman clone. Though the story is mostly nonexistent, and the game's soundtrack is mostly forgettable, Death to Spies: Moment of Truth is a fun stealth game that, as long as they iron out some of the wrinkles in (hopefully) future installments, could become one of my favorite games. This game is a definite recommendation, as long as you don't mind a difficult game.

Like Metal Gear Solid, but not so much your gameplay being interrupted every 10 minutes by Codec chatter and / or Hollywood-esque cutscenes? It grows even tinier if you are in grass and can utilize your camo. There is so much more into figuring out how to beat this game on hardest difficulty as you cannot procure enemy disguises. It's doable though, a trail well hidden / disposed of, garrotted, and chloroformed bodies later and I was damn proud of myself for infiltrating that Nazi airbase near Prague and putting a stop to the prototype Nazi Me-163 new rocket type fighter on the first mission! "When there's no more room in hell, the dead will walk the earth."
A tribute to the highly acclaimed film series in which the above quote originated from, No More Room in Hell (PC Gamer's Mod of the Year 2011, ModDB's Editor Choice Multiplayer Mod of the Year 2011), is a co-operative realistic first person survival horror modification for the Source Engine. Taking inspiration from George Romero's "Of the Dead" series, the mod is set during a time in which the world is on the verge of collapsing into chaos from a disease whose origin is unknown. Many experts and organizations have their theories and ideas on how such a disease emerged and started to systematically destroy our very way of life, but one fact is clear to all. Whoever perishes from the disease gets up and kills, and the people they killed get up and kill.
The chances of you surviving this all out war of society and the undead are slim to none. Already, there are millions of the walking dead shambling about, searching for food to eat. There's no known cure. One bite can possibly end it all for you. However, you aren't alone in this nightmare. There are still a handful of uninfected survivors left in this god forsaken hellhole, and with co-operation and teamwork, you may live long enough to fight your way to salvation.

Well, DmCDevil may Cry was a reboot of the fabulous, beloved and awesome Devil May Cry Series, courtesy of Ninja Theory and  CAPCOM. It retells the story of the origins of Dante, Vergil, Sparda and the iconic Eva, in a twist that breaks the cadre of the story from the previous Devil may Cry series.
Review: The story was a (bit) half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ character development was shallow, and as such, the previous touch and flair that Dante is known for ( Balls, bravery, awesomeness, cool dude) and Vergil's nature ( Loyalty, skill, distaste for firearms, etc) have neen washed away and in their place, are shallow, under-developed and uninspiring characters for whom no fan of devil may Cry series can connect to easily. The fabled Sparda, and his legend is gone. So if you're looking to reconnect to the awesomeness that Devil may Cry used to be, this is not it. It may feel a bit insulting to the series' die-hard fans.
Gameplay: Acceotable. Fluid mechanics,  and the camera can get glitchy at times. For the love of all thats' awesome, why did they leave out Lock On to targets out of a hack and slash game? This makes combat cumbersome, especially in Boss Fights (Mundus, anyone? ). The game also has a short learning curve, and as such, new players to the series will be at ease hacking and slashing demons at the comfort of their seats.
Graphics: Pretty average. Nothing spectacular. Runs in DirectX9, powered by the Unreal Engine 3. If you're on catalyst (Running an AMD/ATI GPU/APU), ensure you're using the latest driver. The game is known for being glitchy with old versions of AMD Catalyst, and micro-stutter is  relatively common in CrossFire-based systems. Your mileage may vary.
The music is great,m if you're into industrial metal. Noisia and CombiChrist worked up quite the charm here, so you'll be in for a blast if its' your kind of thing.
Overall rating: 88% in my personal opinion. Despite its shortcomings, this is a great game with excellent gameplay and many hours of fun, especially when you throw in the Vergil's Downfall DLC and the other mode similar to Devil may Cry's 4 Bloody Palace. Again, your mileage may vary. This is a personal opinion and as such, is subject to personal bias.
Play the game, and be the judge.

It was almost morning, waking up from the American Dream. We are willing to suffer, to die for the things we care about. For love, for the right choices, Because of her, I had solved the case. My case. All of it.
Two years after the events of the previous game, Max Payne is a NYPD detective. Senator Alfred Wooden has kept his promise, and released Max from his history of violence. Max got back to working for the NYPD to keep himself busy in life. After a series of events, Max investigates a group of contract killers called: The Cleaners. Mona Sax, who was presumed dead, is under investigation for killing Senator Gates, a member of "The Inner Circle" from the previous game. The leader of the Russian mob, and Max's old friend Vladimir Lem, finds himself in a heavy mob war with Vinnie Gognitti. Max is determined to find out about the unexpected return from Max's love interest Mona Sax, and who The Cleaners are working for, and what they want.
Max Payne 2 plays very similar to its first installment. The new and polished bullet-time is back, and better than ever. The animations of the bullet-time just look better, and the bullet-time diving won't lower your stamina bar. The game has like its previous installment 3 parts, each with seven to nine chapters. Next to playing Max, you'll also play as Mona Sax for a few chapters, making the characters bond together even better. There are more guns to choose from, and are in my opinion far more fun to use.
Max Payne 2: The Fall of Max Payne is in my opinion a better game than Max Payne 1. It has one of the best game stories I've ever played, and it takes a few nice twists and turns. The gameplay is amazing and fun to play, and still plays a lot like Max Payne 1. That being said, the only bit of negativity I have for the game, is that it's really short. An average gamer completes the game in six or seven hours. But the story fits perfectly in this time span, nothing needs to be added or left out. But a little bit more time to walk around and shoot is never a bad thing. Max Payne 2: The Fall of Max Payne is a phenomenal game, nothing more I can say about it.

Pros:
It had strong feels.  It has remarkably good detail in its environment.  The music is pretty moving, too.  I only paid $5 for it on a Steam sale.
Cons:
Duration; even with the run button forcably disabled the entire game, I still finished it in under 5 hours, including wandering over hill and dale trying to find more snippets.  Though I did not find them all, I read an article and confirmed that I found the lion's share of the story.  I could hunt achievements, but it looks like they're a bunch of ironic jokes to play on achievement hunters.  For all practical purposes, 5 hours is the complete experience: game uninstalled.
This game defines the "walking simulator" genre.  It's more an interactive narrative, a 3D world based visual novel, than a game.  Worse, it's a less interactive example of its kind, where nothing the player does really makes any difference.  The story will end the same way every time.  It's not much of a game when the player is irrelevant.
I am most annoyed with the deliberately hobbled level of interaction and slow walk speed.  Invisible walls and locked doors abound, the player must slowly walk up to them, discover they can go no further, then slowly double back.  I know the developers did a great job of providing fine details to the environments, but their pride is getting in the way of the players' experience.  Just because the game world ended doesn't mean I have all the time in the real world.
On the fence:
The story.  The entire game is about a catastrophic event that might be good, might be bad, is not literally The Rapture, but has pretty much the same effect.  Hey, it's not a spoiler if it's in the title.
We learn about this by encountering memories left behind by the people of the small town.  However, because this is their memories, it largely derails into drama about the characters.  Really heavy-handed drama, of the likes of infidelity, pregnancies, terminal illnesses, and bitter mortality.   Just dragged out and shoved in your face to see if it evokes an emotional response.
Maybe you're into heavy-handed drama, in which case that'll be your cup of tea.  Maybe you're not, in which case it will insult your intelligence they're breaking out these big guns at the drop of a hat.
I fell a bit into the latter category, the tendency to unapologetically employ sledgehammers wherever a mallet would suffice offended my logical sensibilities a bit.  Subtlety probably would have worked better.  Yet, this emotional carpet bombing certainly had some effect: at times, I was moved.
For best results, do not overthink the story.  It will fall apart under critical assessment like most stories do.  The ambiguious bits are deliberately so, if you go seeking answers you will be tasked with inventing your own.  None of it really matters anymore anyway: Everybody's Gone to the Rapture.
My rating:
I don't hate the walking simulator genre.  I gave a thumbs up to Stanley Parable and Diaries of a Spaceport Janitor.  Taken in a very specific light, Everybody's Gone To The Rapture is an masterpiece, it is certainly prettier than either of those games, but this perspective requires just enough suspension of criticism of its various parts that I can't quite recommend it.

While it has it's flaws (mainly a pace that often crosses the line from "meditative" to "painfully slow") this is a formative entry in the genre. The quasispiritual sci fi plot and the lives of the prior inhabitants of a small English village make for generally fantastic storytelling and the score and graphics (mainly the lighting) make for some melancholic perfection in terms of atmosphere.
As a fan of interactive fiction I would call this more "nonlinear" than "interactive" but I really liked it  nonetheless. I also loved Gone Home though and it had very similar gameplay so if that's not your type of game, move along.
PRO: Fascinating story and unique setting/atmosphere. Solid voice acting.
CON: Very slow pace (both physical movement and story beats).

This is why I can't stand the Steam review system.  I hated Dear Esther which hadglowing reviews, I loved this which had mixed reviews...and most of the negative reviews for this game seem to be from people who either don't like walking simulators, or simply don't have any patience.
Nice scenery, phenomenal music, great voice acting, and great method of relaying the "story".
As I'm sure you're aware by now, the game is first and foremost a walking simulator.  Relatively slow pacing, but the way this game is constructed I really think it works well.
My only serious gripe with the game overall is the ball of light "guide".  The AI for that thing is really terrible.  Sure it looks cool, but I often found it travelling back and forth between the same locations for no reason.
If you're on the fence about it, sure wait for a sale.  But I really recommend this title for people looking for a different experience.

Hardware: Win 10 x64, i5-3570, nVidia GTX 1070. Looks great, runs great.
I picked this up because I'm a fan of post-apocalyptic fiction, and don't really care HOW the world ends in my stories, only that it has.
I assume most people viewing this game are at least passingly familiar with the term "Rapture", which derives from ancient Greek / Latin words for snatching or seizing, with the idea that believers in Christ will be taken away to join him prior to the Tribulation (a period of wars, etc) that precede his return to Earth (the "Second Coming"). The idea comes from the Bible, 1st Thessalonians, chapter 4 verse 17:
Modern "pre-Tribulation" Rapture Theology, meaning believers get snatched away to Heaven before the time of troubles, was developed in the early American colonies, and though the concept existed in earlier Christianity, it's a fairly American idea. The Rapture is an event, not a place, so the game's name is somewhat of a misnomer. You get raptured TO a place. You don't go to it.
Anyway, on to the game:
It's set set in a British village called Yaughton, nicely modeled and well detailed. There's a voice you hear early in the game coming over the radio, an American female scientist married to a local British astronomer. You get the sense that you're that person, though in the game I've played so far it's not entirely clear. Gameplay consists of trudging around the village, listening to brief audio clips played on various radios, and encountering the ghostly, lighted spirits of people as they re-enact the events of recent days prior to being taken away.
The British voices are all well-written and acted; the American protagonist is also well-written, but I didn't care for the actress, Despite winning a BAFTA award for her role, I found her unconvincing as a scientist; she sounded more like the narrator of a car commercial. Using that same croaky-husky voice that has infected 95% of young American female actors in the last 10 years, she delivers her lines with excessive force while mutilating vowels whenever possible (for example, in the opening line in the game, she pronounces "I'm the only one left" as "I'm the only one laughed"). I looked her up and was surprised to learn she was in her 40's. Tsk.
The movement speed is as slow as others have complained. Worse, the RUN key (shift) doesn't actually work; you hold down SHIFT like you're supposed to, and your move speed doesn't change in the slightest.
Moving slowly wouldn't be so bad, except it's clear that the game won't advance to the next stage until you've triggered specific event(s), and, as you can wander anywhere you want in the rather large play area, you can miss things. Having to trudge all over the map trying to find that one event you overlooked, with absolutely no direction from the game, is frustrating. This frustration is compounded by some odd interface choices; there is some sort of right-click-slide action you're supposed to do with your mouse at key moments, and I could get that interface to activate despite the gaming experience of a 40 year habit.
The game only auto-saves after specific events. Thus, on my play-through, I spent 45 minutes fruitlessly wandering around the village trying to advance the game, only to learn I would lose all that progress upon quitting. If I want to finish, I must either randomly wander at a turtle's pace for who knows how long, or resort to a walkthrough. Both are unappealing options. Who designs games this way in 2017?
Anyway, it's probably worth the $5 I spent on it, but it's a thunbs-down at the $20 asking price unless the interface, save game structure, and player direction get some work.

Starting point:
I slogged through this game and I can finally say that I gladly uninstall it from my computer.
Let's start off with the good:
-Good music
-Good graphics
-Diverse townscape to walk through
-Good voice acting
-An
(but not amazing) story concept
All of that said, it's lost in what can only be described as the player being held hostage in a pretty world that only lets you move around at a painfully slow pace set as your normal speed.  You can have a nice story, and an experience presented to a player like this, but if it feels like your character is constantly walking in sand, it kills the enjoyment of it pretty quickly.  The developers say they want you to 'experience' the world, which is why you're at the pace you're at, but it's hard to want to do that when your world is lifeless, and doesn't let you interact with anything more than a few tape recordings, and phone/radio messages.  Your main objective besides that is to find flashbacks of people in the town interacting with each other which range from boring to slightly interesting if you decide to try to get invested in the characters.  But overall nothing about those interactions made me want to forgive the movement handicap.
But wait!  There is a sprint button you might be saying...except it only works after holding a button down for 5-10 seconds and even after it activates, it's still too slow for how big the world is.
If you don't mind taking your time and you actually enjoy looking at graphic textures and a town layout in some kind of interactive tour sort of way, then you might actually like this game.
But I can't recommend this for anyone outside of that.

When I started playing I thought this was the best Hitman game since Blood Money, by the time I finished I thought it was the best Hitman game period. Initially I was put off by the episodic format and held off on purchasing until I could get it all at once - I've since realized this is a game almost uniquely suited to a episodic release schedule because each level is absolutely packed to the hilt with things to do/challenges to complete/details to drink in etc. It's actually extremely overwhelming to have it ALL available right from the get go.
Dumping a lot of the trashy sexualization prevalent in earlier games (such as the shower scene from Absolution), this is all about Agent 47 traveling to a variety of stunning locations where you're given a target or 2 to kill and maybe some kind of extra goal and then are largely left to do it in whatever way suits you. There are opportunities and challenges to guide and suggest, but the choices are ultimately left up to you and there is a huge amount of replay value (as my close to 200 hours of game time can attest).
The loose connecting cutscenes tell a largely forgettable story that exist mostly as a framework to tie together 47's disparate targets/locations. It's well produced though and doesn't go completely overboard in the same way Absolution did.
If you avoided this because of the episodic format or the fact it's a single-player game that wants you to connect to a server, I recommend giving it a shot. It didn't sell well and apparently there won't be a season 2, so sadly for now this is as good as it gets. Happily, it gets VERY good indeed.
