If you like the Hitman series, have an interest in espionage or WW2 this game is for you. It is a bit dated now, and you can see this by the graphics and the UI however that doesn't harm the game in anyway as even now it is very playable.
WEAPONS
The first reason I liked this game was the detail in terms of authenticity and gameplay. There is a large amount of historically accurate 'spy' weapons availiable including a Nagant silenced revolver and the classic silenced sten gun however if you are looking for a shooter this is not for you. Most of the weapons feel fairly weak - mostly because they are silenced but even the machine guns feel a bit 'odd' for example the STG 44 doesn't sound right and doesn't give a real kickback it should do, by affecting you physically, it instead just seems to tilt up when you fire. The guns are hardly the main meat of the game but for an authentic game such as this they could have done better.
VEHICLES!
Moving onto a positive note there are vehicles in the game, and correct me if i am wrong, but i do not think hitman or any other simular stealth games include the ability to drive vehicles whilst useing them as a tool to hide bodies or escape. Sure they don't drive very well but it is not a racing game and they are slow, but it is nice to have the option to hide a german officers corpse in the back of your bad♥♥♥♥♥opel blitz.
AI
The AI is competant at what it does, the detection system is good - the sense bullet noises, if you are near them or in their line of sight and yet still allows you to use morphine or take out a guard from behind. There is always problems though-AI can be a bit stupid sometimes by repeatably charging into a room you are camping in whilst you gun 20 of them down, you cannot just walse through missions like this though as in the end they will pull back and wait for you, or 'lob' a grenade into your hiding spot.
STEALTH/TOOLS
The main component of any game of this genre is stealth i.e the ability to have to avoid, usually enemies, without being noticed. In Death to Spies moment of truth there is a variet of ways to do this...
You can go in quiet using morphine, silenced weapons, diversions and patience to outwit the enemy or you can play it on easy and run-and-gun, but the latter doesn't work often and why would you want to anyway? The stealth is statisfying but you don't have the ability to do much in the way of interesting tactics. The interactions you are given throughout missions are good but they can be hard to find sometime, I spent ages trying to work out how to get passed a party of german officers only to find that the plumbing had to the solution.
Good points:
-A Completely solid game, I have had no problems with running it and the aesthetic and the gameplay complement each other perfectly (although the art direction is nothing to write home about- but the normal 'trying for realism' graphics suite it well).
- Authentic levels, objectives, weapons, uniform (there is disguises in the game).
-Up to you in how you complete the mission, big level design with choices of which way to go and what you do and (I think) sometimes even say.
Bad points:
-Lack of direction, doesn't really tell you the options you have to complete missions, and figuring it out as you go along on harder difficulties ends in death.
-Boring mission objectives (Blow A up, kill B officer, find C secret documents - very cliche)

If it's on sale, definitely.  If not, perhaps watch some gameplay before you buy, just so you know what you are getting.
There's a lot wrong with the game.  The story trys to be serious and fails, the voice acting is meh, and the climatic battle at the end of the game ends up being rather underwhelming.
However, the combat is fun, the scenery not only looks great but is creatively designed, and there are some really cool ideas on display.  But my favorite thing about the game is how well is sets up players for success, rather than failure.  The mechanics are well-explained, the pause combos are marked with a visual cue that takes the guess work out of learning and using them, frequent checkpoints, boss fights are their own level so you never have to slog through a dungeon just for the priviledge of trying to beat the boss again.
You can skip the cutscenes, even on the first playthrough, and after you beat the game a mode called Bloody Palace becomes available, which is just the fun parts--combat.  So that's nice.
One final word: this is a reboot of the Devil May Cry series.  I gather that fans of the original games aren't too fond of this one.  I'm not sure of the specific reasons beyond the games obvious flaws as I never got into the other games. Perhaps the combat changed significantly, perhaps the character redesigns were just too much for the established fan base, maybe the plots of the original games weren't nearly as bad as this one...I really don't know.  I only mention this because if you, like me, didn't play the original games, it's important to separate genuine problems with the game with problems established fans have.  Not that their issues are small.  Lord knows I've panned games for lesser sins than they list, but the reasons simply don't apply to me as a non-fan, so perhaps they don't apply to you either.

I originally groaned when I heard they were going to remake the Devil May Cry series from the glorious old PS2 days, it was a case of if its not broke don't fix it. A few people however recommended it to me and I finally relented. I have to say, I am very very surprised. The gameplay is really good and I mean really good, it makes an almost seamless blend of cinematic experience and gameplay, the environments can really pop out at you, there is some seriously good level design here. That's even before talking about the combat, which is electrifying and addictive. The way of blending between weapons and styles is amazingly well done, switching out to three different weapons in a single three button combo is completely do-able, however I never managed to pull of using all 5 weapons in a single stream, that takes some practice. The let down is that there are rarely any moments in the game that really challenge you in terms of combat, they made Dante a powerhouse while leaving the demons a little wanting, which makes the game a little too easy at times. The final boss was more of a cinematic delight rather than the gritty battle I was really hoping for. The story is a bit loose and there were a few moments that made me roll my eyes but it serves the purpose of stringing the hack'n'slash together. The style of story telling is intriguing, much more so than the story itself, this is Capcom so you do have to take it with a pinch of salt. All in all I really enjoyed the new Dante and the series reboot, they got so much right, it's stable, fast, fun and great to play. I think what turns most people away is that £30.00 price tag when it is coming up to its second birthday.

A hidden gem of not only 2017, but for Shoot 'em Up fans everywhere in my opinion!
4 out of 5
PROS: A well balanced, yet challenging shmup. Banging music. Great arcade-y and charming look. A small, yet diverse enough array of pick-ups to combine and use at your disposal that offer some imaginative use. Specials that can get you out of a sticky situation. Unlockable characters (tanks) with different playstyles. Boss Training Room (a mode I find necessary for Shmups), and difficulty mods to increase the challenge this game has to offer. Also, it has a rewarding level up system where you get permanent upgrades to your tank(s). Such as triple shot, a spread shot pattern, and depending on what tank you are using, specific artillery adhering to the characters play style.
CONS (but mainly personal gripes [which may sound more like nitpicking due to the fact that is nothing seriously wrong with the game]: If, and WHEN you die the music repeats (of course), yet it feels (or more accurately: sounds) as if it is looping. It gets irritating real quick. But, hey! Don't die and no problem whatsoever lol. Some hit boxes need to be adjusted immediately, though. The biggest one, and the most glaring is the radioactive goo/slime/acid/whatever you call the green substance on the floor! You could be a decent pace away from riding onto the green goo yet still take damage as if you stepped your little tank feet onto the goop. It is a run ruiner that also is a big issue that needs to be addressed especially since this is also a side scroller where perspective and perception mean life and death!
Another issue is that when there is too much of ANYTHING on the screen you just cannot see hits coming. Which, I know is the norm in shmups, BUT, when you are firing nonstop wiht lasers and flamethrowers AND the enemies have the same colors/palettes as their projectiles and/or background/level, well things just feel unfair and feel like complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t because you cannot bloody see! In moments like this in the game, where they are apparent, it feels like you need to use the specials you acquire just to be in the safe side of the temporary fray, to avoid unwarranted damage.
And speaking of specials. They are a mixed bag, or just too situational to depend upon. You have three specials to toy around with. Which are the Flame Thrower. An attack where a huge fire-y hitbox covers the right side of the screen doing acceptable damage to all enemies inside the parameter. The second being a Tesla Lighting Shocker (of sorts). Which goes out a into a large "V" shape arc doing respectable damage to foes caught in the sight of it. Finally, the third is a Homing Missle Barrage that barrages onto enemies that it locks on too. Now, the specials are all fine and dandy, but due to the fact that they take way too long to charge, and picking up more special ammo tends to rotate to the latest pick-up means that you will hardly use them when they are needed most. The ammo for the specials are abundant, yet their situational behaviors and long cooldown kind of hold them back from being more of an aid in the mix of things. This could have been treated more fairly, if not, just been designed better off if you could rotate between ready-to-use specials manually. Giving more choice when planning a repeated run. But, regardless the specials due not make or break the core gameplay since you can defeat the game without using specials.
THE MAIN ISSUE is the green goop of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t hitbox detection, and the times when it seems as if you can dodge a projectile only for the games perspective and/or perception of invisible walls (edges of the screen) ♥♥♥♥ you over, and you end up getting hit regardless. Plus, the final boss is too much of a bullet sponge. Who, on its first phase relies heavily on the damn ♥♥♥♥ing hazards, its size that covers the whole right side of the screen, and has random starting attack patterns that sometimes come out seemingly on the first frame when in the middle of exchanging projectile. It's second phase is alright. Still could end up being tough for you, but it is handled fine.
ALL IN ALL. These "cons" are more like personal gripes and are minor fixes that can improve the game, yet as Lil' Tanks is right now, it's balanced, fair, and fun! To be honest, these minor problems can fixed by minor changes. Such as adding an extra THIRD heart (hit point) to even things out more fairly. Or, adding a separate shield for each of the two hearts. Giving more of a reward to those players who are more evasive and better reflexed.

P.S.
I found a potential GAME BREAKING BUG/EXPLOIT that makes the final boss, if not, the entire game so much more easier and trivial. Instead of pressing and holding down on the attack button like you normally do in shmups, you can repeatedly mash in a quick rhythm which spouts out your attacks at such a fast(er) rate that it ends up dealing what seems to be (at least) double the damage at twice, if not, thrice the normal rate of just holding down the attack button! It's super fun. And it works best with your tank fully upgraded while using the Flame Thrower as your primary fire. BUT, it works with all weapon pick ups, so you can choose how you want to use the exploit/bug. :)

Lil Tanks is a retro-styled shoot-em-up. You control a tank and his smaller assistant and try to singlehandedly repel an alien invasion. One of the innovative things about the game is the small assistant that also shoots and follows you. Its movement is comparable to movement in a snake game: the head moves, the tail follows in its track.
•	Nicely drawn enemies / backgrounds, the game has its own visual style
•	Intense gameplay, a lot of things are going on at the same time
•	Difficult, challenging
•	Good music / solid sounds
•	Four different tanks that can be levelled up, eventually increasing in power. Each has special ability that can be used to your advantage
•	Different enemies with different movement patterns
•	Only 3 different bonus weapons, not much variety bonus-wise
•	Level 6 deserves an extra mention: drive for >1 minute almost without enemies
•	Enemies do not spawn randomly, but bonuses do: especially on level 5, your fate is decided by random: if you get flamethrower bonus in the beginning on the round, you’ll probably do much better than if you get it at the end
I’ve played for ~4 hours and got to level 6 (I did not complete it, but as I understand, this is the last one). I’ve beat 4 levels on hardcore mode before that, but the 5th was just too overwhelming and it felt more frustrating than rewarding. I still say the game is good, but with 6 levels I honestly did not feel like it has enough content to justify $9.99 price. I’d suggest waiting for 50% discount.

If you enjoy The Chinese Room's other works, particularly Dear Esther, this holds a lot of parallels in both style and substance.
There are no puzzles, and interactivity is sparse. The environment is, however, beautiful to look at, and very authentic of a little country town in Shropshire. The voice acting is superb, not once did I find weak dialogue, and there is a lot of it. The music is also very nice and fitting for the setting and atmosphere, even if you're not in to "choir music" as it were, it really adds to the feel the developers were trying to give.
You wander around from area to area, with each area being open for you to explore, discovering phones, radios, and "ghosts" that reveal more about the story of what happened leading up to the "event". It's very very character focused, so if you're not the kind of person who gets invested in characters and people, you probably won't enjoy this. I DO recommend turning on subtitles though, as it tells you who is speaking, as there's not really any visual indicator as to who is who, unless you can easily differentiate between voices.
Overall, I enjoyed my experience, even if the pace was a little too slow (also, unskippable credits AAARGH). There is a "run" button, and it builds up over a few seconds, but even that feels slow, and sometimes it just doesn't work at all.
In short, did you like Dear Esther? Yes? You will probably like this. No? Turn away, we don't need another person whining on the forums because they didn't know what they were buying.
FINAL NOTE: If you are having performance issues, run Steam in Big Picture mode. It's weird I know, but it worked for me.

The Fall of Max Payne is one of those games that has pitch perfect writing. Sam Lake is a god amongst video game writers. What it comes down to is Max's inner monologues that subdue the player into escaping reality and entering the stark world of Max Payne.
Taking place two years after the events of the first masterpiece, Max Payne has been reinstated into the NYPD and is on the case of a group of hitmen that dress up as a cleaning crew. Max follows their trail while uncovering a conspiracy involving the Inner Circle, corrupt politicians, and dirty cops. Mona Sax reemerges early in the game, surviving her apparent death after getting shot in the head in the first one. She's on the run from the police but works with Max as they have similar goals.

The fall of Max Payne is that he falls in love with Mona Sax, he can't bring himself to turn her in or fight her; which makes the game a film noir love story (as stated on the iconic cover art).
The gameplay is very similar to the first one, why fix something that isn't broken, right? But the graphics are substantially better, Max's face doesn't look like a distorted Sam Lake and the models are certainly more polyganyl. The nightmare scenes are easier but still kinda crazy. And the music, the music is SO good. I would at times just pause the game and let the music play in the menu while getting some water or pop.

Ori and the Blind Forest is a beautiful and immersive game. The graphics, storytelling, gameplay, controls, and responsiveness are all top notch. I love how this game progresses. As you make your way through the game, you learn new abilities that allow you to interact with enemies and your environment in many different ways. These abilities also allow you to unlock items and parts of the map that were previously inaccessible, so there's always something new to find in old areas of the map. Though this game does feel like a fairytale, the gameplay is most definitely not a cakewalk. There is plenty of challenge to be had in the world of Ori and the Blind Forest. Some situations require you to be on your toes at all times, utilizing all of the different moves that you have learned throughout the game. I would definitely recommend this to anyone who wants to enjoy a beautifully designed and executed platformer.

Pirson Architect well to start off I've been with this game since the early alpha days and as such I've seen this game go throw many phases that bring us here. So the game as is, is a really well made prison simmulator of what a prison would be like if you built one in your design. Now this is not saying this is how it would excactly work in real life as let's face it humans are a bit unpredictable at times and can break any boundry we or just about anything sets for us. But we aren't talking about humans we are talking about AI driven prisoners that have two goals programmed into them. One keep their needs up, and two escape the prison. And once you know that you can use those to goals and exploit your prisoners for your own gain more or less.
Now some problems the game suffers from. 1 the more prisoners you get the harder it becomes for the game to run as you will noticed as your prison grows you frames seem to steadly drop as well, unless you got a god PC. 2 the game still has certain assits that have no use in game, one example of this is posion as you can pick it up but you can't use it for anything. 3 the economy is 90% done, as from the stand point of the warden the economy is just fine as for the prisoner AI's can trade with each other no problem but when you the player decide to join your prisoners you will find out you can't really trade with anyone but you can just drop items and wait for a near buy prisoner or guard to pick it up and use it later. 4 Players really can't create a gang all that well and for sure don't have as much control over unites like AI drive gangs do, yea I know you can recuit prisoners into a crew/squad but that's not the same as a gang where you have no limits on how many members you have or being able to order prisoners to do out and capture prison territory or pick fights with other prisoners why you stay out of the fight.
Now I know that's a lot of negitives but trust me they are only minnor problems and theres a lot more to the game as you can easily mod it or even make the mods yourself as it's fairly simple programming.
I hope this review has help you in some way or another and thank you for your time. Now have a nice day.

Much like a rainy day in Yorkshire, this game is beautiful, has quirky accents but is ultimately dull.  The point of a 'walking simulator' is to tell a story, and often to feel involved and attached to the person you play as.  In this game you play as no person. I feel in this game I learned of a lot of characters but none in any meaningful way, more just a bit of gossip about each stretched thinly over 4-5 hours of... what I resent to call gameplay.  The whole plot is understood rather quickly, in the first hour or so of the game, and then you're just left running around like a headless chicken trying to find more dialogue so you can unlock the next bit and progress.  Much like an archivist looking through old reels of tape taken by some videographer to try and get a grasp at what happened in a time; this game ultimately feels like work.  Disappointingly the only vaguely interesting bit about the story is never really explained. Here is the interesting part of the story summarised: "There are two scientists at an observatory, who discovered a thing in space, and then it did stuff to yourkshire people". That thing is never explained as to what it is, its backstory is never shown, the games secrets are ultimately never revealed.  I can only reccomend this game if you want to take a stroll around a pretty, virtual, lifeless but lived in Yorkshre. If you're looking for more than scenery I suggest you look elsewhere, such as the Life is Strange games, or Firewatch; much better entertainment value.

Everybody's Gone to the Rapture is a (very) slow game, but one that is thoughtful and with a surprising amount of depth.
Growing up in a village in England, I found the game's setting of Yaughton to be immediately familiar, the entire experience is exactly like wandering through a real old English village. The visuals are not state-of-the-art, but they certainly do a good job of making Yaughton feel like a real town, and the writing and voice acting peoples it with a cast of engaging characters. As you wander around, following 'guiding lights' you discover certain points of interest, scenes which play out with ghostly echoes of events that happened before. This forms a non-linear narrative, where you wander through the valley slowly piecing together the ways in which the lives intertwined and how things played out during a mysterious apocalypse.
The game surprised me in that the premise is laid out almost entirely before you in the opening area of the game. There is little twist or deviation from this, but instead you learn more and more about the people, their actions and histories and conflicts and desires. It is a sci-fi story with a very grounded, very human heart. It shows you a community, and whilst the plot doesn't exactly twist and turn, becoming familiar with the stories of these folks is definitely engaging. They are all brilliantly voice-acted, too.
For all that I enjoyed Everybody's Gone to the Rapture, I must explain that this isn't a game that respects your time. I should state that I'm a very patient person, and a big fan of 'walking simulators', but I found myself feeling frustrated at the slowness of the movement speed. There is a 'sprint' button, which it took me a little while to work out actually only kicks in a few seconds after you've held it down, and then it only increases your speed marginally. I would consider this 'sprint' speed to be too slow for base movement, let alone the maximum speed. On top of this, the game continually slows your movement speed even further (to a very deliberately painful crawl) at certain sections, presumably for dramatic effect, which again results in frustration. Additionally, once you have beaten the game there is no way to skip the credits or bring up the menu (I watch credits anyway, but again, the game felt it wasn't being sparing with your time).
Another testament to this is the achievements...
'Passive observer' - Do nothing for five minutes.
'Last Orders' - Wait in the two pubs in the game for three minutes each.
'Wrong Number' - In the first phone booth in the game, enter it, close the door, and wait three minutes.
'Perpetual Motion' - Stand on a children's playground ride for two minutes.
Now, I'm not an achievement hunter, but these seem a bit random and mean-spirited to me, there are other things they could easily have implemented rather than 'go here and stand still for [X] minutes'. Not ultimately important, but I think it does show the lack of respect for your time that the game seems to have.
Additionally, the guiding lights in the first section of the game felt like they were pulling me all over the village, and often moved too fast for me to catch up to (further infuriating the issue of movement speeds), and it took me a few 'sections' of the game to get to grips with what is essentially the core mechanic (discover minor plot points around an area, before moving in for a larger 'central' plot point to play out, then be guided to the next area). I felt this settled down in later areas, but still occasionally found the guiding lights frustrating... They would occasionally double back on themselves whilst I was following them, and sometimes just hover somewhere, whilst I was unable to find any point of interest nearby. Exploration is fun, but with the movement speed being so slow, the idea of quickly checking down a side-street before going into a building, etc becomes more of a chore than a pleasure. The world is beautifully rendered, I just wish the game let me explore it at my own pace (which is, a little faster, but more thoroughly).
So, for all its faults, Everybody's Gone to the Rapture is a very, very slow game, one with a premise that is laid out before you almost immediately, but one that has a lot of heart, and explores its theme thoroughly. I became very invested in the lives of the villagers, and seeing how their stories played out and what fate they came to was engrossing. The game has several ways to interpret it's endings and themes, and I found it interesting to read up discussions afterwards. Very engrossing, just be aware that it does require patience.

This game is brilliant and just what I have been waiting for. Why?
Preamble:
Well for the longest time now, I (and my gameward comrades) have been waiting for something quick and fun to play rather than Rocket League, now don't get me wrong, I frickin love Rocket League, but its been quite a while now of endlessly smashing the ball about and arguing about whos going to stay in the goal, so to have something to pour some time into which isnt over in 5 minutes comes as a welcome relief, I think in the Astoneer we may have found a lump of gold!
Why:
Firstly, it is very visually stimulating, the graphics are balanced just right between cutesy and practical and this lends to the fun Gameplay. Its not quite "visually stunning", but goes a good way towards being fully convincing and is sufficiently pretty to keep you fully engaged, from standing on a plato and viewing the vast valley below and gazing up at the stars and other to be explored planets above, to wandering deep into the depths of the "earth" within the vast cave systems, the visuals are pretty dam good and do a great job of conveying the experience of what its like to be alone on a atmoshereless planet, although any of those in doubt about the visuals should bear in mind that the strengths of this game lie within the intoxicating good gameplay.
The Gameplay is great (did i mention it was fun?), just the right balance between quizzical and testing that lends to extended periods into the early hours for "just got to do this first, then i will definately, definately, go to bed". The bulk of which will be exploring, which there is an exuberant amount of in order to progress and which is fun and interesting.
The games progression rate is very well balanced in my view, from the early days of locating compounds next to your base in "Eureka" style moments from which you then learn to craft new buildings and facilities. This progress inevitably encourages the desire for "more stuff" and generally gravitates towards the production of far reaching air/power lines around the "local" area in order to facilitate more efficient collecting of a sufficient amount of materials to fabricate indeed more machines is very rewarding and the sandbox nature allows you to progress at your chosen rate and doesn't force anything onto the player. Inevitably you will end up collecting enough resources to produce that mobile lander you wanted from the start and it will seem great, but then you realise it needs more storage, you need a trailer!! - (out you go again!) Then additional vehicle tools to help harvest the resources (I will go to bed in a minute.....) you will be absorbed with the conquest of land and apparent never ending requirement for more resources, the great thing is, these are fun to collect and look for and is the essence of the game.
Playing single player is great and you can achieve all the things you need on your own, however if you have a couple of buddies and if you can get a team of you working together then this quickly ramps up the progression speed and the enjoyment factor another couple of notches (understatement detected!).

I hate Counter-Strike: GO. Now, the reason I led with this is because it's true (more on that later). However, that doesn't necessarily mean that CSGO is a bad game. Admittedly, it's a fantastic game with almost 6 years of polish from a dedicated team of devs. The gunplay is absoultely fantastic, centering around controlling your accuracy, which is impacted by movemnt, firing pattern and many other factors. The big difference between a game like CSGO and, say, Call of Duty is the gunplay. Where, in CoD, you aim down the sights, always stay on the move at top speed, and where accuracy isn't really a concern, in CSGO, you won't get anywhere without focusing on your accuracy and aiming down the sights only works with a few guns (those being mid-ranged ARs and snipers). And with movement, you want to move as slow as possible most of the time so that you can actually hit anything.
The one thing that really stood out to me about this game was how balanced it was. Despite some assymetric elements, it's possibly the most balanced competitive game I have ever played. The main gamemode is bomb defusal, where you can play as either the terrorists, who are tasked with planting a bomb at one of two bombsites and/or killing as many CTs as you can, and the counter-terrorists, who are tasked with splitting their team and defending both bombsites, in an effort to stop the terrorists from planting their bomb or, failing that, defuse the bomb before it detonates.
The maps are extremey well designed. Most competitive players actually memorise entire maps and callouts for landmarks in said maps just to communicte efficiently with their teammates and gain a strategical advantage. In fact, many of the maps are quite memorable (like Dust 2, Inferno and Cache).
Now, I led with the statement that I hate this game, yet, after all of the praise, I've given it, you may be wondering why. Well, the game is fantastic, but the few flaws it has are pretty big. First off, the dev team, like the rest of Valve, it seems, have recently been making some pretty poor decisions and major slip ups (like the launch of the R9 revolver). Additionally, the game has been undergoing a few changes to the balance between the two teams and weapon stats lately, which has thrown the balance off a little. But, this can be forgiven, to a certain extent. My biggest problem with CSGO lies not in the game itself, but the community. The casual subcommunity can only be described as a throbbing brain tumour, the competitive community, while nice and friendly, are also far too competitive for my liking (most people chalk this up to me being bad at the game, although, I'm actually pretty decent. I just prefer less competitive environments), and in any other gamemode, it's just one great big ♥♥♥♥♥how.
So, despite being an amazing game, I was put off CSGO by those things. Also, the game itself just isn't really my cup of tea, however I certainly recommend it to everyone. It can be a lot of fun and despite being not my kind of game, it certainly shone when I was playing with friends and having a gay old time.

Pros:
- Good sized open world that's easier to traverse thanks to Batwing fast-travel points
- Many locations previously unseen: Gotham City proper, the Batcave, Wayne Manor, Blackgate Prison, "Arkham City" BEFORE it's urban decay, the GCPD, etc
- Solid cast of characters we haven't seen, nor heard of in the past two titles (Deathstroke, Copperhead, Firefly, Shiva, Anarky, etc)
- Enjoyable, challenging "boss" battles
Cons:
- No real serious improvements in regards to gadgets, enemy types, or other basic gameplay elements
- Combat is less fluid and responsive than Arkham City
- Conroy (Batman) and Hamill's (Joker) talents are missed but their replacements aren't bad
- Traversing the world is easier but there are still some areas that are unnecessarily hard to get to
- Technical issues
- Lower quality cut-scenes
- Story starts strong but falls apart and becomes erratic by the mid-point
The Bottom Line:
Many write Origins off as a bad game due to the simple fact that Rocksteady wasn't at the helm. Granted, perhaps if they had developed this game we would've gotten more improvements and new gameplay elements but WB Montreal didn't do a poor job with emulating the basic structures and aspects of the Batman: Arkham franchise.
However its that lack of anything entirely new and game-changing that makes Origins one of the weaker installments in the franchise. Combat is much the same as Arkham City save for a little less fluidity and responsiveness, the gadgets are either exactly the same or are different looking but serve the same purposes, and the open world is larger but still relatively empty except for roving groups of enemies.
All-in-all, the only "new" ideas Origins brought to the table were the "martial artist" enemy type, fast travel points, more boss battle engagements, and the crime scene/detective-mode investigations (the latter being good enough to appear again in Arkham Knight to some degree).
For me though what holds Origins from being a favorite is the story. It's not a bad story, I actually liked the idea of Blask Mask putting out this bounty on Batman and having eight different villains/assassins come after you. Yet, this plot gets abandoned only a couple hours into the game and suddenly the antagonist changes two or three times and the remaining 75% of the story just feels like a series of side missions that you play one after another. It loses focus and thus any kind of consistency, pacing, or enjoyable resolution/climax.
So while Origins certainly isn't the best of the Arkham series it really isn't as bad as some would have you believe. It's enjoyable for numerous reasons - most stemming from the never before seen characters/locations and intense boss battles. Definitely a must-play for Batman fans.

In my opinion, this is the best Max Payne game of the series, and it holds up surprisingly well given its age. Released alongside titles such as Call of Duty, Beyond Good and Evil, and Knights of the Old Republic, Max Payne 2 suffered the same issue as Psychonauts: a great game with great reviews, although nobody bought it.
The gameplay and gun mechanics are only really comparable to the original Max Payne (another great game that has aged well), except they're much tighter and more refined. The infamous Bullet Time ability works quite well here, and the shoot-dodging mechanic is almost perfected. The weapons all work fairly well, although the pistols and shotguns become a little too situational to be practical at the end of the game.
The story itself is fairly cut and dry, although the Noir comicbook style of storytelling gives the game it's real charm. Unlike the first Max Payne, the comicbook segments are intercut with cutscenes which serve only to enhance the overall experience. The gameplay has enough variety to remain fairly fresh through its runtime, including pseudo-escort missions which don't actually suck.
The biggest criticism this game received was its short length, and, too be fair, that's not too far off the mark. In comparison to the original game, this one is certainly shorter, although this has the added benefit of substantial pacing. The environments are varied enough to be quite distinct (an attribute many modern games can't compare to), and the comparatively shorter length helps make this game an easy pill to swallow.
To anyone interested in the Max Payne series (and, if you like artistic games, well crafted single player storytelling, or fine-tuned slow-mo gun battles you should be), this is the crown jewel, although this game can be best appreciated after a playthrough of the original game for context and a better understanding of how this game's engine improved significantly in two years. The third installment, Max Payne 3, is certainly fun in its own right as well, although, with so many little things changed, altered, and tweaked, it simply doesn't give as good of an appreciation of the Max Payne franchise that this game can provide.

At first, I liked this game.  The initial area you visit is fairly small with the story events close together.  As the game stretches out throughout its story, the areas become larger.  It becomes easy to miss events or stories.  The walking/jogging speed you read about is true - it is far too slow.  Yes, there are mods you can use to increase it, but the game had so much potential that was ruined by the slow movement speed.  The developers have stated this was a design choice so a running player didn't mistakenly trigger a proximity trigger for a clue or portion of the story.  This could've been easily remedied by having a button to press to allow the encounter.  There is already a mini-game for the major story events.  By the time I reached the ending areas of the game, I stopped caring about the story and just wanted to finish the game, I wanted to go back and re-explore areas, maybe even play it a second time. This game seeks to achieve an interesting narrative, however because of poor game design it fails greatly.
I really tried to like this game, but can't recommend it in any way.
My reasoning:
-The walking speed is ATROCIOUSLY slow. There is a hidden sprint button, but you still run extremely slow. This makes exploration tedious, and not fun. If you get lost, you'll waste your time walking around at an aggravatingly slow speed. It's a walking simulator with a terrible implementation of walking.... I can't recommend this game on any mechanical level.
-The fragmented nature of the story made me miss critical plot points. I felt so discouraged from exploration due to the walking speed, I missed critical plot details and often found myself confused with what's going on.
-There is barely any character introduction, and it's extremely ambiguous who is talking. Everyone is a particle system and not a human being, You NEED to use subtitles, otherwise it's impossible to tell who is who. It was very hard to engage with the characters, and I often was dismissive of the dialogue all together.
-The technical performance is pretty bad. There is constant stuttering, and what seems like frame rate drops. I have a 1080Ti, I should not be experiencing these issues.
There are much better games in this genre, like What Remains of Edith Finch. Go play that instead.

(NB - paid £3.99 in sale)
No gameplay at all. You just walk, and find radios, phones and incident spots, and hit a button to witness fragments of the story. There is a cruel "move faster" button, which barely allows you to move faster than the game's standard crawl. EGTTR has a major flaw in that it virtually punishes you for being interested in it; because the designers did not know if you would visit every story beat, the diligent player will end up being exposed to scenes that cover the same details in a different form. And if you take a diversion to see if there's something down a road, you do so knowing it's going to be a long haul to bring you back again. So, it can become boring, and you have to be a person who doesn't mind being bored.
But it's incredibly beautiful, and that's the selling point. If you like good game soundtracks, EGTTR has one of the very best. If you like beautiful graphics, and have a beefy GPU, EGTTR offers a beautiful depiction of a 1980s Shropshire village and the surrounding countryside. If you're the kind of person who slows down in games to see the way reflection effects play on a rain-soaked road, or who intentionally looks up to see the light beams scatter through tree leaves, you'll love this. If you run past for the next thing to shoot, you'll hate it (and you won't get to shoot anything. Sorry). If you have the patience to listen to British radio plays, this is a very well acted little drama which eventually reveals a bigger point (if you join the dots are figure out the meaning behind all of this). That's a lot of ifs, but it worked for me.
TL:DR - The Archers: Apocalypse.

Sort of an upgrade from Dear Esther, and the fact that you can open doors and interact with with objects does not put it in the walking simulator category anymore, in my opinion. The slow movement also encourages you to look around and enjoy the scenery and beauty of the CryEngine. The game looks very good graphics wise. The full playthrough will take a lot more, played it once, and I still have yet to figure out the story completely, because you can miss some dialogue. The score is great, well done to Jess and of course, the very Rob Briscoe scenes with darkness and lights, just like the caves in Dear Esther.
Now performance wise, this game is a port, runs pretty poorly, appears to be very GPU intensive, keeps steady console fps (that's 30, in some cases had drops to 15).
Can recommend it to adventure game players, but this is very slow, it's more like you exploring the world slowly, getting an idea of the story from different viewpoints listening to characters. You can't change the outcome, it's like a book, just in 3D. Never seen such story telling "through light", no models, no characters technically appear in the game, only light and their voice, which creates a unique atmosphere, it might even scare you or creep you out at some parts, because you hear conversations, but nobody's there.
In the end, everybody goes to the rapture, and no matter how sad the story may be, it's a happy ending.

When I first purchased this game, I did not understand what kind of game it was.  At first, I thought it was a classic platforming game, but I quickly learned it actually is a Throw-Your-Controller-Simulator.  Upon learning that this was the kind of game it was, I excelled at it and began throwing my controller constantly and must say that this is my favorite Throw-Your-Controller-Simulator our there.  Sometimes the throwing seems so real I feel like I threw it in real life.
You may also notice that there are no expansion packs, no addons, no DLC, nothing else that is needed for this game.  That, however, is misleading.  Do not be tricked by the low price tag, it really is as expensive as some of the most expensive games on Steam, almost as expensive as Train Simulator.  The addons for this game are actually back-up controllers needed to keep you going.  After purchasing 17 controllers from various systems, I was ready to play this game.
The reason this game is so expensive is because the big guys in video game consols, Sony and Microsoft, were not satisfied with simply taking everyone's money from their consol sales.  They needed more controller sales, so they commisioned the creator of this game to create Super Meat Boy.  After many attempts, the creator knew the game was perfect when he turned all his friends insane after playing this game.  He submitted it to Sony and Microsoft, but neither one would take it on account that the game is too evil and they would get sued by everyone for creating a game that turned all their customers insane.  So the creator simply published it himself and this was the result.
Note that this game is not without educational value as well.  Several of the lessons learned from this game include keeping maggots away from meat, being environmentally friendly, and teaches the dangers of nuclear weapons.  Also, after my 352 death on the final boss I discovered that this game demonstrates what the inside of a butcher's shop looks like, so it is a wonderful game for any children desiring to be butchers.
This game also taught me that the guy doesn't always get the girl.  If the villain is desperate enough to create ominous death traps to keep Bandage Girl from Meat Boy, who am I as  Meat Boy to take Bandage Girl away from someone that cares that much for her?   Obviously Dr. Fetus would take much better care of Bandage Girl than anything that I could do, which is the reason that I quit at the final boss and left Dr. Fetus to take care of her
In conclusion, while this game may be quite expensive, it still is one of the best Throw-Your-Controller-Simulators I have ever played and provides a wonderful educational experience about life, how a butcher shop looks, and if a fetus with a Ph.D. steals your girl, who are you to argue with a fetus with a Ph.D. who controls the saw blade industry on who can take better care of her?  I give this game a 10 out of 10 for sending me to a mental institution.

APB Reloaded seems to be a good idea on paper. What is that idea? Make an online multiplayer game that somewhat seems to be based off of GTA. Does this idea work? I'd say it's a tad mix of both "yes" and "no".
To begin, you can choose from two "factions" and these are the criminals and the police. The criminals commit crimes and work together to cause as much chaos as possible. These can be as simple as stealing a car and ramming over many pedestrians or working together to rob stores and escape. Eventually, you will cause enough trouble and then you will become a target for the cops (who happen to be controlled by other players). While creating chaos can be fun, I found myself working alone and seeing many other criminal players doing the same thing. I hardly saw two criminals working together during my playtime. Being a target for the cops isn't much fun either as the main goal for the cops seemed to be just finding you and killing you. They don't try to arrest you or anything of the sort; they just chase you and bring you down with bullets. After you die, you just respawn and do it all over again. There are some sort of missions in the game but I wasn't given the slightest clue to where they were. I found a suitcase and was told to deliver it to some location but don't expect the map to get you anywhere as it wasn't much for help.
After derping around with the criminal faction I played the cop faction. Problem is, I found difficulty in even finding my way out of the spawn area and, as stated before, the map isn't much for help. My best guess is that the cop faction patrols the city area and is given a list of target criminals to find and gun down.
Here's a short list of pros and cons that include some points that were not covered:
+ Vehicles handle differently in an appropiate manner
+ Graphics look fairly good
+ Creating chaos is enjoyable
+ Fair amount of character and vehicle customization
+ Basic free roaming is entertaining
- Map is hard to deal with
- Difficult to find missions
- Little teamwork
- Slight lag issues
- Police only shoot down criminals
- Community is known to be a little less than friendly
Eventually the confusion and constant deaths bored me and I can't recommend this game to anyone. It'll be nice to uninstall this game to make room for a more deserving one.

It's a simple formula: Create an open world, create well thought out mechanics and make them work, listen to the community to make game better after release, add mod support. That way, you'll earn so much goodwill that people will even buy your skin DLCs.
This is the reason ETS2 is the most played game in my library for the last year and I don't see myself getting bored in the near future. Why?
* It's relaxing. This isn't a racing game. You go at your own pace, watching beautiful sceneries.
* It's addictive. You set yourself small goals and try to achieve them. They're your goals, your victories.
* It works. Game is still supported after almost 4 years and bugs are mostly dealt with. Core mechanics like GPS are almost flawless, even with mods.
* Mods. Did I mention mods? Every aspect of the game is moddable.
I would be happier with a more efficient, DX11 engine (dev says it's in the works) but still, I don't regret a cent I spent on this game. If you enjoy driving, you'll love ETS2.

Eidolon is an odd one. When I first played it, I had zero clue what was going on, and kept wandering around, picking up random objects and documents on the way. I caught a fish and got ill because I ate it raw. I broke a leg falling off a cliff. I almost drowned crossing a river, and then I died all the way when I approached a wolf. The good bit was that I didn't have to restart the game; the bad was that I woke up in a completely unknown place, and then got completely and totally lost. It was not a fun experience, and I stopped playing for a while, but the documents I found were intriguing and I eventually came back. I started a new game, made sure to avoid wildlife, and started using 'show me where the nearest document is' button a bit more deliberately.
Once I really got into it, Eidolon was an absolute joy. Was it slow from time to time? Sure, and the hiking was a bit of a drag every now and then. But the experience of finding all of the documents and slowly piecing the story together was absolutely worth it. The atmosphere of the game is amazing and I found it incredibly relaxing, while at the same time I felt compelled to find every last fragment of the lost civilisation. For people who like story-driven games, this is one that I would absolutely recommend. However, the survival aspect, while interesting, can get really problematic, shifting the focus from the story to survival, which quickly gets tedious. So make sure to avoid cliffs, bears, and other dangers.

I was on the fence whether to recommend, but decided yes because, for a Walking Simulator, it does some things right:
- It actually has an ending (though not entirely expanded on, it isn't a visually-pleasing cop-out like usual)
- It has a 'sprint' button (though more of a 'walk briskly' button that ideally could've been faster)
- A unique setting. Who needs another game in New York with its skyscrapers and traffic when you've got the ORIGINAL York with all that farmland, God-fearing and village gossip waiting to be utilised?
- It has some rather heinous Achievements that you couldn't get without specifically looking up a guide and following it, wasting days doing extra-tedious tasks for nothing, eventually teaching many the folly of Achievement hunting, showing they could've spent that time and aggro playing several fun and exciting games in their backlog instead and lead a happier life.
While, like generic Walking Simulators, still nothing happens, you don't meet anyone and the story is told via convenient audio diaries/visual space magic recreations, it at least avoids a couple of the usual complaints.
So if you like your Walking Simulators, get your fill in the West Country countryside, ooar.

When I first purchased this game, I did not understand what kind of game it was.  At first, I thought it was a classic platforming game, but I quickly learned it actually is a Throw-Your-Controller-Simulator.  Upon learning that this was the kind of game it was, I excelled at it and began throwing my controller constantly and must say that this is my favorite Throw-Your-Controller-Simulator our there.  Sometimes the throwing seems so real I feel like I threw it in real life.
You may also notice that there are no expansion packs, no addons, no DLC, nothing else that is needed for this game.  That, however, is misleading.  Do not be tricked by the low price tag, it really is as expensive as some of the most expensive games on Steam, almost as expensive as Train Simulator.  The addons for this game are actually back-up controllers needed to keep you going.  After purchasing 17 controllers from various systems, I was ready to play this game.
The reason this game is so expensive is because the big guys in video game consols, Sony and Microsoft, were not satisfied with simply taking everyone's money from their consol sales.  They needed more controller sales, so they commisioned the creator of this game to create Super Meat Boy.  After many attempts, the creator knew the game was perfect when he turned all his friends insane after playing this game.  He submitted it to Sony and Microsoft, but neither one would take it on account that the game is too evil and they would get sued by everyone for creating a game that turned all their customers insane.  So the creator simply published it himself and this was the result.
Note that this game is not without educational value as well.  Several of the lessons learned from this game include keeping maggots away from meat, being environmentally friendly, and teaches the dangers of nuclear weapons.  Also, after my 352 death on the final boss I discovered that this game demonstrates what the inside of a butcher's shop looks like, so it is a wonderful game for any children desiring to be butchers.
This game also taught me that the guy doesn't always get the girl.  If the villain is desperate enough to create ominous death traps to keep Bandage Girl from Meat Boy, who am I as  Meat Boy to take Bandage Girl away from someone that cares that much for her?   Obviously Dr. Fetus would take much better care of Bandage Girl than anything that I could do, which is the reason that I quit at the final boss and left Dr. Fetus to take care of her
In conclusion, while this game may be quite expensive, it still is one of the best Throw-Your-Controller-Simulators I have ever played and provides a wonderful educational experience about life, how a butcher shop looks, and if a fetus with a Ph.D. steals your girl, who are you to argue with a fetus with a Ph.D. who controls the saw blade industry on who can take better care of her?  I give this game a 10 out of 10 for sending me to a mental institution.

As much as I regret it, I cannot recommend this game. Which is such a shame, too, as most aspects about this game are simply amazing, or at least well above average. Let's break it down:
Graphics: 10/10
Simply put, the game is gorgeous. It's also animated well. It's a treat for the eyes. Ori has a lot of personality just in his or her animations for jumping. It's awesome. Almost as good as a Vanillaware game, better in some ways (dat water man).
Sound: 7.5/10
Soundtrack is good. Sound effects punch when they need to. The sound design is overall very excellent.
Story: 6/10
I only got about 5 hours into this, so I can't comment too much. The first 15 minutes were amazing, but it kinda goes slightly downhill after that. Basically devolving into "get the plot mcguffins for Plots McGufferson".
Controls: 6/10
At first, the controls seem very tight. Not like, Castlevania or Super Metroid tight, but pretty tight. But over time you will start to notice little things that nag at your shins in annoyance. Then they keep adding more and more and more movement buttons. By the time I quit my fingers were really starting to ache with how tired they were of trying to hit 4-5 buttons at once, and I was missing several movement abilities. They aren't the worst, but could use some improvement. Please condense your 5-6 movement buttons down based on context. Glide shouldn't be it's own button, make it to where holding the jump button after starting a descent activates it.
Worth mentioning is the fact that in game you can't rebind any buttons, and you can't disable your joysticks. You CAN pseudo remap buttons through a text file, but it's not done by function, but by button number. Also, prompts for Xbox controller only, with no option to swap to a dualshock button setup. Not unexpected, but it would've been nice to be able to choose. I used an arcade stick mainly anyway as it's easier to mash buttons on that as fast as you need to with the combat mechanics the way they are.
Gameplay: 3/10
Unfortunately, this is where the clear love and care that went into this game just wasn't put. The level design is not the worst ever, but not very good, for a host of reasons. Traps aren't well conveyed to the player, and the rules of the world change all the time. For example: Some spikes just do damage to you, some just kill you outright. Which are which? The only way to know is to fall on them. Even stranger, is there are a lot of non instant death spikes that are in places that you can't get out of anyway, making you just sit there getting hit repeatedly.
Having instant death traps in a metroidvania is pretty bad to begin with, too. But not only that there are often times when you must make a pure leap of faith to progress, only to usally fall on some instant death spikes with no warning.
The platforming is loose as heck, too. The jump arc isn't really clear, and feels pretty anemic to boot, despite this the game demands you make jumps that don't seem possible or require pixel perfect accuracy. Usually conquering such sections doesn't make me satisfied I completed a challenge, but often I ask "was I supposed to pass it like that?", that's how loose it is. Like a mid 2000s physics platformer.
How does the game compensate for all this? It lets you cast a spell to save anywhere. It costs resources for some reason, but eventually you get enough to save after every platforming room, which is what you end up having to do. This turns it from a metroidvania into one of those spike hell platformers, but with not tight enough control. Not fun.
With the save mechanic it's not really "hard", but it is quite annoying to play.
Another problem is conveyance. The game is really bad at letting the player know what does what and how you can use it. Spikes not doing consistent things have already been mentioned, but which walls you can jump on and which you can't is never clear, as are which platforms you can jump through the bottom in. One of the most terrible examples is at the end of a dungeon type zone, I cleansed the water in the game from poison, great right? It released a bunch of it. It then gave me control of the character without telling me, and literally in 3 seconds I died because suddenly that water damaged me. Turns out it's a chase sequence. With no warning, and no indication that the good thing I just released would kill me.
Basically this game becomes a trial and error by death platformer pretty quick. It's just not fun. And certainly not a good choice for a metroidvania game.
After all that you might wonder about the combat? Well, there is no strategy basically. You have a thing that flies with you and shoots when you press a button. It auto targets whatever it wants, so you just mash it while dodging very basic attacks. It's boring, has no depth, and a big missed opportunity.
Another problem is the upgrade mechanics. There are skill trees you can unlock upgrades in. Sounds cool right? Well, it's not bad, but I got several that didn't appear to do anything. They may have required abilities from later in the game, but I got them pretty early on.
Overall, I really really wanted to like this game, and was for awhile, but the platforming just kept getting worse and worse and it became not very fun. It wasn't even challenging, just a literal pain in the wrist to do.

No More Room in Hell is one of the best cooperative zombie survival games out there. The best part is that its free.
Based off of the Source Engine, No More Room in Hell will basically run on anything. I have mantained 60 FPS on a laptop not even meant for gaming, with the only thing I had to turn off being Anti Aliasing.
Though the game is not that graphically stunning, its gameplay makes up for that.
You and up to 7 other players have to either survive or complete a number of objectives. You will either hold a position as the shamblers make their slow approach to your temporary 'fort' or you will navigate through streets full of the walking, rotting corpses, deciding whether to blast your way through (the stupid way) or strafe around the slow ones and only waste bullets on the faster ones (the smart way).
Melee takes getting used to, but ultimately becomes incredibly satisfying, as you hold off small hordes with weapons such as a fire axe. You can charge up your swings for maximum damage or slash quickly instead.
Firearms aren't necessarily rare, but ammunition is. This game will teach you to not waste your bullets and to take your time aiming before you shoot. One wasted bullet could have taken out one or even more zombies. Guns like the Mac-10 and the MP5 have quite a kick to them and are both fully automatic, resulting in heavy ammo consumption. Not really ideal for a game focused on conserving your bullets and being accurate.
Overall, No More Room in Hell is the ideal, free, cooperative zombie survival game.
Oh, it also has a survival map that is an exact replica of the house from Night of the Living Dead (1968). THEY'RE COMING FOR YOU, BARBARA.

Beautiful, absorbing game... if you're patient and if you like walking simulators. Because you'll be doing a lot of walking in Eidolon.
It's not hard to figure out the basic gist of the game: walk around Western Washington and pick up little tidbits of information that paint the story of what happened to the world. It's post-apocalyptic but doesn't really feel like it in most places. It's like camping.
The key to enjoying Eidolon is to buy into the atmosphere and storyline. Explore! See what's over that hill over there. Learn, through trial and error, the limitations of your human form. Like it or not, this IS a survival game. Cold water will eventually kill you, as will starvation, disease from eating bad food, injuries, and wild animals. But none of those things are immediate-- it does take work or carelessness to "die" and even when you do, you respawn in a safe place. This is a great game to play when you have a lot of free time, because the more time you spend in this world, the more real it seems. I found myself getting genuinely frightened by a bear sighting and the sometimes-discordant music contributed to it, while other times I felt giddy because the weather and views were so astonishingly beautiful. I experienced several vivid dreams that brought me back to Eidolon's universe in sleep.
While I appreciated the variety of the fragments, the sheer number of them made it hard for me to follow a cohesive storyline and eventually I got frustrated. For me, some fragments were impossible to reach without "cheating." A simple code allows you to fly, but i strongly advise against using it unless you absolutely have to-- maybe to cross a large body of water or reach a fragment floating high above you. Relying on the flight cheat completely ruins the point of the game.
My biggest gripe with the game is that there is no ending. You just run out of fragments to find. I am someone who likes completing things, so this really left a sour taste in my mouth. I would have loved some kind of profound or emotional ending that ties everything together. But maybe that's the point: for the character (me?) there is no ending. There is only what will happen tomorrow, and the next day, and the next.
Weird game, hard to get into...I'd rather be playing something else.

Ahhhh Eidolon, a forsaken game deep inside the forgotten games of my library.

Eidolon is placed in a post apocaliptic scenario (minus the destruction, or any generic element of it), where all the mankind is gone, no clue of who are you, or where are you, the only option left is to find some wood and make a fire...
Starting in some giant forest, while being alone, freezing and hungry. You must gather food, and keep going.
Again, you have no clue of what is going on, not even a brief introduction, its just *paf* you are in the middle of a forest.
Sooner or later you meet the animals of the earth, after some time, you find some tools to aid you in your unknown journey, and then you find the notes (if not, you are most likely to leave the game).
Learn about the life of lost people, find out there was something going on that caused all of this, explore this giant forest and climb mountains to complete this unsolved puzzle.
I lasted 41 minutes roaming without a single clue of WHAT IS THE POINT OF THIS.
But the real question is..
How long will you last until boredom consumes you?
The game art is.. yeah, its good, quite pretty i must say, it really feels like a forest when you are playing, the ambient, the sky, the water, the atmosphere is very deep, but then, you meet the reality...
The freezing and food meter are just pointless, eat some berries in the floor and you are good to go, every animal is gonna try to kill you and the ones who doesnt are going to run 60 km per hour fleeing for their lives.
If you have the fortune of finding a bow, say hello to the unlimited rapid fire gun that kills the miserable point of survival in the game.
Again, the diary notes you found are quite (very) interesting, but they lead to nowhere, and i mean NOWHERE, you have to walk all the way down until you find some buildings or radio towers.
If you have the time to find out the treasures of eidolon, or you have no problem with the things i said before, this game will be worth a try.
If not, dont even bother to buy it.

Having just finally beat this game, I want to write a review with it fresh in my mind. I'll start by saying that this game deserved to be beaten a long time ago, and it sat in my library uninstalled for far too long. I don't usually enjoy platformers but Ori and the Blind Forest is so well made that it's just too hard to use that as an excuse.
Obviously this game is one of the most beautiful to have graced Steam, but even before considering the visuals it is an excellent example of how games should be. I played entirely with an Xbox One controller and every death I had, of which there were 641 by the end of the game, were very much my own fault. I was never cheated by a mechanic, there was never an off-screen death waiting for me; the game is fair to you for the entire 8+ hours it will take. With that said of course, there were some nights that I just had to stop because I couldn't beat an area, but picking it up the next day, I was always able to figure it out. I chalk that up to my own personal ability in these types of games, as the level design as well is very good in Ori.
You should buy this game. Especially if you are interested in the recently announced sequel. The storylines of the two games will be connected and you would be doing yourself a disservice to skip the first one Finally, thank you Moon Studios, and Microsoft, for making this game. I really do hope that Will of the Wisps is just as good, because you have a returning customer, I will be patiently waiting for the next release.

No More Room in Hell is one of the best cooperative zombie survival games out there. The best part is that its free.
Based off of the Source Engine, No More Room in Hell will basically run on anything. I have mantained 60 FPS on a laptop not even meant for gaming, with the only thing I had to turn off being Anti Aliasing.
Though the game is not that graphically stunning, its gameplay makes up for that.
You and up to 7 other players have to either survive or complete a number of objectives. You will either hold a position as the shamblers make their slow approach to your temporary 'fort' or you will navigate through streets full of the walking, rotting corpses, deciding whether to blast your way through (the stupid way) or strafe around the slow ones and only waste bullets on the faster ones (the smart way).
Melee takes getting used to, but ultimately becomes incredibly satisfying, as you hold off small hordes with weapons such as a fire axe. You can charge up your swings for maximum damage or slash quickly instead.
Firearms aren't necessarily rare, but ammunition is. This game will teach you to not waste your bullets and to take your time aiming before you shoot. One wasted bullet could have taken out one or even more zombies. Guns like the Mac-10 and the MP5 have quite a kick to them and are both fully automatic, resulting in heavy ammo consumption. Not really ideal for a game focused on conserving your bullets and being accurate.
Overall, No More Room in Hell is the ideal, free, cooperative zombie survival game.
Oh, it also has a survival map that is an exact replica of the house from Night of the Living Dead (1968). THEY'RE COMING FOR YOU, BARBARA.

are the final deciding factors, and not Pay 2 Win weaponry and gear... then APB:Reloaded is where you want to be. There are no shortcuts. No matter how good you think you are... in APB:R you

Remedy took everything that they've done right with Max Payne 1 - gameplay mechanics, bullet-time, story, humour, graphics, physics, music, level design - and greatly improved it to a whole another level. For me, easily the best chapter in the whole franchise and maybe even one of the best games ever made.
Very good level design and the overall atmosphere makes almost all of the levels memorable and unique - Mona's noir playground, dream sequences, cpt. Baseball-Bat escort mission, one mission from both Max and Mona's perspective to name some. The developers really put a lot of care to this game; the incredible amount of tiny little details (like usable world objects or bystander dialogues) shifts this from a video game to a consistent living piece of art. Only downside is that everything feels a tad too scripted - but I must add that it's scripted very well.
The game aged very well and didn't lose any of its shine throughout the years. If you're a bit computer-savvy then - after some small effort and googling - it WILL run on Windows 7 64-bit in widescreen no matter what some users are reporting. At least it worked for me.

I'm not usually one for writinng reviews, but the more I wander through Eidolon, the more I'm appreciating the magnitude of the effort, work, and love that went into making it, and I feel obliged to write a praising note.
Eidolon delivers incredible atmosphere, a unique yet unpretentious art style, and a surprisingly involved and well-written back-story. This is definitely dead-centre on the slow, meditative, "walking simulator" genre space, so if you're looking for action, something you can complete quickly, or fast, densely packed drama, this is DEFINITELY not for you.
But for those looking for a pensive, meditative (and surprisingly relaxing!) experience -with a fantastic, slowly unravelling, backstory to boot- Eidolon is it. Despite the surreal feeling of picking up "clues" that are just pulsing blue dots, or watching animals move around like cardboard cutouts, this oddly adds to the dream-like feel of the game.
I'm so glad that indie developers are willing to put in the time and effort required to produce unique experieces like Eidolon, and I hope we see more from them.
(My advice: Don't go looking online for story spoilers, not even for a rough "what is this game about" - go in for the atmosphere, if the style appeals to you, and let the story be the icing on the cake, the end result is worth it)

Everybody's Gone to the Rapture is a beautiful looking walking simulator. There are no enemies, no stressful scenes (stressful as in to the player), and has some great audio.
But beyond that, it's pretty lifeless.
I had waited months to see if this game would ever go on sale. It never does, so I finally hunkered down and shelled out the money for it. The premise sounded interesting to me, and as I've gotten older, I enjoy games with story and narrative more than balls to the wall action.
Firstly, I want to commend those who deserve it - the voice acting in this game is phenomenal, and I have a bit of empathy for The Chinese Room as developers. I think the walking simulators they created were labors of love and I applaud them for efforts.
That said, I didn't find a whole lot memorable with this game. Not that it was a horrible story, but there are definitely things not explained (and acknowledged as such in-game) and in general, I didn't find anything surprising in the narrative. I didn't feel there was any big reveal. I've seen it mentioned that some reviewer on here spoiled the story without marking spoilers. In truth, I think you learn mostly what you need to about what's happening within the first two chapters. I think the main focal point here is more not what happened to people in the town, but rather what they were doing prior to their disappearance. There is a LOT of emphasis on relationships, between the townspeople and the main characters, as well as among the townspeople themselves, and the story narrative scenes are really focused on that.
And here, I think, is where I lost interest. As you play through the game, the narrative focuses on the events just prior to your "arrival" (what you are playing as is never explained. We do not know if it is a person or just a bodiless viewer not confined to the world, much like when you read a book), and seems to be told in a rewinding fashion. With each section, you "travel" the path involving a certain character, until the section ends and you move on to the next character and next section. Most of these seem to end during a certain moment in time, and then the next character's story starts up clearly in the past. Problem is, for me, only the first two sections made the biggest impact, primarily because its an introduction to this world and everything going on. After that, as I mentioned, I didn't feel like anything new or shocking happened, and thus it was just kind of exploring the interactions of some other people. And that wasn't terribly interesting to me. Beyond the emotion emitted by the first character, I didn't find anyone else relatable or generally likable, and that created a boredom issue when their lives, and not the event at hand, are the main focus.
Overall, I wanted to like it, but I just didn't find it as interesting as it appears to be.
(Worth noting, the story flow seems very similar to the TV show, Lost. If you've seen the show from beginning to end, you'll notice how this game parallels the basic storyboard very closely)

The game is very nice. It has a rock solid foundation to grow upon. However, imo, ASTRONEER falls right into the 'love it, else hate it' category.
These are what the game is as of the current build:
ASTRONEER is not just another crafting/building game. Considering how the items are handle, how they function, how you manage your inventory, how each module in your base functions, they can be seen as minigame by themselves as you will play with this a lot. If you are going to play like you average crafting game, you will have a hard time doing so.
There is no enemy to fight, no creature to hurt you. The main things you will be doing are exploring, while managing you resources, bases. There are environmental hazards, so you might say that it is player versus nature, though it is not that much from what I have seen so far in this current build. The planet is huge, I doubt that I have seen everything on my first planet yet in these 5 hours.
I am quite positive that ASTRONEER won't be very big in term of available contents as one would have in crafting/building game. The game don't need you to have big/complicated bases, or have to spent hours building thing to be able to enjoy it. You can just pick it up, drop into your friend's game, and have fun with them right away. Not sure how the future will be, but the current roadmap seems along this line.
The game will drop you on the planet right from the start, with minimal instruction on what you can do. You have your tools. All you need is to use them. There is no objective, there is no goal. It is just you doing whatever you want with available tools.
If you are turned off by above concepts, you might be better holding off your purchase until later.
Now, onto something I found in solo. haven't try coop yet.
- There are several weird behavior in sliding animation, not game breaking though.
- Tethering  is currently glitchy, and performance-hungry.
- Interfaces can used some improvement likes hiding them if player is not in certain range/direction
- Bugged item in backpack on load (mostly O2, Power stacks)
- Resources, objects respawn on load
- Stuck in falling animation in places (lands, bases,objects)
There are also balances, and optimizations issue, but it is expected in this stage of development. Anyway, good jobs so far.

Astroneer is the most exciting Early Access game - actually, forget the "Early Access" bit - that I've played in several years.
Its visual style is, to my mind, absolutely perfect. Better than perfect: it's refreshingly different from any other game out there. The gameplay is engrossing - so much so that you'll not notice the passage of time whilst playing this.
The exploration side of things is even more compelling that MineCraft's ever was. The crafting is, at the moment, quite simple and straightforward but already well-polished. As is survival: although not as intricate and nuanced (yet) as, for example, MineCraft, it works perfectly within the scope of the game. Oxygen and energy (power): that's it. Sounds simple, right? Yeah, not so much. You will learn to take a tactical approach to everything: especially exploring the planets you come across. And you will die. A lot. And you will love it.
I'll add more to this review as I experience more of the game, but let me just say that this is one of the two best Early Access games available on Steam as of this moment. Don't let Astroneer's "pre-alpha" status put you off. This game already has more than most "completed" games of this genre (yeah, looking at you, Sean Murray).
My opinion? BUY THIS RIGHT NOW! You will not be disappointed. If you are legitimately disappointed, you can send me your fecal matter through the postal service. That's how confident I am that you'll love this title.
If you've ever played any game ever, then you'll fall in love with Astroneer within the first 20 minutes of gameplay.
11/10.
