I've always been a fan of the Devil May Cry Series. As this game is now on sale, I thought it's a good time to write a quick review.
Dante might initially get a pretty strong reaction from some fans, he's no longer a cocky badass, instead he's something of a lowlife rebel. That will sting on occasion, because the cocky badass persona had been built up over several iterations and had gained some pretty good (if cheesy) characterisation in Devil May Cry 3.
But given that this is the game after Devil May Cry 4, it's a vast improvement in almost every way. The story is ok (in that the character development is there and the plot is solid) but never shines, or at least not in the way the gameplay does. Fighting is smoother than ever, switching between weapons feels seemless, and no one weapon is ever distinctly bad for a given situation (the game may sometimes force you to fight opponents immune to certain weapons but is otherwise happy to let your style dictate how you fight)
I think the best game to compare it to is Devil May Cry 3. Both have Dante at the start of his story, both have him meeting with Vergil, his brother but they both take it in different directions. The gameplay is better in DmC, the story better in Devil May Cry 3, but both still have the cheesy dialogue and incredible action sequences.
In short, if you loved the old games, you should love this one just as much. If you loved the old Dante however, it might take a while to adapt.

A Servicable Batman Title.
-
I grew up in an era when you only had to see a licensed game title to know it was a pile of poop. The Batman series has changed that perspective on its head - each of the Arkham series (Asylum, Origins, Knight) has met or exceeded my expectations.
Origins was the middle child of the set, though it's a prequel title to the rest of the story. If you play this one first you won't hurt your expereince at all. And of the three Arkham titles, this one felt the weakest overall in terms of the scope, presentation, and quality. The game is smaller and shorter than its bretheren. There are a few bugs hiding in the code (mostly to do with maps, position, getting hung up on object edges). The gameplay hasn't evolved beyond Asylum's recipe, and you'll see some of the set pieces common to the rest of the franchise: Scene with young Bruce looking at his dead parents? Check. Trippy hallucinatory sequence? Check. Nearly losing someone important to you? Check. All the oldies but goldies.
The bar for this game is still set decently high. The game plays well; the graphics are decent; the scripting for the content is good, though I preferred the stories in Asylum and Knight. One notable change is that Mark Hamill doesn't voice the Joker in this title. His replacement on Origins does his best with the role but it's a bit like someone else trying to do voice acting for Mark Hamill's Joker. Might have been better served if it were taken in a new direction entirely (a la Behind The Red Mask).
If you like the other Batman titles you'll probably like this one. Find it on sale.
For: Fans of the Batman Arkham franchise.
Not for: Stan Lee.

I'm a patient gamer who enjoys a "walking simulator" every now and then as a break from my usual FPS and racing games. I just finished "The Old City: Leviathan" and LOVED it so I figured I would try another of my many walking sims. I thought Eidolon might be similar to "Proteus" (short but excellent game) due to a similar art style. Unfortunately, it is not. I just spent (wasted) several hours "playing" Eidolon and got NOTHING from the experience other than the ability to collect mushrooms, blackberries and wood. It is boring, repetitive and pointless -- the map is hard to decipher and it doesn't show where you are -- useless. This game is neither fun nor interesting. Not worth a buy at any price.

So much of Eidolon doesn't work.
The poetry each time you wake up? Too out of context to be more than a jumble of words.
Forests to explore? They feel stark and empty.
Trees and plants to observe? They are too lacking in detail to be very interesting to look at.
Wild animals? They are more likely to be stuck running in place than flashes of shy wildlife.
But the landscapes? I expected them to be visually beautiful. I was disappointed.
The stories? Hit and miss. Some are definitely intriguing, some are mundane.
Survival resources? A simple chore. I like how the food deteriorates so you have to keep gathering.
Survival tools? They feel out of place.
Navigating? Not for the faint of heart! You will still get halfway lost after planning your path carefully.
Yes, I still recommend it.
The game is found in how it blends together. The ponderous pace, the passing titanic trees, the conscientious pauses to plan your eventual destination, the forced attention to what lies beside and ahead, the beckoning twinklings of a lost epoch... it is a long quiet desolate trek. It feels like lying in the grass for hours and staring at the flickering leaves. The desolate wilderness was an experience in patience, serenity, and meditation. I enjoyed many hours of this muted melody.
Except for how my game ended. I didn't know you could hurt yourself descending slopes. I found myself rudely informed when both of my legs broke. I crawled, nauseous, to a constant food source. There I lay, passing out every 45 seconds, until it became clear that I was not going to get better.
Ever.
I didn't even have a single hint for what to search for let alone where to search. I couldn't try to find an answer in my condition.
So I looked up what to do in response to this calamity. Honey. ???? In some distant forest maybe. ????? I tried to drag myself to the specific type of forest, but failed to find it after crossing half the map. The only solution? (Serene)Ragequit. I never worked up enough desire to go back to Eidolon again.
Yes, I still recommend it.
It didn't mean I didn't like the time I had. Eidolons. Eidolons.
Related games to try:
Viridi. Waking Mars. Mirror Moon. The Swapper. Miasmata.

Astroneer is the most exciting Early Access game - actually, forget the "Early Access" bit - that I've played in several years.
Its visual style is, to my mind, absolutely perfect. Better than perfect: it's refreshingly different from any other game out there. The gameplay is engrossing - so much so that you'll not notice the passage of time whilst playing this.
The exploration side of things is even more compelling that MineCraft's ever was. The crafting is, at the moment, quite simple and straightforward but already well-polished. As is survival: although not as intricate and nuanced (yet) as, for example, MineCraft, it works perfectly within the scope of the game. Oxygen and energy (power): that's it. Sounds simple, right? DmC Devil May Cry is a reboot of the popular game series which eventually had an anime based off of it. I thought it was the other way around since I watched a couple episodes of the anime a few years ago.  It’s a good thing that the game is a reboot since I probably never would have bought the game if it was #5 in a series. (I’ve never played the old Tomb Raider games either and I loved Tomb Raider 2013). It’s my understanding that the previous Devil May Cry games were known for their high difficulty but fortunately for me, DmC Devil May Cry wasn’t too hard at all (at normal difficulty).
The game world is a little hard to explain since there are various “layers” to consider. There’s a Heaven and Hell which you never see (kind of like Darksiders). The whole story takes place in the “real world” and in Limbo, which is sort of a “twisted copy” of the real world infested with demons. All the game’s combat takes place in Limbo. Powerful demons attempting to attack you will pull you into Limbo for the fight, and you can also go in through magical rituals (only happens as part of the story). You play the part of Dante, a loner with mysterious combat abilities and powerful weapons, working to take down the demon king Mundus. Mundus has sort of taken over the city (possibly the whole world) through various evil ways and the humans don’t even realize there are demons among them. Dante teams up with his long lost brother Vergil and begins killing Mundus’ allies one by one in awesome boss battles.
DmC is a hack and slash game with anime physics. This means for example that you can knock around a bunch of enemies with a single swing of your sword or launch them into the air and follow them upwards with a 20 hit combo. Like the game Darksiders, you unlock various “moves” by buying them with orbs that dead enemies drop. There’s a lot of platforming involved in the game as well, where you need to get from one area to another by double jumping around and using your 2 grappling hooks (one to pull yourself to a target, and another to pull the target to you). Fortunately there aren’t many puzzles, though there are quite a few secret items to be found. The reason I said earlier that DmC wasn’t too hard is because if you don’t care about your score, you can just keep “continuing from checkpoint” until you win. I believe your score will get chopped in half for every time you die. The same goes for using purchased healing items in the game, your score goes down. The game is broken up into missions, and you get a score at the end of each mission based on your time, secrets found, style (combos), and whether or not you used items/died. Keyboard and mouse controls are very intuitive and worked well for me, but I expect people who are used to controllers would enjoy that more.
Pros:
+Feel like a badass smacking a room full of demons around with combos and magic weapons.
+Very nice graphics including huge demonic bosses. I’m a fan of Angel vs Demon artwork too.
+You can beat the game pretty easily if you don’t care about your score.
+A lot of humor in this game. Dante doesn’t take♥♥♥♥♥♥from anyone and you get in some insult matches.
Cons:
-The game is still rather pricy despite being close to 2 years old. I think $12.50 is the lowest historical price.
-There are maybe 1 or 2 times in the game where you might get lost in a large level. The platforming is three dimensional so there are a lot of places to go. The game doesn’t have a waypoint system or map so it’s possible to get turned around. The levels are mostly straightforward though.
-That’s about it actually, the game is very polished despite being a console port.
Overall DmC Devil May Cry is definitely recommended. If you enjoy hack / slash games like Darksiders, you will appreciate the flow of combat in DmC. You don’t have to worry about missing collectables in the game since you don’t necessarily need the upgrades. The story is told through gameplay and cutscenes, and more or less makes sense to people who haven’t seen the anime or played the previous games. Wait for the price to drop, then buy the game!

If you're a lover of the original Devil May Cry series and the characters, then you are going to have a really, really hard time enjoying this game. The characters are changed dramatically. The gameplay, however, remains the same and is very fluid in transitioning between different weapons making the battles very stylish. Combat will definitely not disappoint you. I'd definitely rate the combat as being better than that of DMC 3 without being as cheap as Nero's Devil Bringer in DMC 4. The only disappointment is a lack of boss fights. DMC 3 and 4 got me used to fighting a boss almost every level, whereas there are 6 in the entirety of this game.
As for how the plot has changed, you're getting an almost pre-DMC 3 type of storyline (although they don't line up, obviously, as it is a reboot). The humor from previous games has been preserved, although rather than ridiculously showing off, it has more one liners befitting a youthful generation. Dante has plenty of good quips for certain. However, Dante and Vergil are dramatically different than their previous selves. If you compare to the originals, you're going to hate them, but if put the previous games out of mind, then you'll only really hate Vergil. So sad, Vergil was great...

It will be interesting to see where they take the franchise from here.

Huh. I'm gonna start this off with, a long time ago, I wrote a really simple one or two sentence review for this game with a not recommended.
That's gone. I'm pretty confident I didn't delete it without redoing the entire thing. Sooo... Yeah. Cue dem lofted brows.
So, let me explain: I don't recommend this game. I don't recommend it because it not just because of my opinion of the game at the time, but because I went back to DmC:DMC to try out some moves and mess around with the unique things the game offered.
...They didn't work. Any shoot+jump input move doesn't work in an consistent performable matter. That means: Kablooey can't detonate on its own, you can't perform Rainstorm, and I *believe* you cannot perform Fireworks. Frankly, I forgot whatever the god damn hell the shotgun did, but whatever it does for its jump and shoot,
, unless you completely change the keybindings forcefully - at which point, good luck chump, because Ninja Theory wastefully used up the entire god damned X360/Dual Shock controller and there's not really a better place to put it.
Mix that in with everything that happened during this game's development: Tameem & Co. insulted gamers, insulted DMC players, insulted Dante - all while making what was essentially a clone of Heavenly Sword. So you know what happened? Eventually, the community
that the game mechanically resemble DMC on some level, giving us the minimum: a jump cancel. So while Tameem was sitting there, writing out his self-insert, the people who maintained interest in the series he specifically took an opportunity to jab at - even though they are the only reason why this game isn't just Heavenly Sword. They are the
reason why this game gets any marks which might threaten to put it "above average,".
Meanwhile: there's those other mechanics Ninja Theory put in that Capcom had their port company strip out when the game was rereleased on consoles: specifically, that colored enemy nonsense, and include lock-on in the game, high level design decisions that put DmC:DMC in a position that solidly remind the player of its average action game roots: crappy mechanics to bar the player from dealing damage unless it's done in a specific manner in order to create some false illusion of challenge. We won't get those, ever: this game didn't actually sell well, especially not on PC.
Finally, putting aside the concrete shoes the developers decided to put on the game, we need to tackle story and cinematic value. I hate to say it, but there are interesting venues which one can travel around to breathe life into the Devil May Cry series for telling a story. You shouldn't expect them here, instead, here, we have a distinctly worse retelling of Dante's origin - which is arguably the best game in the series. All the notes pretty much got missed, misconstrued, or just... Badly interpretted. Dante doesn't get any cool equipment that he proceeds to demo like a boss in a cuhrazee cutscene. Here, in this game where the developers were eager to tell the world how
video game stories were... We have pretty much the worst characterization, bad cutscenes, terrible scene writing, and more:
You fight an unborn fetus. Vergil shoots an unborn fetus. Mundus is basically a ♥♥♥♥♥ier Kingpin, and the entire story is better viewed in Spanish than its original English - a testament to those voice actors and the flow of the Spanish language, really.
But hey: DmC got us DMC4SE, and DMC4SE is going to get us DMC5, so it's not all bad. The game got enough kickback that it made it clear there is interest in DMC, just not DmC. That's a good thing.

To preface: I can totally see why some people wouldn't like this game. If you want action, or don't like exploring for the sake of exploring, this is not the game for you. That said, if you DO like freeform exploring and rich lore, then this game is brilliant.
I figured I'd like it, but I didn't think I'd like THIS much. There is an incredible story to piece together here, and while there is often a lot of mundane walking around and foraging for berries and not doing much else aside from that, the environments make it worth it imo. This is one of the few games where the environments have been so lush that I could just wander around sightseeing all day. Eidolon does so much with so little, graphically; despite the low-poly environment, it never ceases to be beautiful. (It's also very good at making things look deceptively close, and then you find yourself freezing to death in a lake and praying you make it to the other side before you die, but that's just how life is sometimes).
I've definitely only scratched the surface of the underlying plot in my 10 hours of play time so far, but what it presents you with is so intriguing that you just feel compelled to keep searching. It sucks you in. The survival elements spice things up without being overly demanding. I love Eidolon.

One wouldn't think the idea of driving a truck would ellicit such praise. However, ETS2 pulls it off spectacularly. This game is not so much about the tasks of delivering goods from point A to point B, but it is about how the world around it presents itself. I bought this almost 2 years ago, and still play it with continued fervor. Here's why, it truly is about all the scenery you pass on your travels. The world is beautifully scaled properly to not be a literal 1-to-1 simulation of real life. The world is detailed and varied enough that you never feel that you are going through persistently recycled assets.
Graphically, the world is well presented with a great variety of road structures and traffic.  The day/night cycle and lighting systems have been consistently upgraded, and the game looks far more polished today than when I first bought it. Add to it that the technolgy in American Truck Simulator is being integrated into this engine, and Europe looks better than ever.
The economy of the world starts with an approprite pace as you can only take quick jobs where you are driving other company trucks. You build experience and level up to open more types of jobs that include rush shipments, fragile goods, and dangerous substances. Eventually, you will have the cash to get your own truck, garage, and then begins your quest to expand your company.
Even now, the Vive La France DLC is approaching, and with the rework of France (v.1.26 in current open beta) in preparation of the DLC, France looks so much more believable.
In the end, I purchased this game at a highly discounted price. It cught may attention and love so much that I paid full price for the Scandinavia DLC. Mostly because I felt I got too good a deal from the initial purchase. In seeing the rework of France, I am already hype for it.
SCS has done a spectaular job with ETS2 and their continued support of the game through the years,

Max Payne 2 came out eleven years ago so it seems odd to do a review of it. I'm sure that not exactly very many of you are going to be swayed to buy the game or anything like that. Yet I still want to recommend an absolutely fantastic mod that caught my eye for the game and I have been playing through.
Payne Evolution takes a classic game and makes it even better by refining it with some of the features and improvements of Max Payne 3. Every gun is replaced by a new variant from Max Payne 3, new dialogue is is introduced when Max picks up painkillers ("I was self-medicating, like a good American") and the MP3 bullet time effects are introduced. New sounds are added for so many things, of especially good quality being the new weapon sound effects. It really is a wholesale improvement on what was already an amazing game. Here is a link to the mod:
I was surprised by just how much fun I had with the classic film-noir love story. The game holds up really well too in terms of aging. The revolutionary at the time physics and environmental interactivity is still really impressive. The level design is something else (it's really refreshing to have this big wide open level design to explore, in stark comparison to the heavily scripted nature of modern games) and the characterisation is strong. Like Max, you find yourself falling in love with Mona and hating Vlad just as much as he does. The dialogue is top-notch, with Max's brooding and dark outlook on life feeling a lot more original and fleshed out than Max Payne 3's lines. The comic book style presentation feels really unique too, a fine example of not so heavy-handed storytelling. The game at times made me miss some of the traits I associate with games in the days of yore, truth be told.
The original game's excellence is further enhanced with the the brilliance of the Payne Evolution mod. Hell, if anything can vindicate that then probably the best moment is when the mod maker took inspiration (well, blatantly copied really) the song for for the final sequence of Max Payne 3, which is incredibly haunting and well fitting, and added it to the final sequence of Max Payne 2. If anything, it fits even better.
A real treat to revisit a game I fell in love with 11 years ago and still retains the quality I fondly remember.

One of those rare cases where the sequel is better than the original. Max Payne 2 tones down the difficulty a bit, but not by much as it is still a challenging game. Over all it feels much smoother than the original and was a fun game. The only bad thing I can think of was the story, I'm not really sure what is going on overall and it is kind of hard to make sense of it at times.

I played the original Max Payne years ago on the original CD version (I've never touched my Steam copy).  It was a straightforward third person shooter whose graphics weren't all that great even in its own time.  Its real strengths were its story (an offering of over-the-top noir detective grit with themes from Norse mythology) and its use of "bullet time", which took advantage of the popularity of the contemporary Matrix films.
The gameplay is not much different in this sequel.  It is still a linear third-person shooter with similar graphics and the occasional surreal nightmare level.  The cutscenes look the same and it remains in the noir genre.  However, the story is not nearly as interesting and abandons the interesting thematic choices of the original.  Since that was the main strength of the original, I don't think this one is worth your time at this point.  Just move on to part 3.

3/5
Continuing the narrative of the previous game, this sequel felt like it was just more of the same.

This is a pretty original game concept which doesn't has as much attention as it should of and I do like the idea of the game. The gameplay is fun and challenging and is similar to other hardcore platformers: Super meat boy and n++
In this game you're a red square with eyes (we should name him Frank) and you have to get to the goal (green), but in the way are objects: grill, walls, lava and more that you can't pass without switching the dimension. When you press Z you are in a altered dimension where one or two to the whole level is altered. There are various mechanics when you are playing the levels: lasers and one-way blocks. The blocks can make a confusing puzzle or a insane challenge. There is 90 levels to explore. There is even a whole entire level editor and a workshop to explore (It's pretty insane).
Once you beat all of the levels (or not I don't control your life), there are stars that are quite difficult. The postitions of the stars are in places that can make you think, complete the level again or generally challenge you. For the times for me it feels like you need to be pixel perfect on some of them (but of course you don't have to).
Best part of all is that if you make a level the lead developer (June) will probably play through it on a twitch stream. The next stream is on 16th of June 2017 at 6am (BST)
Overall this is a amazing game which is definitely worth the £6.99 ((£9.99 for anywhere else) I paid more and I still think it's worth it)

DmC Devil May Cry is an action-adventure, hack and slash hailing all the way from the brainchilds of Ninja Theory. Being the fifth installment into the series, yet serving as a reboot, this game received a wide, negative reception from those who are bound tightly around the original series, due to the strong character and story re-telling. Either way, I'm not one of those fans, as I accept this game immensely and greet it as its own beautiful reimagination.
The game's protagonist, Dante; a young, rebellious and hot-headed nephilim, (A hybrid of angel and demon.) who has no memory of the haunting and rather unfortunate past that had happened to him quite a while back. After a heavy night of clubbing, excessive drinking and rough sex, Dante awakens the next day with a hangover and is briefly warned by a young, psychic woman named Kat who hastefully warns Dante in her own words, that ''the demons are after him.'' Speaking of the devil, Dante is subsequently fazed into 'Limbo', a place where the demons are present, powerful and crave Dante's blood. After a few ruthless scenes of both unraveling family revelations and major story plots, you pair up with the twin brother-nephilim you never thought you had, and with his intelligence and propaganda sophistication along with Kat's strong knowledge of Wiccan spells, they'll lead Dante to plunge deep into Limbo and face off a number of demonic threats such as a roundabout circus fight with the baboon-faced Hunter. Taking down a Succubus, who's main job consists of human control through producing the world's most popular soft drink, firing off a middle-aged demon puppet of a TV reporter, and even having to dance with the devil's mistress and their demonic spawn. All of this will depend on the ultimate test of encountering the all-powerful demon king, Mundus. Or Kyle Ryder, if you're wanting to know his human-form alias.
The game's engine is near to being absolutely perfect and intense. Playing the role of Dante, you have a strong and calculative arsenal; such as performing combos by the slice of his sword, Rebellion. Keep the enemies stunned and juggling with his twin, ammoless pistols, Ebony & Ivory. As you progress through the story, you are granted more weapons, each with their own abilities and strategic modes. New to the series, has got to be the inclusion of the Devil Mode and Angel Mode. Dante's sword attacks change to the Osiris, a speedy, long-ranged scythe type weapon, whilst Devil mode uses the slower but more powerful Arbiter. These modes also alter Dante's mobility. Using Angel mode allows Dante to pull himself towards enemies and various points in each level, whilst Devil mode lets Dante pull enemies and objects towards him. With all of this aside, there are still a few more weapons to discover, but I'll leave the unaware player to discover.
It's all worthy to note and check out this games DLC, Vergil's Downfall, which allows you to play as Vergil, in his own side story, which just adds fuel to the fire of satisfying those fans who crave more. I would definitely recommend getting this game around the time everything is on a special deal, as it's only worth buying at that time.
The only thing that I find a problem with this game is the fact that the game lacks a lock-on mechanic, which all previous Devil May Cry games had at it's disposal. You only lock on a specific target automatically, depending on the third person camera angle as well as being in the correct vicinity, as you can fire your guns at targets from quite a mile away if you're standing in the right place. But this also adds to some few minor problems, such as glitching out if you accidently latched onto a target, while a short cutscene is playing.
As a massive fan of the previous, original Devil May Cry games, I still consider this reboot a new step in the right direction as well as a new breathe of fresh air. Negatively looked down upon fans of the original series, due to the story flaws and late and contrasted character development, aswell the differences it has when compared to the original Devil May Cry games that fans cherish so much, Capcom gave their development rights to Ninja Theory for the correct reason; Their originality is absolutely sensational and I have every right to say that Ninja Theory delivers. I honestly prefer this game's visual style, as it's much more surreal, hollow and darker than the previous 'Anime'-esque originals, not saying I hate the originals, as I love them equally to this reboot, but in a different way. By all means, this game is both for the casual and intense gamer, so it's a win-win situation. It's a massive recommendation from me, to everyone.

Very few games have acheived the level of mind ♥♥♥♥ery that Spec Ops: The Line has.
From a gameplay perspective, it's a very basic cover based 3rd-person shooter. The gameplay is purposely boring, almost even a chore at times, but it's all to convey the fantastic story and themes. Spec Ops wants you to think about why you enjoy killing virtual people, it wants you to consider if your actions are forced by the gameplay or out of your own choice. It does these things better than any other game I've seen.
Length wise: it is pretty short. Playing on the normal difficulty I was able to beat it in 4 hours. Though it has some good replay value, with 4 different endings and plenty of choice driven sections. Additionally there are a small amount of collectibles that are worth searching for that add to the extremely interesting world Spec Ops has built.
I would highly recommend picking this game up if you're even the slightest bit interested. A must buy if it's on sale. You are doing yourself a disserive by not playing this game.

Early access. Sometimes you win (Prison Architect, Factorio), sometimes you lose (Godus and many, many others). Thankfully, this conforms to the former, a solid Alpha release that is an intuitive, albeit rather casual, third-person exploration/base building game.
Exploration is a key focus in the procedurally generated environment. Rewards of rare minerals and research development are granted to those brave enough to venture away from the safety of your base.
I am not qualified to comment on multiplayer, I have only been playing single player.

Spoilers Below.
PROS:
-For me, it is a calming experience watching the planetoid rotate in concert with other planets and stars.
-Minimalistic art direction. Not everyone's cup of tea, but I appreciate the aesthetic.
-Music is soothing.
-Backpack mechanic, upgrades will sacrifice precious inventory space. Choose wisely.
-Animations are good; intentionally ragdoll the Astroneer with a debris storm. Oddly satisfying.
-Vehicles are limited but varied, each with their own unique attributes and handling characteristics.
-Kid friendly. Casual game style, no gore, limb amputations or unpleasantness. No shooting aliens. However, you do disrupt the lifecycle of various flora based life-forms.
-Accessible and intuitive.
-No HUD. Think Dead Space.
-Spelunking is rewarding.
-Terrain manipulation is fun.
-Procedural world generation appears to be balanced quite well.
-Obvious pro-active Developer support; so far so good! Well communicated, actively engaging the community-Early Access done right.
CONS: (Early Access, not representative of final product)
-Frame rate issues. After playing for awhile the game gets quite choppy.
-Terrain, flora pop-ins.
-Camera issues (rare)
-Bugs (Clipping, physics, also rare)
-Needs more content.
-Late game needs some kind of reward system/motivator.
As it stands, I am giving this a 75 out of 100, I could realistically see this being bumped to low 90's once the bugs are ironed out,  more content added and everything is optimised. Very promising.

An astonishing exploration game, with some breathtaking moments, that ultimately fails to be satisfying.
Your heart will soar as you glide gently through changing landscapes, weather patterns, and incredibly subtle day-night cycles. There will be moments where you reach a new place and you'll just stare at the screen at awe. You will find well-written documents that will wave together a remarkably rich, sad, and inspiring story.
Unfortunately, you will mostly be bored. The game is far, far, far too slow. How slow? Think that reaching the next location can take 45 minutes. Sure, it's a beautiful ride to get there, but actually the scenery is not so diverse, and it will get boring. With a game so focused on nature, there really should have been more than three kinds of trees and shrubs.
The slowness is exacerbated by a raw navigation system that will not let you easily plan your journey, so that you will surely have to go back and revisit places you've already been. Since it can take 45 minutes to get to them ... you may find yourself looking up a cheat code for faster travel (and it still will take a very long time!), or just quitting and heading to the wiki to read the rest of the documents and get the whole story.
As other reviewers have mentioned, there is a terrible "survival" system that is an entirely unnecessary addition to the gameplay. It's charming for the first 10 minutes, but then it's just a bother. I wish, instead, that there was a good navigation system.
A wonderful idea, and I did thoroughly enjoy some moments in the game, but the execution would have benefited from more development.

This game just about scrapes a Recommended review from me.
I guess it depends on what you are considering buying it for. If you're looking to just play it casually, perhaps with your family, then I definitely recommend it.
It's overall a decent game, and runs well for an older lego title (some of the titles on the older engine have crashing issues on modern operatings systems / hardware). I actually had no crashes at all when playing this game.
However, if you buy these games with the intention of 100%ing them, like me, then that's where this game has a couple of moments that will seriously test your patience.
First of all, there is a minikit on the Arctic World level which sees you having to go through 5 'gates' when sliding down some ice. This is by far the hardest minikit to get in the game. Actual control of your characters on this slope is hit and miss so it's luck more than anything if you manage to do it, and if you miss even a single gate, you have to start the whole level again.
Then, you get to the final 100% hurdle, which is the Wayne Manor bonus level. You have to get 1 million studs, and this is exactly how many there are to be found; you basically have to collect every single stud. The things you have to do to get them are somwhat tricky, but also seriously mundane, it's just not a fun level to play, at all.
Having said that, I still achieved the 100%, and would say that overall it was an enjoyable experience. The two things i've mentioned above do lower the tone of the game somewhat, and if it weren't for those, i'd be much more confident in giving this a thumbs up.
As is, i still recommend it, just with the warnings above.

This is a fascinating game if you are a patient person and if you go into it without thinking of it as a "game" in the traditional sense.  This is an exploration that will take hours and hours to complete, and I find I like it best in occasional small doses of a half-hour to an hour at a time.
Graphically it's very simple and the area is extremely vast, so it can get monotonous if played for long lengths of time.  There are two "hint" systems to the game: clicking on a topic in your journal shows you the direction to the next document of that topic, and a flying bird in the sky leads you to the next closest document regardless of topic.  Unfortunately, the flying bird "hint" is sometimes obscured by the trees which may or may not be intended.
There are many, many intertwining stories and with each document you pick up, you unlock a little more of that storyline.  But don't go into it expecting everything to be tied up with a little bow at the end.  You're expected to think about the stories, and the landscape, and the history of this area.
There are some aspects of survival included in the game but they are very much ancillary to the experience.  You have to eat, sleep, stay warm, and stay away from wild animals that might want to nibble your giblets.  But the food is plentiful and the predators extremely rare (in ten hours I've only encountered a couple), so the survival aspect is an afterthought that is very easy to manage but does give you something to think about other than "walk, walk, walkwalkwalk, walk more..."
So if you enjoy walking simulators, are very patient, and aren't looking for an action-packed experience, and especially if you enjoy the discovery process of uncovering bits and pieces at a time of larger stories, you will probably like this.  Otherwise you'll probably hate it.

I'm not usually one for writing reviews, but with the fate of the Hitman franchise in jeopardy, I felt it necessary to show my support for this amazing game.
Hitman 6 (or HITMAN™) was a welcome return to form after the disappointing Hitman Absolution. Where Absolution floundered, HITMAN™ triumphed :
So what went wrong?
Well, for starters, the abrupt announcment of an episodic model caught many off guard and turned a lot of people off. Many people, myself included, didn't want to get absorbed by the first level only to have to wait a month afterwards for the second, third, fourth, etc. We just waited for the game to be released fully. A game's release is the most important part of it's marketing blitz, so staggering that out over a year killed the hype for casual gamers eyeing the game at a glance. Not to mention the performance issues at launch that now seemingly plague every single PC port, meaning I had to wait for my GTX 1070 before I had the peace of mind to try the game.
The end result was that I bought Season 1 on sale. Having be thoroughly impressed, I was ready to buy Season 2 at full price, confident I would be getting my money's worth. Now that Square Enix and IO Interactive have parted ways, I'm honestly not so sure. I'm not sure if there'll even be a Season 2, and even if they contract another developer, it probably won't be the same. I believe games are defined pimarily by the people who make them. The Hitman franchise was developed by IO Interactive, but they have also developed alongside it. Their creative voice was molded by the hitman franchise, and HITMAN™ is an expression of all they've learned. I'm worried that another team will never capture their same state of mind and design philosophy, assuming they even try at all (*cough*Thi4f*cough*).
Square Enix made a very premature move by ridding themselves of IO, and it's a shame that IO no longer owns the franchise they've created. Guess that's just the industry works...
In summary, HITMAN™ gets my GOTY 14/10 it's okay i guess can't wait to augment my preorder for HITMAN®

When I started playing I thought this was the best Hitman game since Blood Money, by the time I finished I thought it was the best Hitman game period.  Initially I was put off by the episodic format and held off on purchasing until I could get it all at once - I've since realized this is a game almost uniquely suited to a episodic release schedule because each level is absolutely packed to the hilt with things to do/challenges to complete/details to drink in etc.  It's actually extremely overwhelming to have it ALL available right from the get go.
Dumping a lot of the trashy sexualization prevalent in earlier games (such as the shower scene from Absolution), this is all about Agent 47 traveling to a variety of stunning locations where you're given a target or 2 to kill and maybe some kind of extra goal and then are largely left to do it in whatever way suits you.  There are opportunities and challenges to guide and suggest, but the choices are ultimately left up to you and there is a huge amount of replay value (as my close to 200 hours of game time can attest).
The loose connecting cutscenes tell a largely forgettable story that exist mostly as a framework to tie together 47's disparate targets/locations.  It's well produced though and doesn't go completely overboard in the same way Absolution did.
If you avoided this because of the episodic format or the fact it's a single-player game that wants you to connect to a server, I recommend giving it a shot.  It didn't sell well and apparently there won't be a season 2, so sadly for now this is as good as it gets.  Happily, it gets VERY good indeed.

I think the term, "walking simulator," gets applied to more games than it ultimately should. If you ever had the opportunity to play the original Myst back in the day - a title that both revolutionized and became the gold standard for what it meant to be an adventure game - then you might agree with me that Myst could technically be termed a walking simulator based on its gameplay. But that's not really correct, is it? That's not what we think of when we call something a walking simulator, is it? Where then is the dividing line? When does a game cross over from being an adventure game to being a walking simulator?
I've spent the last couple of hours pondering this question as I've been playing Rapture; the very fact that I've been doing *that* instead of being focused on the game, gave me my first clue: immersion. Myst was enthralling; for the player, time stood still. 3am? Bah, I'll just call in sick tomorrow. I've experienced that as well with the "Vanishing of Ethan Carter" and "What Remains of Edith Finch," two other noted walking simulators. And what makes a game immersive? Atmosphere. Storytelling. Exploration. A mystery to be solved.
Technically, Rapture has all of this....but unfortunately, it has serious flaws with each aspect:
- Atmosphere: the creators do a fairly decent job at providing the back drop of a quaint northern England village; it's an attractive-looking game with some fairly stunning visuals at times. The music is effective in places, but in others becomes a heavy-handed distraction with majestic chorals being used far too much and hence losing their effect over time. The voice acting would be adequate under normal circumstances, but other than the main protagonist, it all starts to sound alike quickly, which creates an immersion issue. You see, all of the characters are represented as silhouettes of light with no visual differentiation whatsoever. There are no visual points of distinction or interest, so we're left to fall on their voices to fill those gaps, and the differentiation between the voices is insufficient, as they are essentially all villagers of the same demographic background. This gives the impression of a very vanilla set of characters that we have trouble distinguishing between or empathizing with.
- Storytelling: At the risk of being blunt, the storytelling here is subpar. The intent here is to tell the story through 20-30 second snippets of dialog presented out of order between the denizens of the village and it's up to the player to piece together what's going on. But much of the dialog is inconsequential to the plot and merely helps identify and flesh out the characters, most of whom are also largely inconsequential to the plot. There are far too many background characters here and far too little reasons to care about them individually. Yes, there are undercurrents and subplots, but they are irrelevant to the story, and frankly, make you question why the writers thought them compelling. Several are rather cringeworthy. But again, it's all irrelevant, because this story is really about two main characters, both of which you also  finding yourself asking why they're behaving the way they are. Finally, the story wraps up with a long exposition about the existential nature of life itself and you're left wondering how we got from point A to point B.
- Exploration: At first, this seemed delightful, as you skip from house to house to check out every nook and cranny hoping for secrets to be revealed. By roughly the 5th or 6th house, you begin to realize that the vast majority of houses are just window-dressing and cannot actually be explored, and that you're going to be treated to the same in-game objects again, and again, and again, and again in different combinations. But even this would not be so terrible were it not for the fact that you walk everywhere. Or perhaps I should say, plod. No running, no jogging, not even walking at a brisk pace. No, you plod. In the beginning, you don't mind so much, because the newness is still fresh and curiosity peaked, but roughly 50% into the game you find yourself just sticking to the main objective because the payoff for exploring does not exceed the "plod factor." In fact, the number of interactions you have with the game generally come about every 5-10 minutes, between which you a plod, plod, plodding along. This gets old extremely fast.
I mean, there's even a guide attached to the store page about how to download a cheat program simply to make your character move faster, for crying out loud. The creators of this game seem to embrace the idea of long stretches between actually doing anything; at least four of the achievements are earned by going to certain locations and doing *absolutely nothing* for several minutes. I'm not making this up; you are rewarded for standing perfectly still and doing nothing.
- A mystery to be solved: As I mentioned earlier the gameplay is about locating these 20-30 second snippets of dialog that you're supposed to piece together what's going on. But the problem is that by the end of the first area, you already have a pretty good idea about what's going on. From there forward, it's mostly about uncovering all the little subplots that are ultimately irrelevant to main plot. There really is no payoff, no grand "a ha!" moment that makes you glad you invested in the game.
So to answer my original question - what is the dividing line between an adventure game and a walking simulator - I believe that an adventure game is a superset of a walking simulator that never feels like one because its too busy captivating your imagination. Rapture, on the other hand, is a pure walking simulator - and not even a very well implemented one - and as such I must caution you against buying it unless walking really is your thing.
The soundtrack positively makes the game

Everybody's Gone to the Rapture does a lot right, but it probably should not be considered a "good game."
What it does well: The artistic direction perfectly captures what I think of when I picture the "ideal" english countryside. The scenery and attention to detail of the town and surrounding areas is exceptional. The accompanying sound design for birds, wind, and music fits very well. You can tell it was crafted with care. In your quest to discover what happened to the residents of the small village in their final moments, I came to sympathize with their regrets and shortcomings as their stories unfolded.
What it does not do well: Despite the attention to detail of the landscape, there are very few chances to interact with it and the game suffers for it. As probably mentioned thousands of times, the walking speed is unbearbably slow. The walk fast option is barely noticable but I understand why the developers set it the way they did (they want you to experience the world!) Now onto the story, without spoilers, it is kind of out there and I'm still not sure what the final takeaway is supposed to be.
Rapture has a lot offer if you just want to sit back for a few hours and experience a different world. I do think this game is worth a playthrough, though for some folks this is probably best picked up on sale.

The awaited sequel to the blockbuster Max Payne has arrived, and I´m happy to report that it packs with it a ton of fun and hefty improvements which do a great job of fixing the original´s missteps.
Taking place 2 years after the events of the first game, Max Payne 2 places you right in the middle of the action, and it´s your job to reconstruct the events that led to where you are at the beginning of the adventure. It´s a clever storytelling tactic, and provides an excuse for Max to bust out his witty one-liners and noirish remarks which are dotted throught the entire six-hour campaign, even if they do get a little stale at parts. Twists and turns lurk around every corner, making this is a story you     won´t want to put down until you see it through.
Gameplay hasn´t been drastically improved, which isn´t a bad thing if you were a fan of the original´s bullet-time setpieces and deadly shootouts, but some aspects could have been changed up a bit. One thing I noticed was a heavier use of dream sequences, which are there to provide a breath from the action and push the story forward, but ultimately only serve as boring, linear sections with little to no fun to be had at all. Perspective is also played with, as the focus sometimes shifts from Max to another character I won´t name so as not to spoil it. These chapters are very cleverly intersected with the    protagonist´s own path, and provide a different angle on some key events in the story.
An aspect of this sequel which has received a major overhaul is definitely the audiovisual department. The voice acting is once again top-notch, and the graphics have been redesigned to give Max and the supporting characters a more realistic feel, even though the thugs' faces do tend to repeat themselves far too often for their own good. Lighting effects add to the dark tone of the plot, making this title a beauty to look at.
Max Payne 2 won´t blow you away with new mechanics, relying instead on the aspects that made the original the great experience that it was, but introducing some fantastic touches here and there which make it stand out as what a sequel should be: bigger and better. It´s not a very lengthy ride, but it´s definitely a sweet one.
Pros:
+ Engaging and tightly crafted storyline that keeps you constantly guessing what´s about to happen
+ Gorgeous looking graphics and animations
+ Responsive controls which provide for an immersive experience
+ Outstanding use of the bullet-time feature
Cons:
- Short campaign
- Seconday characters aren´t that detailed, and they tend to repeat their faces often
- Corny dialogue
- Annoying use of the quick-save option
Final grade: 8.5 (Very good)

Here's a short history lesson
The year was 2012, gaming has been a very shallow and safe year for many triple A companies. Usual genres that were put out were shooters as that is what every company thought what their customers want. But what was believed to be even safer, or more importantly insulting were military shooters. Games that glorified the military and tweaked the mechanics of gameplay to give you a sense of power like, brain dead AI, regenerating health and a black and white story of good and bad. Perhaps it was not intended for these developers to make propaganda games and thought it was what the public wanted, given for where the companies were set up. But never the less, they obviously made a foolish story for more mature and experienced players that the idea that one country is morally better then the other.
Going in the background, a team of developers called Yager who were responsible for the spec ops series in the late 90's and early 100's decided to make a game to not compete with major games like call of duty or battlefield, but still act like one to convey a message. A message that violence was not fun and there is no need for unnecessary conflict. their recent games conveyed respect and the harsh realities that these soldiers go through unlike the other brands. This may have not been a game to make major sales, but maybe as a cult classic and to go down in history as one of the greatest feats in gaming history.
I won't spoil to much of the game because it's best to go in with the expectations of cluelesness. You should definetly play it or if you can find a copy, buy it to perserve it, because the latter is why i brought it, i'll explain later.
For the mechanics of the game its boring. Its a mix of terrible cover based shooting with modern military tropes that make it feel like a bland shooter cashing into the fad, but that the point. It purposely does this to make it look boring at first and assumes that you brought it for shooting
.
Infact, its made to look like it has bad shooting mechanics at first and then it alters its minor details to convey the mental state of Walker, the protagonist throughout the game. These mechanics alter how the enemies die as well, in the first hour your given only two small arms but later on your given high powered and explosive wepons, which may sound exciting, but its not and not in the tedious way. Even the new mechanic, exicutions for ammo, changes differently from what weapon your using or how long you are into the game.
This may sound small, but in truth these are put into the game because alot of military shooters don't show you what actually happens when you shoot someone in the head with a high power weapon or when you blow them up with a rocket launcher. This game bravely shows you how sickening it is to kill someone, and when you see that motar loaded with white phosphorus you will know what its like to truely hurt someone badly.
This game is chock full of visual metaphors that enforces the idea of an unsettling feeling that something is not right, where there is questions on whats real or not real and as it goes on from the first act to the last act helps us to understand ourselves of what actions we do. Its not a very pretty thing but it helps with the expeience.
The game is also very self aware that you exist, i don't want to spoil anything about how it will do so but it will make you feel bad and it will do so in ways that will make you embarased and disgusted of yourself. You will notice things that only you can see and no one else can.
But the biggest shocker is that you are in control of your actions and when you hear the line "do you feel like a hero", the major characters mocking you for your pretend heroism and the loading screen contributing as well, the true villian will be put out.

Any companies that tries to cash in on alternate reaities of our future with real countries taking over the world, is going to be decimated because of a fad no one likes anymore, Homefront the revolution for example.

Hitman is a third person stealth/action game where the player takes on the role of iconic assassin for hire, Agent 47. This is the sixth main game in the franchise. I've previously played Blood Money (which was fun) and Absolution (which was disappointing). The difference between those games was essentially caused by their portrayal of Agent 47. In Blood Money, the goal was to be a silent assassin, to kill your targets without anybody ever knowing you were there, often making it look like an accident. Using guns was a last resort. Absolution (and the two terrible Hollywood movies) tried to turn 47 into an action star, running and gunning his way to a huge bodycount.

The good news is that this latest game is on par with Blood Money in terms of quality and playing style. Well, five of the six missions are. Let’s just say that the best thing about Colorado is still the Denver Broncos :)
The level design is fantastic. There are six locations around the world, each of which is quite large and open. There’s a mixture of indoor and outdoor areas, and they all have lots of different paths to reach your target. Each location feels alive, crowded with people going about their business. Some areas are off limits to civilians and certain types of staff. Fortunately 47 is a master of disguise. You can steal the uniform of anyone you kill or incapacitate, to gain access to restricted areas. But you still need to be careful because some NPCs will recognise you as an imposter. NPC AI is pretty good, they’ll run to find security guards and report any suspicious behaviour. If you’re nearby you can even hear them describe your appearance. Each location is filled with objects you can interact with, parts of the environment that you can sabotage to create a distraction. You’ll also overhear conversations that give you information about opportunities to kill your targets in a unique way, or make it look like an accident.

With such enjoyable gameplay, its a shame that the story campaign is relatively short. I finished it in just under 9 hours. The story is also quite basic. Each mission is apparently part of some larger global conspiracy, but you don't get many details. And the lack of a satisfying ending (I wouldn't even call it a cliffhanger, it just feels incomplete) contributes to the feeling that the game is still unfinished, like it needed another couple of missions.
Each location has several bonus contracts and escalation missions which add a few extra hours of gameplay, but the quality of these missions is mixed. Your targets are average NPCs such as security guards, chefs and tourists. Escalation missions have 5 stages, adding more objectives each time to increase the complexity of the mission.
The problem with the contracts and escalations is that most of them require you to kill the targets with a specific weapon and while wearing a specific disguise. You don’t get the freedom to choose how to complete the mission, which takes away the biggest strength of the story missions. Its also difficult to play as a silent assassin, because most of these targets never move to isolated areas where you can kill them unseen and hide the bodies. You’ll almost always get seen by other civilians, which leads to gun fights with security guards and lots of collateral damage.
There are also elusive targets, which are special missions where you only get one attempt to kill a unique character. If you fail somehow or die during the mission, you can never try again. In theory, these are fun ways to test your skills, and beating these missions should be something to be proud of. I managed to kill one elusive target, but then his bodyguards killed me, so I failed the mission. That’s my fault for not properly planning my escape route. The problem is, these missions are time limited – you only get about a week to try them, before they’re gone for good. If you haven’t played the game yet (and I’m assuming that’s why you’re reading this review), you can’t actually play these missions. There have been 24 so far, and you’ve missed them all. I think this is poor game design, which punishes players for waiting until bugs have been fixed and all the episodes have been released. It would be better if players could make their one attempt at each elusive target, any time.
Controls are fully rebindable and work great with mouse and keyboard. I’ve only suffered one crash, so the game is mostly very stable. However, there is a common problem with the physical disk version, which prevents it from installing. I wasn’t aware of this, and my download speed is still relatively slow, so I bought the disks to avoid downloading 50GB of data. A potential fix stated on the developer’s website, didn’t work for me, so I ended up downloading the whole game anyway.
Hitman is a good game and I recommend playing it, but you shouldn’t pay full price because you can’t play the whole game. Wait for a sale.

Prologue: I adore this game. I truly do. This is not simply a 'Walking Simulator', it is a Hiking Simulator! As noted in the description: "Featuring a beautiful, detailed open-world and a haunting soundtrack, Everybody’s Gone to the Rapture is non-linear storytelling at its best." Indeed, it is a haunting soundtrack, however, it is closer to a melancholy hymn than anything else. So, what about all the other aspects of this game? Well, read on, and I shall indulge you!
Gameplay-Slow, smooth, and serene, dying is just not possible here. So, don't even bother trying. Instead, simply relax, take in all the scenery, and immerse yourself in the story-line. Who are you? It matters not, but for me, I was a nameless hiker, along the road and also the trail. Will you encounter any other people? In a manner of speaking, yesh. However, don't expect to see them clearly, for they are nothing more than particles of light. What about creatures and critters? There are a few critters (Like birds) here and there, both dead and alive, so seeing them alive us a plus, at least. Plus, you can open doors, use light switches, radios, computers, and whatnot. Gameplay Score-8 out of 10.
Items-As mentioned before, you'll see all sorts of objects in-game. However, don't count on being able to take anything with you. Yesh, you can turn stuff on and off, but other than this, all those items are there to add to the scenery, whether interactive or not. Items Score-7 out of 10.
Weapons-You don't need any here, since there are no enemies encountered. At one point, you might witness an attack or two, but all you can do is stare. So, just pretend you have a tent, backpack, and a hiking stick and simply walk along the trail. Weapons Score-N/A.
Ammo-Since there isn't a single usable weapon to be found, you won't find any ammo either. But who needs ammo, when you can just keep hiking? Ammo Score-N/A.
Armor-Is this an emergency situation? Kind of, but since you don't ever have to worry about anyone attacking you, then guesh what?...There is no Armor here, either. Armor Score-N/A.
Plot-Slow as a snail, but deep as an ocean is the best way to describe the plot in this game. I won't spoil it for you, but you may not like all of the characters equally, and sometimes, you may even often feel chills run down your spine! This means it is well-done indeed. Plot Score-7 out of 10.
Characters-As mentioned above, there are some nice characters and some...Not-so-nice characters. But every story needs characters or there is no story at all! Characters Score-6 out of 10.
Sound-You may hear the wind blowing, people talking, bird calls and songs, and sometimes, a sudden loud noise nearby or in the distance may startle you. But you can relax, because as mentioned before, there are no foes to be found, so you have no risk of dying whatsoever. Sound Score-8 out of 10.
Music-Something which can only be described as a melancholy hymn fits the music here to a tee. If the music was a little more...Mysterious, it might be better. But since most of it falls under the aforementioned above description, it will be filed under...Mediocre. Music Score-4 out of 10.
Graphics-One of the best (If not the best) aspect of this calming game, the graphics are of epic quality, even on a lower setting. Granted, having this high quality of graphics may make the game run slower, but since it's officially classified as a 'Walking Simulator', then you shouldn't worry about how the graphics appear on this game. They'll be beautiful regardless. Graphics Score-9 out of 10.
Final Score-Everybody’s Gone to the Rapture is one of the most relaxing video games I have ever played. And before I learned about it from a rather controversial video on youtube, I had no idea there was a game classified as a 'Walking Simulator'! Before this, I would often seek out hiking adventures on other games, which featured even small sections of wilderness. But since I now have this amazing game, I can take a virtual hike just about anytime! Final Score-9 out of 10.

Everybody's Gone to the Rapture is more like a piece of art than an actual game. A story you can move and immerse yourself in. The visual presentation is quite pleasing. The village and landscape you are moving in are very convincingly crafted and the music perfectly fits them. The story ebbs and flows between mysterious, sad, elegant and even philosophical in the later stages. Probably the best part about it is the voice acting - really high quality craftsmanship. I especially remember a scene with Lizzie in which her car broke down. The amount of little detail in her voice is absolutely fantastic.
If you like works like Firewatch or The Stanley Parable it is highly probable that you will like Everybody's Gone to the Rapture as well. If you expect much gameplay, this probably isn't for you. If you're an indie movie fan you should give this a try. I've spent 20 Euro on this and didn't regret it.

Batman: Arkham Origins is the prequel to the Arkham series, but will you want to play it ?
Batman: Arkham Origins take place in the first year of Bruce Wayne becoming Batman. On Christmas Eve Black Mask hires 8 assassins to hunt down and kill Batman for 50 million dollars. So it's up to you to capture every assassin and save Gotham.
Gameplay is almost identical to Arkham City. It adds new elements like shock gloves that speed up combat, but do less damage. Overall the combat is identical to Arkham City and if you played that you know what to expect.
Graphics are also identical to Arkham City, but unlike AC they add snow and snowing effects and add Christmas decorations to make you feel like Christmas is just around the corner. Graphics are amazing to say the least even though they are just a re-skin.
The soundtrack is awesome. When you fight some of the bosses and the music kicks in is just awesome and makes the fights even better.
The game is a bit harder than the other titles. Stealth play's a bigger role in this game and the armed enemies do more damage. But the game is still really easy.
Level design is mostly taken out of Arkham City, but there are new locations. Overall it's really well made but there is one location that has horrible design is the Gotham Police station. I got lost and confused multiple times. I would have liked for them for not make it that confusing.
Game is pretty long. It took me 17 hours to finish the main story and complete all side quests. 2 hours more to play the Cold, Cold Heart DLC. Not to mention there's also a lot you can do after you finish the game and also there are challenge maps.
The game is incredibly buggy. During a boss fight, the boss got stuck in a wall. I needed to restart for it work again. Sometimes, I couldn't interrogate people after I beat them up. The game doesn't have any game breaking bugs and restarting from a checkpoint fixes the problem.
The multiplayer mode is kind of fun but now it's full of hackers and it's kind of hard to get into a game. My suggestion is to skip all MP dlc.
Batman: Arkham Origins isn't as good as the previous titles. The game is buggy and it get's boring really fast, but it's still really fun. The boss battles are interesting and are fun as hell. The story is really interesting too. Overall if you are a fan of Arkham games this is a must own. But my suggestion is to get the game on sale only. I give Batman: Arkham Origins a 7/10

I remember, after dumping about 12-15 hours back into this game, just why it is I turned away from the Arkham series in the first place. Don't get me wrong, it is a beautifully crafted game with an interesting story. I'm just not sure that the story is enough to keep me engaged.
The worst of this (and all Arkham games) sins is the sense of reverse progression. In the beginning, you fight guys and beat them up for experience. You level up your abilities which should make you feel more like the superhero that you are. Instead, the game designers chose to negate your progression by introducing progressively more specialized bad guys for you to defeat. Sprinkle in some regular level baddies to keep you from using your special maneuvers and the game goes from fun to frustrating in no time flat. The constant respawn takes away any sense of true accomplishment. After going through the frustrating combat after combat, you turn around and see more bad guys where you just defeated them. It detracts from the mood of the story and the sense that you are in a living, breathing world.
It doesn't stop there though. I want to find whoever invented "collectables" in video games and fire them from a catapult. It is bad enough in games like Dragon Age: Inquisition where you have to collect all the shards and mosaic pieces in an area. Arkham Origins takes this a step further by showing you collectables that you will need then denying you access until much later in the game by requiring story unlocked gear. Hint to game designers: I DO NOT WANT TO GO BACK INTO AN AREA I CLEARED 20 HOURS AGO TO PICK UP A COLLECTABLE. That is not replayability nor extending gameplay. It is tedium.
On the plus side, the game has a fantastic soundtrack. The voice acting is solid as a young Batman meets a lot of his rogues gallery during the game. I miss Mark Hamill as the voice of the Joker, but Troy Baker does a very admirable job with the role. Similarly Roger Craig Smith did a good Batman voice. You can tell the differences, but it wasn't jarring nor did I dislike either role.
As mentioned above, the story is fantastic. Meeting a lot of the supporting cast and enemies during the course of the game is really fun. The time frame involved makes me a little jittery. All of the action is supposed to take place over the course of Christmas Eve  into Christmas morning. I understand the dramatic reasons for that, but the simple truth is that the times don't match up no matter how hard I try to make them. It takes me from the story. I think it would have been better to space the story out over a week or so leading up to the Christmas finale.
I wanted very much to like this game but there are too many little details that detract from an overall great story. I hope that somebody, somewhere will someday make a Batman game that captures the fun elements from this game while leaving the unpleasant "grindy" stuff out. 4/10

text:
Though perhaps odd, this is my favorite game of 2015 (that's when I bought it in a bundle, it was released in 2014). Eidolon is not for everyone: There is very little action. Instead there is a beautiful world, portrayed in a fashion similar to that of Proteus. The game is very peaceful and simplistic. Hunting and fishing are presented in a minimal fashion as activities in the game but are almost an afterthought. You can also die from cold, but there is no permanent death and you are instead respawned, seemingly at random, to a location within one of the games healing swamps.
I believe that many people may be turned off by the endless walking with no apparent goal. There is however a simple beauty behind the story as it is told via pieces of scattered journals located across the map, represented visually as glowing blue orbs. The games apocalyptic tale is revealed in piecemeal fashion  but there is a timeline that slowly unfolds as you gather more documents/orbs.
To enjoy this game, you must be patient, as before mentioned, the endless walking is most certainly not for everyone. But the wonderful pastel color palette is soothing, the music is fantastic and adds to the overall experience.  In this game,  I felt more absorbed in the games world than I do in many more "modern" games. I felt like I was exploring a lost, lonely and decayed civilization. A bird I adopted as my spirit guide would lead the way to new journals, of which there are over 150 entries.
This is my first and potentially last Steam review. However this game impacted me in a way I would not have expected. Though I have collected all of the journals,  after playing viridi ( their recently released virtual plant potting simulator) I now have the itch to reinstall and play again, the first 43 hours I put in the game apparently were not enough.
I think. I liked it. But I grew impatient almost immediately. Definitely going to try once more when I'm more relaxed and patient. Beautiful game though.

I would love to play this game, it really looks great, but I can't because I have an Nvidia video card. It's okay that the game doesn't support any system, but I didn't read the system requirements (where it's explained) before I bought it, since my computer should be more than good enough. When excluding most of Mac users from playing the game, it should be written VERY clearly. I suggest to include the info as the first image in the slide show at the top of this page and everywhere else possible as well. That should be a pretty obvious thing to do in order to let people know that they're most likely wasting their money, if they have a Mac and buy the game.

Eidolon is a fantastic experience, but it requires an unthinking of modern impatience in gaming. You should take your time with this one, wandering the woods to uncover the story told here.
The Journey in Eidolon is yours to make. Rarely is a game this brave when it comes to leaving the game to be explored by the player himself. Even though there is a survival system, hunting, fishing, items that allow for more abilities, a story to follow... the strength of the game doesnt necessarily lie in that traditional kind of progress. This game makes you want to explore like rarely any other. Haunting nights, simplistic and equally beautiful day and night shifts and a sense of "belonging". This game deserves to be heralded for its efforts to deviate from open world norms, which put more and more emphasis on flashy side attractions and instead focuses on the meditative beauty of the journey... your journey.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.
Eat.
