Everybody's Gone to the Rapture is a very story-centric walking simulator. There's no fighting, no enemies, you walk around and uncover the story as you go along using radios, phones and scenes that appear from the past at certain points.
The graphics are really beautiful, with the scenery from the English countryside at every turn, including different weather patterns and times of day. If you're into that sort of thing, the game is really a lovely time just for that. I took many screenshots just cause it was so good looking.
Again, being a walking simulator you can expect to do one thing - walk...a lot. If that's not your thing, then pass on by, but if you've played games like FireWatch or The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, you will most likely enjoy this game.
The story is slowly uncovered by progressing through the game as you arrive in a lovely English town out in the country only to find that no one is there. The mystery of why and how is revealed through the course of the game. For the most part the game never holds your hand, you are free to walk around, explore houses, yards etc. A lot of the story scenes are only discovered, in fact, by doing it this way.
You are guided through the MAIN story scenes by a mysterious ball of light, which will wait for you if you go off wandering, so never fear of missing out. Of course you can miss things by progressing, and need to turn back, so you will have to figure it out by yourself.
You also run across radios and phones which you can listen on previous conversations and messages that help reveal more of the story. The side scenes, as I said, are discovered mostly by just walking around, there's no indication that they're there until you walk into it.
At this point I'd like to say the voice acting is very well done, making such scenes and messages interesting as well as engaging. I'd also like to say the overall production is top notch: the music, the voice acting, the little details here and there, the graphics, everything invites you to just enjoy the journey, you never know what you'll find.
By the end you'll have met many people, in a way, and I personally will replay again sometime in the future.
A couple of nitpicks - the game has an auto save system that only saves after certain things, which can be pretty far apart. They are looking to patch in a manual save system, which is currently in Beta if you check the forums. I applaud this as some saves were 15 minutes or more apart, and I'd not want to have to redo everything from that point.
The other thing is the walking speed - even "Running" doesn't feel much different than walking. It's a small point, but it would have been nice to have about twice the speed normally, given how long it can take to get from one point or another, or if you backtrack.
I highly recommend this game to anyone interested in beautiful scenery and an interesting story that will draw you in. It's a great way to pass the time if you're just wanting to relax, it can be very calming indeed.

This is one of those games I kind of wish I had a MIXED feelings button for.  Let's go over Everybody's Gone to the Rapture here, and explain why.....  So, Sony's Santa Monica Studios decided to deliver us a Steam port of this very interesting Walking Sim, about a scientist who is the only one left in town alive it seems to determine what happen to the town as it was getting ripped apart.  This is a pretty good story on paper, and I enjoy the idea of the "last person on Earth" feeling.  To keep this review simple, i'm gonna be quick about this on it's Pros and Cons...
PROS
*Fun Story
*Great voice acting
*Relaxing
*Good writing
*Controls...Work
*Beautiful environment
Now, the Cons, and this is where I feel torn..
CONS
*Optimzing issues (Ran on all settings and they all work the same, and have the same frame issues, so I played on Very High)
*2 MINUTES to load your progress
*Frame Rate issues (Sometime's i'm running 60 frames per second, and then with no warning or reason, it'll do a sharp drop to 30 or 25)
*Can't run, and the town is big
This all together is where it's leaving my torn. We have a really good idea for a game under the shell, but this port however has issues.  With that being said, i'm going to recommend it, but on a very thin minimum reason why. This is a good game at heart, but shouldn't be totally avoided. If you want to get into this and try, get it only on sale.

While not my favorite entry in the Max Payne franchise, Max Payne 2 is still an excellent, though short game. The gameplay is inherently the same as the first title, though there are several changes to the trademark bullet time mechanic. For one thing, it can be used basically in every fight. As Max kills more enemies, time slows down even more, which also you to reload faster, in an appropriatly cinematic fashion. The visuals are also essentially the same as the first game, with the welcome addition of ragdoll physics- blowing random thugs away is much more satifying. The storytelling is again similar, with the comic book style cutscenes overlayed with Max's familiar deadpan. To me, the story is the best part of the game. It ties in closely to the original game and features many of the same characters. Without going into to much detail, there are many twists across the game's 5 to 6 hour length. The relationship between Max and Mona is especially good, though I wish the sequences where you play as her stood out a bit more, as she plays exactly the same as Max. Sam Lake's writing is solid and I would say a tad better than the first game, several of Max's quips are very poetic and the ending of the game left me thinking.
All in all, I would recomend this game to any Max Payne fan, though I urge anyone to check of the first game before playing this one!

The presentation is excellent. The visuals are breathtakingly gorgeous. The sound effects and music contribute significantly towards the game's impressive atmosphere. The level design is impressive; exploration is rewarded and backtracking, when used, is never dull. The game always finds a way to reuse existing areas. The gameplay is tense and exploration feels rewarding. New abilities are steadily introduced but at no point (excluding the intro) does your character feel gimped. The player is presented with a lot of different environmental mechanics - all of them are effectively used. I recommend Ori and the Blind Forest for everyone, especially fans of 2D platforming/metroidvania titles.

This game is just so beautifully done, from the obviously beautiful graphics, to the music, to the perfectly done controls, to the animations, to the world design, to the story, Ori and the Blind Forest is just an incredible game.
If you have any interest in metroidvania games or the idea of games being art, this game is an absolute must buy for you. Back before LEGO games started using actual dialogue came LEGO Batman. LEGO Batman is one of the original themed LEGO games and it follows the adventures of Batman and Robin as they take on numerous villains from the Batman Universe. There are three 'episodes' that each contain 5 levels, so 15 levels in total. Most levels have some sort of boss fight where you fight a specific villain (such as Mad Hatter, Killer Moth, Mr. Freeze, etc.). At the last mission of each episode, you have to fight the main baddy. This could either be Riddler, Penguin, or Joker (depending on which episode you're on). All of the levels are incredibly fun and action-packed!
Since Batman games are famous for their combat (looking at you, Arkham City!), how good is the combat in this? Well, if you've played any of the other LEGO games before this, the combat is pretty similiar throughout. You can punch guys, hit guys with different melee weapons (Like Nightwing's stick thingys (Yes, I know the actual name for them, I just like 'stick thingys')), shoot guys, and even throw batarangs at them! Best of all, you can blow them up Michael Bay style!
This game was pretty creative back in the day (in terms of LEGO games) with its mechanics. First off, you can use a grappling hook in certain segments to get up higher (Kind of like in Lego Star Wars, but this one you can control). Also, this is the first LEGO game to include a tightrope to get from one building to another.
Whilst playing a LEGO game, have you ever thought, "Wow, I like this character, but I wish they had more abilities" ? Well, in this game, there are different suits for Batman! Batman has a suit that allows him to glide, one that makes it so he can place bombs and blow them up, and one that can break glass.
All you Robin fans out there don't worry, Robin didn't get the short stick. Robin also has different suits, like a suit that allows him to walk up metal surfaces (Magnet suit), a scuba suit, a technology suit that he can use to control a RC car/do other things, and the attract suit (which I like to call 'the sucky suit') that, when activated, sucks up red, green, and yellow pieces that are used to build things (When you have 24 pieces). You find these suits throughout the missions. Also, when you unlock Batgirl and Nightwing, Batgirl can use Batman's suits and Nightwing can use Robin's ;)
This game can be pretty toxic sometimes, thanks to the introduction to toxic waste. Think of it like lava, you can't walk through it...well, unless you're  a character that has that ability (Like Joker). This is also the first game that uses the strength ability, where some characters are super strong and can pull these orange handles that are attached to heavy objects. By doing this, they can move these objects (which usually block the way to something).
Like all LEGO games, there are tons of characters to try out! If you're familiar with Batman, you'll definitely recognize some of these iconic characters! In the levels, there are also 'mini-kits' to collect. If you're not familiar with 'mini-kits', they're these collectable pieces that unlock things. When you play the game, you'll also hear the iconic Batman music Danny Elfman created, which is a nice touch. Now, I know what you're thinking , "I think this guy has covered it all."
But wait, there's more! There's actually 'counter levels' to the main levels. Ever wondered what the villains do before Batman and Robin show up? Well, you can play through each level as the villains in separate villain levels (And yes, these are different than the main levels).
Overall, this game is absolutely amazing! If you're a Batman fan or a LEGO game fan, I highly recommend checking this one out!

It's like Mountain, only less philosophical.

I really want to recommend this game, but I can't. It's pretty (for 2003), expansive (enormous and empty), has a good story (chopped up and scattered over literally hundreds of square miles of identical forest), and has a nice blend of exploration and exposition (gimmicky survival elements slapped over a walking simulator).
Joking aside, I honestly can't recommend this game to a wide audience. Yes, it has a good story, one that is leagues better than that of a lot of modern games, but even though that story is so interesting, the method of actually uncovering the story is painfully dull. I do like it when a game rewards exploration, and I love it when a game will focus on story rather than the old tried-and-true 'shoot anything that's not the same color as you', but the massive amount of story (150+ items, or so I hear) is diluted so badly by the amount of walking you need to do to find them that even though I was hooked, I couldn't come back to it after a while because finding another thread of the story was not worth holding down my shift and W keys (yes, I know there are auto-walk and auto-run settings, but don't you think that's a symptom of the problem?) for another half hour, occasionally stopping to click on story fragments to watch the green flare point to the next story fragment or eat some fish.
It seems like Eidolon is trying to marry purely story/exploration based games like Kentucky Route Zero and solo survival games like The Forest, and I can't say I'm a huge fan of what resulted from it. The survival mechanics are barebones, but in such a way that it's not an added challenge to survive a day, more of just an added 'collect these unrelated items to continue' minigame. I won't rip on survival mechanics being unrealistic, they're minimalistic and that's understandable, but it seems like it's too easy to survive. All you need to be able to run for a day is two cooked fish, that's it, and after you find the fishing rod, you can get fish within about a minute or two of walking from nearly any point on the map. In fact, the only ways to die are starving (via illness or stubbornness), falling to your death, getting mauled by a bear (I never saw one), and freezing to death. If you don't jump off cliffs continuously, catch more than one fish a day or press E every time you see a prompt come up for mushrooms or berries, and don't stand in water for too long, you won't die. It's more of an added chore than an added challenge.
The art design is sort of a balance between 'minimalistic' and 'lazy', with everything in the game rendered with solid-color polygons, which in the right circumstances can be quite pretty, but most of the time is just bland. For the lazy part, some of the design is just cutting corners. If you're not within 30 yards of a fox, deer, or other animal, they either stand stock-still like a statue or glide around in the same pose a few inches off the ground. Objects are almost always half in the ground, half floating in the air since they don't really account for local geometry. Skyscraper remnants are strangely even more low-res than the rest of the game, with blurry, off-color edges.
The rest of the game is quite well executed, though, the story is intriguing and engaging, the music is appropriately minimalistic and atmospheric, and the game occasionally has moments where I need to stop and take a screenshot. However, unless you're a fan of walking very long distances to read single pages of books, I can't recommend this game to you. I think that the story would probably be better executed as a collection of vignettes and the rest of the game as a minimalist but immersive and difficult survival game, but that's just me.

Once again I go head to head with Spec Ops: The Line. I think this might be the game that has frustrated me the most as somebody who enjoys a good story based game that leaves an impact on you. Not only did Spec Ops: The Line's story fall completely flat, but the gameplay did it no favours either.
Spec Ops: The Line is a gritty yellow and grey third person cover based shooter where you play as a hoorah military man sent to dubai to attempt and fix a situation that has gone completely south. Things proceed to get worse and worse, leading to a climax where you make a choice that changes your ending.
This sounds like the most generic concept for a shooter ever, and it is. But before we continue on, It's important to note when this game was released. June 2012 was during the period where people were just starting to get tired of these yellowed desert war shooters, similar to how people are slowly getting tired of open world games now. This was a time period where literally everyone and their dog was still talking about Modern Warfare 2 and 3, and every shooter that came out was trying to be them. I think Spec Ops: The Line is partially a frustrated response to these tired shooters, and we should acknowledge that. However, to me, this doesn't excuse any of Spec Ops: The Line's problems.
Spec Ops: The Line is largely bogged down by it's mediocre story, choiceless actions, and absolutely abysmal gameplay. The part where this gets more complicated with all three of these things is that it's very clear that in a way they are deconstructing the genre at that time and it's conventions in those areas.
Spec Ops: The Line's story is often what the game is heralded for. As previously explained, you and a small group of soldiers go knee deep into dubai to clean up somebody else's mess as a bunch of military groups occupying the region have begun infighting. The character development of your team is handled very well- at first they seem like the kind of people you'd stop giving a♥♥♥♥♥♥about 20 minutes into the game, but when push comes to shove they begin to each grow different arcs that all climax throughout the story. Even the main character, while having potentially offensive interpretations of war related PTSD near the end, has a semi-decent growth and conclusion. It's too bad that all of this completely gets sat on by the message of the game, which is trying it's best to shove itself down your throat.
It's honestly hard to continue from here without spoiling things, but I'll try my best. The main problem with Spec Ops: The Line's storyTELLING (not the story itself) is that it constantly wants to show you how bad a person you are both in the game and past the fourth wall. I'm not entirely sure if this is just because it's aimed at the dudebro audience that loves violence and shooting things or the developers just think you're an idiot for purchasing the game. This leads to the game explaining extremely basic, overdone messages to you like you're four years old and constantly wagging it's finger at you like you were a dog that just crapped on the carpet. You are given choices, but both choices always mean nothing. Either the other choice you didn't choose happens immediately after anyways, or the person/thing you saved/did whatever with just goes "thanks!" and never shows up ever again. But no matter what you choose in these choice segments, expect to be berated for it. Your teammates and the game's tone itself will constantly remind you that you are literally hitler and did a bad thing by choosing the action you chose. This is extremely obvious at probably the most famous scene in the game, in which you have no choice but to do an action. Then for the rest of the game, you are yelled at for doing it. The only thing stopping you from not doing it is an invisible wall, as it's been previously established through past fights that the threat in front of you is no match for your arnold schwarzenegger accuracy and powerful grenade launcher. The game itself is stopping you, not the narrative. This may all be the point and what the game is trying to tell the players- that you have no choice when war is involved and every action you take is a bad one. But is a slightly more complicated message than "war is bad" really worth tanking an entire pretty decent story for?
The storytelling itself is also not done any favours by the absolutely abysmal gameplay. At the very least the gameplay could compliment the story and message by making things more dire and hard to deal with as time goes on, but it doesn't even
to go that far. It is THE most generic third person shooter you might ever play in your life, and plays exactly like those terrible Kane and Lynch games I try and forget about every time I look at my PS3 collection. It's actually even worse than other generic third person shooters: multiple actions are mapped to the same button, the snapping to cover is buggy (sometimes you'll just run past cover into a guy's gun), grenade trajectory is faulty and sometimes acts completely different than expected, and at points cover that should be protecting you randomly fails to do so as a bullet clips through concrete straight into your head. The game advertises "[commanding] an intelligent and powerful squad of Delta-Force soldiers" when realistically you just press a button on your keyboard and one of your dudes eventually decides to shoot the guy you're looking at. Sure, you could say this is all to accentuate the point of third person cover based shooters being boring and terrible and compliment the deconstructivist view of the military genre at a whole, but beyond the gameplay being ♥♥♥♥ing bad it makes no attempt to match itself to the story. You are in a water starved, sand ravaged dubai, yet everyone has infinite ammo and act livelier than ever. You constantly regenerate health despite being beat to♥♥♥♥♥♥through cutscenes and having no further medical supplies or water. The city is buried in sand, yet the most that comes into play is three points in the game where you can shoot a window and sand comes out, and a sandstorm part near the end that has barely any bearing on gameplay. Things get more mentally tough for your crew, yet they still scream "♥♥♥♥IN A" and "HOOAH" whenever you kill somebody, and other than a hilarious hallucination part at the end your mental state has no impact on gameplay other than walking segments and a way too "trying to be deep" ending.
I'm running out of space so I'll make it brief: Spec Ops: The Line may be a visually gorgeous game (its goddamn beautiful), but has a story that is euthanized by it's own storytelling and gameplay. These two problems gangbeat the whole point of this game down, making what could have been a great timepiece of gaming in 2012 and a decent look at the horrors of war into little more than a dying whimper of a good concept. I appreciate it's attempt, but it just doesn't work.
I feel like the only way you can positively look at Spec Ops: The Line is by blinding yourself to it's negatives just because the negatives are intentional without looking at how the negatives actually impact the experience.

A side game mode born from a mere project 9 years ago became one of the most known CoD playlist to this day. Casual or hardcore Zombies is appealing to everyone that's a fan of smashing hordes of unending undead that charge at you from every corner of the map. Sadly it will never receive full attention from 3arch since Activi$ion's main focus is only revenue, yet 3arch has managed to enrich it title by title accomplishing what Zombies is known as today. Grief is also an exclusive sub game mode to BOII which puts 4 players against 4 players in team deathmatch Zombies style existent in 3 maps.
Definitely one of the most hated if not most hated map to this day, many people don't realize without this test map we wouldn't have the buildables system that is present in every map after TranZit. A very eerie experience with the whole area covered in fog haunted by little creatures that hug your face every time you trespass their territory. Map also features a bus drove by one auto-bot that doesn't appreciate hostility towards it and will kick you out mercilessly leaving you fresh dinner for the undead. While it lacks a powerful wonder weapon TranZit can be played as survival in closed off areas which brings a bit easier time surviving all around. While Town & Farm are albeit smaller similar to classic survival maps Bus Depot is truly a hardcore zone with nothing but the mystery box.
In my opinion the least played and talked about 3rc brought this map originally from BO in BOII in both MP and Zombies, while it is indeed small it's packed with a bunch of easter eggs that tell pieces of the story. Absence of a wonder weapon which would have filled many strategies' missing link is not enough to ruin and belittle it that many exiled it for; Nuketown is a hardcore mini-map designed not for the faint-hearted where perks drop near you from the freakin' Moon. It's little known the events in Nevada occur at the same time as the events in the last BO map, Moon, if you survive enough time you can tell by clues that pop up.
One of the least memorable BOII maps Skyscraper features a unique map design within Zombies universe with lots of heights. Classic perk-a-cola PhD Flopper is teased but unreachable; truth be told it would ruin the whole idea of the map taking no fall damage. The Hellhound round also returns introducing Jumping Jacks, agile cousins of gas zombies that teleport and jump from ceiling to your face however their low health makes up for the annoyance. 3arc tried to innovate a new Quick Revive but from many's point of view failed to do so as Who's Who is a gamble depending on whichever area of the map you got downed.
Creepiest experience by far in the BOII universe that occurs within the famous Alcatraz Island featuring a new game mechanic called Afterlife mode. It can be used in various ways such as self or reviving teammates, levitate through walls/doors opening up parts of the map or simply zapping zombies away teleporting them to ease up your recovery after being downed. It's one of the few maps with an upgradable wonder weapon that's mandatory in a long term strategy against the waves of endless undead. Sunset Strip also starring the notorious Brutus a fearsome mini-boss that doesn't have it's own round but randomly spawns whenever you use the mystery box too much or apart every few rounds; while not as deadly he's a tank that will chase you throughout the whole island given that you don't have a powerful weapon to rid him rapidly.
Well known to be the easiest map that only casual fans tend to enjoy the map brings more than few new things to the Zombies experience. NPC you can ignore or aid in which he'll give you an easier time surviving in this old west town. To pack-a-punch your weapons you'll have to trespass a mansion haunted by ghosts that will steal your hard earned points, then finding your path through a maze which changes it's layout every time you exit it. What brings down the difficulty is how little effort you need to survive being able to use 3 traps that instantly kill zombies at the same time, same location.
Fan's favorite and the biggest non stop action packed map featured in BOII with arguably most fun mechanics and replay value. When you talk about Dig Site you can't help but remember the 4 different iconic staffs which overpower the undead in a fashionable way with blizzards, lava, tornados and lightning chains. Aside that you can ride a freakin' tank throughout the map while falcon punching the undead meters away showing 'em who's boss, nevermind the G-Strike nades rainstorming the field with napalm. Undeniably Origins has an abundance of things to do for hours with a single downside tons of mini-puzzles required to unlock them.
> very high replay value
> weapon diversity & customization
> well thought map design
> intriguing story & easter eggs
> good optimization (at launch)
> connection crash (p2p)
> lack of mod support
> activi$ion pricing

The end of an era, and arguably the best title in the series. After this game, the developers changed engine and most of what made this franchise famous was lost.
There was never anything too flashy and glamorous about Call of Duty : Solid gunplay , good weapon variety and great map design. By trying to always be the next cool kids thing, the next iterations lost those core elements in favor of arena gameplay jumping and moba class skills.
You could argue that the series would be more beloved if it had not fallen victim to the Ubisoft syndrome : A greedy publisher spreading the name too thin.
At any rate, if you are interested in a solid competitive multiplayer platform and, to an extent, a piece of video game history, give this one a try!

I silently wend my way through derelict streets where the only light comes from the abandoned police cruiser  up ahead. I check to see how much ammunition I have left in my 686 revolver and it's almost full. Then I hear a slow moan come from the darkness on my right, so I flick on my flashlight to see how many of them are there. It looks like 5 of them but my light also picks up a glint of green and white on a small box, and that means 12 gauge for my Mossberg 500. The shamblers are already approaching and I take careful aim.  The first of the group falls with one shot, and I've already lined up the next. I fire and I turn her head into a canoe. As I slowly back up to keep distance, I realize that I've cornered myself. No matter though, as I have enough bullets to finish the fight.
The next two fall with each successive trigger pull and the last is two feet away. I fire and graze his ear... I quickly line up another shot and... click.♥♥♥♥♥♥ I pull out my shotgun and bring up the sights... click. I realize that I forgot to reload after the last encounter.  Now it's too late and his teeth sink into my arm as I shove him violently away. I then pull out my machete and bury it into his skull. He slumps sideways and I step over his body to retrieve my spoils, but my vision goes blurry and my skin prickles and crawls. I know it's only a matter of time now before I share their fate and turn. I calmly walk over to the shotgun shells and take inventory. I have 10 shells now, which means I have 9 zombies to blow away before that last shell ends me... This scenario actually happened, and it's a new experience each time you play. This game is the closest thing to zombie apocalypse training you will come by.  The zombies are slow and traditional unless they have been freshly turned.  In which case they run quickly towards you and make it extremely difficult to line up that critical headshot.  Which also makes it more interesting when someone in your party gets the infection.  Do you take the time and effort to find the medicine that will slow the change and risk him turning into a speed demon? Or do you end it quickly and take whatever gear he was carrying. More than once I found myself infected and I wound up dropping all of the gear I had and sprinting headlong into a horde in order to buy my friends time to slip by.  It's those moments that make this game truly special.
The cardinal rule is also broken in this game, because it features zombie children.  They are few and far between but that makes encountering them all the more disturbing.  The guns are the most realistic I have ever played, and that is a true compliment.  Never before have I seen a better depiction than NMRiH. The models and animations are SPOT ON, as is the time it takes to reload.  You have to physically check your magazine to know an exact count if you've lost track, and that makes the tension rise.  Attention to detail is astounding, as the more you play the more you realize how much effort went toward making this beautiful game.  Forget realistic hunting simulators, if you're looking for gun porn it's right here. If you are using a mic in game people can only hear you when you are within a certain distance.  Zombie Apocalypse Simulator  has arrived and it is a joy to play. NMRiH is also free so there is no damned excuse for you not to enjoy the delightful horrors within. 9/10

The gameplay was a lot of fun.  There are multiple weapons and different combos to use that keep the game fresh.  I know that the style meter is supposed to be a big draw, and perhaps to some people it i, but I rarely paid attention to it.
You get most of your equipment pretty early in the game, which makes the gameplay pretty deep and fun right from the beginning.  You can get some neat combos going, and some of the enemies require different weapons to damage them.  That sounds tedious at first, but makes you plan out some battes once the game starts mixing the enemies it throws at you.
Speaking of enemies: I have heard some complaints about the enemies, but I thought they were done pretty well.  Some of them are pallette swaps, (which just means they are succeptible to different attacks) or just upgraded versions that take more hits, but there are some that are completely unique and can be fairly challenging when they appear with a horde of different minions.
The graphics are pretty good, and the stages do have some variability to them that makes them feel fresh, without getting too stale.  One of the best parts of the world, are the morphing of the world around you as it changes.  Looking down a hallway as the exit zooms away from you is a really cool effect.
The game will also give you hints at how to kill certain enemies, but only after you have fought the enemy a couple of times, which means you still have time to figure out your favorite way to kill a type of enemy before the game just says, "yeah, this is how we meant for you to do it."
Combat - One of the main draws from the original Devil May Cry was that you used a sword AND guns.  Your starting guns in this game, the pistols Ebony and Ivory, are absolutely terrible.  I never used them unless I was fighting the one enemy in the game that was only vulnerable to bullets.
Bosses -
[strike[all the boss battles[/strike] all the boss battles except
are dissapointingly easy, and tedious.  Most of them go a little something like this: fight to expose boss weakness, hit boss weakness, repeat steps one and two.
Characters - The characters in this game are so bland, so boring, so awful.  Hands down the worst part of this game.  I feel like every review touches on how Dante is terrible in this game, and it is true.  Dante is supposed to be cool, but he is just an absolute♥♥♥♥♥♥  Every time he said something,  all I could think was, what-a-tool.
Story - There never was anything surprising about the story.  There were some things that just confused me, like how the real world interacts with Limbo, and vice versa (the rules seem to change depending on how the story writers wanted craete tension).
the main problems with the game don't prevent you from enjoying yourself as you are actually controlling the game.  You may just want to hate yourself during the cutscenes.  With that in mind, the game is really enjoyable, and provided me with a bit of fun.  There are a fair amount of levels, it isn't too short, it isn't too long.  And if you enjoy challenges there are quite a few higher difficulty levels that allow you to have some replayability.

Only a clarification before all - MaxPayne, the original one from 2001 was a far superior product.
Max Payne 2 recycled everything strong about it . Lacking though the doomsday gloom of the 90's occult gothic. Though often unnamed - that's what added the spice to the tragedy. Instead it attempts to portray that tragedy replayed as Max tries to overcome it.
The story of this game seems rather a rehash of the previous levels with new skins, physics, weapons and so on.
What is left of Noir, is buried under the monotonous (in the bad sense of the word) interiors. Build sites, endless apartment halls, streets and only by the end some sort of a palace with many awkward and glitchy moments.
The strongest sequences are the beggining one, another one with the Police HQ... and that's all I remember memorable. I never understood why Max Payne 2 was good because the romance was weak, the antagonist was a joke and... overall it's just like making Die Hard 2 after Die Hard 1.
But how silly, insulting the cliffhanger comes around.
What were they thinking?
The game might be worth it for one playthrough to see if you enjoy the new "autumn" setting contrary to the winter "Ragnarok" of the first game.
It attempts to show a relationship

of the first game (and does so poorly in my opinion).
In fact, even the ending seems like a repetition of the first game's marvelous conclusion of an epic, whereas here - it seems as if I already played this somewhere... Stereotypes and old characters are back. Yet I would prefer them to remain in the dust as they unfolded, much, much more mysteriously and enigmatically in the previous game yet again.
Only for action fans.

The overall plot feels a bit lame if you compare it to the first game, but it has a lot of redeeming moments, and the gameplay and graphics have both been finetuned a lot since the first game, which makes it very enjoyable. It is definitely worth a play if you haven't played it before. As many classics, however, you have to keep in mind that the game is set in a different era of gaming, and that the gameplay isn't the same standard as it is today.
If you plan on playing Max Payne 3, you will definitely want to pick this one and the first one up as well.

This game is unique, to put it mildly. I can understand how some people got bored with it, but, for the right people this game will grab ahold of you and not let go. At times, there is a zen-like, meditative calm in which you float thru this homely yet alien world, untouched by the ruination. At times there is the feeling of utter desolation and fear, even anger at the long dead people who have left you so alone, One night I huddled against the overhang of a ruin, hiding behind the firelight. The next day, I climbed a mountain and stood alone, open to the world watching the sun rise and set and the rain, fog and clouds swirled around me. With no clue as to who or what I am, I vacillate between a noble phantom and low, mean, wild beast. *ahem* Not many games make you wax poetic like this. Not  many games achieve beauty with minimalistic graphics.  And once you get past all that, there are the stories....the eidolons (that word means spirit, soul, phantom). You can follow one at a time or wander freely. I've by no means found them all. I believe that will take a very long time. Yet, the glimpses you catch of lives long vanished are so engaging and enigmatic that you are driven to find more. There must be an explanation among these far-flung eidolons.
As for the practicalities, you can negotiate with compass and map, or let the terrain and foraging guide you. Both are rewarding enough. The basic survival tools are easy enough to acquire in the first few minutes if you keep your eyes open. There is no combat, unless you count shooting a deer or running from predators. The survival part of the game is basic common sense. Stay warm, dry, fed and rested. Armed with a fishing pole and a brain, this should prove quite easy.
TLDR: Just buy it if you've ever enjoyed a poem and don't expect FPS killkillkill constant stimulation.

Though I have not played Super Meat Boy for a long time. This was one of my most enjoyable games to play. The idea is simplistic, the controls are basic, the outcome is devastatingly fun.
Move right, left... Jump, run. Okay. Now you know everything you need to play the game. Jump gap. Get to objective. Next level. Jump gap. Fall to death. Re-spawn. Run. Jump Gap. Get to objective.
Every level teaches you that new skill you need to learn in order to accomplish later levels. After a while you have learnt all of the [mentioned above] basics. You have learnt to jump and bounce up walls. Wall too wall, platform to platform, mastering that running will allow your velocity to increase, meaning you can control jumps using the run, as well as left and right. You have also learnt the lessons. Spikes. Saws. Salt. fire. Fish. All bad. Do what ever you have learnt to avoid these. Now this game is all based on pure skill of the player.
Whilst you are playing, you will also unlock other characters, using bandages you have collected from the levels you have completed. These are found hidden in maps, often stopping you from getting the A+ if you go for both the bandage and the objective. But you can do the level two times, once for speed and once for the goodies. Other goodies also include vortex rifts, where you are able to play some retro SMB along side some other basement collection characters.
If you have not got this game. Get it.
If it is on offer, which it is often. 100% get it.

I should probably give my short thoughts about this game, considering that I have played this game a lot and is mostly fun for me. Here we go:
Pros:
+Graphics and scenery are amazing. The maps not only look good, but are well designed for this kind of gameplay. Sapienza and Hokkaido are my favorite maps out of all.
+Sound design is even better than the graphics in my opinion. Snapping necks never felt so good.
+Music is alright. Fits with the action you commit (so it's dynamic), but isn't interesting when listened separately.
+Fairly good amount of options for PRO players. Such as switching off instinct and opportunities. Fits for players of all skill levels. Also includes professional level.
+Many ways to eliminate targets. Sniping, silenced pistol, poison, drowning, different sort of accidents and of course, snapping necks.
+High replay value. The game includes a lot of challenges for fun and some of them give you items, which you can use for all missions.
+Other challenges and special missions. Elusive targets for example can only be killed once and if you die during the mission, you can't restart it. Plan your assassination with ease and care.
+The game can sometimes be hilarious for various reasons. Check videos on Youtube to find out.
Neutral:
*The game seems to be unstable for some people. I have encountered a few crash, but it doesn't happen that often, gladly.
*AI is serviceable, but really dumb. Also the way the AI/the game reacts to your actions is weird. There is a serial killer on a loose.....calling the cops or evacuating the whole area doesn't seem like a reasonable thing to do. How about we search the area for 30s and always take bodies to somewhere without proper investigation.
*Boring death animation. Not an issue, but I prefer full physics rather than pre-animated deaths.
Cons:
-There's simply no good justification for DRM. Even though I haven't encountered any technical difficulties with it, it's plain stupid to punish all players because of a few pirates out there. This just makes the situation even worse. The players should have the ability to gain stuff without internet connection. It's a single player game after all.
-Lack of maps for 49,99€ game, budget issues or not.
-Lack of diverse voice acting. Why does every guard and civilian sound american even though you could be in Japan, Thailand or France.
-Will eventually get repetitive and you spend most of the time screwing around.

Maybe I was lucky, but the online-only thing hasn't caused a single issue or crash in my 50 hours of playing Hitman. So I'd advise you to be cautious of the naysayers. In my opinion this is an absolutely marvelous game. It was made with lots of love and it lets you feel it. As I am writing this review (in 2017) the game runs smoothly and the loading times are very fast which is important in a Hitman game - I do have a good rig though.
Here are some things I love about this game:
- The levels are nothing less than gooorgeous! Best level design I have ever experienced in a game. So many ways to do your thing, so many things to discover. A lot of love was put into these maps. They are huge, complex and full of life!
- Some of these maps I have played over 30 times and I still keep coming back to them. Replayability is A+, which has always been the major plus for Hitman games (except Absolution).
- The game is easy to learn, hard to master.
- Contracts and Escalations give you an even greater amount of replayability.
- You feel like a badass Hitman. You can just kill everyone or you can sneak your way to your target without leaving any trace. It's completely up to you.
- Professional mode is cool. Once you reach level 20 on a level you unlock Professional mode on that level which makes it much harder and removes a lot of the easy ways to get to your goal. It's great to experience a level that you have played 30+ times already again with fresh challenges.
- The NPC dialogue is hilarious. According to the developers there is more dialogue in this game than in the entire LOTR novels, and it shows. Listening to the NPCs keeps making me smile.
- Music is great.
- Sound is great.
- David Bateson's voice is back again and a joy to listen to. I wish this guy would have played Agent 47 in the Hitman movies as well.
- HUD costumizabilty is great. Remove everything for a challenging game or leave it all on to make it easy.
- Graphics are great.
- Controls are great.
- Unlockables motivate you to retry the level again and again.
What I don't like:
- The scoring system is too simple. I would love to be able to filter leaderboards for certain conditions such as starting locations, weapons, challenges, etc. There's so much more potential in the leaderboards and the devs should improve them.
- Gunsounds are bad.
- Most of the cutscenes are boring. I wish they would have just ignored cutscenes completely and focused their time on a better scoring system. I love good story but in this game it is completely irrelevant in my opinion.
- It would be nice to have the extra Escalation completion conditions (not the 5 stages system) available when creating contracts.
I am surprised on how much fun this game is. I was sceptical because of buying into too many negative reviews.
Definitely one of my favorite games of the past couple of years.

I will preface this with a statement:
I wouldn't call myself an avid DmC fan. I have the other games. I've played them, and they were fun. Heard varying opinions of this game and got it on sale to see for myself. First off, a lot of the people saying its horrible and the spawn of Satan and the like are wrong. Kinda. It has its good points, it has its bad points, and it has quite a few just plain mediocre points, so I'll try and be as fair as I can here.
(Warning. Warning. A new Wall of Text approaches.)
First off, how does it play? Decently. Combat is nice and smooth, flows really well, but... it's not at all that difficult. Some of it just gets kind of silly too. Once the grab mechanics got introduced, I almost immediately figured out how to just return to my home planet without much difficulty at all. While things like this are usually possible, in this game it seems rather hilariously simple to discover and then spam them to your heart's content. Also, Dante's devil trigger is kind of silly. He freezes time, which would normally have me :D'ing, but then he flings everyone up into the air where they are annoying to hit, invalidating every single ground combo I have, basically. Anyway, I didn't find quite as much depth or challenge to the fighting mechanics as I would nessecarily like, but this is coming from a guy who loves Dark Souls and plays everything on the hardest difficulty he can, so my definition of challenge is a bit different from most casual players. Aside from being somewhat more simplistic than I expected, however, there isn't much of anything you can call a fault in the combat. It's pretty looking, very smooth, and kind of mediocre, really.
Plot? Look, let's be honest here, no one plays the original DMC games for the plot. That was one of the many mistakes they made with 2, in fact. That said, unlike the original games, which were trying harder to be entertaining that tell a really detailed story, this one has one. A rather large one that I'm not really a fan of. However, all matters of opinion aside for the most unbiased review, it's mostly another "Eh" from me. Despite usually being an obsessive gamer who watches every cutscene and searches for all the little details etc. I just wasn't that interested in the plot. It's there, yes. Is the writing horrible? No. Is it fatastic? No. Looking at it as a whole, I can't really say there is anything about it that ever goes above average. Some is below, most is right on the line, and none of it really gets very much further than that.
Next we have DmC Dante. Gonna say it straight out. I think he sucks. I don't find him funny or entertaining in any way, shape or form. This is without comparing him to the old Dante at all. had I never played another DMC in my life, I would still get a headache almost every time he opens his mouth. I have laughed at literally none of his jokes, I have completely failed to care about any of his actions at every turn, and in general just been unamused by his existence. He is whiny, thinks he is so cool for being a punk, blah blah blah blah I don't even want to listen to him any more. It seems from where I'm standing that the writers just went with any uninspired bit of excessive vulgarity they could come up with to make him seem "cool" and then went to lunch. That isn't me being a prude. What with all the time I spend online I'd probably have an aneurysm by now if I was. However, all of the teenage-class stupid that spews forth from his every orofice has gotten mindbogglingly old, so unless you giggle at "dirty words" there isn't much there that could possibly be called humor. Once in a while, he makes some comment that gets my hopes up and I think "Is this actually going to be witty and intelligent?" and then he finishes what he was saying and it all comes crashing back down to dull. And do I even need to bring up the infamous "**** YOU!" "NO, **** YOU!" exchage? he is absolutely the worst part of the game, as far as I'm concerned, and it says a lot that my feelings about any game can be summed up with "The main character is the worst thing about it."
Music... is really another matter of personal taste, I suppose. In my opinion, the main game's soundtrack sucks, but that's just because I hate most of that genre to begin with. That said, it suits the character just fine, so if that's what they were going for, great success! Considering that the Vergil's Downfall DLC switches to a totally different theme, it probably was what they intended. (That music is a little eh, too, though. It's there, it doesn't sound out of place, but it isn't stellar for the most part either. Maybe I haven't payed enough attention to it, but that it can't grab my attention does say quite a bit.)
With all said and done, my final opinion on this game is mostly just "Meh". If I had never bought it, I would be perfectly content with my life. If I had bought it full price, I would probably regret it a bit. It runs well, plays decently, and I can't say I wasted the time I spent on it any more than it would have been wasted on another game, but I still find the combat lacking the challenge I looked for, and the new Dante spent a good portion of the game giving me a headache before I just ragequit to play Vergil's Downfall for a while instead. My statements that the combat lacks depth should still be taken with a grain of salt, as the combat will probably be perfectly acceptable to most casual players, but if you are looking for all sorts of tricky shenanigans like in certain other games in this genre, you probably won't find a ton of them here. The plot was uninteresting, at least to me, and way too full of dropping anvils (That's TvTropes speak, for those uninitiated in that specific internet timesink) for me to take it seriously, and as characters I find the new cast bland at best and generally annoying at worst.
As far as I'm concerned, if it's on sale and you feel like it, sure, go ahead and get it, I suppose, but if I had a choice between this and DMC3 or 4, I'd leave this one sitting in my games library collecting digital dust, which I can say with complete certainty, because that would be what is happening this very instant, and will probably still be happening whenever you, whoever you are, come by this little corner of the web and read this particular post. However, since there is no button that says "Meh" and displays a shrugging stick figure, I guess I'll just say reccomended, with the imaginary caveat of "When it's on sale".

So here it is my first review on Steam. Enjoy it as I review one of my favorite games right now to play.
* Very easy to learn but hard to fully master it.
* Amazing Scenery and Graphics (You do need a good PC for the highest settings).
* A large map in the base game. You can drive in 12 countries including Luxembourg! (expanded in the DLC expansions).
* Up to 13 Trucks in the game spread across 7 brands, all fully licensed.
* Constantly being updated with new content.
* Possibility to create amazing screenshots.
* A very well made Truck Purchase System, you can buy Trucks easily which leads to...
* Great Truck Customization (You can customize it how you want).
* Realistic Truck and Physics Damage System.
* Some countries are very well designed in game like Switzerland, the Netherlands and Austria.
* A good community (except some bad eggs).
* A good variety of trailers to deliver to various different pickup points (You can transport everything from Basic Pressure Tanks up to Chemicals and Fuel).
* Great way to alleviate stress (most of the time).
* Finding all the Discoverables, while time consuming, is very rewarding.
* Steam Achievements and Trading Cards.
* Steam Workshop Connection.
* You can customize the way you play it in a variety of ways.
* World of Trucks connection(You can complete jobs online and from time to time win prizes in the World of Trucks site).
* Built-in Radio System (You can choose a variety of different Real life Radio Streams whilst driving if that is your preference or you can add in your own.).
* Built-in GPS System (Sometimes it gets a bit wonky, but use it if you want).
* No Multiplayer officially supported by SCS, however, there is a mod out there called ETS 2 MP that adds it.
* A Huge variety of mods to choose from that add new content into the game (You might need Going East and Scandinavia for some of them like Promods and TSM).
* Driving on Highways can be very boring for many people as it is tedious and monotonous.
* Some of the Scenery looks the same in many countries.
* The United Kingdom and Germany assets are reused from previous SCS games UK Truck Simulator and German Truck Simulator.
* Huge variety in customization like Paintjobs Packs and Cabin Accessories but you have to pay for them if you want them.
* To get the best out of the game you definitely need a Controller at least and/or a Driving Wheel.
* Some Highway exits can trick you.
* The AI can be very aggressive and may ram into you for no reason.
* France and Italy are not fully completed (In case of France this will be fixed soon).
* Some Pick-Up Points are tricky and it can be annoying to get into Quarries.
* There's a lack of variety on Highway Exits. (Many countries will have the same exits in multiple roads).
* To get 100% Map Completion you have to drive through some off road paths, which can be very annoying.

A wonderful experience, and a work of art.
The pros:
+ The story is layered into the whole world, not just in terms of narrative, but also in the various bits of context you gather up throughout the game; you can glimpse the personal history of each character, and this gives the world texture.
+ The soundscape is amazing. The voice acting is terrific; the background music is great; and the sound effects all around immerse you into both the narrative and the world.
+ The graphics are great; the light effects are incredibly well-rendered, as they are especially important to the story, but everything else is top notch quality.
The cons:
- The graphics are *really* heavy; my gaming rig was clearly suffering until I reduced the details from the defaults. I have a fairly beefy machine, and I still lost frames.
- The pacing of the "main character" is way too slow. Coupled with the frame drops, it makes walking around a slog. I know there's a "do a short sprint" key, but even with that you won't really be walking any faster.
- The interaction model to "unlock" parts of the narrative is a bit wonky, and you never know if it's working correctly.
All in all, I deeply enjoyed this game. I'll probably just play again a bunch of times just to squeeze every single bit of the world of Rapture.

I'll keep this short and sweet.
This is one of the best, and most frustrating games I have EVER played.
Yes, it's walking simulator, but the story is beautiful and gripping, and leaves you thinking about what it all meant for days following. Without ever seeing a single character, with only voices, you get to know each of them intimately, and grow to care about them throughout the course of the game.
And the soundtrack- SO. DANG. GOOD.
Now the bad- I have a decent computer, it's not the best, but it doesn't have trouble running games. I've NEVER had as many issues with other games as I did with this one. The lag. I had to turn down the resolution almost all the way, which is a bummer because this is a beautiful game. And the CRASHING. Over, and over, and over, making the game take twice as long, forcing me to repeat certain scenes, and miss out on a lot of the story because any time I tried to go certain places (like the windmill, for instance) I knew it would crash again. And since there's no manual save, you're basically screwed.
That being said- it's still a worthwhile game to be played. I just wish it ran better.

Ok, if you're like me and a bit squeemish and not into horror, don't worry!
Within 10 minutes of playing, I was getting characters telling me of nose bleeds, headaches and death. But don't be alarmed, you don't see any of it. I got concerned at that point, as I hate horror, but there's nothing graphic.
ANYWAY:
Really nice story driven experience.
Good for those who like walking simulator story type games. Amazing graphics and very detailed.
Quiet enjoyable, and nice and long (just under 6 hours to complete)
DETAILS:
The story is good, although it can be quite confusing at times. You never actually see the people that the story is about, just their silhouette, so it can be hard to remember which charater is which and you need to remember their names (something which I'm not that great at!)
Also, I'm sure I went the wrong way at some points. The story seemed to be a bit disjointed and out of order.
Maybe it's supposed to be like that though, as there are lots of smaller stories running through it too.
Final thought is this. I STILL have absolutely no idea what it is that has affected the villages in the game.
The game doesn't show anything graphic, but the language used is very philosophical and over complicated. It's something to do with light coming from somewhere that affects the telephones, but I still don't know how it came about, why it happened, or why it was causing people to have headaches, nosebleeds and eventually die.
I think it could be explained a bit better, as the ending to the game felt a little lazy compared to the rest of the game.
But it's still an interesting and exciting story.

In these wonderful times of ours, there are many first-person games that emphasize exploration. There are almost none that focus on it exclusively.
Eidolon has a few token survival elements - you need to eat, you can't leap off cliffs, and you can only spend so much time in freezing water - but they're window dressing. If you want mechanic or systemic challenge, look elsewhere.
Instead, Eidolon is a meditative exploration of a landscape. As a native of the Seattle area, it perfectly captures the sense of scale of our forests - dense yet empty, far sightlines from our mountains muddied by constant clouds and fog. The story uses the "fragmented narrator" method popularizied by System Shock to tell the story of this largely post-human world.
And it's slow. You will spend many minutes walking between finding notes or bits or narrative. You will get lost, and need to use your natural sense of landmarks, a compass, and a few maps to find where you are.
But there's nothing else like it, and it's one of the best before-bed games I've ever found; contemplative, calming, yet thought-provoking.

long lost child of the "Arkham" series. The combat system is pretty simple. If you don't already know you have one button to "strike" and another to "counter" with the ability to mix various gadgets in your combos rather fluently. There are also stealth sections throughout the game though they are pretty bland and don't have very much depth in my opinion. You are offered various methods of taking people down in the stealth sections, but I don't see much reason to use them when a silent takedown is the simplest, most effective way of taking enemies down. One thing to note in this game is that
.The ratio is something like for every 4 combat encounters there is a 1 stealth encounter. Even that ratio feels a little too generous though. There are many, many more upgrades in this game and a system t hat rewards experience based on a grade it gives you during encounters. However, the stealth upgrades are not nearly as good as getting the combat upgrades, especially since there are more combat sections. Otherwise the game is prettier and has a much better"feel" to it than its predecessors. The game is still enjoyable, but is tainted by an unwanted multiplayer and bad DLC. The Cold, Cold Heart DLC is fun, but the rest is just skins and challenge maps! I wanted to 100% this game like I did the other two, but multiplayer achievements and the fact that there is no "Perfect Knight" achievement makes me not want to at all. If you are choosing to either buy this game or one of the others, then buy one of the other two plays. Otherwise, it's still a fun game besides these things. and I would recommend getting it if you're a fan of the series.

BACON BROWNIES
4 oz bacon (thin rashers, finely chopped)
2 teaspoons golden syrup or corn syrup
10 tablespoons softened unsalted butter
1 ¼ cups soft light brown sugar
¾ cup unsweetened cocoa
1 cup all-purpose flour
1 teaspoon baking soda
4 large eggs. beaten
6 oz chopped bittersweet chocolate (or dark chocolate chips/morsels)
Preheat the oven to 190°C/375ºF and line a 25cm/10 inch square tin or a throwaway foil baking tray measuring 30cm x 20cm x 15cm / 12 x 8 x 6 inches.
Heat a heavy based (preferably non-stick) frying pan, and when warm, add the bacon bits and cook, stirring occasionally until they begin to crisp. Add the syrup, stir again to mix and transfer the sticky bacon bits to a cold surface, either on some foil or a plate. The syrupy bacon juices left behind are just delicious when mopped up with some bread: a cook’s treat!
Melt the butter over a gentle heat in a medium sized saucepan and when it’s melted, add the sugar, stirring with a wooden spoon.
Now take the pan off the heat and stir in the cocoa, flour, and baking soda. Next, add the beaten eggs and then stir again to mix.
Add the chocolate and the bacon bits, breaking them up with your hands if necessary. Fold together then pour and scrape into the tin.
Place in the oven to cook for 20-25 minutes; you want a little gooeyness inside still.
Transfer the tin to a wire rack and sit until cooled a little (but not to the point of coldness). Cut into 16 squares.

Pros:
-LEGO
-Batman
Cons:
-Everything else that matters in a video game.
This game succeeds by combining LEGO and Batman, and that's about it.  It's got all the quirky fun of every other property LEGO has churned out a game for, but it's frustratingly broken in so many ways.  Collision detection is unpredictable, the AI is moronic and will often fall somewhere between dying during or immediately after a two person puzzle (requiring another attempt) or straight up just failing to cooperate, the camera angles can be incredibly deceptive, and as a result of all this, the level designs, while aesthetically good, are terrible.
I don't know how many times I've fallen because I was looking half a degree to the right which caused my character to overshoot the platform by 5 feet.  Or all the times I jumped and went nowhere because I guess my toe was stuck on some invisible ledge in front of me?  Or the times I held "A" for a quarter second too long so Batman would glide instead of jump, causing me to completely miss the mark.  Or all the times I stood on the stairs instead of walking up them--something I would expect to be possible since they're STAIRS.*
This game should be good, and the first level plays fine for the most part.  After that, numerous levels have constant issues that aren't in any way a result of gameplay mechanics or otherwise poorly conceived concepts--those are all as good and familiar as you'd expect if you've played any other LEGO games.  It's the execution that makes this game borderline terrible.  I don't understand the problem.  I might chock it up to being the first in the series, but this is merely the first Batman game in the series.  This is not their first rodeo with the LEGO games property.  Then again, maybe it's just an issue with porting to PC.  Who knows?
I haven't played the rest, but I can only hope and assume they at least fixed these problems.  Then again, maybe they didn't.  Unless you're like me and insist on playing through game series from the beginning, there's no reason to grab this one.  Skip ahead to 2 or 3.  It's not like you're exactly missing out on important story elements or character development.  I'll no doubt complete this game before I move on, but I won't enjoy it.
Having completed the game (story-wise; still only about 70% total completion with regards to secrets and unlockables), here are a few updated thoughts:
Regarding the stairs issue, it seems that turning on V-Sync is a fix for this.  Most of my previous criticisms still stand, but certain almost game breaking glitches (walking up stairs, driving remote controlled cars up ramps, etc) seem to be resolved by turning on V-Sync.  If you're having issues, try that as a quick fix.
The villains storylines are FAR better than the Heroes storyline.  The lack of boss fights is a bummer, but some of the boss fights are painfully bad.  Harley Quinn, for example, will backflip away if you get close.  How do you beat her?  Just chase her around the circular room until she gets dizzy, hit her a couple times, beat up some baddies, repeat.  That's it.  I know LEGO games aren't known for their difficulty, but there is ZERO challenge in this fight (and many others).  It's like they designed it to be a waste of time.  So missing boss battles isn't really always a bad thing.
Where it shines is that the two villains you get are chosen specifically to navigate the level.  There are plenty of secrets that must be accessed with other villains in Free Play, but you can make it through with those two characters.  The Heroes levels with Batman and Robin, on the other hand, require different suits.  The idea sounds good, but it becomes more tedious and annoying than anything else to constantly have to change suits just to solve a single puzzle before rendering that suit and its abilities worthless until the next suit change.  Plus, rather than seeing some cool classic (or at least established) suits from Batman lore (like the armored Batman from The Dark Knight Returns, for example), we get lame "magnetic" suits and "heat resistant" suits.
Ultimately, my recommendation isn't changing.  Even though V-Sync fixed game-breaking bugs, the other mechanics are still very poor.  And while I really enjoyed the Villains storyline playthrough, it hardly offsets the tediousness of the Heroes storyline.  Ya know, with Batman, the part that everyone bought this game for.  The main storyline should not be worse than the unlockable storyline.  I love the LEGO games and I have high hopes for the sequels, but I still can't give this a positive review, despite generally enjoying the second half of the game.  Too little, too late as they say.

I had not planned to try another LEGO game so soon after the Harry Potter games, but my eldest really wanted to play this one on her computer, so I decided to play, too.  I reached 100% completion last night, just a few minutes ahead of her :D
This game is nothing like the Batman: Arkham games that I so adore, nor is it like the story-driven LEGO: HP games.  Gameplay is standard fight, explore, build, destroy everything possible and grab all the coins (studs) possible.
There are three chapters from Batman & Robin's perspective, plus three chapters from the villains' point of view, with each chapter spanning five episodes for a total of
.
- 300 mini-kit pieces (10 per level)
- 30 red bricks (which unlock new abilities - don't forget to turn on in the Extras menu once you purchase!)
- 24 hostages
Why are there only 24 hostages when there are 30 levels?  Because one episode in each chapter is done entirely in a vehicle, and there are no hostages - only shooting, exploring, simple puzzles, and collecting. Vehicle types:  Automobile, watercraft, aircraft.
Our home base is - not surprisingly - the Batcave for our heroes, and Arkham Asylum for the villains.  Once you unlock and purchase the extra characters, you'll find them wandering around in their respective area, and can switch to them when they are nearby.  You can also choose whichever character you wish to play as when you enter a level in Free Play mode.
Characters are mostly unlocked during gameplay.  For instance, you may want to play as The Joker, but you won't be able to unlock him until you complete the villain level that has him as a playable character.
To be honest, I found the stories and combat to be a bit on the ho-hum side, especially when we were playing only as Batman and Robin (the first three chapters).  True, they both have a variety of suits with their own unique abilities, but Story Mode was still kind of boring.  Once the villains started unlocking, though, things got more interesting.  Once unlocked, Nightwing and Batgirl were my preferred characters on the heroes side (they have the same suits as Robin and Batman), and Man Bat my favorite villain to play.
There are a couple of minor annoyances along the way, with finicky ladders, and glass that just did NOT want to break when using the sonic suit unless you were standing the right distance away from it.  There's one glass window that will not break unless you bomb it - something that will not work on any other glass window in the whole game. :\
LEGO Batman is not an
gaming experience, but I really had fun getting my 100% once I got past Story Mode and had everyone unlocked for Free Play Mode.  The puzzles are pretty easy, but there's something satisfying about mindlessly demolishing everything in sight and collecting all of the coins and hidden things.  Recommended for all LEGO game fans!

Personally, I really like this game, and have devoted quite a while into it. The patches and all do move along at a somewhat slow rate, given the small dev team, but I think its actually a really good game. I read some of the other reviews and I will address some of the issues mentioned.
Pay2Win-
Basically every gun in the ARMAS Marketplace is a reskin of a gun you get from in-game progression, and the few execeptions have lots of downsides to balance their upsides. Anyone who claims that guns are p2w most likely hasn't gone to the cash shop and trialed the guns, which by the way, you can do, trialing all of the guns for 30minutes/3hours depending if you have premium membership. Really though, the in-game progression weapons are on par, or even better than their cash shop counterparts.
Hackers-
This community is so paranoid of hackers, its pretty much a given that either one person might seem like they are hacking, or you will get hackusated. Just realize that its possible that people are better than you, because some people have been around 4-5 years, since the start in RTW times.
Lag-

If instinct could be used to help evade enemies as in Absolution and the game had a more  meaningful storyline this would have been almost the perfect Hitman.  As it is, while it's a decent game with plenty of scope and options the frustrations hinder the gameplay experience.  Buggy AI also detracts from the potential of the game to be great rather than merely good, being asked to give a character 'Some Privacy' in a crowded room does wonders in killing immersion.
The leaderboard system is also a waste of coding time, this should have been a true single player experience and judging by youtube videos of leaderboard hits, the scoring is suspect at best in any case!  If players wanted a leader board experience it could have been added as an opt-in, but with the coding deficiencies in the game the time spent on leader boards and online elements would have been better spent fixing bugs and adding polish.
I have no problem with episodic release, it could have been better presented though if the game relied less on meaningless online stats competitions and more on roll out of a coherent set of assignments that built into a meaningful storyline.  In this respect it is a significant retrograde step for the franchise.
Still recommend it but you should be aware that there is some poor coding and the overall gameplay is slightly below Absolution.
Next release should be treated with caution until it is known if development continues in the same direction.  Are devs going to revert to Absolution grade stealth and storyline and try to improve on that or are they going to continue along the meaningless online competition path that apparently draws kids who want bragging rights at school as the target audience?
