If you don’t want to read my reasons why then let me save you some time and suggest you jump down to the ‘Conclusion’ heading at the bottom of this review.
My in depth review:
It’s 1984.  A village in Shropshire.  A celestial ‘event’ occurs.  A quarantine is put in place due to an unknown malady.  The village is now completely devoid of human activity.  It appears that everyone has vanished without a trace.  You enter the village.  The game begins ...............
In the genre of science fiction, the game is presented like a radio drama (think ‘The Archers’ meets ‘The Twilight Zone’) by means of interaction with supernatural orbs of light.  Once these orbs are triggered, ‘echos’ of the last few hours and days are replayed as they happened in that particular location in the game.  Radio and telephone messages also play a key role in the development of the story.
As the story is non-linear you can follow the light rigidly or develop the story in your own way following the light and triggering the story events as and when you wish.  How much of the story you consume is up to you.  The end result is the same.
This is an open world, exploration, walking type simulator driven by narration.  There is little interaction with the open world.  Some doors and gates open but many do not.  Some electrical appliances can be activated but that’s about it.  This side of the game is slightly disappointing as on the surface there is so much eye candy but that’s all it is.  In my mind, exploration involves using your hands, not just your eyes but there just wasn’t enough of it for my liking.
Game/story progression via the orbs and the ‘echos’ of the past are well presented and make for interesting and unusual game play.
Even the human side of the game works.  The village is a close knit community.  Everyone knows everyone else’s business which has its advantages and disadvantages.  The story also addresses the matter of prejudice in the form of the games protagonist (Kate) who we learn is someone of colour and how the insular views of others affect her and her relationship with others.
The voice acting is of a high quality.  The script is well written and the dialogue feels natural across the board to the point where I often felt like I was standing behind people prying into their conversations.
The atmosphere is nicely balanced.  It’s eerie but not creepy or frightening at all.  The mysterious orbs of light never feel malevolent but rather benevolent.  There is an overarching melancholy to the game but it stops short of being overly sad or depressing.
Tourist maps are frequently placed around the open world and were occasionally useful.
The layout of the world felt natural and believable and there always appeared to be at least 2 routes available.  You can stick to the road system or go off road across fields and through forests via public footpaths.  Even this didn’t feel forced as many rural parishes in England still work like this today.
This is an area of the game of which much has been talked online.  It basically comes down to the player’s speed of movement.  It’s so slow.  Now don’t get me wrong, moving through the game like Lara Croft would be ridiculous and completely wrong for this game but the default speed is just too slow and feels unnatural.  For a game that is relying so heavily on immersing the player in this world you don’t want the player to be constantly thinking “why am I moving so slow?”
A ‘run’ button was revealed late in the day for many.  If you’re using an Xbox controller, it’s the right trigger button.  This button name is deceptive though as what it actually does, and apparently only in certain environments, is makes you walk faster ................. by a fraction.  The game doesn’t allow you to run anywhere, ever.  This ‘fast walk’ button is a more natural in game walking speed and should be changed to become the default.
The bottom line is that, while developers should be able to fulfil their vision, the player should be able to choose the speed of movement in which he/she wants to traverse the world and ultimately how much time they want to invest in it.
A second but less problematic issue was the triggering of the orb ‘echos’.  When you first encounter one a visual animation of the Xbox controller appears and highlights the buttons and movement needed.  “Ok, that’s useful,” I thought to myself.  However, this animation by itself doesn’t accurately describe the mechanism or the objective.  I had to search online to find the answer.  In my book that’s unacceptable.  That’s the responsibility of the developers, not Google.
The solution is to think of it like tuning in an old analogue radio station, like manually turning a dial back and forth.  Once you locate the signal you need to hold it in place until the signal locks.
If you prefer not to interact in this way then this feature can be switched off in the settings menu.  Presumably, you will then get a much simpler interface to use when encountering the orbs.
The world created is exquisite and at times jaw dropping.  It was easy to forget that this village doesn’t really exist but is someone’s creation.  The attention to detail is amazing and particularly the period detail.  All the paraphernalia of the 1980’s is on show - Rubik’s cubes, old analogue telephones, brick sized mobile phones, playground equipment that would probably be banned these days due to healthy and safety issues.  House decor, furniture, transport, pub menus - nothing has been overlooked in giving the game a fully authentic feel.  The research in to this period has to be commended.
Being a game set in the rural English countryside the vegetation had to be done right else it would be too distracting.  They nailed it.  Despite walking through miles of forest, fields and green spaces not once did I think I was walking through the same patch as I did say 10 minutes ago in another location.
If I was to be a touch nitpicky then I’d like to have seen more realism within the homes themselves.  It seemed like this was an area of the world that needed more time in development.  It’s not that they were sparsely furnished but rather that there was too much similarity and not enough mess and general appearance of being lived in.
The soundtrack is beautiful and shifts in relation to conversations and significant game events.  There is much choral music with the backing of stringed arrangements which adds to the ethereal mood of the game.
Another nice touch is that depending on location you can hear ambient noises and voices that appear to travel as if on the wind but are actually wrapped up within the moving orb.  For example, when on the football pitch you can hear the crowds and when in the playground you can hear the children playing.
Everybody's Gone to the Rapture is a fully fleshed out and atmospheric open world which is engrossing and believable.  It’s exquisitely designed and visually a joy to look at.  It’s almost like going on a weekend break in the Cotswolds except without all the people.  The story has depth and is thought provoking.  The game was still lingering in my mind days after playing it and I love it when a game does that.
The issues discussed above proved to be minor frustrations that, whilst always present, didn’t spoil the overall game experience.  You soon adapt to the speed of movement.
I really recommend it but due to the game play issues and the length of the game being relatively short, I would wait until it is on offer before shelling out.  The speed of movement issue would also deter me from replaying it so that also has to factor into the overall value of the game.

Let me start off by saying the scenery and music in this game are fantastic. However, these game aspects alone are not the benchmark I hold a recommened game to.
1. The story here is lackluster. It did not leave me satisfied. Not even the subplot got me really interested.
2. The speed at which the character moves is extremely frustrating. I'm talking snail's pace. Plus when you enter a building you slow down even more! Note for those who do play there is a run mechanic. From what I hear it does not help much, but figure it out before you play.
3. While details are fantastic you will see many assets used over and over. Many buildings are laid out the same. Every person has the same exact shed out back with exactly the same things in them. I know this is a bit nit-picky but it started to get on my nerves.
4. Lack of settings options. I am noting a few things here I would have expected. No sensitivity controls as well as no brightness settings. This was frustrating as the game can get very very dark at times.

I was a bit worried starting this game. There were quite a few bad reviews ranging from "slightly boring" to "borderline unplayable because of the slowness". Although I can see where these people are coming from, they started Rapture with the wrong mindset, I think.
I myself am a big fan of the so called "Walking simulator" because they play like you are part of some of the most original artsy movies I've seen. And that is mainly because they give you time to explore gripping stories at your own pace.
And boy, is this a gripping story. Scratch that, it's so many stories interwoven. It's a glimpse into humanity and daily life. It's absolutely ****in brilliant, this. If you take your time to explore Rapture (and you will need some time, there's a lot of walking around to do, and you are slow-footed), the result is one of the most human storyline I've seen told by  a game.
After I finished I went to look up what everyone else was saying about the people and the stories in this game. And that for me tells of a good story: one where you keep thinking about it, long after it has been told.
Tl;dr: Play this. Please.

The game is short, and outside of replaying the game to experience the story after gaining the perspective from completing the first time, or minor collectables, won't bring you back much replayability. That being said, replayability is not this game's focus. Spec Ops: The Line will take you on a ride through the terrible and seemingly impossible choices in the moment of war and make you reflect on the choices for the future. Definitely a recommend if you're looking for a low-key enigmatic third person shooter.

To date I've played several 'walking simulators' (there *has* to be a better description surely): Firewatch, Dear Esther, Gone Home... but none of these moved or intrigued me like 'Rapture'. It's not a puzzle-solving game in the traditional sense but you do have to spend time wandering, listening, interacting and sometimes just standing in the beautiful, lush visual landscapes and soundscapes taking it all in so you can put the pieces together.
The English village where everyone has vanished is beautifully rendered and amazingly detailed. The sound design is a step above this again. The music, ambient noises and echoes from the departed residents are so immersive. Headphones are highly recommended.

This is truly a beautiful and very involved story.  While you see snippets of different people around town, the main character stories involved Father Jeremy, Wendy, Frank, Lizzie, Stephen, and Kate.  I don't want to say anymore about the story as it is something to experience on your own, but there are a few cautions.
1.  If you are an achievement hunter and very impatient, you will probably get frustrated with this game.  It took me quite a bit to get all the achievements, and some of them were agonizingly ssslllloooow

2.  Your game only gets saved after motion control events.  So if you have been roaming around for an hour and feel like taking a break, best to leave the game running.  Which brings me to...
3.  The end scene (when you arrive in the dark room with the table and tape recorder), refrain from doing shift+tab or alt+tab.  I did this a couple times in the same spot to make sure, and I crashed every time.  And in order to get "The End" achievement, you have to watch all the way through... even the credits.  So unless you want to redo the slow observatory events over and over, leave those keys alone.
Apart from those few things (and the painfully slow walk), if you can hack it through those, you are in for one helluva story.

I will preface this with a statement:
I wouldn't call myself an avid DmC fan. I have the other games. I've played them, and they were fun. Heard varying opinions of this game and got it on sale to see for myself. First off, a lot of the people saying its horrible and the spawn of Satan and the like are wrong. Kinda. It has its good points, it has its bad points, and it has quite a few just plain mediocre points, so I'll try and be as fair as I can here.
(Warning. Warning. A new Wall of Text approaches.)
First off, how does it play? Decently. Combat is nice and smooth, flows really well, but... it's not at all that difficult. Some of it just gets kind of silly too. Once the grab mechanics got introduced, I almost immediately figured out how to just return to my home planet without much difficulty at all. While things like this are usually possible, in this game it seems rather hilariously simple to discover and then spam them to your heart's content. Also, Dante's devil trigger is kind of silly. He freezes time, which would normally have me :D'ing, but then he flings everyone up into the air where they are annoying to hit, invalidating every single ground combo I have, basically. Anyway, I didn't find quite as much depth or challenge to the fighting mechanics as I would nessecarily like, but this is coming from a guy who loves Dark Souls and plays everything on the hardest difficulty he can, so my definition of challenge is a bit different from most casual players. Aside from being somewhat more simplistic than I expected, however, there isn't much of anything you can call a fault in the combat. It's pretty looking, very smooth, and kind of mediocre, really.
Plot? Look, let's be honest here, no one plays the original DMC games for the plot. That was one of the many mistakes they made with 2, in fact. That said, unlike the original games, which were trying harder to be entertaining that tell a really detailed story, this one has one. A rather large one that I'm not really a fan of. However, all matters of opinion aside for the most unbiased review, it's mostly another "Eh" from me. Despite usually being an obsessive gamer who watches every cutscene and searches for all the little details etc. I just wasn't that interested in the plot. It's there, yes. Is the writing horrible? No. Is it fatastic? No. Looking at it as a whole, I can't really say there is anything about it that ever goes above average. Some is below, most is right on the line, and none of it really gets very much further than that.
Next we have DmC Dante. Gonna say it straight out. I think he sucks. I don't find him funny or entertaining in any way, shape or form. This is without comparing him to the old Dante at all. had I never played another DMC in my life, I would still get a headache almost every time he opens his mouth. I have laughed at literally none of his jokes, I have completely failed to care about any of his actions at every turn, and in general just been unamused by his existence. He is whiny, thinks he is so cool for being a punk, blah blah blah blah I don't even want to listen to him any more. It seems from where I'm standing that the writers just went with any uninspired bit of excessive vulgarity they could come up with to make him seem "cool" and then went to lunch. That isn't me being a prude. What with all the time I spend online I'd probably have an aneurysm by now if I was. However, all of the teenage-class stupid that spews forth from his every orofice has gotten mindbogglingly old, so unless you giggle at "dirty words" there isn't much there that could possibly be called humor. Once in a while, he makes some comment that gets my hopes up and I think "Is this actually going to be witty and intelligent?" and then he finishes what he was saying and it all comes crashing back down to dull. And do I even need to bring up the infamous "**** YOU!" "NO, **** YOU!" exchage? he is absolutely the worst part of the game, as far as I'm concerned, and it says a lot that my feelings about any game can be summed up with "The main character is the worst thing about it."
Music... is really another matter of personal taste, I suppose. In my opinion, the main game's soundtrack sucks, but that's just because I hate most of that genre to begin with. That said, it suits the character just fine, so if that's what they were going for, great success! Considering that the Vergil's Downfall DLC switches to a totally different theme, it probably was what they intended. (That music is a little eh, too, though. It's there, it doesn't sound out of place, but it isn't stellar for the most part either. Maybe I haven't payed enough attention to it, but that it can't grab my attention does say quite a bit.)
With all said and done, my final opinion on this game is mostly just "Meh". If I had never bought it, I would be perfectly content with my life. If I had bought it full price, I would probably regret it a bit. It runs well, plays decently, and I can't say I wasted the time I spent on it any more than it would have been wasted on another game, but I still find the combat lacking the challenge I looked for, and the new Dante spent a good portion of the game giving me a headache before I just ragequit to play Vergil's Downfall for a while instead. My statements that the combat lacks depth should still be taken with a grain of salt, as the combat will probably be perfectly acceptable to most casual players, but if you are looking for all sorts of tricky shenanigans like in certain other games in this genre, you probably won't find a ton of them here. The plot was uninteresting, at least to me, and way too full of dropping anvils (That's TvTropes speak, for those uninitiated in that specific internet timesink) for me to take it seriously, and as characters I find the new cast bland at best and generally annoying at worst.
As far as I'm concerned, if it's on sale and you feel like it, sure, go ahead and get it, I suppose, but if I had a choice between this and DMC3 or 4, I'd leave this one sitting in my games library collecting digital dust, which I can say with complete certainty, because that would be what is happening this very instant, and will probably still be happening whenever you, whoever you are, come by this little corner of the web and read this particular post. However, since there is no button that says "Meh" and displays a shrugging stick figure, I guess I'll just say reccomended, with the imaginary caveat of "When it's on sale".

Ignore the complaints about Dante's re-design. While it's true cosmetically he's changed the vast majority of his personality remains unscathed. Except rather than being arrogant and cocky in the manner of an anime badass his dialogue is a lot more natural and far less forced. The same can be said for his appearance with him looking a lot more human, both of these factors made it easier to empathise with Dante while witnessing his origin story. I think for all but a small niche the new Dante is likeable, relatable and much more natural as a character.
The game plays in a similar manner to other action games of this genre, throwing a group of enemies at the player and encouraging them to combo their way through them to advance the story. The better the combos the more rewards along the way. This works really well thanks to two mechanics, switching weapons mid-combo in DMC is very quick and simple allowing the user to swap weapon sets in real time at the push of a button. While this is a series staple DMC adds greater emphasis to the mechanic with enemies that can only be killed by certain weapons, something that encourages players to think tactically about how they approach a melee. The other can only be described as a god send for the series, in a similar manner to DMC4's 'Devil Bringer' players are given a weapon early on to drag enemies towards them so as to keep combo's going and create a faster flow. The twist this time round is that there's also a weapon to drag Dante TO the enemies which doesn't sound like much but married with the previously mentioned 'X weapon kills X enemy' system this creates a small ecos ystem the player has to manage in each battle. Just hacking away will not wash in DMC. In what has become a staple of the action genre now the game also features your typical "rage mode" which allows Dante to regain health while dishing out extra damage, against regular enemies this more will also slow down time and launch all the enemies into the air for you. It feels a bit like a get out of jail free card on the first run through but on higher difficulties you'll be thankful for the few sweet mnoments of down-time before the bloodbath resumes.
One minor caveat to this though (one that is not so minor for the more hardcore DMC follwers) is that the average level of difficulty has been nerfed. While this is dissapointing for some it never mars the experience on the first run and with harder difficulties available after completing the game it's not a big enough issue to put you off the game. Another drawback in this new entry is the camera system, there's no lock on option available and while this isn't so bad as you can work around it it does make it unnecessarily difficult early on when trying to target particular enemies.
For many players Ninja Theory's decision to use UE3 was a strange move, on consoles at least the game is capped to 30fps a bold move by any action game let alone it's founding series. Thankfully this not an issue on PC as the framerate has been unlocked to reach that silky smooth 60fps and boy does it look fantastic. This is quite easily the best looking game in the series by a long shot with many levels featuring a wide colour palette in the majority of levels (sorry no "UE3 browns here). The most enticing aspect of the levels though is how they move and shift as Dante progresses through them, you really get the impression that even the world itself is against Dante in his quest with large chasm's appearing as a building seperates itself into multiple pieces or a plethora of deadly buzz-saws appear as if out of nowhere. This is made even more epic by the fact that Dante is able to traverse these new dangers freely with the weapons mentioned earlier allowing him to drag himself accross the map or pull platforms out of walls.
While the overall story isn't much to write home about it is engaging enough the first time through but not something you'll be talking about in years to come, or even weeks later. It does present it's characters well with all the main characters avoiding the cringeworthy dialogue the series is known for whilest managing to get a few pot shots in on modern culture along the way. All of this is voiced well with Dante and Vergil being the standout performances. The other star on show is the music in what can only be described as a perfect marriage between dubstep and death metal the games soundtrack fits right in and manages to help make each area feel unique.
Despite it's minor flaws and the vocal niche baying for it's blood DMC is a highly enjoyable action game that manages to be accessable to newer players while still providing a good time to series veterans. It doesn't offer up much in terms of replayability other than some achievements and artwork and the expansion DLC while offering a new character mars the experience with a poor plot and recycled enviornments.
In conclusion if you're an experienced fan of action games or a newbie looking to get into the genre you're likely to have a great time with DMC.

The Short:
This game shows promise but it's got a long way to go. Unless you're VERY into pre-alpha games and all that comes with it, I suggest you hold for a while until a few major patches have come through.
The Long:
I'm not going to get into all pre-alpha / early access bugs. That's the nature of the beast and there's no point complaining about or even pointing out that sort of thing in a review. Note to other reviewers: this stuff belongs on the forums as feedback to the devs, not here.
This game shows promise but as of right now there's just not a whole lot to do.  There is no true "build a bigger, better base" .  There is a handful of stations (e.g. research, printer, vehicle station, etc.) and there's no real need to build beyond that. There's really no real need to build half of them.  But even if you do, it takes like 1-3h depending on RNG for you to farm / research / construct virtually everything.  Hopefully the dev roadmap will include building actual structures (e.g. walls, platforms, doors, etc.).
There are deadly plants, which sort of count (e.g. plants that release toxins, spike you, or strangle you when you get near them). Beyond that there are no real monsters to fend off against. Hopefully the dev roadmap will include this in the future.
Unless the multi-planet vs.  interplanetary travel is completely rebuilt from the ground up as a different concept / function, I don't really know how they can feasibly expand on what they've done now without feeling moreso "gimmicky" and "forced". As of now there are only like 5 planets and a moon, and they all kind of do this weird rotation around each other, the center one being whichever one you happen to be on at the time.
p.s. - I can't seem to understand why people are unfairly comparing this to NMS. There are a number of things in this game NMS fell short on, on launch. But there are also a number of things THIS game fell short on, on launch, that NMS did well. My advice to others is to ignore the NMS rhetoric in these reviews, because this game is definitely NOT everything NMS (allegedly) isn't.

[Copying over a review I made on my tumblr because I am lazy.]
This is a very interesting game. If you’re a fan of massive worlds with basic survival needs, but you aren’t much into digging or building, and have an eye out for a story, this might be a game for you.
Eidolon plops you into a post-apocalyptic western Washington. You have no goal, no purpose. The world is immense and beautiful and it becomes what you make of it.
There are documents from the past littered around the world. If you so choose you may search for these documents (as you find them, you can request a light to shoot up into the sky to guide your way toward finding more), or you can simply explore the landscape, creating your own goals. Reach the top of that mountain, see what’s on the other side of that lake, follow this river, explore these ruins of a once-great city.
As stated the game is set in a post-apocalyptic world. I’ve yet to find out exactly what happened, personally, but apparently things started some time around the 2070’s, when a massive earthquake destroyed Seattle. More than that, I am unsure. I did find some documents in Bellevue pertaining to some fanatical cultist. I’m unsure what to make them as of yet. The story really draws me in and I’m excited to continue exploring the world and discovering more of it.
Eidolon has a very slow pace. Your first goal is survival before you can do anything else. There are berries and mushrooms to sustain you, but you can also fish or hunt if you choose to do so. Watch out for bears and wolf-like creatures that will attack you on sight. If you get wounded it may fester, causing illness and increase your need for food and sleep. There is some way to treat wounds and festered wounds but I’ve yet to discover it. I ended up looking at a guide and apparently there are bee hives you can shoot down from trees. The honey you collect is what has the antibacterial properties to treat those wounds.
The simplistic art style lends its way beautifully to the size of the world. The only downside is the lack of a physical sun or moon in the sky, but all other aspects of the colors changing makes the passage of time as smooth as possible. Perhaps the lack of the celestial entities is what truly drives the powerful movement of time. The world is simultaneously beautiful and simple, such that exploration is hardly boring, but you can also turn your focus to collecting documents for the story without missing much by ignoring the scenery.
I’ve only spent a few hours with the game overall so far. Spend an hour and you’ll accomplish very much and very little at the same time. You can find the game on Steam, but it’s also available for purchase from the developer’s blog. Buying off their blog brings you through Humble which grants you access to both a Steam Key and a download for a DRM-free version of the game. It also helps support Ice Water Games a bit more. I look forward to more games from this team!

I've tried to like this game so far, but there's just too much sandbox for me. On my first attempt, I was eaten alive by a wild cat animal as soon as I spawned. On the second try I froze to death within minutes. Third and most recent attempt: starvation. In the time i've played this game, I haven't come across a single note, transcript, tool or other noteworthy item despite doing my best to look for them,
The closest I ever got to finding something interesting was just recently when I saw something that looked like rows of little cottages along a swampy lakeside. I had emerged from the forest at the wrong side of the lake and so I had to get around it. After several attempts and a few in-game days later, I reached the cottages. To my great dissappointment, they turned out to be trees with oddly shaped foliage. I remembered that one of the "cottages" was located a bit further away from the rest and had a bit of a different shape, so I decided to check that out for the hell of it. At this point however, I was fatigued. cold and hungry, so I decided to rest for a bit. When I woke up a thick mist had crept in, covering the entire lake and the surrounding area. I tried to make my way to the cottage-shaped piece of mystery through the mist, but then I starved to death.
Frankly I really want to like this game, but it´s just too unforgiving for me to enjoy. Be prepared to sink some time into this if you want the most out of it. I will give credit where it's due though; the soundtrack is pretty good, even great in some cases, but it triggers far too rarely to compensate.
-EDIT-
Just now I gave this game one last, serious chance. I summoned every bit of patience I could muster, and set out to explore the world. having already tried going in multiple different directions, I decided to try venturing past the giant, snow-clad mountains, hoping to find something beyond. I gathered mushrooms and tinder for days, planned my route to the best of my ability and set off.
After travelling for what felt like an eternity, barely avoiding freezing to death by building campfires along my path, I finally passed the mountains. For the first time in a long time, I was actually excited to see what lied beyond the misty veil that greeted me.
Then i fell off the end of the world and got dumped back where I started.
And then I uninstalled.
Also, someone said this game has stories on notes in it, but I never found any. Supposedly there are tools too, but I never found any of those either.

Batman has a long history of escaping from some of the deadliest, most elaborate traps a brilliant criminal mind can devise. In his bat-utility belt is a gadget to get him out of nearly any predicament. But in Batman: Arkham Origins, there's one trap Batman can't escape from: the trap of expectations. By now, there are two things that define action in the Arkham series: rhythmic, free-flow combat and stealthy predator rooms. Arkham Origins has those elements in spades. But it doles them out in a straightforward, predictable fashion that lacks the inspiration of the earlier Arkham games.
The most noteworthy difference between Arkham Origins and its predecessors is a significantly larger open world. But that larger world has little meaning when the things you're doing in it are the same things the smaller world of the previous game accommodated perfectly well. Grappling up to rooftops and gliding through the air still feel great, but they don't feel any better here just because you have more rooftops to leap from. And there are side quests that have you doing things like racing to and fro to disarm bombs set by Anarky, which is much like racing to answer Zsasz's ringing phones in Arkham City.
The city is bigger just for the sake of being bigger, and while these side quests make interesting use of characters--Anarky's willingness to go to any length to liberate the downtrodden from the oppression of the rich and powerful makes him a fascinating figure, for instance, and the game gives him his due--the things you're doing are exactly the same as the things the previous game had you doing in its open world. Even the crimes in progress, events you can choose to respond to or ignore that come up on the police radio, aren't a chance to protect hapless citizens of Gotham from criminal elements, but just to fight more groups of thugs, something you do plenty of anyway.
Free-flow combat is unchanged from earlier Arkham games, aside from the fact that there are a few new enemy types in the mix, most notably a martial artist who has an attack you need to counter twice rather than once. The animations are still excellent, and getting into a rhythm where you're dishing out punishment while perfectly countering every enemy attack still feels good, but it also feels exactly the same as ever. At a certain point in the game, you acquire shock gloves that make your punches more powerful, but this doesn't prevent punching dudes in the face from feeling routine.
Predator rooms are also what you'd expect them to be, no less and no more. Of course it's still satisfying to sneak up on a goon and take him down silently, or to be perched on a gargoyle, waiting for a clueless criminal to walk right under you so you can do an inverted takedown. But it's also starting to feel rote. By this point, the mechanics governing these systems have become apparent, the process of sneaking up on enemies or of countering attacks overly familiar. You and Batman and the game he's in are all just going through the motions.
8/10

Mixed reviews, positive and negatives ones everywhere! Oh god, should I buy this?! I'll try (I say try, lol...) to give you a quick run down of everything you need to know in this improvised review.
I was afraid of buying this game due to the contraversy surrounding the offline mode etc. Thankfully, I haven't had any connection issues, aside from when I first started up the game for the first time, it took a good moment for the game to connect, and had no issues after that. But seriously, you ♥♥♥♥ed up Square Enix and IO, big time with that.
Well, the first question you'll probably have on your mind is: Is it better than Blood Money? No. It isn't. Is it still worth buying? Yes. I'd pay £20 at most for this game due to its very short campaign. Granted, you have contracts and customised ones to master and learn how to play but realistically, you're not getting a fully fledged game, so you shouldn't pay the full price.
There are plenty of ways and means to eliminate your targets, and many ways to reach them. The levels are very big, so there's plenty of exploration and discoveries to be made to make future plans to pick them off. Not only that, there are subtle storyline hints here and there which is a nice touch. It does feel a little similar to Blood Money, but not entirely. Infact, it feels like a much better version of Absolution more than anything due to the movement and gameplay feel and it definitely has a modern feel to it, so try to come into the game with a clean perspective and slate, and try not to compare it to the older titles too much.
The graphics are beautiful, very detailed and immersive. I've had to lower a few shadows to keep my frame rate above 60, but I can still rock this game with good anti-aliasing and high textures, so I'm happy.
The audio is fantastic and very immersive, doors, sinks, weapons, the ambient atmosphere of the locations, it's wonderful. The soundtrack however is a little unfitting to me. It makes me feel as if I'm playing as Tom Cruise in Mission Impossible due to how modern, fancy and kind of over the top it is. I'd rather have the subtle strings like in BM, but hey...
The gameplay is really fun, challenging, and has a large variety of ways to
Negatives: The game lacks weapon customisation, e.g. Silencers, accuracy addons, different ammo etc. You're unable to look through keyholes, and no matter where you go the characters ALWAYS have British and American accents which seriously kills the immersion! Especially in Morroco and Japan!
The main menu is atrocious. It's beyond confusing and you have to load up the level as a new session and then manually load your save to access your save files. Maybe I'm doing it wrong and being an idiot, but they really need to tone it down and simplify it more. It feels very much like a console main menu due to how big everything is.
Overall: A fun immersive experience that will last you many hours, much better than Absolution, but many steps away from being a successor from Blood Money.

I finally found my way to "Max Payne 3", and as preparation before the third installment, I decided to revisit the first two games to brush up on the story, get in the right mood, and simply to see if they still hold up as well as I remembered them. They do. In fact, they're even better, with me being a more mature gamer and properly appreciating the work of art that is the MP franchise. After being done with MP1, I jumped to MP2, which is also the first MP title I ever played and a such holds a special spot in my gaming heart.
Is it a sequel worthy of the first game? Yes, yes it is. 100%, and then some. Basically, all that was bad in MP1 was fixed in MP2, and all that was good was made better. MP2 features even better comic book style narrations. The script is equally well-written as before. In addition, the game now has proper cutscenes which provide a good transition between some scenes.
Gameplay-wise, the tempo has been balanced a bit. Instead of the relentless onslaught, there are sections in MP2 which are exploratory only. The infamous dream-like sequences have been remodeled and made far less frustrating. Bullet time has undergone a few subtle changes, all for the better. There are some graphical improvements and fancy animations, of course, but the most important one is in the gameplay mechanic.
Remember how in MP1 you would shoot-dodge (that is, dive in bullet time) and if you weren't able to clear the room of enemies in that one slow-mo leap, you'd be forced to watch an animation of Max standing up, during which he'd be powerless - and most likely dead, considering MP1's punishing difficulty. Now, after shoot-dodging, Max can remain down, firing his guns from a prone position. This makes a world of difference.
The game's difficulty has also been adjusted. That is not to say the game is easy. You'll still die, but nowhere nearly as often as before. Quick save is still present, but it won't be your #1 button anymore. I admit the adjusted difficulty made for a more enjoyable and fluid experience. And for those wanting an extra challenge, there are tougher difficulties to choose from once you beat the game - including unlocking and alternate ending for beating the game on the highest difficulty.
And lastly, visually, for a game 11 years old, MP2 is stunning, and only the most shallow gamers would condemn it for "looking bad".
MP2 is a must-play game for anyone who deems himself a lover of 3rd person shooters - or simply great games in general.

Very pretty and inventive game, with an inspired story and beautifully designed worlds and characters. Generally worth it for that alone, though I have a few nit-picks regarding the manual saves.
The shared energy that is used for saves doesn't work all that well, considering you might find yourself in an area where you have to choose between using your last remaining energy to help you get through a difficult platforming section, or to open the path you actually have to go down. The game is generally pretty good at providing energy refills in this type of area, but it is still an annoyance at times. Add to that that it is rather easy to accidentally waste energy in a needless save or a miss-clicked power attack and the player may find themselves in a far more difficult situation than intended.
My biggest issue with the saves is that it creates scenarios where the player, through ignorance of the level design or poor planning, may strand themselves in a long, difficult platforming area with no energy in sight to help them along. It makes certain parts of the game feel far more difficult and tedious than I think the developers intended it to be, and is especially noticeable when the music and environments paint a far different atmosphere than the one the player experiences. Such sections make the game feel unpolished, as if it were an oversight on the developer’s side and create disconnect between gameplay and the emotion that the game otherwise masterfully delivers on.
I’m aware such minor flaws aren’t enough to make Ori and the Blind Forest a bad game by any means, but I doubt the developer’s intent was to make me call Ori a little ♥♥♥♥♥ 40 times.

The phrases "Visually stunning" and "Aurally Impressive" come to mind when I think about Studio Moon's massive success Ori and the Blind Forest. The controls are really tight and responsive, the puzzles are inspired, yet simple, and backtracking is actually fun and interesting in this game. Ori and the Blind Forest may seem like a simplistic side-scrolling platformer on the surface, but in reality it is surprisingly deep. Every new ability Ori obtains widens the range of world exploration drastically. Places you visit will have obstacles that are insurmountable at the present and will require you gain new abilities to access new areas within an existing area, in which the player will be rewarded with extra life or energy. (which definitely comes in handy.) This game looks and sounds good, but it's not a pushover by any means. Ori and the Blind Forest offers many challenges to the player. There are four difficulty settings,


and for the masochists
I beat the game on hard and it lived up to It's name. In addition to the set difficulties there are sections in the game (most of them are optional.) that challenge the player immensely. (I raged a couple times.) The objective of Ori and the Blind Forest is to restore Nibel (the land in which Ori takes place.) and defeat the final boss Kuro. Ori and the Blind Forest is an incredible journey that is bite sized compared to similar games and leaves a lasting impression with it's players. Ori and the Blind Forest is as close to a perfect story-heavy platformer as you can get, it contains minor flaws and delivers so much entertainment for what it is. That's why I give Ori and the Blind Forest an 8.5/10. I'm also excited to play the sequel Ori and the Will of the Wisps.

No More Room in Hell. I'll just put it simply: It's not good.
Yet another zombie mod that only exists because it's a zombie mod, NMRiH claims to be an intense survival horror coop with good replay value. But what we get instead is a crawling, boring slugfest with unreliable servers, broken hitboxes and unconvincing animations and voice acting.
To elaborate: Everything moves at a crawl, survivors and zombies alike (with the exception of the rare "28 days later" running zombie) resulting in gameplay that strains the attention span making the player slam their shift key hoping for a sprint.
NMRiH's combat is just plain broken, melee weapons only register a hit once every twelve swings and even then a zombie will grab you and kill you before you can even wind up for a second attempt. Guns are slightly less broken, with a shot that also hardly registers but at least giving the player a second attempt.
The games server browser is one of the worst aspects, most often when attempting to connect to a server you'll be kicked to the main menu for many reasons, such as the server being a LAN party or the server being offline which in both cases such servers shouldn't even appear in the browser to begin with. Difficulty finding a server in a game that's supposed to be multiplayer does a game no justice.
To conclude, I recommend saving yourself 1.5GB of space and let this particular apocalypse pass by. No More Room in Hell is in it's basic form nothing more than an uninspired attempt at an exhausted concept.

I love Devil May Cry games, i have been a huge fan of them since the first, I've played them all, even that one we DMC Fans don't talk about..
Does DmC stack up to the reputation that it's name has gained over the years? Yes, yes it does. While it will never be anywhere near as good as Devil May Cry 3 (Possibly the greatest game of its kind) It's still a solid Devil May Cry experience, It's fun, Fresh but easily recognisable as an addition to the franchise.
First off i think you should ignore all of the fanboys, those players that have only probably played DmC4 and think they are some kind of authority on the franchise, most of these complaints come down to a single thing "ERMAHGURD WTF DID YOU DO TO DANTE'S HAIR!?" I mean really? To crap all over a good game just because they changed his hair is pathetic.
The gameplay is what you expect form a devil may cry game, It's fast paced and fun with a variety of weapons to use that you can switch on the fly, certain weapons being slower or faster than others and certain weapons having to be used against certain enemies to down them fast and keep your combo flowing in true DMC Style. When an action sequence starts it is literally non stop until you have mowed down every last enemy.
Between the combat sections you will find a lot of platforming, almost jumping puzzle like sections of the levels, this is actually a fresh experience as DMC has never really put a focus on your out of combat movement abilities but these platforming traits are not just limited to out of combat platforming, you can also use them in your combos to rack up the points and slay some demons.
Everything you expect a DMC game to have, this game has it and does it in a style that is similar, yet fresh, new and interesting. Secret doors are here, life and devil trigger upgrades are here, the store to purchase abilities with collected red orbs off enemies are here, the level rating system is here that rewards your end level with a style rating like the ones found in combos.
I found the Combat to actually be faster and more difficult than DMC1, While this new DmC is pretty easy on the lower difficulties it does amp up to an insane degree in true DMC style with the higher ones, all of the difficulties you loved from previous games are here including a new one, Hell or Hell mode which mixes Dante Must Die mode and Heaven or Hell mode.
in Hell or Hell mode Dante still dies in one hit like Heaven or Hell but the enemies do not, the enemies are the difficulty that you'll find in Dante Must Die mode rather than also dying in one hit like Heaven or Hell mode. Ninja Theory brought DmC and all the trimmings into an updated and modern take on the DmC Universe and in my opinion they did an amazing job.
Every single second of this game pays major respect to the previous titles while staying fresh and interesting, Some might say this isn't true due to the "Not in a million years" part of the game but that was more to slap angry fanboys in the face that think the game is garbage because of a stupid thing like a change of hair style.
Amazing Devil May Cry combat, Above Average visuals, great platforming, smooth and responsive controls, masive replayability and a kick♥♥♥♥♥sound track from Noisia and Combichrist all come together to make this what i consider to be one of the best entries in the franchise.

Gameplay
----------
Gameplay is very smooth, if you can get past the fact that geared guys will kill you 300 times in a row before you can actually get a little shack built.
Controls are simple, not very complicated at all.
Graphics are good depending on what you set it at.
The Playerbase
----------------
Rust is a very fun game if you can manage to ignore the amount of 7 year olds that will chase you with rocks on the beachside.
Basically impossible to trust anyone as you will either get shot in the back of the head, or if you can find one of the 0.999999999% of players that you CAN trust, some random guy will come up and mow you and your buddy down with a Thompson.
Also, beware of micspammers.
Also, beware of zerg clans.
Combat
--------
Combat in this game is uneven as hell. I can't tell you how many times i've been in a fight against someone with an AK, while I have a bow and a few arrows.
Armor barely does♥♥♥♥♥♥ because if you get hit below half health, you pretty much have a 100% chance of death.
"Base" building
--------------
Unless you play on a modded server, you are very unlikely to build a full scale base.
But assuming you survive all the geared guys, and zerg clans, you have made yourself an entire, whopping 1x1.
There's really no use to expand from there unless you're part of a clan, as you will probably get doorcamped when you try to expand your territory.
As of recent updates, many new decorations and building items have been added. I feel they definetly improve the game overall if you want to make your 1x1 look all spiffy.
Radtowns and Monuments
----------------------------
I for one enjoy the way they present Radtowns and Monuments as ways to gather loot.
That is, if you don't get shot by geared guys, or beaten to death by a Naked zerg clan.
Also, never build your base near a Radtown or Monument as you are 100% sure to get you base raided.
Tips
----
Have good aim before you play this game.
Never build by highly populated or popular areas. (The Dome and Rocket monuments being some examples)
Trust nobody.
There are no friends in Rust.
Expect to die a good 4000 times.
Expect to want to ragequit.
Expect the unexpected.
Rating
-------
If you like a challenging game, I would say this is 100/100
If you like a casual game, I would say this is 47/100
If you like fun games, I would say this is 84/100
If you like unique games, I would say this is 100/100
If you like survival games, I would say this is 100/100
My personal rating: 76/100

text:
**** Discusses details, but no true spoilers. ****
you have to ask yourself before you begin this game: Does the slow pace of walking sims attract or repel you?
If you can't stand a walking sim's pace, you won't like this game. And if you review it, you'll whine about how slow it is and you will thereby deserve to burn eternally in hell for ignoring my advice. I don't like professional sports. What do you think would happen if I presumed to review a football or basketball sim? I wouldn't like it. And my opinion would be
, because I should never have reviewed the thing in the first place, lacking a basic sympathy for it. Just as your opinion is
if you basically don't like walking sims.
If you are able -- notice that I don't say "willing," you can't will yourself to change your tastes -- if you are
to let yourself sink into a story and absorb it slowly through a multitude of environmental details, hints, and suggestions, and to sort out the tangles when you trigger story information in the wrong order, as you will -- it is superb.
June, 1984. You're in a picture-perfect little English village, the type you're used to seeing in glossy magazines. And it's empty. Why? Well, the world just ended. Again, why? That's what drives the story, but the story isn't a story, it's an interlayered and intermingled series of tales of the people who lived here, the crisis they faced, how they reacted to it, and how some of them may have helped it to happen by their snobbish insularity. The story is told in six chapters, beginning with the village priest, Father Jeremy, and ending with Kate, the American astronomer who married a local man and came back with him to work in the observatory near their village. The human characters express themselves through swirls of light which re-enact scenes from their lives and interactions, allowing us to watch the development of what has already taken place.
"Rapture" is a lyrically depressing game, often shading into tragic. For me, the most hanky-worthy moment was Rachel's final scene. She's a bit of a "bad" girl because of a supposedly dodgy boyfriend, but when an irresponsible couple abandon their baby to her care in an attempt at a speedy flight (which ends in their deaths), her boyfriend stays by her. In her last scene, she's trying to rock the baby to sleep while struggling with the realization that it's all over, whatever is happening, none of them is going to see the sun rise, sobbing through the words of her lullaby, "When we're called, we needs must go..." but still considerate enough to tell another who comes to see if she needs help that he ought to get some sleep himself. And then all of them are gone.
One point that isn't made sufficiently clearly is that Kate is black. Her encounter with Barbera, one of several local busybodies whose main retirement hobby seems to be minding the business of others with an unhealthy intensity, is a masterly depiction of hyper-refined bigotry, an unprovoked insult carried out from sheer racist spite covered with a gloss of "niceness." But of course it isn't Kate's skin color that is the problem, another of them, Wendy, explains later. It's just that "she won't fit in here." That attitude may have ended up being a major reason the world has ended. But there are a lot of other candidates.
[Later note: Another viewing made it clear that Wendy isn't quite the monster she appears to be in the scene above. She's herself clinging desperately to what she still has, whether by meddling in her son's marriage or conducting a moralistic crusade against Father Jeremy for an incident in his past. The only things she really loves are her birds, and the first sign of strange occurences is when all the birds in the village die. Her last meeting with Father Jeremy, at the village war memorial, where they finally settle their old quarrel and forgive each other, is another sad and wonderful scene.]
The village is done in magnificent detail, and the score by Jessica Currie is by turns ominious, lyrical, and mournful, funeral music for a world. The ending is a bit difficult to understand, but one must remember that the sole witness was not necessarily entirely sane at that point. Too often, criticism hinges on confusions and mistakes that would be natural for a character to make.
So by all means play it -- if you like the genre. If not, avoid it. You'll be missing nothing but a headache and the scorn of those who realize that like an anaconda swallowing a baseball, or me trying to throw one, you took on something that wasn't meant for you in the first place.

I want to give the art team a big hug and thank them for making something so beautiful and evocative. This game is a pleasure to look at.
Sadly it's not a pleasure to be in. I want to have a frank conversation with the game designers and ask them about all the baffling decisions they made. Why do we have to walk so slowly, with a weird "run" mechanic that doesn't work half the time? Why did they think that following a yellow dot around the village would be more fun than exploring it organically, following clues? Why did they ignore the opportunity to make anything at all interactive, except radios and telephones?
Lastly, based on the audio recordings we hear, the population of Yaughton was generally so unpleasant and dreary that frankly I'm glad they're all dead.
We spend a lot of time hearing characters moaning, yelling, or crying about the sci-fi nonsense that underpins the story and yet throughout, we never anything interesting about anyone  - I can't come up with any words to describe any of the characters without resorting to job descriptions and ethnicities. We don't even learn anything interesting about the aforementioned sci-fi elements.
This game is in many ways a spiritual successor to Dear Esther: it's gorgeous, empty, not as smart as it thinks it is, and entirely misses the point of why someone might want to be told a story as a first-person experience rather than as a film.
So why am I leaving a "thumbs up recommended" rating with this review? Because I can't unequivocally say you shouldn't play it. *Contains spoilers* Eidolon is a game that doesn't tell you what to do, or what your objective is. In fact, it really has no objective. You're dropped in a world with nothing. Absolutely nothing, and must wander to find items to help you with this quest to find out what happened to civilization.
*Spoilers* You can find items near your spawn point that can help you with your quest, such as bow and arrows, a map, binoculars, a compass and a fishing rod.
You may wander a seemingly endless landscape, finding notes, stories etc. in the form of glowing green cubes. When a cube is somewhere near you, you can hear a small "ting" in the background once in a while, as well as on occassion, you can see birds flying around or towards a collectable/note. Notes will often contain clues of what direction you can go to find anothenote pertaining to the specific story you're reading.
Fall damage is indeed a thing, and will cause you harm, as well as jaguars and wolves etc. If you are injured and leave the injury for a few days, it will start to fester. Let it fester for more than 1 day and you will get extremely sick. You will start to get extremely exhausted, hungry, and nauseous. If you eat, you throw it back up. Finding healing items is actually quite hard, so try not to get hurt.
Food: Blackberries, Mushrooms and meat are essential for food. Note: They will go bad and become poisonous if you eat them. You can also fish (For food or notes).
Hunting with the bow: I found that the target being slightly to the left of the tip of the arrow is the place where it hits. Try pulling the bow all the way back, and targetting something to the left (about an inch or so) of the tip of your arrow.
9/10 for lack of interactive items. Still an amazing game though.

This game is a beautiful and solitary exploration of western Washington returned to nature. Unlike many exploration-style games, nothing (at least for me so far) reaches out and tries to kill you. It's the equivalent of yoga in video game format - meditative and relaxing. Finding scraps of the former culture is highly rewarding; the journals are beautifully written. Stumbling upon something in the forest is equally as exciting - a watch tower, a former town, a deer - all of it is rewarding.
As someone from western Washington, the simple aesthetic of this game truly captures what it feels to wander around the forests - the fogginess, the smattering of rain, the different vegetation, the solitary nature of the experience - it all adds together to form a perfect rendition of what the great outdoors is like.
I unintentionally played this game for several hours without noticing - it's a highly recommended experience.

Awesome game if you're into slow-paced, open-ended exploration of a huge world with some very basic, relatively low-pressure survival mechanics. Everything about that is right up my alley, so this is probably the best game purchase I've made in the past year. I can understand how the gameplay style might bore or frustrate some players; and while the survival aspect is less than frantic, if you make a wrong move or two, it can also be brutally unforgiving.
Eidolon is a relaxed game and has been described pretty aptly as a "walking simulator." You simply roam the vast landscape (really vast) seeking to piece together the story of what happened to the people who once lived in the area in an apocalyptic scenario and its aftermath. You can follow specific story lines from one clue to the next as you discover them, or you can just explore freestyle.
The graphics are minimalist, but in my opinion they are gorgeous and beautifully successful at evoking the character of the Pacific Northwest. I rarely find myself being critical of the graphics. This is good for people playing on less-than-beefy computers, as the game isn't terribly taxing on resources.
Staying alive in Eidolon is just a matter of eating enough and avoiding sickness or injury. There is really no crafting to speak of, and no building. Mushrooms, berries, and fish (after you cook it) are your staples; it's also possible to hunt for meat if you find a bow and arrow, but this is really difficult and I've only had one successful kill after a lot of trying. You can collect tinder to build campfires. Wounds from fall damage and aggressive animals (wolves, bears) are the main sources of injury, and eating spoiled food or freezing are the main ways in which you can be injuried, as well as from wounds which fester. You *don't* want to get sick from a wound -- the situation can get really dire quite fast.
I've only found one bizarre bug in several hours of gameplay, and that was a deer that got stuck in the side of a hill at the very beginning of my game and couldn't seem to get out. The animal AI behavior is a little "blocky" and unnatural, but I didn't find this to be a serious problem since interaction with animals is pretty rare on the whole.
Things I love about Eidolon:
- Sparse graphic style and massive open world work well together in this particular context
- The documents and maps that you find are beautifully designed and rendered
- The writing with respect to the characters and their stories is excellent, some of the best I've seen in a game
- Soundtrack and audio are atmospheric and appropriate to the game
- The survival mechanics are not unnecessarily cerebral and convoluted just for the sake of being fancy, and are fairly realistic, e.g., it's a low-key piece of cake until something awful happens and then you're f****d.
Improvements I would suggest:
- A slightly (not greatly) more involved system for hunting and fishing. As-is, it's so basic and easy as to be unrewarding, particularly the fishing.
- The graphics for manmade structures are not up to par with the graphics for natural flora and fauna; the discrepancy is pretty damn glaring at times.
- A more nuanced system for moving from one story clue to the next. The clairvoyant "Now that I've seen this, I magically know to go *this* way" thing is a cop-out; a little more intensive writing and design centered around the maps and documents themselves would be more realistic and engaging. This was the only aspect of the game that broke my sense of immersion.
- Some reviewers have suggested that the game needs more density of interactivity overall; while I agree that this wouldn't hurt, the sparseness and slow pace are part of the game's basic aesthetic and I wouldn't want to see that sacrificed for the sake of giving bored people "more to do." So maybe a few more interaction possibilities, but just a few.
- I also think this game could benefit from a slightly more involved cooking system, such as the ability to make a few different basic campfire recipes with different special properties or bonuses for the player (cold resistance, movement speed bonus, healing bonus, that sort of thing).
In short: one of the best games of its kind, and an awesome experience if you're into the genre and don't require a constant life-and-death struggle or lots of shiny, flashy things to keep you involved in a game. Kudos to the producers of Eidolon!

Going through the list of my most played games one will find FPS after FPS, for hundreds of hours. But this wasn't always the case - I grew up playing platformers and puzzle games, and I have to tell you, it feels great to play a game like Ori after "slaving away" in Counter Strike Global Offensive. The visuals are stunning, the gameplay is easy to learn but hard to master, and the story is just the cherry on top of this delicious cake.

One of the most interesting aspects of Max Payne 2 was how much it expanded upon MP1, but also how different a game it was in general.
While both games borrow from old detective stories and graphic novels. Max Payne 2 is moreso inspired by romance stories. The main character is portrayed far more realistically, as a depressed lonely individual who has gotten everything he wanted at the end of the last game. And then a girl from his past re-enters his life and thrusts him on another adventure into the night. I wouldn't say the story was perfect, it is a little short and doesn't have the same mythological basis as the first. But it does it's job and I respect Remedy for attempting to do something different.
The gameplay was greatly improved, with a true physics engine and reworked AI. The maps were also made a lot larger and the action a lot more upscale. With friendly AI and a survival mode referred to as "Dead Man Walking". Max Payne 2 was a great way to finish Remedy's involvement with the franchise, and is truly a smashing successor to the original.

Call of Duty: Black Ops II is a military first-person shooter developed by Treyarch and published by Activision (Square Enix in Japan) for the Xbox 360, PlayStation 3 and PC on November 13, 2012. It was later released as a launch title for the Wii U on November 18th, 2012.
The ninth official installment of the Call of Duty series (and the sequel to 2010's Call of Duty: Black Ops), the game shifts from the 1960's Cold War to near-future 2025, where military technology has advanced significantly and a new "Cold War" has arisen between the United States (with its Joint Special Operation Command, or JSOC) and China (with its Strategic Defense Coalition, or SDC).
In the main single-player campaign, players take the role of JSOC Lieutenant Commander (and DEVGRU operative) David Mason, son of Alex Mason (a CIA agent and the main protagonist of the game's predecessor). David (codenamed "Section") must investigate and stop the plans of Raul Menendez, a wealthy Nicaraguan narco-terrorist who is using cyberterrorism to fuel the new Cold War. As David puts the pieces together (both from playable 1980's flashbacks from his father's aging comrade-in-arms Frank Woods, and from infiltration missions with fellow DEVGRU operatives Mike Harper and Javier Salazar), he begins to draw a disturbing connection between Menendez and the two Masons.
Along with a main campaign that introduces branching storylines (with multiple endings), per-mission challenges, and custom mission weapon/gear loadouts to the franchise, the game introduces side-missions called "Strike Force", in which players must complete objectives as a soldier, a remote operator of a combat vehicle, or as a tactical commander (in a mode similar to real-time strategy games), switching between these modes at any time. Completing all available missions directly affect the main storyline (even affecting the game's ending), but each single-player campaign has a limited amount of retries ("strike forces") for all Strike Force missions.

Both Zombies and Multiplayer modes return, each with their own unique enhancements. For Zombies, the game adds a variety of new modes (including a large "open world" co-operative mode, a 4v4 competitive co-operative mode, and a duel mode in which one player tries to respawn by controlling the zombie horde). For Multiplayer, the game adds a unique "Ten Point" Create-a-Class system in which players can add and remove components of their class to shift priorities (sometimes breaking traditional Create-a-Class rules, such as adding a second Perk or replacing lethal grenades with another tactical grenade). Multiplayer mode also adds a new game mode (Hardpoint), enhanced Wager Matches (now Party Games) and Combat Training playlists (integrating them with the standard public playlist system, including granting experience points), a Weapon Prestige system (in which players can re-unlock attachments to grant new cosmetic perks), and enhanced social integration (including the ability to livestream via Twitch).
The main soundtrack was composed by Jack Wall (previously known for the first two Mass Effect soundtracks). The game's main theme ("Theme from Call of Duty: Black Ops II") was composed by Trent Reznor (front-man for Nine Inch Nails, whose previous video game soundtrack was Quake).
The campaign includes official appearances by comedian (and television host) Jimmy Kemmel and retired USMC Lieutenant Colonel (and political commentator) OIiver North. Rock/metal band Avenged Sevenfold appears in a post-credit "easter egg" music video. The campaign also includes characters based on former CIA director David Petraeus, former Panaman dictator Manuel Noriega, and former Angolan political leader Jonas Savimbi.

As of December 23rd, the game has made leaps of improvement.  The game is now playable in both singleplayer and multiplayer, but it still has FPS issues and various annoying bugs.  The FPS very quickly reaches unplayable levels if you venture too far into one direction, even on very high end hardware.  The framerate will continue to chug until you start new on a new planet.   In multiplayer if you collect more resources from a vein than you can store in your backpack, the extra resource will drop on the ground and you will not be able to pick it up.  There are many other small annoying bugs that make the game less enjoyable, but Astroneer is definitely at least playable in its current state.
If you can look past the buggy state of the game, Astroneer provides a very compelling experience with plenty of potential for improvement.  There's several different types of biomes with different terrain features and aesthetics.  It seems like every cave you enter is unique, and they seem to go on forever.  The terraforming tool is very intuitive, allowing you to raise, lower and smooth the terrain any way you please.  You can even build a skybridge to space, or tunnel right through a planet to the other end.  If you start to get bored of your surrounding, you can build a spaceship and fly to a different part of the planet, or go even further and explore new celetial bodies.  There's six different types of planets in the game, and they all have unique environmental hazards and resource distributions.  You can colonize all six planets in one savegame, and travel between them easily. Currently there's about eight hours of content avaliable in the game.  That's a fairly small amount for a sandbox type game, and I hope to see the game expanded in the following years.
The game has more content than most games fresh out of early access, and it just went on sale ( in early access) a couple days ago.  The devs have fixed the biggest issues with the game in record pace, and they're already working on new features to add to the game, surpassing my expectation of slow moving development.  The game was unplayable in multiplayer on launch day, and now it seems to be mostly stable, despite framerate issues.

Before I bought Eidolon I looked up some reviews, and one thing kept showing up: walking for unbearably long distances. They weren't joking. This game's massive environment is comparable to Minecraft, except without the interesting landscape and things to do.

I'd like to start this review by saying that I have some mixed feelings about this game...  I really like the concept, but I might have done a few things differently on the execution.
Firstly, I'd like to give a little overview of the kind of game this is:
Eidolon plays fairly simply as games go.  It takes place sometime in the future (it is not clear exactly how far).  You wake up somewhere deep in the forest in Washington and you need to explore to find out where you are and what happened to the place you are exploring. This is done by walking. Lots of walking.  Lots and LOTS of VERY repetitive walking.  Thankfully the developer did include a way to push a key for auto-walk so my "W" finger didn't get too tired.  Still though... you walk incredibly slow and the map basically covers all of the greater Seattle area including the Olympic Penninsula... and while it may not be "to scale" it certainly feels like it due to the time it takes to get from place to place. It would seem like the gameplay is meant to feel immersive and realistic, although the graphics are very artistic and simple due for the most part I'd imagine to this being an indie game that is meant to be able to run on a lot of computer systems (did I mention the HUGE map size?)  I'm sure there were other creative reasons for the particular graphical style chosen, but I won't get into that really... it suits the game fine and it doesn't need to be "realistic" to get the appropriate feeling across to the player.
Okay, back to the gameplay... near your starting position you can find a few items to help you in your journey: a compass, binoculars, bow & arrows, and a fishing rod.  All these items are useful in either staying alive, or finding "clues".  The items and clues both appear in the form of flashing orbs that float above the ground: white for items, green for clues.  Clues can be either a map of a portion of the game area (usually in a hand-drawn style) or snippets of paper letters, notes, or sometimes photos of events or people that have been in the area before you but are now gone.  I don't want to give away any of the contents of the clues in the explanation of the game-play, so I won't say more about them.  Instead lets focus on the process of obtaining said clues.  These glowing orbs you will find clustered all over the map... there are a LOT of them.  Each one has a link at the bottom that, when activated, sends some flashy lights flying off into the sky in the direction of more clues that touch on that subject.  Unfortunately, you will spend the majority of the time playing this game in-between clues just walking from place to place.  It starts to feel very tedious after a few hours... Did I mention the HUGE map size?
Okay, sorry, getting distracted again... So clearly finding these clues is the driving motivation behind playing this game.  I actually really enjoyed the part about discovering the history of the area and what happened to make it so different.  There are some very well thought out stories explaining the events that took place that "ruined civilization" (I don't think that's giving away too much... I'm still trying to keep this "spoiler-free")  So now I'm finally going to go into the part of the game I wasn't so satisfied with: In order to travel from place to place you obviously have to traverse the natural envirionment.  You can sprint, which I highly recommend because walking is PAINFULLY slow, but only until you get tired and have to sleep, and sleeping makes you hungry when you wake up.  So, aside from a lot of walking, which I think I've mentioned a few times now, you will also have to gather food and eat it to keep yourself from starving, one of two ways that I think you can die in this game.
(Quick disclaimer: I haven't tried dying to see what happens yet... not sure if you lose all progress or what.)
There is plenty of food to find in the game, though the bow & arrow was next to useless as you can't aim with it well enough to hit a moving target. Despite that, I didn't have trouble finding enough food to keep me from starving. The other way you can die is by freezing, which is fairly easy to avoid so long as you stay out of the water and don't climb any mountains. You can swim in water for a short period, but if you stay in too long I assume you die of hypothermia.
In the wilderness you also have to avoid predators... they will attack if you come too close or try to shoot them, which brings me to my biggest gripe of this game: wounds. Unlike most "survival" games where you have a health bar of some kind, Eidolon instead has a kind of system where whenever something bad happens (eg. you fall from a height or get mauled by a predator) you pass out for a few hours and wake up with a "serious wound" which either heals over time... or doesn't. This happened to me several times while playing and kinda caused me to stop eventually. I think there is nothing wrong with the system of getting hurt... that keeps with the realism of the game and the seriousness of surviving in the environment.  My issue really stems from the system for getting BETTER. When a wound gets better on its own you don't have anything to worry about... however when it becomes infected, it won't go away.  In addition, it causes you to become "ill" which wastes a lot of your food becuase you can never stop being hungry, and makes you have to sleep a LOT (which uses up even more food). Most of the time you have a "festering wound," you will be ill. When this finally happened to me from falling off a ledge in the game, I nearly quit on the spot... however I wanted to see if there was a way to heal the wound, as it says something about "put an antibacterial on it" in the game interface. After hunting around the steam forums I found a post that was somewhat helpful... it said there was an item called "honey" in the game that you supposedly find in beehives up in the trees that will work. Only one person had ever found it by the looks of it, but if it does exist in the game, I never could find out where.  There was only one other thing in the game that can cure wounds, and that is a special swamp. I happened to have found said swamp earlier in my exploration because it is not too far from where you start the game, but it contains some warm "brown" water with floating will-o-the-wisp lights over it that miraculously cures all wounds and illness instantly... this would be great except that when my wound became infected, I was probably about a 5 hour walk away to the north (this swamp was in the south-east end of the map).  And did I mention that you have to eat a LOT more when you're ill? That means stopping to fish or collect berries almost constantly, and then you have to keep sleeping so you can continue running instead of walking, because lets just say a 5 hour run is a lot longer when you're limited to walking. So needless to say I just wasn't up to the time commitment. I had to finally resort to console commands to try and free myself of the festering wound.
I am probably almost out of space here, but I didn't really get to mention the day/night cycle with weather... It goes from foggy in the morning to clear in the afternoon, to dark at night... with rain mixed in a lot. Which is accurate to the region, but it makes the exploration really annoying when you can't see where you're going half the time.
Also, there were a few bugs... mostly things that break immersion like floating grass and stuff, and campfires cast no light on the surrounding terrain. Nothing major.
The only part about this game that really feels broken to me is the inability to cure wounds that become infected.  If you're going to say "put something antibacterial on it" and then give a decent percentage of the inflicted wounds infections... PUT MORE ANTIBACTERIAL ITEMS IN THE GAME! Seriously! If beehives do exist, they should be a LOT more common. It is a critical design flaw, in my opinion.
