Devil May Cry is one of my all time favorite game series and when I found that Capcom relinquished the title to ninja theory, I was rather upset.
STORY
This game is about Dante and his brother Virgil who are both nephilim (angel and demon cross-breed). Their father, a demon named Sparda, fell in love and developed a secret life with an angel named Eva. The mother was killed and the father banished and torured in Hell. Dante and Virgil, along with a spiritual medium named Kat, seek to destroy the demon lord Mundus who controls humanity with lies, propaganda, and chemicals disquised as soft drinks.

INACCURACIES
Now let me tell you what upsets me about this. In the originals the brothers were merely half demon half human, Eva was a human. Secondly Sparda sacraficed his power to close the hellgate ending the great war and saving human kind, the parents both died and it isn't really explained how but it is strongly suggested in the first game that Mundus had something to do with it so that part is somewhat accurate. My next point is that [SPOILER ALERT] Mundus is killed in this game when he makes apperances in both the first and the third of the original games (FYI: the third is the prequel to the first) making the killing blow in this game either extremely misrepresented or another story change. About VIrgil, when he first appears in the originals he views humans as beneath him, if he didn't slightly pity them he would loath them. Virgil has no intent on ever working with a human or showing them respect.
DISLIKED
Now things I just didn't like about the game (feel free to skip because this is my opinion). I don't like Dante's bad attitude in this game, in the others he was kinder, funnier, and actually cool instead of a wannabe. They give you half your arsenal within the second mission and postpone the devil trigger until half way through. Emphasis on "give you half your arsenal" I felt like I hadn't earned a single weapon that I had. The other games made you find your guns through extra puzzles and the melee weapons were only earned after extremely difficult boss fights, the bosses in this game pale in comparison (some had multiple stages). The levels were rather stream lined, once i passed something more than likely I couldn't go back to get it nor could I explore like the other games. I would think that being part angel as well as demon would offer some kind of physical strength but, he cant even throw an axe into the air. The old Dante was throwing enemies, vehicles, and boulders regularly and he was half human.
LIKED
Don't get me wrong, I did enjoy the game just not the story or characters. The weapons were pretty cool and mostly originals, aside from classic Rebellion(sword) and his trusty pistols Ebony & Ivory. They did have gauntlets for brawling but, that has litterally been in all of the others. the play style was smooth, though it did seem like I was being hit by things I clearly shouldn't have been. It's basically the play style of DMC4 without the fighting styles. The enemies were more gruesome than ever and over all the game was beautiful.
SUMMARY
Over all this game is worth playing though I only reccomend it to people who have not played the originals and fallen in love with that story. This could almost pass as a prequel to the third game though that's impossible in my eyes. I give it a 7/10 for the awesome play with the botched lore.

Finally the 3D Castlevania SOTH game the world's been waiting for, forget what you heard about previous DMC games, this runs, & looks awesome!!! Full X360 pad support. 99-100 (no multiplayer so no perfect score)

I'm going to be unpopular opinion puffin and I'm
going to recommend this game. I finished the 'definitive edition' of the game, which means that it should be the least buggy and most balanced version with the most stuff to do - i.e. it should be the best the developers can offer. However, despite the name ("definitive") this version was not much different from the first, albeit with only 1 extra hour's worth of content thrown in.
Moving on, first I will talk about the bad things, seeing as I am not recommending it, and then I will talk about the good.
Firstly the bad:
1. Short Length - The game is only about 9 hours long if you want 100% completion rate. I finished the game with 100% completion in exactly 9 hours 21 minutes and 24 seconds. So for what it was, I finished it completely in 2 sittings.
2. No Replay Value - After finishing the game 100% and collecting everything, there is literally nothing else to do except hunt down a couple of pesky achievements. I managed to get over 75% of them in just a single playthrough and I could probably get most of the others in under an hour if I was bored enough as most just involve killing enemies enough times with a certain skill.
3. The Price - Given the game costs $20, takes only barely 9 hours to beat casually 100% and has no replay value. I think that it's somewhat expensive. Hollow Knight took me over 50 hours to get 100% completition in, and had 10x the variety and depth. Not only that, it's 25% cheaper.
4. Performance - I actually found the game lagged a bit at critical moments which made me die a couple of times. It wasn't such a big deal, but I wasn't impressed with the fact that there's no way to customise the graphical options. Having said that, I shouldn't have to because my machine cost over $3000 and I can play games with far better graphics that do not lag at all. The frame rate did spike enough times to warrant me mentioning it.
5. Enemy variety - Ori and the Blind Forest has very little variety in enemies. There's about 12 or so enemies total. Blobs, bigger blobs, rhino things, frogs that spit, jumping frogs, spiders, spitting tentacles, balls of energy that fire lazers and owls. That's pretty much it entirely. There's really no other enemies in the game, and instead of making new enemies they just recloured each enemy at least once to signify it being stronger. For comparison Hollow Knight had over 80 different enemy types, not even including the 20 or so bosses and both had lots of mehcanics that had to be learned.
6. Boring Combat - Basically a light follows you and you just mash attack to shoot auto-guided lightning at enemies. You can shoot from safe distanes or behind cover. There's really little skill involved. Upgrading your attack just increases the range and damage. You do get a few other skills like a stomp etc, but your other skills have more movement and environmental usage than combat usage. Oh and you get way too much health. 15 energy and life at the end which is a crazy amount even on hard.
7. Platforming Issues - Some parts of the platforming are really bad. Granted, a lot of bugs were fixed from the original version and the platforming is WAY better on this version. However, I still felt that some parts were unncessarily stupid and at times (and even with all skills) it was just too easy to fail a task by just an inch or split second. In addition to this, I didn't like the addition of a few areas that were only 1-way.  Ex. Ginso Tree and the right area in Black Root Burrow.
--------------------------------------------------------------
All in all the game was pretty good and features some of the best music of any game and a really beautiful story. However. compared to other metroidvania/platformer games. I felt a bit let down after realising that a casual playthrough could completely finish it in under 10 hours. I have to compare it to similar games like Hollow Knight, and maybe if I hadn't played games like 'HN' I'd be able to recommend OATBF, but for the price and given the above issues, I can't recommend it.
It's fun for a good portion of the 9 hours, but at times it's frustrating and finishing it left me feeling disappointed in the depth, variety and length. Buy it if it's about $10 bucks. That's my honest opinion.

This is hands down one of the most beautiful games I have ever played and also one that has an atmosphere and emotion second to none. A brilliant use of the Cryengine gives a believable segment of the English countryside and the aftermath of a mysterious incident. With eerily abandoned buildings, lush fields and picturesque woods accompanied by strange lights and one of the best music scores and audio around you explore the story of the valley and it's inhabitants at your own relaxed pace. Piecing together the fragments of peoples lives to find out what happened and what made them who they were makes is a masterpiece of interactive storytelling.
It's no shooter, you don't run but it has more emotion and soul than any game of CoD or Battlefield. It's not about framerate either, it runs excellently on my 2 year old kit as you don't need steady 60fps to enjoy it, heck films are 24fps and they work. Enjoy the beauty. Take your time.
If you like a mystery and want an experience like no other, enjoy true art with Everybody's gone to the Rapture.

I'm not quite sure why people have a problem with Everyone's Gone to the Rapture, I would have thought a majority of people by now would know they were buying a Dear Esther successor. I do agree the walking/slightly faster walking (run) controls are too slow and the developers shouldn't assume the player  should have to crawl around to be able to take the environment in, I found myself wanting to backtrack and check out other details but not feeling particularly bothered to due to the time it takes to move around so it feels by trying to force the player to take the environments in by slowing their movement down it's having more of an opposite effect where it makes you give up wanting to recheck or go to that building in the distance.
Being primarily an environment artist I found the world to be quite beautiful (perhaps being an artist I can appreciate games more focused on the visuals of an environment), performance wise I was reaching 50-60fps which I don't mind at all- perhaps some people should just turn the fps counter off, if your mind knows it's running at a particular fps it will become more obsessed with moaning about it. Whilst it can be annoying for people with medium spec machines, look at what you are trying to get your machine to run- maxing out the settings is giving you visuals that should only be run on a high spec machine (don't bring a Ford Fiesta to an Formula 1 race). I tested on a development machine with no hitches and a medium spec with barely any stutter at all, so if you are experiencing any performance issues try lowering your settings to something your machine is more capable of running smoothly (although it's beautiful temporal anti-aliasing can be costly and lowering the mesh detail can help).
All in all, I would recommend a play of this- it's something to relax with and enjoy when you want a quiet stroll through an english village. It might not be everything it could have been (lack of interactivity breaks the immersion at times) but it's worth it if you want to experience a story and world at a more leisurely pace.

CONS:

Astroneer is a space exploration adventure with some survival aspects as well. The game is currently in its pre-alpha stage of early access.
You can play this game solo or in up to four player online co-op. The game starts off with you launching your pod, and landing on a random planet, with just your tool in your hand and backpack. You venture out from your pod in search of resources and items to build your base, and discover new technology.
The fact that you can mold the environment is an amazing feature. It sort of reminds me of Everquest Landmark, but with a lot less customization. The functionality is already in place, and I would love to see more options  added to the tool to allow players to more precisely shape the world around them.
Exploring, collecting resources, improving your base, and discovering new research technology is very addicting. The entire time I played it seemed to fly by and before I knew it, it was two in the morning! There are storms on the planets as well, and they are sometimes deadly with debris flying everywhere. Also, some of the plant life will kill you too if you aren’t careful. There isn’t a lot of diversity right now, but it’s a good start.
The main survival aspect is maintaining your oxygen levels. Venture too far out without an bringing oxygen supply or finding some on your way, you will probably suffocate. Dying causes you to drop all the items in your backpack where you died and spawn you back at your habitat. You can go and collect your stuff, so while it’s an inconvenience, it’s often more of a lesson to teach you to be more prepared in the future. I’ve had a lot more fun playing this game than I did playing No Man’s Sky.
Playing alone is enjoyable. Playing with others is really awesome, but there are some problems with the multiplayer that might give some players a negative experience. The game’s performance for whoever is running the server will be worse than when they are solo. Whoever is hosting the server needs to have a good computer, and even then there will be frame drops. The people playing on the server also experienced several disconnects, and would have to retrieve their items from their bodies when they returned. Overall, I think we all still enjoyed the time playing, and weren’t too upset by the issues.
I have played over 11 hours so far, and experienced both the single player and multiplayer gameplay.
Sure, the game has some bugs, and glitches, and the multiplayer needs better optimization, but issues are expected in a pre-alpha state. The fun factor alone is enough to look past the annoyances, and really appreciate the great start that Astroneer is off to. There is a ton of potential here, and this is a game I recommend. The framework for an amazing game is in place, and I really look forward to seeing where they go with it.

Max Payne has been taken by the police and is about to face charges for his killing spree. However, he is cleared of all charges, thanks to his relationship with a very influential member of society, Senator Alfred Woden. A few years have passed, and Max has returned to work for the NYPD as a homicide detective. During a routine murder investigation he finds himself face-to-face with the fugitive Mona Sax, a woman he thought was dead. Max and Mona team up to solve the answers to Max's past that left his wife and child dead.
An incredible leap in gameplay and graphics just 1 year after the release of the first game. The story does not dissapoint. Starting off with the cleaners and finding out Mona is alive (Its not a spoiler its on the game description) dealings with the inner circle and Alfred Woden. Meeting people from the first game, Vladimir Lem & Vinnie Gognitti. Leading up to a massive climax, dark and gritty as in the first.
This time the gunplay and bullet time is far superior and you get to play as Mona as well. Certain missions you play both in alternating sequence to get to the goal.
James McCaffrey reprises his role as Max and the superb poetic and dark monolougue continues.
One other point about this game. It basically introduced the world to Poet's of the fall with their song Late Goodbye. If you like your Scandinavian rock/metal (I do \m/) check these guys out for some lighter rock. Late goodbye can be heard throughout the game from a janitor humming as he cleans, to a cleaner playing it on a grand piano right before (most people blow him up with a grenade) and of course the final credits.
One of my favourite PC shooters of all time.

This game is deep and well thought out.  Though it's a bit complex at first, prisons need to be planned carefully. There are too many bland, boring and lacking simulations. Fortunately this game is not one of them, it will keep you playing for many hours.
I never get sick of building things and can always come back to this game when Iam not sure what else to play. I have played for over 200 hours at the time of writing this review and have not had any trouble with bugs or any crashing.
I don't satisfy all prisoner needs as I like drama and having my prisoners riot regularly is fun.
Otherwise it's boring if they behave and don't do anything wrong.
So far I have sold 2 prisons and am building my third prison as it costs quite alot to build the prison you want. Though you can opt for unlimited funds, I built however I wanted, but my bank balance ended up being -2.5million in the red. Didn't like it, my prison felt worthless. You should first start out with getting all the grants you can, build along with what the grants require  and then sell when you run out of grants. Though what brings profit to a prison is workshops and a forestry.
My second prison was a female prison and I did not like having a female prison as you get mothers who bring their babies with them and they need a much larger family cell as well as a seperate nursery area for them to eat with their baby, plus they have different needs than males, seem to have hygeine first, males exercise and aren't as violent as males.
After 200 hours I ended up with a 1000+ prison valued at over 9million with 6million in funds without using any cheats.
Escape mode seems like a tacked on after thought, not very exciting, quite boring. As the prisoner, you just damage things to get heaps of rep points, use points to skip punishment and repeat until you max out skills, it's rather quick to do. Then one hit punch kill guards and escape out the front door. I escaped when there was a riot happening, even though I was carrying keys, guards just ignored me as were busy trying to handle the riot and I just ran past them all and out the front door, when I ran out I had 3 groups of riot police chasing me, but the quick skill was maxed so managed to sprint and escape.
Even though I like the game there are things that could be improved, but unfortunately looks like the developers are finished with the game, which is sad.
Things aren't categorised well enough, objects in a object menu are a mess and can be hard to find unless you type out the name first, difficult for new players that may not be sure what they are looking for.
I dislike that things aren't explained very well in this game, I was not sure how many cookers I would need or how many clothes a laundry provides, I had to look it up on a wiki to find out. That info should be in game, at least have it as a tooltip when you mouseover the object.
But overall I recommend this game as I enjoy it mostly.
Get this game if you love building, simulations and micro management.

Overall this game had a lot of potential and it really delivered in some aspects. The graphics and the feel of the guns when shot are still great even after a number of years.
But that's it really, if I'm being honest.
The combat is great at the start, until you reach sections of the game where enemies spawn in waves after waves and you gun them down with no problem. The game actually gives you a lot of ammo when you're low, so it wasn't as punishing as I initially thought. The melee units are a joke and even the special troops near the end of the game are easily taken out. The only trouble would be the heavy units, but even they're done in with a shotgun to the face a couple of times. All in all not a very difficult combat system, and in a vacuum, would be actually fun to play once in awhile.
Until you mix that with the A.I.
Now, the A.I of the enemies is actually pretty good for a game from 2012. They flank, they wait for you to pop out to shoot, they cover each other and pin you down when other enemies move up. Nah the enemy A.I is commendable. The only problem is your teammates. The dumb soldiers do the worst possible imaginable thing almost every time. Attempting to melee enemies in full armour and an LMG is a common one. Running towards grenades is also pretty much the norm for these great american troopers. Time and time again I would have to restart simply because the 2 dumb bumpkins the game calls soldiers would rather hug each other and cry when a grenade lands at their feet then move to the adjacent cover about 2 metres away. It would have been acceptable if it had happened once or twice, but the exact same scenario happened at least 5-6 times in a row.
The biggest issue I have with the game is finally here. Something so easily changed and tweaked almost had me wanting to throw my pc out the window with Dark Souls levels of rage.
The controls and autolock.
So many times the leader of Delta team (i.e you) would get gunned down because he couldn't lean on a pillar to literally save his life. Alternatively, would get his legs blown off by a grenade because he
. The janky♥♥♥♥♥controls was the main thing making this frustrating to play and the game would have gone so smoothly. The biggest qualm I have with the game.
Had the fairly common audio bug where some or all sound in some cutscenes would not exist, e.g no sound at all in a cutscene, or no dialogue audio in another cutscene. Tried fixing it a few times throughout the game, but gave up around the same time I gave up on the game.
The story was rather eh. You get dropped off with no idea on what you're doing and the game just throws some expo and leaves you to figure it out. Granted, its not a whole bunch of names and expo dumps but it still leaves you with a sense of "uhhh...?" for half the game, and the next half you're not paying attention because you really don't care by that point.

Overall okaish game with decent combat, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ A.I and such broken♥♥♥♥♥controls it would make Sean Murray (circa No Man's Sky launch day) blush.
. I can definitely see why the game's story would be a major appeal for some, just not for me. Sad really, was excited for the game and had high hopes after hearing from friends and other reviews.
tl;dr just get it on sale with low expectations, won't be too disappointed like that.

As a fan of the series for maybe 14 years Hitman is one of my top games of 2016.
It wasn't apparent at first just how much there is to do, every mission has about a dozen paths already laid out with objective markers and clues, and it's fun to experiment whether you just follow the crumbs or turn off the guidance and let yourself mess up on occasion. Messing up is actually part of the magic, and it's not without frustration but failing can be fun in Hitman.
Eventually you decide to go off path and dispatch of the targets your own way, then you realise there are just as many options the game doesn't tell you about at all, indeed they're probably easier than those the game suggests. You'll replay missions over and over trying different approaches, either to get achievements or just for fun. Then you'll go on Youtube and realise there are things you can do you never noticed, not because they're secrets, just because you never considered looking for them.
Then you have Contracts, Escalation and Elusive Targets. The quality is hit-and-miss but I've had great excitement, fear and joy playing them and I appreciate that the devs have been able to experiment with the formula and create some awesome moments in the process.
There are things about the game which nobody is happy about, they have definitely effected me from time to time. Some have been improved yet there is still more that could be done, but Hitman's negatives are almost inconsequential to it's positives and IO have built not only a great game but a great system for delivering more missions and new types of content in the future.
Hitman gets to the core of the franchise while stretching the entertainment well past anybody thought it could be stretched to, and throughout the whole experience it manages to match or exceed expectations. And they're still working on it.

HITMAN™ is really, really good. It blends the great stuff from Hitman: Absolution such as the improved combat and graphical fidelity with the traditional hardcore stealth elements of classic instalments such as; Hitman 2: Silent Assassin and the infamous and well-loved Hitman: Blood Money.
It lets you approach objectives anyway you want to; whether that be never being detected and only killing your targets or going completely guns blazing.
Enix gives you seven missions, (that may not seem like a lot but just keep reading I will say why it is ok) that are all spread across different parts of the world;
-ICA Facility: this is your training stage.
-France (Paris): this is at a massive home where a fashion show is currently taking place.
-Italy (Sapienza): this is a small little town on the coast of Italy with a mansion that you have to infiltrate.
-Morocco (Marrakesh): this is a city currently under military control giving you an even harder job at completing your mission.
-Tailand (Bangkok): this takes place within a hotel resort along the coast; due to it being in a hotel resort it has lots of things the targets can do to seek pleasure such as massages, this gives you loads of opportunities to kill them in a variety of ways.
-USA (Colorado): this is within a small rural town. This is an interesting mission in itself because you can play that stalker like role within the cornfields and pretend to be scarecrows pinned up.
-Japan (Hokkaido): and finally this is set in an extremely high tech tower facility thousands of feet above sea level.
Now you may be thinking: "These missions don't sound interesting at all mate..."
In which my response is: "Words do not do the mission design any justice."
Going back to the idea that seven levels aren't a sufficient amount for a full priced AAA game. This game centers its longevity and replayability around one thing VARIETY. Whether that be as simple as mixing your playstyles up between levels or trying to master one level with all the weapons and strategies possible making you a 'Silent Master Assassin'. The game's beauty like all the other so called 'Hitmen' games comes in mastering the levels so you know them by the back of your hand no matter the size of them so you feel like you know each targets movement cycles and where to go to kill them with certain things; practically making yourself as proficient as possible at killing HVTs.
The missions are not only just on their lonesome. You have the standard missions of course with literally dozens of mastery challenges to complete but you also have things called 'Escalation Contracts' which place you in the same mission but give you different targets within them such as a particular high ranking security guard or a private investigator. In addition to this, there is also complete revamped versions of the standard missions you get, for example; in Sapienza there is a mission where you have to kill an actor while he is on set shooting a new movie. (This occurrence is not happening in the standard mission by the way).
So, like I said the game prides itself on it's replayability and value for money. It's quality over quantity but the latter half is not lacking at all. They blended the quality of content with the amount of content well.
It is worth noting the graphics are fantastic, the gameplay is fun; you don't die too quickly like in some games but you don't take that many bullets to be taken down (it's realistic and authentic), the story is kind of hit or miss for me; if you are a die hard Hitman fan (and you haven't already bought it) you may dig it - it's very simplistic and barebones but it gets the job done so it's fine.
All in all, definitely worth picking up!

Astroneer is a space exploration adventure with some survival aspects as well. The game is currently in its pre-alpha stage of early access.
You can play this game solo or in up to four player online co-op. The game starts off with you launching your pod, and landing on a random planet, with just your tool in your hand and backpack. You venture out from your pod in search of resources and items to build your base, and discover new technology.
The fact that you can mold the environment is an amazing feature. It sort of reminds me of Everquest Landmark, but with a lot less customization. The functionality is already in place, and I would love to see more options  added to the tool to allow players to more precisely shape the world around them.
Exploring, collecting resources, improving your base, and discovering new research technology is very addicting. The entire time I played it seemed to fly by and before I knew it, it was two in the morning! There are storms on the planets as well, and they are sometimes deadly with debris flying everywhere. Also, some of the plant life will kill you too if you aren’t careful. There isn’t a lot of diversity right now, but it’s a good start.
The main survival aspect is maintaining your oxygen levels. Venture too far out without an bringing oxygen supply or finding some on your way, you will probably suffocate. Dying causes you to drop all the items in your backpack where you died and spawn you back at your habitat. You can go and collect your stuff, so while it’s an inconvenience, it’s often more of a lesson to teach you to be more prepared in the future. I’ve had a lot more fun playing this game than I did playing No Man’s Sky.
Playing alone is enjoyable. Playing with others is really awesome, but there are some problems with the multiplayer that might give some players a negative experience. The game’s performance for whoever is running the server will be worse than when they are solo. Whoever is hosting the server needs to have a good computer, and even then there will be frame drops. The people playing on the server also experienced several disconnects, and would have to retrieve their items from their bodies when they returned. Overall, I think we all still enjoyed the time playing, and weren’t too upset by the issues.
I have played over 11 hours so far, and experienced both the single player and multiplayer gameplay.
Sure, the game has some bugs, and glitches, and the multiplayer needs better optimization, but issues are expected in a pre-alpha state. The fun factor alone is enough to look past the annoyances, and really appreciate the great start that Astroneer is off to. There is a ton of potential here, and this is a game I recommend. The framework for an amazing game is in place, and I really look forward to seeing where they go with it.

It's a shame that they decided not to add anything new to this game, because it's lacking a number of things that would make it a really good prison simulator. Namely, the only way for your prisoners to escape (other than leaving the door open) is to dig an escape tunnel, something only certain prisoners can do. They won't try and attack your guards to steal keys, they won't try to climb fences, nothing. Prisoners also do not exist to each other at all, except as things to beat up if they go on a tear, or murder if they are randomly assigned traits like Snitch and Ex Law Enforcement. These are the only kinds of prisoners that will have hits called on them; they will never be called on any other prisoner. They do not talk to each other, they do not form bonds with each other, they do not band together or dislike each other except as part of the optional Gangs system. The problem with the Gangs system is that gang leaders will frequently be assigned traits that make them extremely volatile troublemakers, rather than subtle string-pullers that never get their hands dirty. They will murder your staff, and then the rest of the gang will riot when they are punished for it, rendering the system more of a nuisance than anything.
The game reeks of unrealized potential that was cut short when the dev team realized they had been working on this title for 6 years and wanted to be done with it. It may be released, but it is nothing approaching finished. They didn't even bother to hammer out a flexible, powerful modding API before they ditched it, so these holes will never be filled. Despite this, it's still a very enjoyable, fun game that you should buy and enjoy. But when you've played it as long as I have, you will always have that niggling at the back of your head that it's lacking a lot of important things.

A good game usually falls into two categories for me: Good gameplay, and good story. Prison Architect has somehow fell into both of these categories.
I picked this game up for $7.50 (£6.05) fully expecting great gameplay and a very detailed and intriguing game system. Not only did it deliver, but I have been playing for well over a cululative day and I am still finding new things to implement into my prison. The way that the game is set up is so wonderfully complex and deep, yet with its great UI and helpful tutorials, I have no problem navigating and interpreting everything that the game has to throw at me. You can tell that the game devs had a wonderful grasp on exactly what the people wanted and they delivered and then some.
I may have been expecting the great gameplay, but what I did not expect was surprisingly well-written campaign/tutorial that not only had me intrigued, it got me thinking about the penal system nowadays. I can't say that it is as good as Portal or even Grim Fandango, but it surprised me that so much effort went into characters and plotlines while still getting me introduced to the gameplay mechanics.
Overall, I cannot recommend this game enough to management game fans, strategy fans, simulation fans, and people who are curious about these genres of video games (this game is a wonderful introduction). I have never played a game so avidly right after purchasing it. 11/10

Do you like Arkham City? Do you want more of it? Well, Arkham Origins is exactly that. It feels more like an expansion pack to Arkham City than a whole new game, as it doesn't do anything gameplay-wise, even going so far as to reskin some gadgets from Arkham City that didn't make sense to carry over into Origins's prequel setting in their original form. Even The Joker returns as the main antagonist, something Rocksteady was clearly trying to steer away from, but on the bright side, despite Mark Hamill's departure, Troy Baker did an excellent job picking up Hamill's legacy. You'll probably miss Kevin Conroy as Batman though; I know I did.
The same old Arkham City gameplay holds up in a new story with new characters and some memorable moments, especially a tense cat-and-mouse (bat-and-mouse?) fight with a monstrous Bane hopped up on super venom. (Speaking of Bane, I wish writers would stop making "breaking the Bat" Bane's entire two-dimensional reason for existence.)
Arkham Origins wouldn't have been worth a $60 purchase at release, but if you like the "Arkham" series, it's worth grabbing, especially on sale.

A fairly standard third person cover based shooter with an interesting story it fails to deliver correctly.
This game has its moments. Three of them to be exact. First of them being sand falling through the window for the very first time. Second is a single scene that would include spoilers and an epilogue. Outside of that it's pretty forgettable.
The graphics are nice although a bit dull with all the sand and not much space to roam about. The level design is extremely linear and there's next to no room to maneuver. All you do is follow a set path, cover behind obstacles and shoot the opponents.
The story is strange. You start in Dubai not really understanding why you're there, what happened and what exactly you're trying to achieve. For whatever reason you need to shoot your fellow Americans, there's CIA involved and you're not exactly sure what's going on. In the larger scheme I think the game tries to do something like Apocalypse Now but I wasn't sold on it. It wasn't bad though. There's a big plot twist near the end but it's nothing you can figure out along the way.
The gameplay as mentioned is forgettable. It gets a bit better towards the end but feels really boring for the first half of the game. The AI is extremely stupid. You hide behind the cover and enemies come in waves. You kill some, another bunch comes and so on until there's no one left. You progress further and repeat the same thing over again.
It's a good thing that this game is fairly short and I enjoyed the cinematics for the most part. Good if you're up for some mindless shooting.

What I think about this game.
Everybody's Gone to the Rapture Review:

I feel like most of the negative reviews here involve mainly technical issues, which is fair, but the game is perfectly playable as long as you have a mid-range computer. Full disclosure, I have a 6700K with a 980ti for my desktop, and an i7-4702HQ with a GTX 870m for my laptop. There's definitely some frame-pacing issues, and some areas need some optimization (framerate drops at random times in the game), but nothing game breaking, and nothing that breaks immersion. My take on the game: If you liked Dear Esther, or if you felt that it had potential but needed more depth, then Everybody's Gone to the Rapture will be everything you expect. If you dislike "walking simulators", then move along.

A walking simulator. You walk (slowly) and explore and the story unfolds through conversatiions left behind by the dead and from recordings also left behind. Beautiful graphics. Good voice acting, Some have praised the music but it's elevator music to me. It's sci-fi in an open small world. It is ultimately boring. The story is interesting but not exciting or engaging. If you like walking around looking at the scenery this is for you. It does have it's flaws. The biggest of which for me was the lack of the ability to save the game which meant I played it and lost it all twice. The game tells you that it automatically saves after certain keys scenes but It never happened. So prepare for a 4 to 6 hour (approximately) stroll in the country but don't count on saving and coming back where you left off. Save your money.

Ori is a platformer/metroidvania game with also some interesting, although limited, combat mechanics. You play the role of Ori a...light squirrel?? I don't know what is exaclty, but you soon discover that the forest is dying and you have to restore it by claiming three magic macguffin to place back in their correct place. travel the different, but coherent landscapes of this vast forest, populated by a somehow limited set of creatures which will attack you. You will progressively discover new abilities that will help in traveling the map with more and more ease, access previously locked places and learn few more ways to fight.
The strength of the game is in the platforming. Ori moves very fast and can combine, by the end of the games, a vast set of jumps, dashes and slingshots which hook on projectiles and enemies, shooting you in one direction and the thing you hook on in the other. Chaining all of these abilities is very satistying, creating a great flow of movement that really makes you feel as if you are made of immaterial light. Despite of the fast nature of your movement the animations look fluent and almost rich, maintaining a very high level of reactivity, which is key for a good platformer. Imagine a super meat boy which animates like a "Studio Ghibli" anime.
The combat and the enemies are both rather limited, it is not the focus of the game. Nonetheless they are still used to provide xp points which you can use to gain new abilities and strength, although they best use in the level design is as animated environmental element to traverse, using them to access higher places or to break barrier while airborn. Defeating the enemies is not the best and most enjoyable interaction you can have with them, the best thing is jumping from one to another untoutched...which is quite in line with the morale of the story about the balance of nature.
Xp points can also be earned in bunch by exploring and collecting them around, but if you want to go for filling all of the power ups available (not necessary to finish the game), you will need to grind some enemies. Exploring will also allow you to find life and energy increments, the first will allow you to resist more hits, the second are necessary to mostly use some special abilities and saving. You can save almost anywhere, but creating a new save point in the map uses a resource which has to be properly managed. When you die you restart with almost no lag at your previous save, the song goes on which to me is important in not making you feel bad for dying...and you will die...a lot. I am not ashamed in sying that my first play ended with about 600 deaths, but I did not feel frustrated about it, because the game makes a good job in letting start right up immediately.
The story is rather generic, but there are a few touches of bonding moment which make you feel involved in the charachters. This is instead a problem I had in Super Meat Boy, although it is a good game, I often felt a lack of motivation in pushign through every level. Here as you are part of a coherent story and a defined map it is much easier to feel involved.
Upon the key points of the game you will have what corresponds to "Boss encounters" which are in the form of very creative levels to traverse and navigate, with a whole specific set of rules and mechanic, most of them learned in the normal map, but definetely pumped up.
Sound design is very coherent and well fit to the theme, not very memorable maybe.
The game ran well on my machine, and would on probably most of them nowadays, although I sometimes had some glitches in the ligthing of enemy projectiles. You can change resolution up to 1920:1080, abilitate or not Vsync and motion blur..pretty basic stuff, but that's just good enough for the type of game.
One thing I really did not like is that YOU CANNOT REBIND KEYS!!!! The game is even out in a "definite edition", but this basic option is not available. Luckily the key setup in the keyboard/mouse function is functional enough, but I do feel sorry for anyone that would not find the standard setting to be suitable for their way of playing and are stuck with it. Even in a first release I do think that not allow for key rebinding is very disrespectful...in a "definitive edition" which sould namely correct problems with the initial release. On steam forum you can find ways of modifying some game files to rebind keys, so check them out if you do need to.
.
In conlusion I do recommend this game as it is a very good example of a platforming/metroidvania game, with artstyle and animation level that have almost no equals. I enjoyed all my time with the game (which is much more than the one indicated by steam, I played a lot offline for reasons).If you like at least two of these three things (platforming, metroidvania, anime) you have to try this game.

Hitman is a game which, whilst not perfect, I have thoroughly enjoyed playing. 8/10
• Excellent graphics
• Stunning map design
• Creative and amusing methods of assassination
• Always-online DRM (
)

The
reason this game has Mixed reviews is because of the always-online DRM. Playing the game offline, whilst possible, severely hinders your experience. This is a potential deal-breaker if your internet is too unreliable to play the game. Despite this, far too many people are leaving ‘Not Recommended’ reviews because of this feature alone which is not fair.
I will review all of the maps on their individual DLC page but, since Paris doesn’t have one, I’ll review it here.
Paris ranks 5/6 (6 being my least favourite) on my list of maps. Whilst strictly speaking not entirely inside, the map design feels slightly sloppy. Many rooms are near-enough empty. This, in fairness, may be accurate to real life but that simply means that the map should be different. You’ll spend little time traversing the public end of the fashion show and more time sneaking through near-empty rooms and corridors. With that said, I still enjoyed this map. I originally bought just Episode 1 as a ‘trial’ of sorts and it convinced me to buy the game.

Let's get one thing straight. To unlock the achievements, you need a constant internet connection. That has ruffled a lot of feathers among several reviewers but I think it's a small issue.
That being said, this is definitely one of the best games out there. I've played the series all the way from Codename 47 to this one and I have to admit, it keeps up with the Hitman feel. There are multiple ways to eliminate a target and the disguise system is much better. Unlike Absolution, where anyone wearing the same disguise could see through you, there are specific NPCs who can tell if you're not one of them; NPCs that change with each disguise. The game has great replayability, partly because you'll want to try all the different ways to kill a target or to infiltrate and partly due to the Mastery system. There are plenty of missions on each map in the form of escalations, even though they do get a bit repetitive; and one Mission in Colorado is definitely broken, but doable. The Elusive Target is a great new addition to the game.  All in all:
Pros:
1. New Graphics Engine gives the game a much nicer feel
2. There isn't much in the way of a Story but the cutscenes definitely keep you interested in what happens next
3. Multiple ways of killing a target
4. Some funny moments for fans of the franchise (I'd rather not spoil them by giving an example)
Cons:
1. Controls can sometimes be a bit clunky
2. Needs a constant internet connection in order to record achievements
10/10 would buy
Edit: They've added more missions for all owners of the game. This is the kind of positive response I think most gamers want from developers. Waiting for Season 2

A good game usually falls into two categories for me: Good gameplay, and good story. Prison Architect has somehow fell into both of these categories.
I picked this game up for $7.50 (£6.05) fully expecting great gameplay and a very detailed and intriguing game system. Not only did it deliver, but I have been playing for well over a cululative day and I am still finding new things to implement into my prison. The way that the game is set up is so wonderfully complex and deep, yet with its great UI and helpful tutorials, I have no problem navigating and interpreting everything that the game has to throw at me. You can tell that the game devs had a wonderful grasp on exactly what the people wanted and they delivered and then some.
I may have been expecting the great gameplay, but what I did not expect was surprisingly well-written campaign/tutorial that not only had me intrigued, it got me thinking about the penal system nowadays. I can't say that it is as good as Portal or even Grim Fandango, but it surprised me that so much effort went into characters and plotlines while still getting me introduced to the gameplay mechanics.
Overall, I cannot recommend this game enough to management game fans, strategy fans, simulation fans, and people who are curious about these genres of video games (this game is a wonderful introduction). I have never played a game so avidly right after purchasing it. 11/10

I played the original Max Payne when it was first release [and I still use the free mouse pad that came with the box! (had to wash it a few times)]. I thought the first game was fun but I put off playing the sequal because I never heard much about it. Well, I finally played through the game and actually enjoyed it. It's rather short, the graphics are a bit dated and the story arch wasn't as epic as the first (going off of memory here), but it brought back some good memories of playing the original Max Payne. If you liked the first one I suggest you give this a shot, otherwise you'd be better off trying the original.

In contrast with its previous iteration, Max Payne 2 feels like an action crime-thriller rather than the paced noir style of the original. The production values increased, which is a positive note unless you miss Sam Lake's lovely constipated look as Max's face. The story is taken to a whole new level, with more twists and turns than the writer can throw Norse Mythology references at you. Just like the previous game, I really enjoyed the little touches like the TV shows (which you should watch) and continuity checks (Captain Baseball Bat Boy, how I have missed you!). This crime-thriller/action/ psychodrama is something I would always smooch with my bloody lips if I didn’t had to clean it afterwards. On a side-note, check out Alan Wake if you can, another Remedy game with the same lead voice actor, fantastic writing, and with some quirky references to the man who gave us a late goodbye.

There are a number of indie, puzzle games out there, most of them very similar in both concept and functionality. A lot of the time using a simple graphical style, with a mostly basic story-line and more often than not, reusing the same puzzles and mechanics. So what sets See No Evil apart from the endless stream of clones and failures.
To begin with I’ll start by mentioning the fact that it’s not too dissimilar from a lot of games in the genre. The puzzles are somewhat familiar; pushing boxes, standing on switches all to reach the level’s exit. There is a bit of twist, however. Sound plays a very important part in the puzzles, in some more than others. Blind but dangerous enemies patrol some of the levels. If they hear your footsteps or your shouting they will hunt you down. Standing still can sometimes help you survive, but very rarely. This gives See No Evil a slight stealth feeling to it. Watching the enemies patrols and waiting for the right moment to move can feel very sneaky sneaky. You can distract them too with bell flowers or huge horns, allowing for you to tiptoe past while they check what’s going on. Some of the puzzles are quite complex and take time to think about before actually setting things into motion. Some blocks will lower when the matching pressure plate is pressed, which in turn can raise other blocks instead. Sometimes enemy patrols will prevent you from getting to where you need to be. There are a number of different obstacles to overcome in order to reach the exit, and as you progress through the game things gets tougher and a lot more complex.
Graphically the game has a charming, hand drawn style to it. Levels are mostly simple, with an obvious theme running through them. Whether its through a crumbling castle, a lush, green woodland or an abandoned factory the style is somewhat refreshing. As well as that, it’s not overly cluttered or distracting, allowing the player to easily see the sound indications as well as which objects can be interacted with and not.
The sound effects are very clear as is the music. Each area has a different music track, which at times can get a little bit grating as it plays on a constant loop. But it has a somewhat retro or classic feel to it, along with most of the game for that matter. Even though the game has a dark and foreboding story running through it, the music almost lightens the mood.
Talking of the story, you play as a Seer, whatever that is, and are guided by a journal left in your prison cell. You’re opposed by a group of blind evil doers that are afraid of what they don’t know. It’s not all that in-depth, to be fair, but it stops the game from feeling dry and emotionless, not to mention it helps with that feeling of progression.
Lastly lets talk about the games mechanics. There are always small problems with indie games, when it comes down to mechanics. Sometimes they’re things not even worth mentioning. But there are some that affect a game in such a way that they can’t be overlooked. In See No Evil there are a small number of glaring mechanical problems. Interactions with certain object require the player to be in a particular spot for it to actually work, which can be frustrating when you might be against the clock or trying to avoid an enemy patrol. Alongside that, some of the walls seem to be made of glue as the player might find themselves getting stuck to said walls. This doesn’t count for every wall, infact I found it to be a rare occurrence, although it was a small annoyance when it did happen. Lastly it would be nice if the player were able to move even a smidgen faster. Moving about the levels seems to take a long time, a small sprint function or maybe just an increase in movement speed would be a welcome thing.
But, to conclude, I’d say See No Evil feels almost original in its ideas. The graphical style is pleasing to look at and the music is refreshing to boot. The story is lacking however, but I guess you can’t have everything. If you want a different angle on the indie, puzzle genre then See No Evil might be worth your time. Good Day!

This review is being written maybe 1 day after the games early access was launched on Steam.
For a pre- alpha ... this is an AMAZING experience.
Love the music. Love the look and feel of the planets.
Even without a tutorial you can work out how things work and what to do with them just like games back in the day.
Started the game in the evening and was playing till about midnight without even feeling like i had been playing for long.
i have no idea what the game developers are thinking for the future of this game. but even as it is, i can just load it up. and set up a base, and it actually feels relaxing. i don't feel like i'm being pulled in too many directions. the materials needed for crafting are simple to aquire and use.
I would love to see future updates including travelling to other planets. i would love to see more vehicles. more building types. and different base expansion options( like 2 tiered pods and upgrading to larger storage tables).
This PRE-ALPHA feels MORE polished than " no mans sky" did on release. i am impressed and as i said before. Am looking forward to future updates.
PRO's
- Game runs really smooth
- Control scheme is really well thought out and feels natural
- Love how adaptable and fluid building feels.
- Day /night cycle nice and quick which also adds to the feel of the planets.
- Researching feels rewarding.
- Exploring caves is fun and interesting
-being able to choose between carry quantity or more power and oxygen with backpack slots doesn't feel punishing.
- Tether system!!!! AMAZING!!!!
CON's
- Multiplayer struggles a little with more than 2 people in the game.
- 2nd player seems to disconnect occasionally.
- game does crash occasionally (its a pre alpha DUR)
- lack of tutorial will leave some players wondering what to do. (and frankly they just need to use their brain a little because its not hard to work out).
- Items not stacking with existing stacks e.g. 5 tethers left. pick up one that was placed accidentally. takes up new slot on backpack. (i'm sure they'll fix this.)
- After a long time on a planet. and with a large base and LOTS of tethers. the games frame rate will start to chug. (once again Pre-Alpha DUR).
Honestly the Cons just feel weak because it is mostly just early access things that i'm sure will be fixed. but i wanted to write a review straight away because i have been enjoying myself thoroughly. and this game DESERVES support.

I'm going to start my review with a caveat: I do recommend this game, once it's closer to a real beta level state.
Now with that out of the way, for a pre-Alpha I must admit the game's beautiful and was a ton of fun for the first 5 or 6 hours. Sadly that's about all there is for content right now. After building an elaborate base, researching dozens of unusual and alien items, exploring the surface of 5 planets and their deepest depths (they are small worlds to be honest) and stockpiling more resources than I can even use... I'm out of things to do after only 8 hours of gameplay.
I think this game has OODLES of potential and what we have now is a rock-solid foundation, but I'd like to see a lot more depth added over the coming months. I'd also like to see the planets made larger - I was a bit stumped at the fact I was able to complete a full circumnavigation of the moon in under 5 minutes (on a Truck, not on foot). It also seemed far too difficult to establish bases on the other planets as many essential resources seem to be completely missing on remote worlds and we don't have the ability to bring much with us in terms of materials. Also, based on the small size of planets, I fear that in a single game it would be possible to completely exhaust every resource on every planet with enough gameplay, especially in multi-player.
Base building has some issues I'm sure will be ironed out quickly, but long-term I'd like to see the ability to build bigger, better base components like a REAL "habitat" that players can enter and walk around in. And a real landing/take-off pad for the ships instead of permanently tying up my vehicle assembly bay once a ship has been built. We should also be able to build things like hydroponics pods to grow renewable resources (Organics, Resin and Compound) if for no other reason than to have something to trade for other resources once we've completely mined-out a world.
Again, major kudos to the dev team for a graphically stunning game that's fun and easy to play. It's been a real pleasure. Sadly it was just short-lived in this pre-Alpha release. So I had fun for a couple days and I will be eagerly awaiting the next major content update. Until then, keep up the great work!

A fairly standard third person cover based shooter with an interesting story it fails to deliver correctly.
This game has its moments. Three of them to be exact. First of them being sand falling through the window for the very first time. Second is a single scene that would include spoilers and an epilogue. Outside of that it's pretty forgettable.
The graphics are nice although a bit dull with all the sand and not much space to roam about. The level design is extremely linear and there's next to no room to maneuver. All you do is follow a set path, cover behind obstacles and shoot the opponents.
The story is strange. You start in Dubai not really understanding why you're there, what happened and what exactly you're trying to achieve. For whatever reason you need to shoot your fellow Americans, there's CIA involved and you're not exactly sure what's going on. In the larger scheme I think the game tries to do something like Apocalypse Now but I wasn't sold on it. It wasn't bad though. There's a big plot twist near the end but it's nothing you can figure out along the way.
The gameplay as mentioned is forgettable. It gets a bit better towards the end but feels really boring for the first half of the game. The AI is extremely stupid. You hide behind the cover and enemies come in waves. You kill some, another bunch comes and so on until there's no one left. You progress further and repeat the same thing over again.
It's a good thing that this game is fairly short and I enjoyed the cinematics for the most part. Good if you're up for some mindless shooting.

A desent into madness that is worthy of praise for the story alone. This is honestly one of the few games I could recommend on story alone. I don't want to spoil anything but I'd argue this is a strong contender for best story in a shooter.
That being said, if you're like me a game is a complete package. Just because one element is strong doesn't mean it's automaticly a masterpiece. For me to consider a game to be 10/10, A+, Five stars etc all elements must be near perfect.
First off the game looks great. Character models are the strong point. The way Walker's face changes as he takes damage is great. The world looks convincing and some injuries look genuinely disturbing. Sound design and voice acting are also on point and support the desent into madness.
But then there's the gameplay. This is the big weakness to this game. Don't get me wrong it's not awful, just average. This is a a basic cover based shooter with regen health, dumb AI and enemies that are only tough because they can eat two magazines from an assault rifle to the face without dying.  I do understand this game is suppose to be poking at the ludicrous power fantasy mentality that comes along with most shooters but that shouldn't be an excuse.
AI is my biggest complaint. It was not rare for teammates to charge ahead and leave cover, often getting them and myself into very bad situations. To be honest they felt more like a burden than an asset. Enemies are also fairly stupid and will bunch up making them very vunerable to grenades. Later parts of the game feel too small for the enemies, as they are unable to spread out enough.
My other big complaint are the controls. For the love of God having take cover being the same button as sprint is beyond frustrating.
Overall I'd recommend this game. I don't think it's a masterpiece as a game although it is a masterpiece in story telling. The only reason I wrote this review is that I think people who love this game oversell it. I'm not saying this can't be your favourite game like I'm some big authority on gaming. Plenty of games I love are deeply flawed. Just go into this game knowing that gameplay-wise, this is a basic third person shooter.

This is a cheap game and definitely run easily on high settings on low end PCs. If you appreciate it, I'd definitely suggest to purchase the Eurotruck Simulator 2, which has some awards as one of the best Simulation Games.
Let's start with the cons of the game:
- Basically only highways (with passing lanes on the right ??)
- Cities are ridiculously small (a couple of business companies, a garage)
- Really bad driving behavior from AI, as an example, they always slow down to 40 km/h on highways because of an acceleration lane on their right even if there is no car or they will horn for no reason
- Speed limit is bad, as the limits variy from 50 for cities to 90 out of cities (AI won't drive at 90 km/h if they ain't on a highway)
Let's go to the positive notes:
- Accurate truck movement, especially when it comes down to backwards driving with cargo
- Driving with cruise control possible and best highway speed seems accurately to be 80 km/h
- Different camera perspectives which may be useful (May favorite in all situations is still the perspective from inside the vehicle)
- You can get tired by driving (if it's enabled)
- You can run out of fuel if you haven't refulled in tank station - you'll have to call emergency service which isn't cheap
- Accidents may happen, which can be sometimes on odd places (in front of your city's garage)
- You will get fined if you drive too fast, without light during night or if you crash against another vehicle
- A fine will be issued for the damaged cargo
- You'll have to repair your truck and you can tune it
- You need to purchase specific licenses if you want to transport fuel/oil etc.
Definitely some issues, but in all a bug free Simulator it seems and for sure a good and cheap way to start getting into a Truck Simulator. For those who have their driving license, it should definitely help them get a foothold in it.

As someone who is less than stellar at platformers, Ori initially was a frustrating experience.  The mechanics took me a little while to understand and at certain segments I found myself dying over and over again because of improper timing.  After realizing the game intentionally becomes easier the more you play due to acquiring new skills which allow you to do more things and access new areas, I instantly fell in love with it in every way.
Simply put, Ori can be described as a work of art.  It is one of the most aesthetically pleasing games I've ever had the chance to play.  The art style is gorgeous and I love the environments as well.  The colors are so vivid and you can just tell so much work was put into the art.  This alone sets Ori apart from basically any other game, not just platformers.  Visually appealing is an understatement to say the least.
Controls and overall mechanics do feel tight and responsive but less experienced players may struggle at first.  If you do, don't stop playing! It gets considerably more enjoyable as you familiarize yourself with how to control Ori and what to expect from your surroundings and enemies.  Once you nail down the mechanics, you're on easy street.  There are certainly points in Ori that are much more challenging though, especially if you play on higher difficulties.  This makes replayability a factor particularly if you want to unlock some of those insane achievements (beating the game without dying) for example.  You will have your work cut out for you here.
The typical platformers I have come to know are incredibly basic with respect to how much control and abilities your character has.  In many all you can do is run, jump, and die instantly.  With Ori you have skills that help you progress, find powerups (Extra health and Spirit Energy) and secret areas that are well hidden.  At first you start with almost no skills and must acquire them as you progress through the many environments.  It takes a little while but as you acquire new abilities, the game becomes significantly easier and more exciting because you can go more places and aren't going to die as quickly.
To top it all, Ori has a legitimate story and that is fantastic.  The soundtrack is fitting too - peaceful and soothing.  Sound design in general here is as perfect as you can ask for. This goes to show just how much effort and detail was put into it.  Ori is definitely a unique title that rivals essentially any other platformer I have ever played.  It has everything a platformer needs and everything other platformers sorely lack.  I say this with complete confidence.

Everybody's gone to the Rapture is an interactive Novel/Walking Simulator similar to the likes of: Dear Esther, Gone Home, Vanishing of Ethan Carter etc.
If that isn't your kind of thing, simply don't bother with this.
Tldr:
- Walking Simulator
- Minimal Interactivity
- Slow Paced
- Beatiful Environments
- Excellent Original Score
- Non-Linear Narrative
Now that's out of the way: Everybody's gone to the Rapture is the best example of "interactive fiction" I've experienced to date.
I couldn't put it down. The entire environment is immersive and emotive, with an intriguing plot brought to life by believable characters with some excellent voice acting.
I genuinely sympathised for the plight of the villagers (despire any and all of their flaws).
Although beautiful visually, I found I appreciated the subtlety in its direction more often than not.
You are free to Roam and discover at your pace, although ultimately funneled towards the end, in vaguely whatever direction you choose. However you are often drawn to certain areas by visual or audio cues (light trails or a shift in sound to church bells ringing for example) to give you a nudge without forcibly dragging you by the hand.
The original score and sound direction also complements the events perfectly and are well used to enhance the atmosphere.
Although valid gameplay criticisms can be raised at it (slow walking pace, lack of minimap/menu screen map etc), the majority of these I feel are down to artistic choices to aid the immersion.
The 'focussing' mechanic for some of dialog can be a little frustrating initially, but there is an option to simplify this.
I had no issues performance-wise on high settings with a mid-range PC (i5-2500, 16GB RAM, R9 270x), although I note the lack of quick save is a shame as the autosaves are quite sparse.
Everybody's gone to the Rapture is worth the asking price for the general attention to detail and care put into crafting the environment alone.

This is one of the most beautiful games I have ever played. It won't be for everyone but many of its criticisms miss the point - this is an experience rather than a pure game. I hope there will be more like this in future (particularly with VR) that push the boundaries of interactive storytelling.
I previously played on PS4 (so I've bought this twice). The PC framerate was higher (on GTX 970 and i7-4970k) - on high settings 60 fps (30 at times) vs 20/30fps on PS4. This is a graphically advanced and demanding game, it's not poor optimisation in my opinion. Unlikely to be mistaken for Doom 4 Everybody's Gone to the Rapture is slooooow and beautiful. This is the slow movement from Beethoven's Pastoral Symphony, not Symphony of Destruction by Megadeth. It felt like being in the kind of dreams I have when I've read too much John Wyndham. It's slow, intriguing and beautiful. A trascendental dream, it is. A blast, it is not.
The story set in an English village owes a lot to John Wyndham and this is to the game's credit. Move slowly from house to house piecing together the story in an other-wordly setting. The village feels and looks breath-takingly convincing. The graphics are superb.
On the downside very few of the objects in the world allow you to interact and there is nothing to actually "do". I never thought I would say this in a game and I understand how saying this out loud sounds kind of odd. But I'm not saying it out loud I'm typing it so I'll say it anyway - this game isn't really about "doing things". If you're interested in actually "doing things" you might prefer pretty much any other game in existence (with the possible exception of Big Rigs). But if you like walking very slowly round an atmospheric village looking at things and bumping into invisible walls and getting frustrated that you can't pick up that thing over there and why am I wasting my life playing this and - oh my god that thing that just happened was the most beautiful thing that ever happened in any game I've played and the music and all my hair's standing on end and everything.
This isn't really like any other game I've played. It isn't even like Big Rigs. It's slow and it's beautiful and it's a work of art and it's £15 and it's in my gaming library and should be in yours too.
Be gentle with it and it will love you back.

It's hard to believe that Max Payne 2 came out over seven years ago. This remains one of the best third person action games ever. The first one was also good but BRUTALLY difficult at points, and Max's hilariously constipated face made for great times, but part 2--pardon the pun--remedies whatever flaws the first one had. Aside from a graphical upgrade, they changed the bullet-time mechanics to basically be Cyborg 009's acceleration mode. As one of the first games to use Havok physics aka "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ physics" in conjunction with ragdoll effects, the gunfights always looked and felt unique.
The other great thing about Max Payne 2 that hasn't really been explored since is the ongoing meta-narratives explored by overhearing radio broadcasts and television. A lot of it is referential to the first game, but several of the tales serve as "Shadow Play Girls" / "Tales of the Black Freighter"-esque parallels to existing developments.

This game suffers from the same issues all old Lego games do, which are easy to forget in light of the newest gems. Awful level design, repetitive boss fights and a dull fight mechanic break the few interesting features this game brings to the collection. The humour falls flat, the characters are inexpressive and some mechanics, such as having to tow mines with the boat, are extremely frustrating and poorly implemented.
The levels and boss fights are so poorly design that by level 4, I had already resorted to a guide three times because what you have to do is so unclear - a problem I never faced in the Harry Potter games. Other typical issues also purvey, such as no sense of depth for accurate platforming, slippery edges around pits and one-hit kills – annoying, but not game-breaking. Unfortunately Lego Batman also suffers from ugly shading issues on the characters' faces (making them look very polygonal) and absolutely aweful AI. Make sure your buddy is always on-screen, because if he isn't, chances are he's stuck on something and you'll have to backtrack to get him - there is no catch-up-teleport or switching to the other character when you're that far away. Even some puzzles are made very frustrating because of the AI's broken behavior.
That being said, there are some very nice features - the Batmobile level was some of the most fun I've had in a Lego game, and for each of the three Batman story arcs you complete, you can go to Arkham Asylum and play from the villain's perspectives (this isn't a bonus, it's the second half of the game). The highlight of the game for me is Danny Elfman's fantastic score from the original Batman movie, which I will never get tired of hearing. Everything else is there: millions of studs, a fair number of characters/vehicles (think the original Lego Star Wars), forced replay to unlock everything and custom characters, if you're in to that.
If you're hankering for some Batman and don't mind the clunkiness of old Lego games, then this offers exactly what you'd expect. Having now played Lego Batman 2, I can EASILY say the sequel is FAR superior in every way. That said, this stll contains all that lego-y co-op goodness you love from the series and makes for a fine casual game. 5/10 for Gameplay, +1 for Soundtrack

Far as the game play itself the gun play is a loose as you can tell it is truly meant for a controller and a console but over all falls in line with COD and BF games. The gameplay is fine, but nothing to write home about. Basic third person shooter stuff. It works, but it's nothing special. You've got two support characters who help out in firefights, but they can take about 20 sniper bullets to the face before they go down and you need to revive them, so you don't have to worry about them. Ammo management is really well done too. You're always low, but you're never out.
The combat can get a bit tedious though, since the entire game is nothing but cover-based shooting sequences stitched together. Difficulty is good, I went too the game on Normal, and the difficulty was fine. In the last hour the difficulty really gets cranked up though, and the last mission ♥♥♥♥ed me over good a few times.

I watched tons of videos back in mid 2014 about this game and got addicted, 2 years later and still as addicted as I was when I got the game. I've been through so many updates ever since 2014 and they're only getting better, I'm really proud of SCS for making such an addicting game. It's relaxing, yet concentrating to make sure nothing goes wrong on the road. Everyone compares this simulator to other driving simulators and nothing can actually beat it. I highly recommend this game for a chill time and fun while your at it. While it says I have 326.7 hrs on record (as of today) I have well accounted up to 1000+ hrs on other comupters, while this is my new computer.
Pros:
- The most realistic simulator out, from the way the engine starts or fails to start, to realistic fuel consumption and air brakes simulatiom (only naming a few)
- Graphics are stunning especially on my current pc, everything ultra.
- AI cars end up in realistic situations and accidents do happen, while this may be 'stupid', it definately simulates situations happening in the real world
- Branded trucks and unique real sounds adn textures for every truck just adds to the feel of the game
- Much more but I'm running out of time!
While every game isn't perfect so isn't this one.
Cons:
- Graphics engine does feel outdated with unusual times where the frames drop yet there is hardly anything spawned (they especially drop in heavy cities and with AI cars bunching up)

The game itself is a classic, but this version is absolutely terrible. The mouse completely fails to work in-game unless you alt-tab after starting the game, open Task Manager, right-click the GTA San Andreas process, and set the CPU affinity to a single CPU (and users have to learn this information themselves if they want to play the game they purchased). This has to be done every time the game is started. The mouse still tends to break randomly after setting the CPU affinity; sometimes alt-tabbing temporarily fixes it, but sometimes restarting the game is required.
There's also a graphics setting called "Frame limiter". If this is turned on, the game is limited to 25 FPS, which is nearly unplayable for a PC game. If it's off, the FPS is unlimited, but apparently having it off can cause all sorts of bugs because the game uses frames as a way to measure time in the game.
Furthermore, the game doesn't save the mouse sensitivity setting; it must be reconfigured every time the game is started.
Finally, the game has terrible performance on a GTX 660M; draw distance can be maximized, but turning up visual effects or AA causes the framerate to drop to sub-20 FPS. It's absolutely unacceptable (but perfectly in line with Rockstar's low-effort PC ports) for a PS2-era game to run this poorly on a computer that can max out Far Cry.

I'm going to start my review with a caveat: I do recommend this game, once it's closer to a real beta level state.
Now with that out of the way, for a pre-Alpha I must admit the game's beautiful and was a ton of fun for the first 5 or 6 hours. Sadly that's about all there is for content right now. After building an elaborate base, researching dozens of unusual and alien items, exploring the surface of 5 planets and their deepest depths (they are small worlds to be honest) and stockpiling more resources than I can even use... I'm out of things to do after only 8 hours of gameplay.
I think this game has OODLES of potential and what we have now is a rock-solid foundation, but I'd like to see a lot more depth added over the coming months. I'd also like to see the planets made larger - I was a bit stumped at the fact I was able to complete a full circumnavigation of the moon in under 5 minutes (on a Truck, not on foot). It also seemed far too difficult to establish bases on the other planets as many essential resources seem to be completely missing on remote worlds and we don't have the ability to bring much with us in terms of materials. Also, based on the small size of planets, I fear that in a single game it would be possible to completely exhaust every resource on every planet with enough gameplay, especially in multi-player.
Base building has some issues I'm sure will be ironed out quickly, but long-term I'd like to see the ability to build bigger, better base components like a REAL "habitat" that players can enter and walk around in. And a real landing/take-off pad for the ships instead of permanently tying up my vehicle assembly bay once a ship has been built. We should also be able to build things like hydroponics pods to grow renewable resources (Organics, Resin and Compound) if for no other reason than to have something to trade for other resources once we've completely mined-out a world.
Again, major kudos to the dev team for a graphically stunning game that's fun and easy to play. It's been a real pleasure. Sadly it was just short-lived in this pre-Alpha release. So I had fun for a couple days and I will be eagerly awaiting the next major content update. Until then, keep up the great work!
