Been playing this game since early Legacy, and have nearly 1000 hours on it. Played mostly solo or with one friend. The game is a gem, it's incredibly fun and challenging. The devs are very motivated and updates and new features fly out by the week. The amount of variety there is in how you can play this game is immense. Playing in massive groups of 10+ people and building castles versus playing solo, or even playing on a wide variety of different servers with mods and different rules that change how the game plays.
I love this game, but it isn't perfect. Que the love-rant about the current state of the game: There is still a lot that must be done - especially about player interactions and how the game has turned into a glorified pubg with crafting and building. Look to other hardcore survival games and you will see very quickly why this is an issue. We need weapons, especially high tier weapons, and ammo to feel extremely valuable and rare. At the moment you struggle for an hour or so and then you start creating an armory inside of your base as if its WW3 and roll around with the sole purpose to just kill and raid - that's all. There's zero danger from the environment, animals, radiation, etc. Running through the radiated towns is easy and getting loot is as well. We've moved in a good direction with the BP update recently, but we need to go full on back to the survival game roots. I don't want to just have the goal of the game to not be raided, survive player interactions, and raid other people. The game gets boring fast, as it would be more worth my time playing CS:GO or pubg if I want to role around shooting at as many people as I can. We need sickness, dangerous animals and weather conditions, rare weapons and ammo, bounty systems for the server, variation in injuries, struggle for food and water. Terminus servers are doing something right - and thats by making the game difficult and posing you with more varied and difficult decisions to make. DayZ is a truer survival game than Rust has ever been (for a lot of the reasons I've already stated) but lacks its polish and dedicated staff. I have faith that the game will eventually end up where it needs to be, the devs need to just ignore the crying little children who want a CoD-esk game experience from this. The dev team is amazing, the quality of the game and how it plays and looks is superb, we have everything we could want but: hardcore progression, incentivized and varied player interactions, hardcore survival mechanics, etc.
All in all, this game has been beyond worth the initial 20$ I spent a long time ago and has continued make that purchase way beyond worth it. I just hope that the devs heed the words their long term player base and aren't afraid to make drastic survival based changes to the game. If they do this, Rust will become the single best survival game ever created (it's already very close to that title even with so much more improvement to be had).

This is one of the best platformers starring a supersonic nuclear lemur that I've ever played. Since it's been exactly 2 years from when I first played it, I decided that this is a perfectly arbitrary time to write a review.
Unless you're some sort of uncultured swine, or worse, a reasonable individual with different opinions who simply doesn't like this aesthetic, it should be readily apparent that the game looks and sounds great. That's all well and good, but the big thing here is that it actually plays as good as it looks and sounds. In other words, this game offers top-notch moment-to-moment platforming gameplay on top of very pleasant visuals, audio and music (your mileage may vary). That's not all though, whenever you're not too busy being dazzled by all the pretty lights while trying to not get brutalized by spikes, lasers, water, or frogs, you might notice that the game has a story.
I don't have very much to say about the aforementioned story other than that its minimalist presentation is both its main strength and weakness. However,
that depending on your testosterone levels, blood type, horoscope, and various other scientifically proven factors, the fairly minimal narrative will either resonate with you to some degree
come across so schmaltzy that it might put you into a diabetic coma? Scientists have yet to discover any kind of middle-ground regarding this phenomenon.
In conclusion, I give it 5 brownie points out of 5. If I had to be pedantic, I'd dock one point due to the lack of replay value on offer if you don't happen to be a crazy person (like me) who goes out of his way to beat the aptly named one-life difficulty and/or simply enjoy replaying games for the sake of it. My main issue with the game is basically that the developers did not give me enough excuses to keep playing it forever.

This game is decidedly old school: basically linear progression, collect new skills and powerups, go to new dungeons and restore each of the elements to save the world. You know the story.
The challenge level on normal felt pretty appropriate, in any event you can scale it up or down to accomodate your skill.
The biggest drawback, and this is a PC specific complaint: you CANNOT change the controls besides toggling between a couple of presets (i.e. Keyboard only or Keyboard plus mouse). It makes absolutely no sense to me that you can't re-map the keys. Some of the ones you're going to need to be holding down and clicking a lot are shift and ctrl, which is really frustrating for a game that requires some fast twitch (my god, the hand cramps, oh the hand cramps) It's also always great when you're running from a wall of lava only to have the "sticky keys" popup minimize the game because you hit shift a bunch of times. What I wouldn't give to just be able to map the dash button to the mouse wheel...
Overall if you're into traditional platformers I'd recommend it.

Probably the best platformer I've played. Beautiful artstyle, great music, almost perfect controls, and a Disney/Pixar-like story.
The game is somewhat difficult once you've progressed a bit, but nothing too hard that I get frustrated (this is coming from someone that sucks and rages at platformers normally). All in all, I totally recommend it.

Excellent game. I can't think of another game that rivals its aesthetic beauty. The "escape" scenes can be a bit infuriating. They are kind of nostalgic in the way that old videogames made you memorize every aspect of the level in order to be successful.
Well done and beautifully made.

The water escape segment in this game was a perfect representation of the amount of tears I shed during the first 10 minutes of this game. Ori and the Forest of Feels are one of those games where you'd do anything to experience it for the first time again.
The soundtrack is absolutely gorgeous, an emotional rollercoaster for sure. Probably a new favorite of mine.
The artwork along its visuals are eye candy and so are the very fluid animations for the characters.
Gameplay is great too, didn't expect it to have a combat system to begin with, but it actually delivered quite well to the game's pacing.
Very Rayman like in a way, which is another platformer I adore. But this one takes the cake over the best platformer I've ever played.
It's a very challenging game too, if you play it at Hard difficulty especially, which I recommend for the platform lovers out there. Normal difficulty provides with quite the challenge too if that's more suitable for you.
Never go one life mode though, it's an eternal torment (unless you're a speedrunner dude, or just plain insane).
So yeah, what I'm trying to say is; what are you waiting for? Go and get the game! It's only 20 bucks and has about 10+ hours of content, it's an amazing deal if you ask me.
Show the devs some love for their hard work. Your choice.

This is clearly one of the most annoying games I've ever played.
You may have already read that the difficulty is too high? Well, no. But yes.
First, there is a difficult setting. I have no idea what it does. It certainly does not make the game "easy" if set to easy.
I assume it makes enemies less dangerous or something like that, but enemies aren't your problem in this game.
The main problem you will face is controls, reflexes and quite challenging physical riddles. Also, you will die. A lot. I think I died ~400 times in this game. The last game I remember killing me like that was the original Super Mario on the GameBoy.
So why did I come back to this game for 18 hours to complete it? Because it is beautiful. It is smart. It has a very touching story. Because of the feeling of accomplishment you get when you did solve the physical riddle after dying 20 times trying.
Still there is something you should know before you buy and definitely before you quit: If you cannot do something there are multiple possible reasons for that:
1. Everything is accessible from the start, but you lack the skills. Learn more, come back later.
2. You have the skill but don't know how to use it. Controls are complex, check youtube if you're stuck. Tutorials are not where this game shines. Deflections can be aimed if right mouse is held, who knew? Certainly not me until the Finale. Makes things a lot easier...
3. You are not there yet. Mastering Controls in Ori is hard. You actually need practice. Lots.
If I could go back in time and request one thing from the developers it would be to skip the scenes where you are hunted    by time, Lava, whatnot. It's hard enough without that and too many repetitions suck the feeling out of every well made scene.
Last piece of advise: Don't play with loved ones within hearing range. You'll be making a lot of annoyed-noises and that might annoy them.

Arkham Origins is the third game in the Batman Arkham series, though it is a prequel. It is obvious when playing through the game that the developer of this game is different than the previous two installments, Arkham Asylum and Arkham City. The game feels clunkier and is not as well optimized but the game still has a sort of charm that drives through, which makes it a unique, though flawed, addition to the series.
The story in this game caught me by surprise because of how honestly interesting it was. The game takes place on Christmas Eve and features the first night Batman encounters The Joker. There is a twist that happens during the beginning of the game, but do not expect anything of Arkham City caliber. The character interactions are fantastic and honestly my favorite part of the game, especially the relationship portrayed between Bruce and Alfred. To see the beginnings of many characters and their involvement with The Dark Knight is interesting as well, including Officer Gordon and Barbara Gordon. Many parts of the story actually portrays Batman as a ture detective, which is very well done and satisfying.
The voice acting in this game is pretty solid, even thought the actors Batman and The Joker have both been replaced. Troy Baker must be commended for his outstanding job as The Joker and filling in the big shoes left by the much talented Mark Hamill. A huge negative for me though is how awful the lipsyncing in real time is in this game. It looks extremely clunky, unfinished, and just plain bad, especially by 2013 video game standards. The cutscenes, on the other hand, are a big plus because they are extremely stylized and are a huge factor that sets this game apart from the previous installments in the series.
The graphics in this game are nothing special and even when they are maxed out, they do not look as good as Arkham City does. That said, it is definitely not a bad looking game (though the fire effects are absolutely atrocious). The funny thing is even though the game came out two years after Arkham City and does not look as good, it also does not run as well. I have a pretty solid PC which can run games such as Battlefield 4 on high smoothly and at a constant framerate but for this game, it manages to lag (though not frequently) at random locations throughout the game, and especially prominent during the last couple portions,
The gameplay in this game consists of what you have already been accustomed to in the series, except it just seems to be a bit clunkier. Though the flow of the combat is fluid, sometimes the takedown controls did not seem to work which got quite annoying in specific portions of the game. Also, the combat in this game is much easier than the other games because once you get a flow going, which is easy enough, you can attack enemies that are stunned and already on the ground which somewhat removes one of the only challenges in the beat-em-up combat this series did so well. There is a return of stealth portions within the game but it plays quite differently because of the very different level design compared to the previous installments. In this game, the stealth portions really just seemed easier and if you are caught sneaking around, it was also simple enough to dodge the enemies' bullets and take them down non-stealthily, which honestly should not be the case. So one of the biggest gripes about this game is the fact that it is really a lot easier than Arkham Asylum and Arkham City. There are also many new weapons introduced in this game, which does not make sense since Batman could have used them in the other installments, which take place later on the timeline. Though when making a prequel videogame, it is inevitable to run into problems like that. One of my favorite additions though is the grapple accelerator, which allows Batman to increase his speed when grappling on to any surface, which happens a lot in these games. This is one feature I definitely want to see carried over into Arkham Knight.
The map in this game is slightly bigger than that of Arkham City, though it may feel emptier because of the lack of interesting and engaging sidequests. The game takes place in Gotham this time around and it does not make a whole lot of sense since the only people we see roaming the streets or the rooftops are criminals. It made sense in Arkham City, since that is an entire area infested with criminals, but the same cannot be said about this game. One great addition though is the fast-travel using the Batwing. There are multiple fast-travel spots that can be unlocked throughout the map and this idea works very well and I hope it is implemented into Arkham Knight.
Though the game is still pretty fun, even compared to the first two installments, it is lacking something huge. A variety of Batman villains. We get some interesting bosses in this game but we also get some fairly unenjoyable ones with villains I don't really care about. Arkham City had an assortment of crazy and fun villains, but this game takes a slump in that department. Bane returns for a total of three different boss battles here and though they are fairly fun, it would have been more interesting to change up the formula. There is a boss battle with Deathstroke early in the game and it is very well executed, and one of the highlights in this game for me. One thing to note is that one of the boss battles is very annoying to play with a mouse and keyboard, so using a controller for this game may be a good idea.
Overall, Batman: Arkham Origins is a solid game muddled by being unpolished and some poor design. However, it is still a good game in my opinion and one that is worthy to be in the series. WB Montreal did a good job at portraying these characters in a new light and I really appreciate that.

I was happily surprised by this game. I rarely play a fps game's story mode from start to finish anymore; usually just skipping to the multi player. I played the entire game almost in one sitting and loved every minute of it!

I wanted to enjoy this game after reading so many positive reviews. What I've walked into is a drawn out game with mediocre mechanics. That entire swath of the story from the wall until the helicopter crash serves no purpose to the overall plot, and honestly this severely hurts the game.
Reason being is that the gameplay is plain repetetive and the only cause of death throughout the entire game for me was the clunky cover system placing me on the wrong surface or simply throwing me out into the open, it is not fluid whatsoever in the way the Gears of War series is. Aside from that the entire combat system if centered around shooting ducks, with enemies "hiding behind cover" with blatant parts of their body hanging out, any decent CS player can just pop all the headshots for an entire area within a few seconds. The only time I was ever "flanked" by the AI was when they spawned to my side and jumped out of some inaccesible area. There is simply nothing dynamic to any of it.
I will admit, the story could have been good, but during the period I mentioned earlier that served no purpose, the same plot points and characterstics of characters are hammered over and over until it's somewhat dull and it's hard to care once the plot begins to progress again. I may be spoiled by the Uncharted series continous rolling plot, but seriously, this game would have been soo good if 50% of the game wasn't boring filler content that just turns into headshotting swarms of useless unchallenging enemies.
If you don't have that much time to play games and try to spend the time you can on solid titles, I can't recommend this title. If you like repetitive shallow gameplay like the Call of Duty series, I think you may be able to enjoy this. I really wanted to like this game, but even the redeeming story is just not good enough to justify the repetitive slog that is the majority of this game.

This game is MUCH better than I had thought it would be.  The storyline is a bit confusing be cause the first cutscene when you start a play through would make more sense to be a mid-game cut scene.  As such, the first 4 DMC games (simply title Devil May cry 1-4) should be played before this one. That said, it is a re-boot done well.  The story feels even more captivating than the original, the character dialogue is some of the best writing i've seen since Borderlands 2, the difficulty curve Is on the opposite end of FFIIIX (meaning that the parts that seem hard are hard because of skill, not some cheap boss fight where tactics are necesarry).  There are a few minor things that I notice for one, all the game play takes place in the alternate demension of limbo, where demons are visible. Granted there are angelic weapons and demonic weapons that revolutionize the god of war esque hit-something-till-it-dies gameplay.  At $50 its a steep asking price, but well worth the cost.  If you dont like the new dante's appearance, if you get the DLC you can use the classic dante's. Capcom definitly made up for their past mistake of making DMC 1-4 have a strange, hard-to-follow chronology(DMC1 was the 2nd or 3rd chronologically, and DMC3 was the first). Admittedly, The limbo dimension DOES explain how the demons control the humans with out the humans knowing any thing.  There are some minor problems with some mid-game mechanics, but im not going to explain them here as to not spoil too much of the game.  I give it a 10/10.

Not really a big fan of "Hold LT for Angelic weapons, RT for Demon weapons," But the weapons were fun to use nonetheless. There's also a nice variety of enemies for you to eradicate, and the bosses also satisfy. As for the graphics and environment, they were spectacularly done. Crisp textures and engaging stages were a joy to go through.
All in all, was a very succesful reboot for me, although the original series will forever hold a place in my heart as the true DmC. Looking forward to what comes next!

I owned the original version of Ori. This updated version is exactly the same apart from some extra places to explore on the map, and changes to a few of the puzzles. The mechanics of this game however, much like the last version, are awful. It will often ignore your input when trying to climb walls, bash projectiles or even perform a double jump. This makes the 'Immortal' and 'Unhinged' achievements IMPOSSIBLE to get. There is also a bug where sometimes your coverage of sections of the map will become stuck at 99%, when the gauge is actually at 100%. You can't remap any of the keys, and you can't turn off the immense screen shake that happens during many of the escape scenes. If you have motion blur enabled then the effect of the screen shaking becomes even worse.

This is a good old school dungeon crawl/adventure game that requires a lot of patience in the beginning stages, but the payoff is good.
You find yourself in a dungeon with nothing in the way of supplies or money so you just start looking around to determine your best manner of escape. There are lots of containers to break that offer coins or, rarely, other items needed (sometimes an extra life), so break them all because the coins can be used to buy extra lives.
Move carefully because you can take a game-ending fall which will mean you must start at the most recent checkpoint (hopefully, you'll remember where you were beyond that point). Unfortunately, the checkpoints, once used, are gone.
There are puzzles to solve, and monsters to defeat ---- but none are particularly difficult.
The graphics are a bit dated, but the play is smooth enough with enough visual clues so you can find your way to the next objective.
I see that some are unhappy that you are returned to the beginning of the game if you stop for a break, and it took a while to figure out that you have to complete an entire level before the game saves your progress. I don't like that, either, but at least you will be returned to the beginning of the level, not the beginning of the game.

I am new to the DmC franchise, so I don't have an opinion on this game as a sequel.  But viewing it as a standalone game and without specific expectations, I'm finding it a joy to play.  I'm not the biggest fan of the popular genre of action games with pretty graphics, but this one really stands out.  The combat, though fairly categorized as "hack-and-slash," is very satisfying.  The responsiveness of the controls and the fluid feel of the combos make for a visceral experience that is more enjoyable than with any other action game I've played. Added to that gameplay element is the artfulness of the story and graphic design.  I was skeptical on this front when I bought the game since I'm not really into Goth or anything like that.  But the artistry on display here just won me over.  You really have to play the game to understand what I mean on this subject.  The cutscenes, the sound, the art style--everything in this game comes together in a way that makes it more than the sum of its parts.  Kudos to Capcom.

Ahh, Seraph. The game that pushed me over the edge and made me get a Steam Controller. And that is an important thing to note folks; you can play this with a keyboard, but it is awkward and not enjoyable at all. You need to have a controller for this one. Now, with that out of the way, onto the review.
The story of Seraph is an interesting one, told piece-meal by start of level and end of level cutscenes, with numerous log files you can pick up along the way to get the rest of it together. Essentially what happens is that in the game's world, there exists Reality (where we live), Origin (heaven) and Terminus (hell). A divine being known as The Seraph left Origin and possessed the body of a young woman named Talia. Somewhere on the way, she was captured by religous persons, and held prisoner on a ship called the Corangelous for years, being treated as the object of a relgious pilgrimage (think Mecca). The demons of Terminus spoke to her, offering her freedom if she helped them enter Reality. Unwittingly she did, and the game starts with the demons invading the ship, and the Seraph needing to fight her way out. There is a bit more to it, but I don't want to spoil much more.
The graphics are good, but not exceptional, as that isn't needed in a game like this. There are five distinct 'world' on the ship with multiple levels each, and you can easily tell them apart by their appearance. The indvidual levels are trutly procedurally generated, so you'll never see the same levels twice, save for two boss fights. The music fits the game well, but sadly isn't anything memorable outside of playing.
But where the game really shines is the gameplay, which is the main draw and what you should be 'coming to the dance' for. As stated, each level is procedurally generated so you'll never have the same experience. The placement of the exit, enemies, and secret areas change each time. Despite this there is a familiar pattern, as each level involves you tracking down a high powered demon and destroying them, or finding multiple demon fountains and destroying them. This never gets boring or repetitive though as you don't know what you're going to come across each time and exploring the levels is a joy.
You control the Seraph, moving through the levels, running, jumping, and shooting. She will always auto target enemies so you focus on dodging while continually attacking. She gets two 'Blinks' which give the ability to transport around enemies rapidly, or reach new areas in the level. The Blinks recharge every few seconds, but it's a careful balance to avoid taking damage while ensuring your enemies are crushed. They start off easy but can get downright nasty later on.
This is thanks to the games scaling difficulty. When you defeat enemies they drop white 'motes' that add experience to your character. The more of these you pick up, the higher the difficulty scales. If you collect multiple motes in a row without taking damage, a meter fills up and this makes the difficulty go up even faster. So if you're good, you can end up in a rather tricky situation early on. As a matter of fact, I had to restart my own playthrough because it got too difficult. Luckly the game retains all your progress on upgrades when you do so.
So on that note, the progression system is great. You get experience from collecting the aforementioned motes, and level up as you would in any other game, each time getting a health increase and the ability to choose to power up one of four skills, which are selected for you when you start. You can put all your points into one skill or spread them out, but the fact you won't ever end up with the same set of skills twice adds to the replyability. However this isn't retained when you start a new game, so what is?
That's everything else. You gather components as you kill the demons, which allow you to craft stronger versions of your weapons, stronger accessories, and more powerful miracles (which are special attacks). As well you collect shards, which can be slotted into multiple skills throughout three skill trees. There are five rarities of shards, and you can combine three of one kind to make the next one. As well you need to have a certain number of shards in lower skills to be able to slot shards into the more powerful ones. So all the crafting and shards carry over.
Even once you finish the game, you're not done. There are daily challenges which provide extra crafting rewards when you place well, and every week there is a special Survival Challenge, which puts everyone in a fixed version of the main campaign with the goal to go as far as you can and get the highest score, with again crafting rewards for doing well. Eventually, if you want, you can "Rebirth" which is equivelant to a prestige in Call of Duty/Gears of War; everything resets,  but you get small bonuses to all your stats, and this can be done up to five times if you're really that crazy.
All in all the package here is exceptional with tons of value avaiable for the price, and you owe it to yourself to at least try it. I give it a demon destroying, angel blasting, fast paced recommendation.

Dreadbit's second game,
, is a combat-focused action platformer without aiming. You're stepping into the combat boots of the titular Seraph, an angel that just escaped from her imprisonment in a city-sized futuristic vessel. While
, Dreadbit's first game, offered a relaxed turn-based experience, this one is action packed and frantic, yet excels in similar ways.
put a spin on match-3 games by combining the genre with RPG-like mech combat and a very stylish asthetic, and
also takes a well-established genre and twists it into something refreshingly different.
Not having to aim in a game like this feels weird at first, but once you become more familiar with the games various means of avoiding damage (like
ing out of the way, using corners for cover, or just killing whoever is attacking you, thus destroying their projectiles), maneuvering around the levels feels just so rewarding.
Your movement in
is swift, responsive,  and well-animated, although sometimes you might get stuck to a ledge that you didn't mean to hiold on to. The combat rewards taking risks, since enemies drop "motes" on death, that decay swiftly – so blinking into a dying enemy is the most risky, but also the most rewarding strategy. You dispatch your foes with a arsenal of different weapons that favor different play styles (my favorites have to be the autopistols). These weapons can be upgraded in-between levels. These upgrades are part of a global progression system, similar to a rogue-lite (although the game usually does not have permadeaths), in which you upgrade your weapons, skills and protective wards across runs.
This meta-progression is one of the core elements of
, after a few runs you'll notice how much easier the earlier levels will become. But don't worry, the difficulty will become quite punishing later. Difficulty also scales dynamically: you're doing well and are dodging all attacks? Well, your enemies just got a lot tougher way more quickly.
This dynamic difficulty is one of the foundations of the daily challenge, and especially the weekly survival mode, in which you start a new character (but keep all your meta progress), and try to score the most points before losing the last of both your respawn tokens. For me, this mode became the most enjoyable part of
, with enticing rewards for whoever reaches the top-tiers of the leaderboards.
The game offers a new game mechanic, in which you swap your progress for permanent stat improvements. While grindy, the core game mechanics just feel so good to me that I haven't gotten tired of starting a new run yet. Once again, Dreadbit has nailed it for me, and I can't wait to see what this studio comes up with next.

An angel embodies a middle eastern woman on board a derelict ship overrun by a seemingly endless hoard of demons. Physics-defying gunplay and smiting ensue. What more could one possibly ask for?
It's hard to say...
is pretty damn good as-is. The controls and subsequent mechanics are solid -- well-polished. Everything feels as it should. Challenge ramps up appropriately via an unusual but well-executed difficulty multiplier based off your current performance; increasingly hard, yet forgiving.
This is a game that wears its inspirations proudly on its sleeve. From
to
and sprinklings of
, there's a lot of enjoyable meta reference present. Expect some welcome familiarity. The music is spot-on, too -- techy off-kilter edge.
Visually the game looks great, if not same-y. That's not to say the level design is bad; it's by all means good (there's more than enough walls, drops, and platforms to make ample use of Seraph's varying abilities), but aesthetically the repetition is disappointing. The premise of Seraph is as unique as the game itself. It's a 2D platform shooter with an emphasis on acrobatic platforming while aiming is done automatically. Jumping and dashing through the levels is so satisfying that the game gets away with its otherwise repetitive gameplay and grindy upgrade system.
Playing as the Divine being Seraph occupying a human vessel, the player is confronted with the task to escape a facility specifically constructed to hold her captive. On the way out, she is confronted with enemy Daemons and only a select arsenal of guns and Miracles at her disposal. The story is rather plain, revolving around religious subjects and a few foreseeable plot developments. The dialogue and notes that can be found throughout the levels are well written in a semi-archaic language and fit the overall theme of the game. Clearly though, the gameplay is at the heart of the game.
There are five different areas, consisting of a few procedurally generated levels each, that have a very clean look to them. Alongside the sober composition of the levels, impulsive industrial music and electronic sound effects contribute to the overarching futuristic design. Seraph adeptly fuses sci-fi indications with spiritual motifs.
The controls are basic and can be internalised immediately. Simply navigating through the areas is already inherently fun because the look and feel for jumping and dashing is spot on. Seraph does cartwheels in mid-air, graciously leaps in any direction or holds on to walls all the while shooting Daemons. This allows, even requests, for a verticality in the levels that would otherwise be more disruptive than fun. Dodging and killing enemies raises the difficulty scale and provides new attacks to the Daemons after certain thresholds have been reached. That's why learning to read the tells, knowing when to cast which Miracle and a bit of movement practice is crucial to get to higher difficulty levels.
Caution though, Seraph can be a grindfest, designed to be played over and over again. In order to max out Rebirth levels, Oaths and Transmutations, soft resets, repeated replays and daily and weekly challenges are essential. Additionally, the selection of Daemons to fight, including only two bosses, is extremely small. Nevertheless, Seraph is perfectly enjoyable and can be completely played through without any meta progression.
Seraph is one of a kind. The gameplay alone is already worth a try, despite its repetitiveness and optional grind.

I wanted to like this game. I really did. When it first started, I really like the traditional drawing style and the mix of 3D rendered graphics. There's something about this combination that feels *right* or a the very least "appropriate".
Some of the HO games have items that are hidden in such good spots that I actually thought "Nicely done" with how cleverly some items were placed.  The story is standard HO fare, so there was nothing extraordindary there. And some of the musical sequences actually stood out in that I didn't mind listening to them, even on repeat.
But then the questionable choices start to make their presence known.
For example, in one of the early HO games you need to click on an item to perform an action that then exposes the item that you need. Unlike most other HO games, however, you are given no clues - visual or audible - that you needed to click on that item to perform an action.  Okay, that's an issue but it's minor, right?
Then you look at the map to see where you need to go to next, except that the map doesn't tell you. The vast majority of HO games do that. What is this game trying to be? A traditional point-and-click?
Then the really poor and downright AWFUL design starts to show its ugly head.
The first is a match-3 that's not match-3. You need to flip tiles that have one pattern on each side. If you just so happen to find a set of three in a row, it then randomizes to other items, which you then have to flip to try to make additional match-3 combinations. It's an idiotic and frustrating design choice that should have been replaced with a traditional match-3 type of game.
Then you have the kind of puzzle where pushing a button (or a valve in this case) will affect two nearby valves. You've seen these mostly with lights where clicking on a light will reverse the lights around it. That's fine, I can do this -- except that often when a valve would affect two other valves it would only initially affect one! Click it again to reverse what you just did and it doesn't reverse the one valve it affected before -- it activates (or deativates) the two valves that it would otherwise affect! Who the F**K thought that this was a good idea?
Then you come to the traditional "match the pattern" like the electronic game "Simon". It shows you a sequence, you repeat it. It starts out with two and adds another one in a different patern as you progress. Fair enough ... except that it goes up to nine sequences, and if you miss any of those sequences, YOU START THE WHOLE THING AGAIN FROM THE BEGINNING (2 SEQUENCES) INSTEAD OF GET ANOTHER CHANCE TO REPEAT THAT SEQUENCE!! I was at the 8-number sequence when this happened. After all of the sh*t I had to deal with above, this was near-ragequit time!
Wait ... did you just have me change the flavor of a candy from apple to cherry by ... by dipping it in paint? Seriously?
How did you expect me to identify that item in that HO game when over half of it is OFF THE F**KING SCREEN??!
Now the game has turned into a three minute long game of "whack-a-mole" to keep rats away by spraying them with insect repellent! The first 30 seconds is bad enough, but extending this to an entire three minutes after having to deal with everything listed above?! Did I offend the developers in a previous life or something?
I have to lift a bucket of water to put out a fire not once but twice by clicking, holding, and dragging the mouse button several times? Now I have to climb a ladder using the same method? What is this? Is this a dexterity test?
A haricot? A "haricot"? WTF is a haricot? Wait, it's a BEAN? Well, why didn't you say so in the first place! (A haricot....)
Oh, for f**k's sake... ANOTHER three-minute timed minigame...
Seriously, I really wanted to enjoy this game. The old-school book drawings / CG mix was actually very appealing; the story told you nothing but kept throwing hints at at you to keep your interest; some of the HO placements were actually clever. The potential for this to be an enjoyable game was right there from the start. But the rest of the game is so horribly done that the developers wanted to be sadists. They had to be. That's the only explanation for the other elements of the game.
I have all of my trading cards now. I'm done. F**k this game. I'm not going to bother finishing it, and I'll have no regrets. Do yourself a favor and don't start this game. Ever. No matter how bored you are. Watch paint dry instead. It's less frustrating.

I've played a
of hidden object games, and
ends up somewhere in my all-time bottom ten.  There's an arrangement of typical minor issues, like sometimes-shaky English translation and a poorly-paced assemblage of clichés as a plot, with an ending cinematic that seems to presume a romance was featured at some point in the story -- it wasn't, but perhaps it was cut out in development.
More problematic are the actual gameplay elements.  First, the environments, HO scenes, and everything else are modeled in 3D.  A pretty good job was done of the modeling, really, but not good enough. I need to write this down and support the team: HITMAN (2016) is excellent. A really phenomenal example of what video games can accomplish as a medium. There are blantant issues for PC purists, but none of them should surprise, or rightly bother a majority of gamers who already play most of their games online and suffer UPlay. There's the short version, if you have questions, read on:
GAMEPLAY
I better knock this out right now, if you have played or enjoyed PAYDAY 2, the Batman Arkham games, the Assassin's Creed games, or a plethora of other titles, then this game *does* have aspects of the familiar for you. I found the biggest barrier for me was that I was planning to use all the PAYDAY tactics to achieve victory and believed it would be simple. It's not. There are numerous twists and turns that even an experienced gamer will struggle with, but could theoretically be played pretty competently while attempting in various states of unconsciousness. That being said, there are huge aspects of this game that are HARD. Incredibly hard. If you want to get all the challenges, achieve victory in every way, or try everything, you will be reloading your save frequently and at least once scream expletives at your screen. I find this fantastic, because every game should have a "tired-and-bored" setting and a "impress-your-friends" setting. The great variety expressed here is definitely a plus for me and I find it hard not to enjoy a majority of what this game has to show.
STORY
Altogether, I wouldn't put the "season" story in the best scrutiny. The overarching story serves to connect what I believe are excellent mission tales. You are told, and experience, several reasons why these scum need to be taken out, and I never felt evil for what I was doing in contrast to games like Grand Theft Auto V. Altogether, while story is usually overlooked in games like this (ask yourself, what's the story in PAYDAY?), it's nice to see the Developers take their universe very seriously. The story isn't distracting, and nowhere near as frustrating to the player as Batman: Arkham Knight, so it gives you a decent opportunity to brush it off entirely and just have fun.
VALUE
I need to talk value at least once because there are serious pros and cons to PC gamers. While consoles are usually expected to pull stunts like this, PC gamers have usually been free to experience huge discounts in price, freedom to play anywhere, and better command of settings and graphics. For this game, this is really not the case. Let me be clear, I love this game and can openly accept all of its cons, but if any of these are a problem for you, I would seriously suggest reconsidering a purchase.
First, the always online setting. You MUST have a constant internet connection to even play this game in its best way. If it's slow and frustrating internet, you're still okay. It just needs to send a simple ping. For a lot of gamers who use laptops on the go, or sit in the backseat of a car, or play on a plane, this will be an issue. You *can* play, but no achievements and trackers or other mission data, which makes it pretty pointless. That being said, you can't do any of that already if you play Overwatch or Call of Duty, etc. so it's not a huge issue, in my opinion.
Second, the processor demands. Basically, if you can't really play GTA V, you're gonna have trouble here. The graphics demands aren't huge, but your processor needs to be decent. There is a lot of NPC traffic and that is hell on some low-power processors. I'm no expert on the stuff, but if you're looking to upgrade your processor, I would recommed for Intel motherboards the i7-6700k or the i5-6500. Both are expensive (roughly $200 for the i5 and $300 for the i7), but excellent solutions to this and other gaming problems. We're seeing a patter in gaming for processor demands over graphics, which could give us some excellently in-depth games, but will definitely strain lower-end CPUs. Again, not a dealbreaker to actually play the game, but you will probably see some frame-drops. I use the i7-6700k and absolutely love the freedom it gives me at 1080p.
Third, the expense of the title. $60 seems embarassingly high for the game's length. I completely understand that argument. I purchased it on a sale for $30 and will happily purchase season 2 for the $60 cost. Essentially, unless you're on board with the title, please do not purchase for the $60. The clever developers came up with a solution for this. A $15 sample and a $50 upgrade. I think this is fantastic. Every gamer interested should try that $15 version and if you like it, consider upgrading at the next sale or purchasing if you see the real value. You might experience an opportunity cost of $5 or so because you bought the first bit at $15, but honestly, the opportunity to try the full experience of the first two parts is a great way to test it out for yourself. The first Episode is an excellent metric for how the whole game goes, so seek out your value from that. Ask yourself whether 5 more of that mission (Episode 2 is excellent), and a few extra full length missions using the same maps are worth the cost. I think they are, but I hope I can provide extra perspective.
CONCLUSION
HITMAN was a pleasant surprise for me. I have yet to finish even the last 2 episodes, but I will happily play them over again a few more times. I wanted to write this because it has faults for many gamers, but in no way deserves to have a "Mixed" rating. This game is far better than that. I eagerly wait for Season 2!

TLDR: The Batman Arkham saga continues in this prequel to Arkham Asylum and Arkham City. Arkham Origins had technical problems (bugs) but as far as I’m concerned, it’s still a fun game.  8/10
If you’ve played the 2 previous Batman Arkham games you may remember that they were developed by a company called Rocksteady, who did a great job on them. This time around the game development was taken over by Warner Bros, and the quality has diminished, though the general feel of the game is similar to the previous games.
Since Arkham Origins is a prequel, Batman is kind of making his debut in Gotham City with no allies other than his trusty butler Alfred. Nobody knows who or what he is and most people don’t even believe he exists. Gotham city is ruled by gangs and corrupt police, and just like the previous Batman games practically everyone you find on the streets is a thug just asking to have his head bashed (including a large number of cops). Your primary nemesis in this game is the crime boss Black Mask (not sure why he wears the mask since people already know his identity) though there’s a lot more going on behind the scenes. Black Mask has put a huge bounty on Batman’s head, and a bunch of world class assassins are here to collect, including some familiar faces: Bane, Deathstroke, Firefly, etc.
Just like the first 2 Arkham games, Arkham Origins is a third person half stealth/half beat ’em up action game making extensive use of the grapnel boost, which helps launch Batman into the air so he can soar around with his cape like a hang glider. Most of the bat tools from the previous games appear but the key mapping for some of them has been changed for some reason, and if you play the games back to back like I did, there may be some confusion as to why the developers made certain changes. The flow of combat is very similar to Arkham City though, so if you have decent reflexes you should be able to counter just about any enemy attack, as expected.
A couple other noticeable differences from the previous games are the reworked skills system and the reduced number of collectibles. Now the skills that you can unlock at level ups are in a sort of horizontal tree, whereas in the first 2 games you could just pick whatever you wanted. If you’re like me and do a lot of side quests, you may find yourself unable to buy the good skills for a while since they’re locked behind story progress requirements. No critical hits for about half the game this time! As for the fewer/easier Riddler collectibles, this change is welcome to me since I’m not a big fan of searching out 500 collectibles in a game playthrough. Unfortunately to actually face the Riddler you still need to get all of them, which is a challenge even if you are actively trying to do it, armed with an online guide.
Pros:
+The story is pretty good, as expected from a Batman Arkham game. Some people have said that the game uses “third tier” villains, and I guess I can’t argue that point. But as long as they provide an interesting plot I don’t care.
+This time the game encompasses the entire Gotham City, not just a small section of it (although it really isn’t that much bigger than Arkham City). The city map is now large enough that “fast travel” has been added, where you can quickly move around the map via the Batwing jet drop-off.  Again however, the city is filled with thugs to beat up, and since Arkham Origins is kind of an RPG (level ups and skill points) you may want to just glide through the city looking for fights to level up.
+With the 8 “master” assassins who took up Black Mask’s bounty hunt, there are a lot of boss fights, each with different ways to take down your foes. My favorite is probably the Firefly boss fight.
+There’s a pretty comprehensive multiplayer system, where you can level up and play as either a hero or villain, though there wasn’t as many players online as I’d like. The game is really better as single player.
Cons:
-This may not affect a lot of people, but for the first week or so, I couldn’t even get the game to start properly. I could get to the “click to start” splash screen but once I clicked, the game would crash out. The WB support was no help, they didn’t even respond to my message for about 2 weeks (and then it was an unhelpful reply). Fortunately, I found the answer online buried in some forums. (I had to force the game into Direct X 9). The last time I played the game, there were no game breaking bugs, so most problems seem to have been addressed by the game developers. I only fell through the floor a couple of times.
Overall, like many AAA game titles, there were problems that were probably due to releasing the game too early, but it’s been a while now and the big stuff has been taken care of. If you enjoyed Batman Arkham Asylum and Arkham City, you should enjoy Arkham Origins. It’s just not much in the way of improvement.

Batman: Arkham Origins opens with no intention of being anything but what is expected from it. In fact I was dropped into Blackgate Prison with such little fanfare and context that it almost felt as if I'd jumped back into Arkham City by mistake.
This was after all the same Gotham I had run through before, familiar architecture giving way to reflexive movements honed over my time with the first two Arkham games. All of Batman’s high-tech toys were still with him, disrupting Origins’ prequel status though at least allowing my to skip collecting them for yet a third time, and by and large everything would appear to be in its rightful place eager for another excursion into Gotham’s criminal underworld (though by now I’m willing there’s a warrant out for at least 90% of the city’s population).
But, therein lies the problem doesn’t it. That for whatever Origins’ is itself, it’s the third of its kind in five years, and what was once revolutionary is now mundane and ordinary. Arkham Asylum came out of nowhere as one of the best games of 2009, and easily the best Batman game ever released. Arkham City soon followed, blowing the series up into an open world and bringing with it some welcome improvements to Asylum’s mechanics, even if that came at the cost of being rather bloated with content it didn’t have any idea what to do with. So where does that leave Origins’ to take the franchise?
Well, it doesn’t really take it anywhere. Origins’ is alarmingly similar to the games that came before it, only without enough confidence to carry itself well enough to at least be comparable to them. Which, OK, it’s being handled by a new developer so perhaps some rough edges are to be expected as a new team attempts to take over the Arkham series until Rocksteady is able to finish their next game. But Origins’ failings extend beyond minor bugs or the occasional bad level design, into an overwhelming feeling that this is all just busywork to keep people busy until the “real” third Batman game arrives. And that makes it hard to appreciate Origins’ on its own merits, when even it seems to have accepted its role as a filler game.
It feels sloppy and rushed, in little and big ways that snowball into one another as the game seems to progressively care less and less about how it eventually turns out. Combat is identical to past games using the same attack/counter freeflow system, but it fumbles over itself far more often than in past games. I was constantly having combos break when I was attacked from off screen or had the camera fail to center on the next enemy, slipping up on counter timing that never felt right, or just having attacks fail to register properly as Batman shuffled in place as confused as I was. Encounter designs enhance these issues by popping up constantly and having no focus or balance to them. I was tossed into rings of dozens of guys with random weapons or armor, and these weird combinations made it difficult to create any kind of rhythm in the combat because it was constantly being broken by a random enemy with a knife or a car door or some other special attribute that might pop up once or a dozen times during a fight.
The Arkham fighting system is one of my favorites in any game, but less than halfway through Origins’ I was already becoming annoyed anytime I walked into a fight and knew even if I played perfectly I was still at the mercy of the game doing what I told it to do. There is a lot less stealth in Origins’ than either of the past games, which was at first disappointing until I finally arrived at a predator mission and then wished they had been omitted entirely. City had already began to stumble a bit in following up Asylum’s impeccable level designs, but Origins’ up and throws in the towel right from the start with levels that are both far too complicated yet feel significantly less tactical than past games. There are still grates you can hide in and gargoyles to hang from, but levels never account for your need to quickly move from cover to cover as you close the distance between you and a guard and just haphazardly place hiding spots throughout a room with no thought as to how you might use them in conjunction with one another.
Every stealth section felt like I was the one who was trapped, rather than the guards I was hunting, leaving me scrambling to take them out as soon as possible instead of anything more methodical and coordinated. I died more times in Origins’ than I ever did in either of the past two games, and it almost always was because I had attempted to takedown an enemy in any way other than hanging upside down and waiting for them to walk underneath. These sections became very boring almost immediately, when previously they had been my favorite parts of the Arkham games.
Maybe this is simply the result of being spoiled by Rocksteady’s games, but Origins’ doesn’t exist in a vacuum and even seems to assume to player will already be familiar with the formula. It doesn’t bother to explain mined gargoyles or enemies with sonar goggles, because if you have played City you already know how they work. It’s entirely aware of its heritage, so treating it as a self contained work feels pointless and disingenuous. It doesn’t feel like a step forward for the series though, being closer to b-roll content cut from City rather than something original.
Where the Arkham series had the most ground to make up though, and where Origins’ even had the capacity to do so was its narrative, and to its credit this is far and away the most engaging and cohesive plot the series has ever known. The cast has been trimmed down from City’s over indulgent buffet of characters, which allows Origins’ to spend more time developing them into interesting, complicated characters I wanted to know more about. Many of the assassins called in to collect a five million dollar bounty placed on Batman’s head don’t get as much time as they deserve, but they’re compensated by a far deeper, disturbed Batman who is still early in his career as a vigilante and less prepared to face the villains he’s after. At times his sense of justice and methods for carrying it out border on sociopathic, a side of him that’s not lost on those he comes in contact with and which eventually comes to a head as he is forced to come to terms with whether or not his actions are actually justified.
It’s familiar ground for Batman as a character, but its a part of him I never grow tired of exploring and which brilliantly accompanies Troy Baker’s fantastic performance as The Joker. I thought I was ready to be done with the deranged clown, but the interactions between him and Batman are so compelling I simply wish Origins’ didn’t take so long getting to them, upon which it quickly changes the subject again. The narrative as a whole is still inconsistent, but it’s Origins’ one true advancement for the series which I hope will be continued with future Arkham games.
I have a hard time flat-out calling Arkham Origins a “bad” game, but it’s saved almost solely on the strengths of what has been brought over from past games (and then butchered) and carries with it a very qualified recommendation to anyone but the most devoted fans of the series. This is still an Arkham game deep down somewhere, with some exceptional characterization that sadly isn’t given enough time to shine, and by now the rhythms of the series have become so natural to me that it wasn’t difficult to get into a simple groove and fly through the game despite how unimpressive it was. I guess what I find most unpleasant is just that in only five years and three games it already feels like Batman has already shown us all he has to offer, and I’ve only reruns to look forward to in the bi-annual future.
"What have you done this time, Joker?" Batman sighed as he drew his katana.

Prison Architect is a prison simulation game. It was kickstarted by three university students in 2001, now sold with more two millions units on PC and won the BAFTA award for Best Persistent Game in 2016. If you love tycoon and sandbox games. Then this game is definitely for you. Especially this is a rather special simulation, compared to other games that you have played where most of the time you will either run a civilisation or food joint.
What's is like to run a prison? Do you intend to have a highly secured prison where no one escapes from your prison, or a place where prisoners are given a second chance to join back to the society. Although the game may seems very simple to you, with all the "South Park" character designs. This is not just a simple build and run game, but there's lots of decisions to make. Amidst juggling with the prison needs, you need to think of a constructive layout of your prisons to prevent them from tunneling their way out, schedule their timeslots, train guards, finding ways to have gang leaders to work for you, and have informants to share their inside traid secrets.
For gameplay it's rather smooth, but will tend to slow down after more than 300 prisoners. As each individual person have their own AI movements. So it gets a few pauses, but not choppy. The campaign mode is rather short, though all the episodes are glimpse of different perspectives from different prisoners. You get to see the story behind Mafias, people whom killed his wife for adultery, people who are on death rows. There's also an emotional touch, where prisoners are at their lowest point of time, asking for help from their spiritual beliefs to regain faith. All these are small stuffs that builds the game. Yet not just building is the main aspect of it, you also get to play as the prisoners in Escape Mode. Where you have to escape from the prison. Either by force, or allying with prisoners to form a gang and create a massive riot and sneak out when the riots is happening. There's still some simple graphical bugs where the sprites are not positioned correctly on the boxes, and AI doesn't still doesn't work quite well with dead bodies.
Nevertheless this game is worth the keep for a long run, and soon you will come back again to remember the changes it had from the start. Introversion Software is still updating this game, as of 03 Oct 2016. I do hope that there are more sprites created for example the scene where the two brothers tried to have a bank robbery. This will allow community to create their own campaign storylines. Or even multiplayer modes, where one will be the one building the prison, while the other at the same time is trying to escape from the prison.
Psst.. there's also a pseudo-3D look in the developer tools, but is resource intensive.

Seraph is a frantic side-on 2d platformer/shooter hybrid that automates the shooting for you. It sounds a bit like a gimmick but ends up working pretty well, mainly because moving around is so much fun; you get a double jump plus a dash in any direction (during which you are invincible). One of the jump animations even looks like Puss in Boots' cartwheel jump.
And you will need to use the moveset extensively, because soon enough you'll be under damn near constant attack by demons. Things get pretty hectic with several different enemy types requiring near constant shifting around.
Your objectives always are to kill enemies and break stuff, until the exit opens, but there's the odd collectible or 'get to this point before time runs out' side objective.
The characters and enemies look great - Seraph herself moves in a deeply videogamey / 00's gun-fu film way (Equilibrium seems to be a major inspiration). She spends the whole game barfooted; I approve. Unfortunately the environments are deeply uninteresting and the levels sprawl a little, which causes some pacing problems when you need to backtrack through cleared areas. So the exploration side of things isn't that great. The storytelling side of things is ok - there's a decent amount of worldbuilding and character work. Even if it didn't really engage me at any point, it's good writing for videogames, I'll take it - even with the hilariously obvious "twist".
There's also an RPG-lite character advancement and crafting system, because this is a game that came out in 2017, and you get penalized for dying because Dark Souls.
The game is complemented with a couple of game modes - daily challenges and a survival mode which, weirdly enough keep some of your character progression and equipment. This means that people who've played more than you have a pretty noticeable advantage in the leadeboards, which is a pretty strange design decision... I guess at least it helps justify the grindy crafting system.

While this game is relatively simplistic, having a small number of enemies and weapons, no real terrain variation, and an interesting but not enthralling story, what is in the game is done to near perfection.
Having your character auto-aim may sound like a crutch, but it's actually a really clever feature allowing you to focus on your movement. You'll jump, dash, run and do whatever is necessary to keep out of enemy fire, while still allowing yourself good shots. Weapons do still have recoil and accuracy issues, which means that while you'll always aim at enemies just fine, you may need to use all that time dedicated to movement to get as close as possible to your enemies when using the SMG or Shotgun, or if you want to go full-auto on your Rifle, rather than just burst-fire. You'll also want to line up penetrating shots and your non-automatically aimed spells.
Honestly, it's hard to say a lot about this game, because there honestly isn't that much too it. It's just all really well done and balanced. However, I do have to register one complaint about the game. Ascension is part of the gameplay progression loop, wherein you restart your progress in the game but with some boosts to base stats. The big issue here is that the currency used for ascending and the currency used for upgrading your equipment and spells is the same. As such, you're discouraged from upgrading much of your arsenal and each Ascension I felt "I'll be using this primary weapon and these two spells."
Still, if you're not obsessive compulsive, you can easily get your moneys worth without ever ascending. After 60 hours, I managed to get all 5 Ascensions in for a 'whopping' +15% Health and Damage boost compared to an unascended character with the same gear. I'd highly recommend the game if you just want some simplistic but engaging combat. It kept me busy for quite a while, especially for it's low price.

TL;DR - best $25 CAD I have spent on a Steam game in the last 3 months.  Have already gotten my money's worth out of it and I'm no where near finished what I can do in game.  Great holiday pick!
What an incredible game, especially for an Early Access title.  Already it feels like more of what NMS promised and never delivered - just on a smaller galactic scale.  I've been playing non-stop for 30+ hours, and have explored 3 other planets, and after encountering the "oops, habitat deployed inside my spaceship after reloading game", I wiped my savegame and restartd.  Currently I have restarted, logged another 10+ hours and started to circumnavigate the entire surface, and still die too many times to count. :)
Pros:
- Rapid Day 0/1/2 patches to fix big issues
- Surf your own Dune worm terraformations like Tony Hawk
- Die repeatedly to fall damage from Tony Hawk shennanigans because, well, you're NOT Tony Hawk
- Crafting that makes sense (not everything implemented yet)
- Good research progression (love opening up those weird orbs!)
- Caves to explore that can go quite deep and house hazards and ores
- Nefarious alien "fart pods" of death
- Get skewered walking too close to a mushroom (spikes of death!)
- Lighted tether system that is epicawesomesauce; ability to pick up tethers yay!
- Craft vehicles that you can chain together for extra explore fun
- TAB flips flipped vehicles (right onto your head sometimes!)
- Suffocate yourself while creating a pillar under your own feet
- Sandstorms that throw minecraft cubes of death at you
- Incredible soundtrack and enjoyable night sky
- Day/night cycles with impacts to power management
- So many modular construction options
- "Where the heck is my base?" icons easily seen across the horizon
- "Where the heck is my body?" thank you devs! <3
- Built in compass functionality for those who think they are Boy/Girl Scouts
- Trade center capability to trade your plentiful resources for something you're missing
- Nearly everything can be picked up and moved
- Did I mention, so many epic ways to die?
- Plays well with my nvidia 650Ti, Intel i7 2.8ghz CPU and 12GB RAM
Cons:
- After a couple hours, experienced occasional frame lag around base and getting in/out of vehicles (restarting seemed to clear up the worst of it; today after 2 patches not noticing it as badly) ** after 2.90 patch and restarting my game and making fewer habitat errors, working better today by far on the FPS front
- Took a while for me to figure out how to control terraforming tool; my recommendation PRACTICE away from your base lots and get the hang of it
- Camera view sometimes gets a little spasdic around busy bases, vehicles and in caves (pan camera to regain non-epilepsy view)
- Vehicle driving ASDW keys seem to function "in the direction camera is facing", and not based on "facing of vehicle", so again, practice before you roll off a cliff
- Dying JUST as you get inside your habitat pod will make it impossible to recover your body and items
- Tether system sometimes breaks after restarts and when returning to areas you have been away from for a while (just pick up and reposition a tether post and it usually fixes quick)\
- Too many tethers seem to cause some lag, though I'm pretty sparse in my use of them
- Crashed to desktop once at my busy base when camera got "stuck" (but savegame reloaded perfectly)
- Reloading has items on backpack floating in air behind you (just Q into backpack view, and select and re-place them back onto backpack slots to fix for now)
- Trucks chained together increase lag and sometimes tow like you're stuck in molasses
- Sometimes loading "research" orbs onto trucks/transports is a little glitchy
All cons that I've experienced have been only minimally annoying, and my progression has yet to be blocked.  I am looking forwards to additional features they most assuredly will add, but for now, this is fun to kick around in and mess about with the modular base building.  :D

Intel i7 860 2.8Ghz
12 GB RAM

Arkham Origins is a very curious title in a lot of ways. It was made by a different developer than the previous two games, since Rocksteady was busy working on Arkham Knight.
The things Origins does well is mostly in the storytelling department. I really liked how the game takes place early on in Batman's career as a crime fighter. Characters remark with surprise treating the protagonist as a myth and Batman himself comes across as more inexperienced and arrogant. It feels more in-line with the Nolan movies in this regard and it's a welcome change from the previous two games which felt like extensions of the Batman Animated series.
However, Arkham Origins isn't as polished as Asylum, nor does it have the steller presentation of City. It's clear the developers were working with a limited budget and time constraints, and that they weren't interested in innovating on the previous games like Rocksteady was. I still do like Origins but I think of it more of a spinoff to the previous two games rather than a sequel. If you treat it like that you'll probably enjoy it a lot more.

The story takes place when Batman is still relatively new at his work apparently, but the only real way you see it is in how other characters act towards you. Otherwise, all the skills and gadgets are there for you to use. So it all feels kind of disingenous when everyone acts like you are this new vigilante who might not actually be real, but you have the full skillset of the Batman that everyone later knows. Not exactly what this game said its Batman was like.
One highlight of sorts is the voice acting: Batman and the Joker got new VA's for this, and yet I couldn't really tell the difference. They both sound close enough to Kevin Conroy and Mark Hamill that, had I not known in advance that the latter wasn't the Joker anymore, I wouldn't have forced myself to look it up to check for sure. So I guess that's something. Oh, and our new Joker is the same guy who voiced Booker Dewitt from Bioshock Infinite. I thought that was neat.

There is no getting around it, DMC being rebooted by a western studio is shocking. So shocking that a lot of fans cried foul and screamed blood murder. Was it for the best? Perhaps it was, DMC 4 was undoubtedly a step backwards after all. Capcom took a chance with outsourcing the IP and surprisingly it paid off.
Meet DmC: Devil May Cry, a young fresh reboot by the team that brought you Heavenly Sword and Enslaved: Odyssey to the West. With a slick, stylized re-imagining of the world home to the Nephilim Dante. Born of the Angel Eva and Demon Sparda, he possesses the power of both. Hunted down by the Demon king Mundus, Dante is dragged into the parallel plane called Limbo at every turn.
While the initial combat impression and the new look might seem jarring at first. After a few minutes you will find that DMC is very much alive under the hood. The intense high level combat gameplay is still there with some interesting new additions to mix things up a bit. Once mastered you will be able to perform the dazzling acrobatic slashing we all know and love with ease again. I say with ease but do not mistake this for the difficulty having eased up. The challenges are still very much there, though I would recommend people familiar with the series start on Hard.
All in all the reboot manages to be fresh, engaging and most of all fun. It will be jarring to some but that is the case with any reboot. If you've enjoyed DMC in the past or enjoy action hack and slash games, give this a shot.

1: Graphically it’s a cut above the older entries into the series; it’s depiction of “Christmas Time” Gotham is chillingly beautiful and sinister.
2: Arkham Origins story is fun, exciting, and entertaining but it’s not Batman’s Origin story; it’s the “Origin” of the legend of the Batman.
3: Combat is the same refined system from Arkham City; but features a new “Dark Knight” system that put your skills to the ultimate test.
1: Unpolished in comparison to others in the series; while game breaking bugs have been fixed it’s still littered with minor bugs/glitches.

Con: Cold, Cold Heart lacks difficulty selection; once completed it leaves little reason for a replay.

Con: Initiation lacks cinematic narrative and feels shoehorned into an otherwise great game.

My thoughts on Batman: Arkham Origins,
I enjoyed the way Batman: Arkham Origins made the criminal element of Gotham City fear the night; believing the Batman was nothing more than a myth made up by the cops. It was fun to see how his rocky relationship with James Gordon began and how it ultimately grew into a friendship. But now onto the other great things about this game other than the story. Arkham Origins is more of what you love but it does come with some pitfalls but more on that later... AO is in a lot of ways a graphically updated Arkham City; it’s more of the fun you enjoyed in that game with a few cool new toys to play with but really you need to play the game to fully understand the feel of it and how much it's like AC.
Unfortunately, it's this familiarity that also knocks it down a few pegs; it also has a number of issues that can get a bit annoying though none of them are game breaking. On the one hand some of the new DLC skins are actually cool but that comes with some issues too... some of the cooler Bat-Suits require certain challenges to be completed but they must be done in story mode and many of them also unlock new gadget upgrades and if your unable to complete the challenge then you simply don't get that upgrade which really is a letdown. I understand that they wanted to add new ways to acquire these upgrades but I feel this was a very poor way of doing it. And on the subject of poor ways of doing things; one of the skins actually wouldn't unlock when you completed the challenge track which really was the prize at the end of the rainbow but instead of simply unlocking it for everyone to enjoy they removed it all together.
All in all, I'd say that it's a fun game but if you happen to never pick it up you won't be missing out on much. I'd recommend this game for hardcore Arkham fans only.

Without a doubt my favorite Hitman game overall and one of my favorite games in 2016. Now before everyone murders me and parade my head on a pike, try to hear me out. After all, it's just my silly opinion. This game has the perfect blend of Blood Money and Absolution and creates something very special. Agent 47 may have been reverted to emtoionless killing machine again, but at least we have our level playgrounds!
PROS:
-Huge playground in every level with endless ways to kill your target
-Replayability is very prominant and very encouraged
-Oppourtunities can be tracked and listed
-Pretty good soundtrack, music changes with your playstyle
-CGI cutscenes are visually impressive and well acted
-Voice acting is top notch
-Visuals themselves are impressive, especially Sapienza
-Intriguing and interesting story. Hitman is better at telling conspiracy stories
-Elusive targets are a fun and interesting mode, you only get one shot to kill the target, so use your wits
CONS:
-Online DRM, not acceptable in a single player game
-Episodic, I personally don't mind it, but it can inspire shady practices in the future
-Repeating voice actors, nitpick, but can we at least get some different voice actors? Breaks immersion a lot
-The seeing through disguises system is still here...still don't like it
-Agent 47 is back to being a emtionless killing machine, whereas Absolution showed he had some emotion and a moral code. What happened to that Agent 47?
To conclude, Hitman 2016 is a blast to play. You'll spend many hours replaying and finding new ways to kill your enimies. However, let this serve as a warning to Square Enix to the future. You have a great game here because you have a talented studio behind it. If things took a darker turn with the episodes, this would've been a complete disaster. Not to mention the online DRM in of itself is rediculous. So please Square Enix, think before your next move.
Verdict: 9/10
