Seraph (auto) aims high and hits most of its targets.
The primary flaw is that, like any randomly generated sets of levels, the level design never gets any more intricate or more interesting over the course of the campaign; it merely changes skins with each area. Instead, the game opts for giving its enemies more and more new tricks, defined by the game's ever-scaling difficulty system. That's fine, and it means you're too busy reacting to each new threat to let the malaise of deja vu creep in. I still wouldn't have minded things like hazards and such.
But this is a fast and fluid action game all about spraying targets and doing it with flair. Even the persistent upgrade system is not about adding to your moveset but amplifing your stats and buffs. You'll unlock more and more weapons and rings to grab from lockers, different spells (which you can only choose in the main menu), and various perks.
I am not a super great game player, so don't take this as gospel, but the final boss is a pain in the hinder. Even when you know all the attack patterns, it's very difficult to react to all of them in flow. In particular, the boss has one attack that happens almost instantaneously after its respective tell. And it will go to it right after attacking you with something else. I don't have the twitch skills necessary to bob and weave as deftly as the game wants for this, but I can attribute that to my own lesser ability. Still, it's a very sharp difficulty spike, considering the game, up until that point, has been adjusting the difficulty to your skill, in real-time.
The most interesting thing about Seraph is its Challenge game mode. Taking a page from Rayman Legends, there is a daily and weekly challenge where you get rewards for participating or finishing in the top X% in the form of crafting materials (which you can then bring into the campaign). The weekly challenge is a survival mode where everyone gets the same campaign seed, while the daily challenge can be various objectives. This extends the life of the game significantly, and should keep you entertained for at least as long as the campaign itself (which took me about 5 hours).
This game is pretty high on my list of recommendations. The movement is great, it looks gorgeous, and it has a ton of replay value. I'd recommend it to pretty much anybody.

TL;DR: If you enjoy 2D platformers, buy this game.
Seraph is a fast paced platformer that frees the player from the need to aim. This may sound strange at first but spend a bit of time with this game and it becomes clear that the developer Dreadbit has taken full advantage of this conceit to open up a platformer with a strong focus on mobility, positioning and ability usage. Enemies here are faster and more agile than in your typical platformer, with unique attacks that will keep your on your toes and on the move. Few games can convey the sheer speed and nimbleness of their protagonist the way Seraph can.
Graphics:
This game looks good. From the lighting to the animations of the titular Seraph, the unique and colorful visuals help to highlight the speed and fluidity of movement on display by the protagonist and the demons seeking to destroy her. My one complaint however is that the vast majority of demonic enemies you will encounter share the same bland tan colour pallet, making certain demons hard to distinguish from one another.
Soundtrack:
While not an extensive soundtrack, what music is available during the course of regular gameplay is very well executed. The oftentimes foreboding industrial electronic vibe meshes very well with the mix of a high technology setting and a story about an angel fending off a demonic incursion.
Story:
The developers have been quite open about this game being "gameplay first". At first glance, they have been true to their word, with the dialogue occurring between levels being sparse and fairly predictable. Interestingly, there is a second layer to the story, discovered through logs that can be found across levels, a story which slowly unravels the setting and circumstances our protagonist finds herself in. Here is where the meat of the narrative lies, a surprisingly lengthy backstory that will require multiple playthroughs to fully uncover.
While the main story can be forgiven for its brevity, the ending closes rather abruptly. I would have preferred adding an epilogue of sorts to bring some closure past the final boss fight (and the player's choices).
Longevity:
As an added bonus, the game has a surprising amount of longevity. A progression system that leads to persistent stat bonuses, upgrades for your skills and the various weapons you will find on your journey gives the player's achievements a sense of permanence. This is a game you can play in 5 minute spurts and yet walk away with something gained to aid you in your next session. A modular upgrade system allows your Seraph to choose, whether she wants to be the embodiment of Danger Close shotgun wrath, an agile gunslinger or perhaps an angel more in tune with her Holy side, enhancing her abilities more than her guns.
Daily Challenges push your skills to the limit to outscore your rivals. Here, in these short, 2 to 3 minute objective based rounds, the game allows you to fully let loose, refining the perfect mix of aggression, speed and control to maximize your performance with rewards that contribute towards your Seraph's progression.
The Weekly Survival mode forms the true endgame of Seraph's gameplay. While structured similarly to the main game, here, your performance is tracked with a point system, rewarding players who have mastered the controls and game mechanics with bonus multipliers to maximize their score as they attempt to progress as far as they can in a single life.
There is plenty of additional depth to explore for the player looking to optimize their performance. That being said, the Daily Challenges seem to be subject to the whims of random chance for those looking to score in the highest tiers. I have occasionally had perfect runs score poorly due to the slow spawn rate of demons, while my best scores are sometimes earned after having made sloppy mistakes in the face of unrelenting and rapid demonic spawns, earning me an excellent time to completion bonus.
Controls:
Seraph was made to be played on a gamepad as its load screen helpfully reminds the player. Full disclaimer, I do not own a pad but found the keyboard more than adequate after spending some time to familiarize myself with the basic controls. Keyboard commands can be remapped which some players will welcome but I found the default control layout to be comfortable enough that I was consistently scoring in the top 10% to top 25% of my Daily Challenges.
That being said, the default ability layout does not play well on all keyboards. I have noticed some 'stickiness' to certain key combinations preventing me to chaining abilities and attacks as quickly as I would have liked. Additionally, while for the most part very responsive, certain situations, such as landing against a wall, can result in the Seraph coming to a dead stop for very brief moments, something which this game can punish rather severely at inopportune times, ruining an otherwise flawless run.
Summary:
Though by no means a perfect game, this is a very solid effort by Dreadbit with a unique premise. The mix of surprisingly interesting narrative, constantly changing dailies and pure sense of speed will keep fans of the 2D platformer coming back for more.

The driving is superbly implemented. Unfortunately the gameplay centres on an economic model that is hopelessly flawed. It isn't obvious but you actually make more money by playing badly. To see this, take an extreme case where you did no driving but just went to sleep (actually the game won't let you do this but it's an extreme case for illustration). Because you make money from other drivers just by the passing of time, the more inefficient you are, which means more time spent asleep per mission, the faster you make money. If you drive well, you will complete your mission in less game time, and make less money.  The obvious way to correct this would be with a hefty time penalty from the cost of finance. Unfortunately the finance part of the module is so feeble as to be pointless.
Because of this it gets a neg from me on balance. But if you just want some fun from the driving and admiring the upgrades to your lorry, it's certainly a fun way to spend some time.

Story and Characters:  9/10
Batman Arkham Origins is heavily influenced by two of Batman's most iconic stories:
. Despite the less than subtle influences, I found the plot to be freshly original and very entertaining. Following in the footsteps of its predecessors, Origins is rich with Batman lore and Easter eggs that every degree of Batman fan can appreciate. The detail and execution of the characters in this Arkham game is once again of very high quality in everything from design to voice acting. Once again, the Arkham title delivers a large host of iconic batman characters and villains to appreciate. Do not expect an origin story for Batman—this game focuses on the origins of his relationships with certain characters and the circumstances that lead to
and the events of the other Arkham games.
Gameplay and Mechanics:  6/10
Arkham Origins inherited the excellent combat system of its predecessors.  That said, it also adds very few new aspects to the fighting mechanics.  While many would say "don't fix what isn't broken," the lack of innovation left me feeling bored after already having played with almost the exact same combat system in the other two Arkham games.  The same could be said for the predator challenges, side missions, and puzzle challenges.  Those who liked the open world of Arkham City will love the twice as large open world of Arkham Origins.  The new fast travel mechanic is a nice addition and can save you about three minutes when trying to get from one edge of the world to the other.  My biggest issue with Arkham Origins is that there are noticeable gameplay bugs.  I have had to restart a few missions and predator challenges because of glitches.  I have also noticed some graphical glitches as well, including gameworld seaming issues and issues with Batman's cape.  This is not the quality I have come to expect from an Arkham game.
Multiplayer:  8/10
The multiplayer mode of this game is surprisingly fun and, for the most part, balanced.  The learning curve can be kind of steep for those who are not accustomed to third person shooters and those who are not patient.  In the beginning, new players may feel very outmatched and out gunned by higher level players, but players can advance their character  level and weapons rather quickly.  After about three days of play, I felt as though my average performance was at least on par with some higher level players.  A nice additional aspect of multiplayer is the ability to customize the appearance and loadout of your gang member characters.
Overall:  7.5/10

After spending probably an hour trying to make this game playable, it continues to have framerate issues, texture bugs, and some of the cutscenes are still missing, but... This game is just... It's a nostalgia trip back from when vampires were actually creepy, gothic creatures of the night. Lurking in the dark corners of the earth... *wink*, *wink*. However, seeing how this is a 10 year old game, some parts of it don't quite hold up nowadays.
In
, you once again take the role of Rayne, a dhampir set to destroy the rest of her father Kagan's offspring, and her half-siblings, that have formed "The Cult of Kagan" and are trying to make it so, that vampires are once and forever able to walk the street during daylight, by using "The Shroud", a substance rendering the sun rays harmless to vampires, thus creating a new era of vampiric supremacy in the process.

Combat in
, as the name suggests, is bloody great fun! You've got Rayne slicing and dicing everyone and everything, with body parts flying everywhere! Besides from the iconic dual blades, Rayne can kick, dodge around, has a pair of blood dragon pistols and poseses an aray of abilities, including drinking the blood of her enemies. Rayne is faced with fighting various enemies. From Marilyn Manson look-alike goons to gone wrong vampire experiments. The controls play well for the most part, they're standard for a third-person hack'n slash game, but some false targeting and the awful camera can at times ruin the experience.
The game's atmosphere is at all time complimented by its graphics. After applying the mandatory HD Texture/ Widescreen patch
just shines... The varied levels, from a night club to a meatpacking factory, show off the game's artstyle. The simple ragdoll physics and prerendered cutscenes, typical for the time, are also featured.
The soundtrack of the game can be heard throughout the story. It varies from classical piano melodies to 2000s techno music. The different compositions can really set the mood and are reminiscent of the Hitman:Contracts soundtrack.
Overall
, similar to its predecessor, was and still is pretty good for its time. Although it does not completely hold up today, you should still give it a try, just for the memorable concept. However... if you are planning on getting it, expect to have to deal with a handful of problems.
has never been meant to be played on newer systems, and not all workaround methods do the proper job of fixing this game! All in all this is still a solid game, deserving of your time! ;)

Prison Architect is a pretty good indie prison management game with a number of flaws.
The art and audio are functional, but not particularly good. Luckily the core gameplay is quite fun and addictive. You build and improve your prison all the while trying to keep your prisoners reasonably happy (or at least under control). There's a very clear influence from Dwarf Fortress and other managament sims here.
The game has a decent if short campaign that acts as an extended tutorial. Unfortunately, many of the more advanced game concepts are poorly explained in-game and you are pretty much forced to either read through the wiki or work it out yourself through tedious (and expensive) trial and error.
Personally I would have liked to see some custom scenarios or at least more variety with the sandbox mode. As it is, the game gets repetitive fairly quickly after finishing the campaign and building a few prisons from scratch. Furthermore, many of the more advanced features feel quite unpolished or even unfinished.
Prison Architect is a good management game that's easy to recommend for the fans of the genre. However, the asking price is pretty high for an unpolished indie release, so it's probably best to get the game during a sale/bundle.
The good:
- Fun and addictive gameplay
- The campaign does a pretty decent job teaching basic game concepts
The bad:
- Many of the more advanced systems lack polish
- In-game tooltips are lacking and a lot of important information is only available in the wiki/guides
- Sandbox mode gets repetitive after a while
The ugly:
- There are a number of bugs with the campaign objectives
- Pathfinding issues

Being a fan of crafting-style-games where machines or vehicles are involved I thought I would look at ASTRONEER, particularly because it is set in space and seems to be what we all wanted in a NO MAN'S SKY-type game, the latter turning out to disappoint.  Before that I played FACTORIO big time and loved it.  So let's jump in.
Like FACTORIO or NMS, trying to work out what to do is half the fun, particularly as it was in FACTORIO where you essentially start of quite vulnerable.   ASTRONEER is similar.  You have a limited amount of air and power; a vacuum gun that can harvest things and before you rests a brave new world ripe for exploration and exploitation.  Don't go too far otherwise you quickly asphyxiate as I did whilst learning the ropes.
Initially you can build a few basic widgets, then machines that can either refine ore or construct more elaborate components and devices.  Some items require components that you can quickly exhaust so the pressure is on to spread your little mining empire.
Quite by accident I fell in a crevice and found myself in a wondrous cave that was filled with everything I was after.   In my half-crazed harvesting mania I scooped up everything I could but then was faced with an enigma – how the devil was I to get back?   I had lost my orientation to the base during my clumsy fall.  How typical!   Instantly rich but no way to spend it.
I got a warning on my oxygen that it was 50% empty (or was it 50% full?) so I better do something quick.   Fearing the inevitable blue face of death I thought:
“well I got this mining gun thingy, why don’t I just point it at 30 degrees in elevation and keep digging?  I’m bound to come out somewhere.”
BLAM!  OH MY GOD I LOVE MY MINING GUN!  I mean just how satisfying is it to watch it drill a perfect tube of escape appearing right before my eyes.  FOOM! As it drills through the lovely maroon shaded colored rock.
TA DAAA!!!  BLUE SKY!!
Well I think it was orange but you get my point.  FREEDOM!   And there’s my base just over there!
I run frantically towards my base my arms filled with gleaming goodness ready to fabricate the next device of pure joy!
-- CONCLUSIONS --
PROS
- Essentially it’s very much what NMS should have been
- Drilling is fun
- Storms scare the willies out of me
- Unlike NMS; exploration and mining is fun because you're not hounded by NPC droids attacking you every 5 mins
- Vehicles are great
- Good sound design
- Good clean UI
- Performance aside, this is one great little gem
CONS
---------------------------------------------
UPDATE:  beta fix released 2016/12/18 fixed the slow down problems!
---------------------------------------------
- Performance is generally poor.  Game seems to ignore any nVidia override; SLI or the fact I am using a G-SYNC monitor.  Stuck at a peak of 60 FPS; where most of the time its 30 FPS.   A bit odd for my rig that can run BF4; BF1 maxed at 144 FPS and GTA5; Watch Dogs 2 maxed at > 80 FPS
- Once you build up a reasonably sized base the game just slows to 14 FPS (one quarter normal performance).  This game uses the UNREAL engine which is known for being slow (XCOM xx) during certain conditions (like being near your base).  Strangely, loading up a brand new game doesn’t suffer
- would have preferred more automation as in FACTORIO
- replayability may be a problem once you’ve done it all once (FACTORIO Syndrome)

I have never played a Devil May Cry game, and from what I understand a lot of DmC fans were deeply disappointed in this reboot. The criticisms they have of it seem fair - especially about the overly edgy protagonist Dante and his edgy mcedgyton brother Vergil.
While Dante certainly wasn't a very fun character (I was sort of hoping he'd become funnier as the game progressed) he's not completely terrible. I never found myself cringing at his emo edgyness, and some of the lines he had were decently funny. A lot of jokes fall flat because they consist mainly of variations on "♥♥♥♥ you." The story isn't amazing, typical evil dude running the world and you have to take him out. I do think it does a good job of setting up future game stories without a ridiculously stupid cliffhanger or anything. It reveals something, resolves it temporarily, and sort of lets it be.
The gameplay is where I had quite a bit of fun. The action starts out reeeeaaallllyy simplistic, but once you get the scythe it all sort of starts to make sense. The fun comes in mixing and matching the various weapons together for good combos. Each creature has a weakness for you to exploit, and some are more obvious than others. For example there were these ninja dudes who I had NO idea, until the last level of the game, were incapable of blocking the axe thingy. I had completely switched to the fists and thought the axe was useless until I realized that. Of course you can't just use the axe on them though because it's slow, first you have to catch them off guard with something else. The same thing applies to a lot of the battles - you find new combinations as you play and it continues like that until the very end. Hell, in the very final boss fight I discovered a new way to use a weapon I thought I had figured out.
One thing about the combat that sort of fell flat was the enemies which REQUIRED you to use either an Angel or Demon weapon. I can see how that introduces challenge in fights where there's more than one enemy but it still felt extremely cheap. There'd be a red enemy that I can only use the fists or axe on, so I would just spam one of those until it was dead. No fun or strategy in it, just a huge annoyance. It became especially annoying when certain enemies would simply become ghosts if you weren't holding down the left or right trigger. Really?
That said I enjoyed the combat all the way through, and the boss fights were decent as well. I thought the next-to-last boss was a bit stupid because he took up so much of the screen that dodging all of his attacks were nearly impossible, so you just had to get lucky. The raptor news boss fight was the best though - it was funny and well designed. It was by far the most creative fight in the game.
Overall I would recommend this game, especially if it's on sale. It's a solid game with some good design. If you can forgive the edgyness, generic story, and heavy use of dubstep.

Note: The following review was made before V1.03, which addressed a few issues mentioned, and more importantly, demonstrated the Dev's willingness to remedy issues with the game.
This game could have been a lot more than what it was, but unfortunately, what it turned out to be was a frustrating, unsatisfying platformer/bullet hell with a very bland and uninteresting visual design.
There's about 3 different enemy types, and one enviornment, so you're going to be running and jumping through nearly identical rooms shooting the same thing with very little tactical depth, you just hang around holding fire until it dies.
The enemies have different attacks, and the depth of the game comes from avoiding them. Unfortunately, all attacks seem to boil down to two types:
1. Orbs which track you for about 16 hours.
2. Nearly impossible to detect hitscan attacks. They're white, or a shade of white, on a greyish bluish background, with bright white lighting, and bright white motes everywhere, and you've got about a second to see them.
And dodging these attacks comes down to one strategy of keep moving around sort of randomly and sort of just hope you don't get hit. And you have to do this for a long time, because every single enemy is a bullet sponge. And when the die they poof into more bits that further clutter the light colored area with bright white lights.
When I said there was 3 enemies in the game, that includes the minibosses. They too are just basic enemies, except they have 3 health bars that you kind of just have to wait until they deplete. There's really no strategy to any boss except dodging the same attacks you've been dodging this entire time already.
There's a second type of boss which is another giant damage sponge health pool, but this one spawns smaller monsters which you've already fought a thousand times.
The customization leaves a lot to be desires as well, so much so that it may as well not exist. The upgrades start at 2% chances at a proc, and by end game are maybe 10%. It may as well have just been a strict level up system with no customization, with abilities unlocked at certain threshholds. Ostensibly you also unlock more weapons later, but these are all just strict DPS upgrades with an ammo system. You basically change weapons when you start a boss fight and it makes a slightly different noise.
All in all, if they made a sequel which fixes these problems, ESPECIALLY making the visuals more distinct, I would buy it. But as it stands right now it's a well executed shooting platformer thing with a number of fatal flaws that make it frustrating to keep playing, with nothing to reward or incentivize you to do so.
EDIT: I falsely stated there were 3 enemy types. I was mistaken, upon review there are apparently 7. I have left the original text unedited, as I believe it is further evidence of the frustration I was trying to communicate regarding the unclear visual design that is omnipresent in this game.
Edit 2: A recent patch fixed a number of the issues I whined about. V1.03 added large "!" to a fire pillar attack that was previously nearly invisible. I have changed my review from Thumbs down to thumbs up not because this totally fixes the game, but because it shows the devs are listening and improving the game in ways the players found it weak. It sounds small, but it resulted in an large improvement in fun to play.

By and large one of the best running Unity action games I've played. Unfortunately a lack of interesting content and procedural variety, coupled with an MMO level of nearly imperceptible progression tied to a per centage chance enemy drop farming mechanic ultimately make the game a chore instead of an adrenalin rush. The painfully slow progression could've been overlooked entirely if the game were truly completely player skill based, but perplexingly Dreadbit chose to artificially limit the player's freedom to dodge with a two charge meter that has a cooldown period. The end result of this, in union with the built-in dynamic difficulty, is that when playing well you'll inevitably get to a point on the difficulty scale that you'll be getting hit with swarms of enemies that are simply impossible to avoid taking damage from with two dodges. This then enforces the grind, to survive *some* hits from 7.00+ difficulty enemies and to have enough DPS to avoid drawn out encounters, instead of making it a natural reward loop.

After bringing this up on the forum, Dreadbit did respond to me (I will say, always, kudos to developers taking part in their distribution communities), and the game apparently did at one point give the player complete freedom of movement; the restriction on it was actually an addition! The sentiment was that you could essentially fly with unlimited dodges, which is both an empowering (read: fun) mechanical concept and fitting for an angel. Dark Souls, and the stamina meter therein, was used as a point of reference for the logic behind the dodge cooldown. The problem with that notion is From meticulously hand crafts games tailored to a steady and deliberate pace, each encounter is give and take. Seraph on the other hand is essentially a hot procedural mess once you hit that 7.00 and up difficulty mark, vomiting out rainbow colored packs of "elites" at you indefinitely, the majority of which just spam whatever special powers they spawned with. Ultimately, I simply can't abide by the decision to intentionally make a game less fun in the pursuit of emulating somebody else's mechanics, but I can't fault Dreadbit if that's the feel they're going for.

As it is at the time of this review, what you see in the trailer is basically all you get. There's a couple different environment backgrounds, two objective types to clear each floor, a handful of enemies and enemy ability modifiers, a handful of consumable ammo gun types, a handful of cooldown-based powers, and a core dodging mechanic designed to shackle the player instead of free them; which is actually fitting for the plot. With all this in mind, if you really like the trailer then go for it; its far from the worst way you could spend $12.99.

+ defensive dodge/blink ability can get you out of some dicey situations
+ ability & item upgrades provide some progression & customization
+ replayability looks like a key design component baked-in
+ default weapon has infinite ammo, so you're never unarmed
+ daily & weekly challenges with in-game rewards
+ well-designed user-interface (menus, prompts, subtle quality-of-life features, etc.)
- taking damage from unseen off-screen threats
- taking damage from threats that are obscured/hidden by visual effects
- cheap tactics by some enemies (like instantly spawning or teleporting on you)
- movement/survival can feel trapped in some confined/cramped environments
- reduced max health when respawning despite being difficult already at full health
- health & ammo refills/pick-ups are limited & don't refill much
- some pick-ups/bonus-items seem to visually blend into the background/environment & can be easy to miss
- many upgrades look like a very long grind, with incremental steps so tiny that it makes me wonder "
"
(in addition to addressing things listed above that I do not like)
^ mini-map visible or accessible during game-play
^ built-in support for borderless full-screen window option
^ built-in configurable frame-rate cap option
^ longer "magnetic" radius/distance to pull in motes/pick-ups

So far, Seraph has been fun enough to make me want to keep playing. I think it's a good value for its price. This game is the Arkham-series going beyond critical mass in terms of expansion. It is expanding upon the existing elements in the almost worst possible ways, making the gameplay either mundane and bloated or just infuriating.
I'm going to quickly touch on the main parts that annoyed me about this game: The combat (including bosses), the puzzle-solving (detective mode and wayfinding) and the story.
So the combat is familiar, except for a few added extra enemies and even more gadget. The amount of gadgets at this point is just fluff though, as you are likely to use the most basic combat mechanics anyway. The basic formula works though, so the combat can still be enjoyable. The bosses are the exception here, because instead of relying on your wits and knowledge of the system, almost every boss-battle is centered around a variation of quick-time-events or a series of the game showing you what to do, and then you doing it. This makes every boss-battle more like a cutscene with QTE's rather than an actual battle.
So like in the other games, there are sections where you are expected to figure out a certain way to get forward or to discover clues leading you on in the quests. Now... I don't know if I remember the other games incorrectly or if this game just makes me notice the flaws, but the game switches between either panning to the player and pointing directly at where you're supposed to go or having you figure it out on your own. This switching back and forth makes it quite infuriating, as there's not really much to the wayfinding beyond matching skills with the environment akin to matching shaped blocks with shaped holes, making it feel padded and chore-like to do these sections. The game is also filled with all these bonus items but it's never really clear, when you're working towards a bonus-item or the way you're supposed to go.
Lastly we have the detective-sections which is basically the game pointing at something and wanting you to click on it - It's like playing a kids' game! Yay.
The Batman universe probably has one of the best comic-book villain galleries, so the direction they took the story was really disappointing to me. SPOILERS:
.
The structure of the story is also absolutely horrendous. I had to check a walkthrough because I wasn't sure whether or not I had completed the game, which it turned out I hadn't, even though the story the game sets up in the beginning was concluded.

Rayne is back, and continues to slice and dice her way into the 21st century. It’s nice to see her again but the experience was rather frustrating.
At the ground level BR2 looks a lot better than the first game did, there are major graphical improvements and the game looks quite nice, although you are unable to go above 1600 x 1200 resolution and there are no AA options which detract from the overall experience. When I first played it in 2005 I didn’t care about the AA options or about the resolution cap as I only had a 1280 X 1024 screen.
The game play hasn’t really changed very much from the first game. As Rayne you hunt vampires and minions who serve your “father” Kagan and Rayne has been hunting them for a long time. The same dismemberment features from the first game return, and there is a lot more blood and effects as well as new finishers. The game has completely removed all other weapons and now only allows you to use a particular set of bullets that are all blood related and can only be used in a single specific gun. The limited amount of ammo you can carry makes them pretty much useless although they are required for certain boss fights.
Although the game is pretty…the grappling hook/grapple shot was obviously not intended for mouse and keyboard. Trying to aim the hook after you have latched onto an enemy is a very tricky process and often results in death. This is especially frustrating when some of the bosses need enemies to be tossed at particular locations in order to damage the boss, and you often have to toss enemies into machines or places in order to proceed in the level (the game doesn’t tell you that you have to throw enemies in there so it can be quite confusing sometimes). You have a rage meter which is necessary to enable the super powers that Rayne gains after defeating enemies. Only a few of them are really useful and the rest can be hard to remember how to use. Defeating enemies helps power her up and increases the life and rage meter allowing you to survive longer. Some of the fights really boil down to just luck and timing.
While it is nice to see Rayne again, and there are considerable improvements in the graphics and physics…the camera works against you usually and when you combine that with the poor accuracy of the grappling hook things can get very difficult. Once again the game can be very repetitive so you’d better like cheesy dialogue and listening to the same conversations over and over each time you die. If you loved the first Bloodrayne and desperately want more Rayne then definitely pick this up, but while it has aged fairly well the controls on the PC port have not.
Maybe take a look at the PS2 version and see if the handling is any better.
So to sum up…more redhead, more blades, more blood, and a really frustrating hook/camera. I suppose it’s also a classic now so If you like vampires and hack and slash check this out when it’s on sale.

DmC differs from its previous entries by attempting to modernise the story, setting and characters. It partially succeeds but can't avoid slipping into giggly cheap laughs from time-to-time that will make gamers who fall out of the teenager core-demographic roll their eyes (Austin Powers-style covering-up-genitals and "I've got a bigger♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; spring to mind).
But as a "game" it's difficult to fault. The combat mechanics are pleasingly simple to master (use a controller though) and the pacing largely gives you room to breath after each encounter. The difficulty curb is also steady and forgiving, and although the bosses sit on the easy side once you get the hang of their routines, they still feel suitably epic and relatively satisfying, but nowhere near the standard set by previous entries such as DMC3.
On the subject of the previous games, hardcore DMC veterans will scoff at the difficulty (I am a seasoned hack-and-slash fan although no DMC master but I didn't suffer a single combat-related death in the game). There are ways of upping the challenge but don't expect a brutal DMC3 beatdown here.
Overall, it's a difficult one to judge. It's focus-grouped and demographic-orientated to the extreme, making it a pleasing and generally lukewarm experience that will never hit the heights set by games such as God of War 1 and 2, Devil May Cry 1 and 3 and perhaps Darksiders 2, but will still be fun and definitely worth playing once. Recommended.

This is my very first review for a game on steam. So, here it goes.
First of all, I´ll have to admit that 2D Platformers are usually not my first choice for gaming entertainment. I was pleasantly surprised by how easy it was to get the controls figured out. The few negative experiences I witnessed were mostly due to my lack of reaction speed.
Let me list a few very positive aspects of the game overall.

- Difficulty scaling works like a charm.
- Game flow is very fluid. You won't spend hours in menus and transitions into the next levels are smooth.
- It has an astounding replayability value.
- Very little to no bugs at all interfered with my gameplay (The game crashed once, but that's alright).
- Personalisation! Play the game the way you want to. Like getting in close quarters with the enemy? You can do that! Prefer to hit´em hard from afar? You can do that! Like the best of both worlds? Just get the Railgun xD
Of course, there are some negative aspects (nothing to serious thou and are just personal preferences)
- The difficulty scaling was occasional a bit too steep. Me: " Yay, I´m doing good " Game: " lol "
- "Wall-Stickiness" There were times when I wanted to stick to the walls and then there are times I don´t need to and/or got damaged because of it.
- It took me a while to really understand the importance of Miracle+Blessing compatibility just like with the upgrade system.
Twitch-Chat interaction! Those were the words that sold me. Yet another game that tries to appeal both to streamers and viewers. All I can say on this point is: works flawlessly!
Speaking of Twitch, Dreadbit also takes care of streamers by providing a webcam box where no valuable information about the game would be covered up! Great Job (even If I prefer not to use it)!.
tldr: Buy the game, its fun.

I have been with the Hitman series since the beginning and I have always loved it. I was however put off until now to buy it because of the always online feature but so far I have played 16 hours and not one disconnection. Lets get right into it
Pros
- Full freedom - Kill the target how you like, in a rush? throw an axe in their head and run.

- They kept instinct though still a nice touch
- The maps are a good size
- Plenty of ways to infiltrate

It is a great Hitman game but here are the cons
- If you prefer a direct approach you can do most maps in 10 min or less
- Always online (not a problem for me YET)
- It forces you to take a stealth approach, I have always liked to first go in quiet then go in all guns blazing, this game is unforgiving in combat situations, half the guards stay inside pretending nothing is happening, no body armor
- The game forces you to replay the missions to unlock new gear (I enjoy it others might not)
- Prefer a ton of small maps like previous hitman games insead of 6 large ones
- Does suffer the occasional frame rate drop for some explained reason
-Its a massive 64GB in size...It is officially the largest size game I have owned
I haven't gotten close to finishing it I am on episode 4 now, episode 1 has given me about 6 hours of fun, another important thing to note I paid £20 for this for that price I happy if I get 50 hours out of this for £40 I would expect 100 hours + but I don't think I am that patient.
Summary: Good game, not the best as the first few but a step in the right direction, worth £20, it is always online so if you have a bad connection don't buy it. Also remember Steam will give you a full refund if you spend less than 2 hours playing a game in 14 days.

Releasing the game episodically didn't work for me. Bought the introduction pack back when it was released and enjoyed it well enough, but didn't feel like playing the same map over and over. Forgot about the game until I noticed it on sale february 2017 and I boufgt the upgrade pack.
And wow, the game itself is amazing. All six maps are great, vast areas with tons of different approaches, it is the perfect Hitman game, I have warmed up to the challenges and have played the same maps over and over again, finding new ways to assissinate the targets and just exploring the interesting and beautifully designed worlds. I'm simply having a ton of fun.
The story sucks as always but, unlike Absolution, doesn't interfer with the game and it can be fun overhearing some connecting fluff while randomly exploring. I don't get why they keep trying to cram some Bourne-esque story into the Hitman games. It would be great if each individual map contained its own unique story and by playing the map you could piece together who wanted the assassination done and why.
Don't understand why the game has to be always online either. Normally this wierd way of releasing a singleplayer game would annoy me more, but I have just unlocked a sniper rifle which plays "Ave Maria" every time I zoom, and that's just wonderful.
Oh, important tip if you aren't too impatient, use 'opportunities help' for Paris to get the hang of the game, and then turn them off. It makes the game so much more fun and rewarding when you succeed when you figure it out yourself, instead of being handheld.
Anyway, great game!

All my life I've waited for a realistic driving sim. Playing with mods in GTA to make it more realistic, trying, and being dissapointed by "educational" sims, until I found SCS' previous game UK Truck Simulator. Now with ETS2 though it's almost become the game I've dreamed of.
I've never had a particular interest in trucks, I've put in 1000s more hours into riding motorcycles than cars even, but if you're the sort of person that finds driving relaxing, even if you don't think trucks are interesting, you'll probably love this game. And even better there's a Linux release!
The two map DLCs (Going East, and Scandinavia), are highly recommended, as is playing with a 900 degree steering wheel (even a cheap one makes it tons more fun, no need to spend 100s on a Logitech wheel), but the game is still plenty of fun without.
Overall I'd rate this game 5/5. There are some small nuances such as the AIs inability to use roundabouts properly, and poor signage in the non DLC map, but overall they're nothing in comparison to the overall quality of the game.

DmC differs from its previous entries by attempting to modernise the story, setting and characters. It partially succeeds but can't avoid slipping into giggly cheap laughs from time-to-time that will make gamers who fall out of the teenager core-demographic roll their eyes (Austin Powers-style covering-up-genitals and "I've got a bigger♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; spring to mind).
But as a "game" it's difficult to fault. The combat mechanics are pleasingly simple to master (use a controller though) and the pacing largely gives you room to breath after each encounter. The difficulty curb is also steady and forgiving, and although the bosses sit on the easy side once you get the hang of their routines, they still feel suitably epic and relatively satisfying, but nowhere near the standard set by previous entries such as DMC3.
On the subject of the previous games, hardcore DMC veterans will scoff at the difficulty (I am a seasoned hack-and-slash fan although no DMC master but I didn't suffer a single combat-related death in the game). There are ways of upping the challenge but don't expect a brutal DMC3 beatdown here.
Overall, it's a difficult one to judge. It's focus-grouped and demographic-orientated to the extreme, making it a pleasing and generally lukewarm experience that will never hit the heights set by games such as God of War 1 and 2, Devil May Cry 1 and 3 and perhaps Darksiders 2, but will still be fun and definitely worth playing once. Recommended.

DmC is a good game. Like many tough men I typed a lot of♥♥♥♥♥♥about this game and Ninja Theory. Well, they are due an apology because DmC is not garbage.
Dante controls very well. The weapons are fun to use and provide good variety for doing combos. Grappling enemies is stolen from DMC4 and is as fun here as it was in that game. Wrangling monsters is oddly satisfying. Someone should make an entire game about just that.
Framerate is very good on my old as dirt PC. The game looks great, too. Ninja Theory is one of those developers known for great looking games and I think DmC is a good example of that. Technically it doesn't seem to do anything outrageous but the art is neat, what effects exist are used well and overall it's a pretty game.
Enemies are fun to fight. They respond well to getting hit and dragged all over the place by grappling hooks. Many enemies are color coded and only vulnerable to one set of Dante's weapons. This mechanic is dumb and I don't like being forced to use certain weapons.
Bosses are straight garbage. Probably the biggest flaw in the game. Every boss is right out of the Zelda/God of War school. Two or three very telegraphed, very slow attacks repeated over and over while their weak spot gets beaten up. After doing enough damage the boss gets visibly hurt, the attacks patterns speed up or very slightly change, and after another couple cycles the boss is dead.
One boss is very neat looking. He's basically a demonic combination of Bill O'Reilly' and Max Headroom.
The last boss is the coolest but the trick to beating him is foolish. I don't like it when a boss is completely invulnerable except for one specific thing, and especially when that thing isn't obvious. (At least, it wasn't obvious to me; maybe I am too dumb for Ninja Theory's boss fight designers.)
Finally, my understanding is that NT was given this chance to revitalize the DmC brand and one area they were expected to excel was story telling. Well, they ♥♥♥♥ed that up spectacularly. The story in DmC isn't bad but it is every part as dumb, nonsensical and populated with oddball characters and off pitch characterization as every previous DmC. Why would Capcom expect any different? Devil May Cry has an insane premise and trying to present the narrative as anything but outrageous camp is doomed to fail.
NT didn't make a great Devil May Cry but they made in my estimation the best Western action game of the entire HD generation. That's not saying much and Bayonetta, Ninja Gaiden 2 and of course Devil May Cry 4 are all better games. That doesn't mean DmC is worthless to Japanese action game fans. Go in with tempered expectations and I think you'll agree this is a promising step forward for Western action game development.

Rust. No other game has ever consumed me in such a way as this game has over the years.
For those who are not familiar with the games' premise, you're dumped on an island, naked, and need to start gathering resources to build a base, make clothes, find food and get weapons, all the while trying to survive while others are doing the same.
You decide how you approach the game. Play aggressively, kill onsite, raid everything you can, earning multiple enemies along the way. Or, play discretely, hiding your base, and only raiding when the opportunity arises or perhaps not at all, just trying to make it to the end of the map cycle without being raided.
There are no objectives, no backstory, the server you are on, the procedurally generated world and its inhabitants creates the story in itself. The ultra violent neighbours that force you and other neighbours to work together to wipe them out, secretly planning your attack only for it to go horribly wrong and losing a lot, or the finding a weakness in a massive base and making off with all their loot are just a scratch on what makes Rust so addictive.
Graphically, Rust has got better and better over the years, the art direction is spot on. Lighting effects along with the day / night cycle make for some incredible landscapes. The UI is a masterpiece in simplistic and intuitive design.
Considering the size of the map (Typically 4 x 4km), it plays better than a lot of smaller sized FPS shooters in terms of gunplay.
Don't be put off by the fact that this is an Early Access release. I've seen a lot of games out there that are nowhere near as polished that release as final products.
Lastly, I want to make a special mention to the developers of Rust. They get a lot of crap from the community. Each week, they release update that introduces a range of fixes, new items, tweaks, and sometimes major shifts to the games' core mechanics. Some of the updates result in the devs getting a large volume of abuse from what seems to be a hardcore element of the community. While I don't agree with the abuse I get, ironically, it is indicative of just how loved this game is by many. Taking into account how small the team is who work on Rust, they have done a stellar job in creating such an awesome game that has consumed a considerable amount of my time.
Looking at the roadmap for Rust, it blows my mind to think just how much better this game is potentially going to become when I consider it to be already one of the PCs gaming greats.

I went into "Spec Ops: The Line" without any research, maybe just watched a trailer. From the visual style and few memories of American cinema, I expected it to be something like a modern "Apocalypse Now" and boy, was my mind blown!
In the very beginning you have the first big run-in with AK-wielding Arabs, and as you go in guns blazing, immediately there is loud battle music, and it does not look like anything to you until one of the NPCs asks if you hear this music too and where the hell does it come from. Watching it alongside "Westworld" felt unexpectedly satisfying.
Vistas of Dubai buried in sand, and the visuals are beautiful, and the performance is acceptable for a 2012 game. As for the process of killing, controls are mostly OK, your squad's and enemies AI is pretty good, and overall gameplay is OK. A little repetitive and exhausing at times, but I did not complain during these nine hours.
After you finish the game you can probably replay it at harder difficulties for extra visual cues or delve into almost uninhabited multiplayer. But even if you don't (this game would be better without multiplayer, as its german developers said), this game stays with you. It's a short game with a long exposure.

Seraph is a 2D platformer shooter where you don't actually need to aim.  This may sound like a bit of an oddity, but it actually works out fairly well in execution.  The gameplay is more about positioning and avoidance (while looking cool) than it is about aiming.
The Good
- Fun, platformer gameplay based on dodge mechanics and teleporting
- Game is generous with teleport uses making for some pretty intense battles
- Large amount of guns to choose from making gameplay more varied
- Leveling up and skills (Oaths) add more diversity to gameplay
- Miracles (magic attacks) add an extra layer to the combat
- Crafting of guns, miracles, and armor
- Gameplay is fun, so grinding a bit to get crafting ingrediants isn't chore
- Cool story concept
The Bad
- Dialoge can be a bit groan-worthy at times, also no voice acting
- Platforming isn't very difficult since there are so many jump/teleport options (can be good or bad depending on your taste)
- Switches where you have to race to get to a door are more of an inconvenience than an actual challenge since it's so easy to cover ground with your abilities
- Respawn system isn't great, players should be allowed to respawn in any map they've opened rather than only allowing respawn in the last map where a token was found
- Animations are not always smooth.  The jumps, flips, and teleports look really cool, but the character doesn't always transition well from falling, to landing, to running.  Also, there's no way to duck, walk, or pose, so you can't really flourish while or after doing something badass.
The Ugly

Seraph is a well-done and very challenging platforming shooter that kind of makes me think of a mix of Bayonetta and an old Xbox game called Gunvalkyrie, but as a side-scroller.  You also have an upgrade system like that of an action-RPG, where enemies drop resources that can be used to improve your weapons, spells ("Miracles"), and special limited-durability items that are the closest thing you get to armor.  In addition, your character gains passive buffs, either from gathering the game's equivalent of experience points or from using special items called Shards, which interact with Seraph's three skill trees--Munitions, Defensive (which I recommend focusing on first, because your very limited health needs all the increases it can get) and Holy, which is a mix of offensive and defensive bonuses.  Shards work similarly to combining metal in Team Fortress 2: three of Shard A makes Shard B, which is stronger; three of Shard B makes Shard C and so on, and Shard strengths and rarities are represented through colors, similarly to a loot system.
The game doesn't really "have" a loot system per se, as other than finding resources and Shards that enemy Daemons drop, you are responsible for what you want to earn and upgrade.  You can't make crafting decisions while you're in the middle of playing a section, but you can do so in between levels, as well as (smartly) from the main menu, which comes in handy if you know you're facing one big enemy instead of many little ones.  However, you also don't have true weapon loadouts: other than your dual auto-pistols, which are always with you and are your only infinite-ammo weapon, you can carry a second weapon by gathering one from numerous lockers spread throughout the game.  Which weapon you get--shotgun, assault rifle, submachine gun, railgun--is randomly generated, though some lockers might instead just offer extra ammo for the one you already have.  Weapons don't have randomly generated prefixes or suffixes that determine their capabilities, so their power generally depends on your investments into upgrading their stats.  Don't neglect your pistols, as they're invaluable when your stronger weapons run out of ammo.
Even basic enemies can severely damage Seraph, and health pick-ups are very rare and rather meager when they do appear; in some cases these will barely replenish the equivalent of taking one hit.  The game's central mechanic is its 360º evade system, whose two quickly recharging uses also function as a quadruple jump.  You're meant to rely on the invincibility frames this gives you.  Seraph targets enemies automatically and is generally smart enough to prioritize the close ones, though you can also lock onto them if you want the camera to focus on enemies instead of you.  At times I'd like to zoom the camera out before blindly jumping into an area I can't really "scout out" beforehand.  Along with replenished health, you get three lives per level, each of which having a significantly smaller maximum health than the one before it, so you effectively have 200% health spread over three lives.  Lose all of those, and--this was forewarned but may turn a lot of customers away--you resurrect at the last checkpoint you activated, even if it was in a previous level.  Many levels, which individually are small despite their nonlinear design, have secret areas that have these checkpoints and health/gun/ammo refills, so after you complete an area, you might not want to make a beeline for the exit without also looking for a secret checkpoint, unless you're already about to die.  The game's few major boss fights thankfully auto-save at their beginnings.
You can also find text logs, and for its genre the game actually bothers to tell a decent story; its writing style is flowery yet sometimes vague, but the story tries to be more complex than just a straight good-versus-evil tale despite its techno-religious motif.  It's even a bit touching when it's not being cynical.  These logs, which can be read during gameplay or accessed from the main menu, do a good job of setting up the complex relationships of the game's small cast, especially between Seraph and "its/their" vessel--intriguingly, but never ham-handedly, a Middle Eastern woman, whose interesting backstory brings up a lot of ethical questions.  Character dialogue can be skipped but is worth reading.  Even the weapons, the various Daemons, and the resources they drop have their own little bits of lore, which is a really nice effort despite the weapon designs lacking creativity.  All these bits of story do a good job of explaining concepts other genre entries might take for granted: why are there Daemons, and why do you in particular want to fight them?  How does gameplay death work if you're an angel?  How do experience points work?  Some of the Daemons, however, look like they came out of Dead Space and were then run through a grayscale filter--some more color and design variety would have been nice.  The ending gives you two choices but doesn't really explain much afterward, even if I still had fun overall.
Many enemies also have icons over their heads representing their abilities, but the game doesn't extensively explain those unless you look them up in the main-menu manual; the ones that really matter, however, will probably become obvious during gameplay.  The procedurally generated level designs function well (except for the one time a mandatory enemy spawned inside of a wall, forcing me to exit my Survival run) but don't always have a lot of 'art' to them.  Graphically there's not as much style as something like Transistor or Mark of the Ninja, but the setting concept is thoughtful and interesting.  The soundtrack, which reminds me of a mix of Frozen Synapse and Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory, is a lot better.  On smaller notes, some of the platform supports can be jumped through while others cannot (not sure why), and the "Motes" you gather sometimes look a bit too similar to the light fixtures.
The single biggest reason to play the game, besides its defense mechanism, is its difficulty, numerically represented in a corner of your screen.  This adapts to your playing skill and singlehandedly keeps the game fun: the early levels might seem too easy while the game calibrates, but that won't last.  You can also choose starting difficulty from a few options.  The main story may only take about four hours, but the last boss fight was INSANE even compared to the rest of the game (14 Nov EDIT: This difficulty got nerfed shortly after the game's launch but is still formidable) and took me yet another four hours' worth of attempts, with the difficulty never decreasing all the while.  I'm not complaining--it was amusing and even somewhat welcome to see a game so utterly unapologetic about its challenge, and I most certainly never got bored.  However, (this will hopefully be fixed) that last fight could use better optimization, since the bullet spam repeatedly slowed down my framerate--devastating in a high-speed game like this--and caused one of my two crashes.  There's also a funny but minor glitch where Seraph's graphic got stuck in a prone position but otherwise played fine.  A controller is highly recommended, as the keyboard technically works but makes directional evades a bit of a pain.  Most actions can be rebound, except for pausing and (on a controller) movement and enemy focusing, though the left and right stick functions can be swapped.
You also have daily and survival challenges you can do, complete with leaderboards, and some select rewards from these challenges carry over to the main game.  If you perform well (e.g., top 75%/50%/etc. of players), you can get extra items.
Other than some issues with the art and the game's stability, I've been very happy with this little game that takes a simple concept and keeps it exciting.  Time to start New Game Plus! (Update: I don't even know how many playthroughs I've done now.)

Everything in Seraph comes together well, and I often find myself admiring its polish during a session of gameplay. Although the proceedurally generated stages and limited variety of foes appear to highlight a lack of creativity in visual design, Seraph executes the philosophy of “less is more” with acumen. Even with my screen becomes swarmed with foes, I never witnessed a single frame drop, and the game maintains its fluidity at all times. With the exception of one track that plays during the post-mid boss levels, the music is surprisingly jammin with its techno beats. Players will get out of Seraph what they put in, and its target audience is for those who appreciate feats of skill. This is precisely the kind of game that SHUMP fans should not pass up under any circumstance.

I want to like this game, because it's very polished, and the amount of work and time that went in to some aspects of the game is obviously huge. The levels are gorgeous. Every area is painstakingly crafted in detail to represent a place teeming with life. Each one is an assassin's playground. The music and sound design are great.
However:
The main replayability of the game comes in the form of mastery challenges and escalations, that when completed, unlock items to use in later levels as well as starting locations and drop points for the current one. It sounds like a great, but the amount of times needed to replay the level to finish all of them is absurd. How about an example!
----
Let's take "The Showstopper" mission in Paris. There are:
26 assasination challenges requiring assasinating the targets in different ways (4 can be done concurrently)
5 challenges from the "Holiday Content" version of the mission to unlock a suit.
Then then 18 escaltions. EIGHTEEN. What is an escalation you ask? It's a playthrough of the level with win requirements. To complete an escalation, you have to beat the level five times with increasingly harder requirements. That adds an extra NINETY completions.
But that's not all folks!
There is a "Professional" difficulty with another 20 assasination challenges!
Then you add on the 70 or so miscellaneous challenges, some of which are fun and interesting thankfully, and all the savescumming and learning the level and and it adds up to a lot of time.
----
AND THIS IS JUST A SINGLE LEVEL!
It should be said that not all of these must be completed to unlock 47's gear. But if you DO want to unlock all of the gear be prepared to spend upwards of 10-15 hours replaying a level over and over again.
Unfortunately the gameplay just does not lend itself to replaying a level over and over and over again, at least it didn't for me, which is why I cannot recommend this game. Also, the story was very barebones (it's six short cutscenes between the levels). If you are a completionist like me, then you will give yourself a complex trying to complete all the challenges. Do yourself a favor and play Absolution for a tighter, more concise experience with an actual story!

First off, Dante is not gone. He is not that far off from the original once you finish the game. That being said, most people are turned away from the game as it is not the Dante nor the Universe we've come to know and love. But you have to understand that this game is acutally a reboot for Capcom. And in my opinion, Ninja Theory did a marvelous job with this game.
(Sectioned these off, just look at first sentence for categories. TLDR at the bottom.)
First off, the universe. Before, in previous Devil May Cry installments, Humans and Demons lived on one plane. In this game, not so much. Here, Demons and Humans are separeted by "Limbo". A plane really close to that of the human world. In this universe, humans, demons, anything and anyone can be pulled into Limbo, and the only way to get out is to kill the demon that dragged you into Limbo. In this universe, you have a more stylized and modern intrepertation of demons. They control the world with debt, keeping them docile with soft drinks called Virility, and monitor them from Limbo with CTV Surveilance systems in the real world. I think this is a pretty interesting take on our modern day and might actually be conveying a message.
As for the visual aspects of the game, I have to say it's quite gorgeous. The stylistic combos that Dante can pull off between his human, demon, and angelic form are quite a sight to see. Animations are much more realistic as they represent actual human movements. What I mean by this is that they transition quite nicely. The point system now shows you what you are getting your points from, how much you're getting from them, and what special actions you've performed that netted you those points such as perfect evades and environmental attacks. All the while, the game is running extremely well. I play on a Laptop, which really isn't the greatest for gaming, but boy. I ran this game on Ultra settings, 60Hz refresh rate with HD texture and HD Anti-Aliasing. 60FPS the whole time. Cutscenes are extremely well done, voice acting is top notch, and make the game pretty believable. I can only recall maybe 1 or 2 events where the voice acting took me out of the game.
Difficulty? Not much here until you hit "Dante must Die", "Heaven and Hell", and "Hell and Hell" modes. Hell and Hell can give you a real challenge comparing to that of Dark Souls or Monster Hunter. See, in this mode, if you're not familiar with previous games is a challenging difficulty level where Dante dies in one hit, while his enemies have full health. This right here, this, is the hardest you're going to be able to play this game. Seriously, the difficulty level in this game is a joke, I beat the game on Standard difficulty dying only once and managing an S or SS rank at the end of the mission. As long as you do what the game tells you to do (Angelic weapons against blue enemies, and Demonic weapons on red enemies) you'll be fine. Took me about 9-10 hours to beat the main DmC mode on that difficulty alone. But I kind of want to go back and finish the game on all dificulties in order to get all the achievements and perfect my combos. That being said, this game is a breeze.
Story wise, like I said earlier, this game has an interesting take on today's society and the demons that walk among us as your everyday Joe. I do have to say, Character Development is not a big thing in this game. When there is some, it's kind of out of nowhere and really bland. One of the most interesting characters in my opinion is Kat, but you don't really get enough of her to justify her as an interesting character all that much. Though I do have to say I was EXTREMELY impressed with what Ninja Theory and Capcom did at the end. They set this game up so well for a sequel and in my opinion, stayed true to DmC. I was absolutely speechless, no doubt do you have to play this game for that. With that ending, you know that they also listened to their fans. Hell, it may seem like they didn't at first glance, but they did. Secretly. They did a very good job calming the populus somewhat with Dante's original redesign. Long story short, the story is entirely riding on the ending. It's pretty generic throughout most of the game and the end just leaves you breathless.
Music is okay, not really much to say here. Basically what you would expect Dante to be listening to while murdering demons. Only complaint is that the music sometimes doesn't stop when all enemies are killed leaving you to think that there are still more when there actually isn't when the music is NORMALLy supposed to fade away after you get them all. But that's not the only thing. Sometimes it doesn't even fade. It just stops. Abrubtly, just like that and you're just kind of taken back a bit. Nothing too major though.
Replayability? Hell yes. You'll see collectibles off in the distance far too many times throughout your playthrough wondering how to get there. Simple answer? You can't. You have to gain access to certain abilites and then revisit those levels to reach those collectibles for a higher completion percentage and the mission score screen. Also necessary if you're hunting for those achievements.
DLC, I'd say skip out on it. It's not that good. By the name of the DLC you can tell you play as Vergil and I'll tell you, while he seems cool, you just feel extremely limited with him. After getting SSS ranks in combat with Dante, barely being able to scrape a B rank with Vergil just hurts. You can combo much better with him as your progress, but you don't even get all of your abilities until you finish the sodding DLC. That's right. Your reward for beating the DLC, is an ability that would have helped you clear the DLC. Their choice for this was obvious if you play through it, but it's best to just either pick this up while on sale or just skip it entirely. Another gripe of mine with this is that the cutscenes, they appear to be concept art, Just a slideshow or a quick demo of what the cutscenes should have looked like/portrayed if they were actually animated. Not only that, they switch from concept art into ACTUAL animation out of nowhere towards the end of the cutscence. REALLY takes you out of the experience.
TL;DR: Game stays true to DmC history, just with a few of it's own twists taking place in a more modern universe that resembles our own. It may not look like it at first glance, but it is actually pretty spectacular with what they did with the ending. Gameplay is satisfying, beautiful, smooth as all hell, but extrememly easy unless you pick one of the higher difficulties like "Hell and Hell" which you have to unlock by beating the game several times. Great replayability requiring you to return to previous missions with abilities obtained in later chapters to get all collectibles. Music is okay though music sometimes doesn't stop as fast as it needs to, or ends too abruptly after fights. Story wise, kind of generic, but my god, like I already said, the ending... Left me as giddy as a schoolgirl. As for the DLC, either skip out on it or pick it up while on sale because it's not that good. If I HAD to give it a score, 9.5/10

Prison Architect is a deep sandbox.
If the Dwarf Fortress
console is too hardcore for you, Prison Architect is perhaps its polar opposite.
You still need to manage a mob of unruly violent drunks.
You still need to worry about locking doors and equipping guards...
Major differences
- employees don't slack off or become suicidal when the alarms are ringing.
- There are NO HOTKEYS...
- You can't just kill the troublemakers.
- No HOTKEYS
- Really none - No matter how much you want to avoid the GUI, you just can't.
The menus have some AI built in - zoom in on an office and the menu will show you office furniture.
Great - but I don't want to zoom in that far...
Foundation / Walls: I figured it out - The fate of existing walls depends on whether your new construction overlaps an existing foundation.
It's not too hard to build a money maker - take minimum security prisoners and get them building quality beds.  I assume maximum security is where the challenge is.
Some troublesome annoyances:
- guard 'schedules' are tricky.  Probably shouldn't use them.
When a schedule ends, all the guards leave immediately,... even if the next schdule requires the same number of guards. The new guards have to walk from ... wherever they are. They might take a 1/2 hour of game time to show up - plenty of time for a snitch to get shanked.
- Tunnels are a chore.  The AI 'knows' which way is the fastest to tunnel.. So all tunnels in an area always use the same path.  Learn once, then put a dog on it. Alternatively you can bait the tunnelers to a maze filled with armed guards. They can't learn it's a trap.
If you like design sandboxes, this is pretty good - but it's not without a few boring chores.

Spec Ops: The Line is the latest installment in the until-release relatively obscure Spec Ops series, and on the surface looks, sounds and plays like your incredibly generic Gears of War game, with a hint of tactical shooter. However, it is a
plot heavy game. The game's premise is set around the attempted reconnaissance and rescue of Dubai's remaining citizens, after vicious sandstorms have all but razed the city to the ground.
Everything is presented as a generic shooter.
You have achievements and awards, multiplayer, co-op, difficulty selection, and a trio of military grunts fitting the charismatic leader, wisecrack cold sniper and big scary black dude tropes to the letter.
Graphically, it is decent. A selection of "filters" let you play the game with vibrant and saturated colours, the standard settings or the overused "real is brown". Main character textures and models are good, though the facial animations occasionally look odd, and their details clash with the otherwise technically unremarkable world and enemies. That isn't to say a destroyed Dubai isn't something to stop and gawk at - it's a sight to behold no matter where you're from.
Voice acting is superb, an essential part of character development. Sound effects are on point. The music is pretty banging when it kicks in.
Gameplay, again, is your bog standard cover shooter. Hug that chest high wall like your life depends on it, because more than likely it does. Sandstorms are an occasional gameplay element, which ruin your accuracy and your mobility whilst allegedly doing the same to enemies. They still hit you pretty often. The tactical gameplay extends to ordering your squadmates to focus fire on a single target, which may or may not simply make them run into the open and get themselves incapacitated by the other 200 enemies.
Past this point, dissecting the motifs, the game's design and characters, will be marked as a large block of spoilers, so you're free to skip it towards the conclusion.
The story is short, around 5 hours max from start to finish on Normal difficulty.
While it is flawed and extremely divisive, Spec Ops: The Line is nonetheless a unique experience and a fresh take on a tired genre. Its message and execution have sparked numerous discussions and essays that analyze its story, motifs, symbolism and so on. It is best you go in as "blind" as possible, though - it is a very plot heavy game. And if you do buy it - and I suggest you do, if only for its unique approach to the shooter genre - play only the campaign. You may replay it once or twice to see some previously unseen details, but you can't go back and experience it like it was the first time playing it any other time.
The rather generic gameplay is completely overshadowed by the truly great story.

An extremely well put together jumping puzzle/twitch jumping game with a nice story, fun game mechanics, great graphics, and natural ability progression but with plenty of room to explore on your own.
I played the Definitive Edition first, and thoroughly enjoyed it, even when the twitch jumping frustrated me, and then I went back and played the original to see what the changes were. There are significant changes to the map, minor additions to your abilities, and some mechanic changes (i.e. being able to go back to major world places like the Ginso Tree and explore after you complete the mission, which you can't do in the original) and also making the save shrines warp portals to travel through Nibel faster.
I cannot recommend this game enough, and it's soundtrack. It's soundtrack is fantastic, and several songs have found their way into my regular rotation.
Overall... it's extremely well put together and it will frustrate you in a good way if you're stubborn and you like problem solving. My one negative critique would be the story cutscenes, while good and emotional, weren't really anything that made me go "wow" but it does tell a nice little story, and it's certainly not bad or intrusive.
Definitely check this game out and, hell, spring for the soundtrack too. Because it's awesome. Definitive edition includes the original if you'd like to play both.
Anyone looking for a great metroidvania with an emphasis on crazy platforming will enjoy this game!
