This is a bit lengthy so I'll put my conclusion in first.
This game is just frustrating to play and it wasn't until I tried writing this review that I realised just how much is wrong with it. It's the procedural generation that fails this game the most, I could probably overlook every other flaw I listed if the devs just took the time to craft a compelling set of levels to play.
All the levels are procedurally generated, often badly. By this I mean more often than not the game will place a variety of enemies in an awkward space that makes it very difficult or impossible to evade their attacks. At the beginning of the game this isn't a problem because you can kill everything quick enough before things get awkward. The game doesn't really give you enough tools to help you avoid damage, just a dash with invincibility frames.
Levels with large vertical sections you have to drop down. You take a leap of faith there aren't a bunch of enemies waiting for you when you land, there's no feature to see what's down there. Just another problem with procedural generation.
Odd procedural generation that will place a background under/over a platform and make it look like a wall you can jump off.
With the exception of the last 3 levels in the main game, the other 22 all look very much the same with the same greyish blue color pallette. The last 3 levels has a red color scheme. The screenshots on Steam are a good indicator of all the variety you'll ever see.
Some platforms you can shoot through, some you can't. All platforms you can't jump/fall through. If you can shoot through it then surely you should be able to traverse through it? A confusing design choice.
You stick to walls. The game has a wall jumping mechanic and when you hit a wall you'll briefly stick to it before very slowly sliding down. The problem? a badly generated level means you'll encounter enemies in spaces that are awkward to fight in, so you'll find yourself jumping to evade an attack but then stick to a wall and get hit.
Offscreen attacks. Firstly all enemies will announce what attack they are going to use by showing you an icon relating to that attack somewhere around their body. Of course you can't see this if the enemy has made the attack offscreen. There is one particular enemy who can summon a pillar of flame under your feet, by the time you notice it's already too late. This could have been remedied with better sound design whereby enemies can make a particular noise before they attack or just not make any attacks offscreen.
In total there are 7 enemies. They all look very similar to each other. Look at the screenshots, faceless, naked, pale grey pinkish skin. They all look like that, that is as interesting as the enemy design gets. There are elite enemies like in Diablo where there are modifiers that give them an extra attack and considerably more HP to give a little more variety.
The game makes itself more difficult by increasing enemy HP, attack frequency and maybe decrease the warning time before an attack. Enemies don't get smarter, they just get more spongy. This is especially bad when you encounter an elite (lieutenant) enemy that can spawn in more enemies.
This game increases the difficulty by measuring how many enemies you kill without getting hit*. Why is this a problem? Well you can breeze through a section of the game because the procedurally generated levels were in your favour, then when you get a more awkwardly generated level you'll to have a much harder time.
*it's actually the amount of xp dropped from enemies that you collect without getting hit.
When you die you don't go back to the start of the level you failed at. You are taken back to where you last collected the glowing green checkpoint item. Though not every level has a checkpoint item (procedural generation) so you may be sent back a few levels.
Bad enemy AI. The Serf demon, at certain positions doesn't know how to traverse from a higher platform to a lower platform to attack you, it will just walk back and forth on the edge of the platform until you lead it off. Other flying type enemies sometimes get stuck on wall sections not knowing they need to fly down to get through a doorway. This is just bad AI and I am very surprised it wasn't picked up in testing because these things don't happen rarely.
There's too much for your eyes to keep track of in combat, this isn't a problem until the higher difficulties when enemies become bullet sponges. The game relies too heavily on visual cues to tell you danger is coming. Example, you need to watch your character center screen to see if there are magic attacks that spawn in at your location (flame pillar, damaging teleport) you need to watch all around your character for enemies and keep a sharp eye out for the attack indicator (at higher difficulties this disappears very quickly). If you're using the alternate weapon you need to keep an on the bottom-right for ammo count. If you've used your magic then you need to check cetner-bottom for your cooldowns.

A young woman wakes up in empty strange place with human corpses. Turns out place is not really empty, it is crowded by bloodthirsty demons. The woman (Seraph) takes two pistols and... carnage begins.
The game is full of dense action with shooting, jumps and spells. Heroine is some kind of disgraced angel, so she has some tricks for surviving. Seraph is not very healthy, but she is very mobile. She can do some high jumps and dashes that help her to evade attacks or to reach some high places... or even hang on walls. Also she is a skilled sharpshooter and fluently deals with any type of guns - from dual pistols to railgun. Seraph knows some fancy magic that helps to slaughter demons in more efficient way.
The game looks like Devil May Cry with pistols only with lots of acrobatics in Castlevania-style levels.
Big, randomly generated maze maps are perfect playgrounds for fast and acrobatic gameplay. Big amounts of demons are pretty aggressive and can chase heroine through the whole level. They have different skills and attack types, and game clearly combines them for making gameplay more agile and difficult for staying alive.
Story is told by short chats between Seraph and demons or survived persons. Usually they happen at the beginning and ending of levels, and they are surprisingly good. Dialogs don't seem to be hackneyed cliches, they are well written and show some depth of characters - as much as it is possible in a game about non-stop shooting. Soundtrack reminds British electronic from 90's, skillfully mixed with modern styles. Visuals are nice, neat and elegant.
I recommend everyone to play this game. It's fun, challenging fast shooting arcade with pleasant music and good story.

I want to like this game, because it's very polished, and the amount of work and time that went in to some aspects of the game is obviously huge. The levels are gorgeous. Every area is painstakingly crafted in detail to represent a place teeming with life. Each one is an assassin's playground. The music and sound design are great.
However:
The main replayability of the game comes in the form of mastery challenges and escalations, that when completed, unlock items to use in later levels as well as starting locations and drop points for the current one. It sounds like a great, but the amount of times needed to replay the level to finish all of them is absurd. How about an example!
----
Let's take "The Showstopper" mission in Paris. There are:
26 assasination challenges requiring assasinating the targets in different ways (4 can be done concurrently)
5 challenges from the "Holiday Content" version of the mission to unlock a suit.
Then then 18 escaltions. EIGHTEEN. What is an escalation you ask? It's a playthrough of the level with win requirements. To complete an escalation, you have to beat the level five times with increasingly harder requirements. That adds an extra NINETY completions.
But that's not all folks!
There is a "Professional" difficulty with another 20 assasination challenges!
Then you add on the 70 or so miscellaneous challenges, some of which are fun and interesting thankfully, and all the savescumming and learning the level and and it adds up to a lot of time.
----
AND THIS IS JUST A SINGLE LEVEL!
It should be said that not all of these must be completed to unlock 47's gear. But if you DO want to unlock all of the gear be prepared to spend upwards of 10-15 hours replaying a level over and over again.
Unfortunately the gameplay just does not lend itself to replaying a level over and over and over again, at least it didn't for me, which is why I cannot recommend this game. Also, the story was very barebones (it's six short cutscenes between the levels). If you are a completionist like me, then you will give yourself a complex trying to complete all the challenges. Do yourself a favor and play Absolution for a tighter, more concise experience with an actual story!

When it comes to gameplay Spec ops: The line does an ok job as a third person shooter, but where this game really does shine is in its story and the way it doesn't aim to glorify war but to reveal its horrors and the psychological effect it can have on soldiers. When you first start the game it may not seem like this but as you go on the plot of the game will start to take a darker tone and the objective of your squad's mission, which was to find and evacuate survivors, will change into a hunt for the man which Walker believes is responsible for the chaos in the ruined Dubai. As you go on your squad will begin to question the ambiguous nature of Walker's mission and so will you as the player, even going as far as to ask if the people you are killing are really your enemies. There will also be points in the game where you are forced to take actions for the narrative of the game that will make you question the morality of those actions, even the text on the loading screens will make you rethink your actions throughout the game. Once you reach the end of the game you will be left thinking and asking yourself one of the same questions that the game asked you "Do you feel like a hero yet?", and no matter which of the four endings you get the answer will still be the same.

Like the past B:A games, Origins includes all the features we know and love. However, it takes you back, hence the name "Origins". It takes you to the time when the Joker wasn't a familiar name, when Gordan didn't know Batman, and before many events those of us who watch the movies know of.

Batman: Arkham Origins is very similar to the last game, Arkham City which isn't a bad thing as the previous game was a masterpiece in it's own right.
The story isn't as good as the previous two but it's still amazing, at times predictable but at other times surprises you with a plot twist that you didn't expect.
The general plot of this game follows Batman on Christmas Eve as a bounty has been placed on his head that many major and minor villains will attempt to get from you.
It should be said that this game was developed by Warner Brothers Montreal which is a different studio from the previous two and the upcoming Arkham Knight game which were all developed by Rocksteady Studios, it's because of this that I can forgive this title from not having too many changes from the last games.
There is so much to do in this game even after you complete it, for example there is a most wanted side quest that allows you to try to stop criminals such as The Mad Hatter and The Penguin and bring them into custody.
- Good Story
- Many interesting villains, even some you may not have heard of
- Graphical improvements from previous game (not too much)
- Fun side activities
- Improved mechanics
- Battle system is great with only a few problems
- You can be Batman, who doesn't want a taste of that Batman lifestyle am I right?
- Battle system is repetitive at times
- Not many improvements from the previous games
- A few glitches had to be sorted out, I never ran into many glitches like the fatal error or controlling flight issues however I did have to fix an issue with the cutscenes as mine lagged a lot; I ended up finding a guide on the steam community to help me.
- Some tasks such as the collectables are still a chore in my opinion and I wish they were done more interestingly than they are in this game, for example Arkham Asylam had audio logs from the villains which were interesting to listen too and made me want to collect them.
Like the previous Arkham games but significantly worse. Not really worthy when the other titles are significantly better.

BEEP is an "action" platformer that has you play the role as multiple BEEP robots. Their mission is to explore all the planets they can. This game has you go through three planets (six areas). You'll explore everything from plains, to swamps, to even lava lakes.
In case you just want a quick review, no problem. In short, this game is a tedious, hard to control platformer that pushes you to your (frustration) limits with its obnoxiously long puzzles. It takes forever to get half of the nuggets because you have to do very specific, tedious movements and magnesis tricks, and it gets old fast. There was some good from this game, but by the time you reach the end, it'll have felt like more of a chore than anything else.
Now, if you care to see the full review, proceed downward. Spoilers beware.
The main gimmick of this game is its antigravity mechanic. Upon right clicking, you can move any object (capable of being moved) anywhere you want within a pretty long range. And, of course, they give you a gun too, and some abilities throughout the game. Simple objective- collect big and little nuggets. All the little nuggets = one more big nugget. So, four nuggets per level.
Starting off, the game isn't so bad. Perilous Plains does give you a nice place to test out your main abilites. But then you get to Dangerous Desert, everything takes a turn for the worst. The jetpack mechanic in this level is absolutely horrible. The game is clearly not optimized to handle this. There's no way to see all of the level at once, so most of the time spent in this area, you'll be wasting fuel, mindlessly flying around to find anything you miss. It's just obnoxious, and a few of the nuggets are tedious to collect. Tedious is one word you'll see me use a lot during this review, because that's a word that heavily describes this game.
Luckily...
The game after that is easily the best area (in my opinion). This area was so fun, it actually completely changed my look on the game as a whole. It introduces swimming, and the levels are fun, and fast paced, with unique enemies and controls.
Following that area, we go back to something similar to Perilous Plains, just a little harder. It's similar in the sense that it's kinda boring, and you kinda just go through it to get through it. This area introduces springs, which are honestly easy to work with. This area (in case you haven't caught on, it's Misty Marsh). In my opinion, this was the slow decline back to what I thought of it before- a boring game with little challenge besides the obnoxious deaths that occur that are propelled by unfair enemy placement, and the fact that there's no cooldown after you're hit. One hit right after the other.
However, little did I know, it'd get much worse.
Snowy Slopes was the area I was the most exciting for. I love ice mechanics and snowy themes in general when it comes to games. However, this area is, without a doubt, where most of my deaths came from. The area introduces the freezing mechanic, which means, everytime you go into the water, you have a few seconds before your BEEP starts freezing up and dies after a few seconds. It's brutal, and the game doesn't give you a big enough meter to do much. I died within the first 15 seconds of the area because of this cheap mechanic. This could've easily been so much fun if they gave you more than like 5 seconds to be in the water. On top of that, the area also introduces snow spike platforms, which can have you on walls and hanging upside down. This brings on a lot of rough segments with enemies that are impossible to kill, and the game's asking you to make a jump to begin going on a snow spike path. You get hit mid air, drop into the water, and freeze to death. That's how it goes far too often. And it's not that this is hard, it's simply just unfair. On top of all of that, when you finally do get on the snow spike platform, you get wonky controls that don't exactly help the often dire situations you wind up in when you get on them. As much as I really wanted to love this area, I couldn't. There's simple, small changes they could've made to this area to make it play and feel so much better, but they just... didn't.
So, at this point in the game, after spending an hour and a half trying to get through Snowy Slopes, I wound up at Lava Lakes with very low standards for the rest of the game. This area introduces platforms that, when you try to gravitate them, they pull you in. I thought this was really cool, and I had an easy time getting through the first two levels. However, there were still points when I died unfairly because unkillable enemies or crappy controls. The last two levels were much more difficult and tedious, but at the same time, I do have to give props to the very last level of the game, for making you think outside of what the game has taught you before, as it forces you to make your own path to keep progressing.
After I beat the game, I was rather disapointed to see that there is NOTHING that rewards you for getting all nuggets. Not a single thing. Doesn't even tell you that you beat the game, it just... takes you back to space with nothing new. At the same time, I was perfectly fine with just closing the game and moving on, as it was almost 12am when I finished it.
Overall, BEEP is a game I tried to enjoy. When I was playing through Misty Marsh, I even (out loud, I mind you) said that I love this game, because that was just really fun to me. But other than that, there isn't much to take out of this game. It's overly tedious, there's plenty of ways to screw yourself over and force you to die so you can get blocks and enemies to respawn, and the whole game just feels... hard to play. The hard controls and the awkward fact that it's nearly impossible to grab anything mid air don't exactly help. Most of the time, the difficulty comes from something that's simply not possible because the game likes to mess with you, and make it unfair. By the end of the game, there's more enemies than you can handle, and there's just far too many situations where you die for the stupidest of reasons that you couldn't have prevented.
So, despite wanting to enjoy this game, and not, I'm giving BEEP a
.
The game has some value and charm, but the only real reason to buy this game is to enjoy Misty Marsh.

I have played a LOT of horror games, and I thought I was pretty much immune to being scared by now... but this game terrifies me! Something about being alone in a forest at night with only a flashlight... the sounds are really what does it. As I walk or run along the path, there are constant sounds around me, mostly rustling bushes that make me shine the flashlight in that direction and make sure nothing is sneaking up on me! The music is also unnerving, sometimes building up unexpectantly and making me jump. While playing, I find myself in a constant state of fear, walking and running along and constantly shining the flashlight around, afraid of being caught unawares.
What don't I like? The movement is incredibly slow. On the one hand, it makes you feel more vulnerable. On the other hand, it takes too long to traverse the environment, and seems like a bit of a cheap way to prolong the experience. Also, the character holds the flashlight at a weird angle. Almost like if you held it loosely in your hand with your arm at your side, so the light points more at the ground than the space in front of you. I'd much prefer a flashlight centered on the screen, it would be way more useful.
If you like first person atmospheric horror games, definitely give this a go! It's free, after all.

How to make home made goat cheese:
INGREDIENTS
1 quart goats' milk
Juice of 2 lemons
Coarse salt
Finely chopped fresh herbs, such as parcel and lovage (optional)
DIRECTIONS
In a medium saucepan, heat milk until it reaches 180 degrees on an instant-read thermometer. Remove from heat and stir in lemon juice. Let stand until set, about 15 seconds. If milk does not set, add a little more lemon juice.
Line a colander with several layers of cheesecloth. Ladle set milk into colander. Tie the four corners of cheesecloth together; hang on the handle of a wooden spoon set over a deep bowl and let drain until it is the consistency of slightly dry cottage cheese, 1 to 2 hours. Transfer to a bowl and fold in salt and herbs, if desired. Store in an airtight container, refrigerated, up to 1 week.

10/10, I know that's a very high grade, but let me explain.
After the opening and first bit of the story, you will already be emotionally sucked in and brought to tears. I don't want to spoil anything, so I'll say this: The story, the soundtrack, the game mechanics, and the art style all unite as one to provide an outstanding and truly worthy experience.
The movement and combat mechanics are visually appealing and smooth, with new mechanics being introduced at a very comfortable pace. The soundtrack is, for lack of a better word, eargasmic. The art style is cute but mature, never taking away from the experience and in many cases amplifying it. And lastly, the story is beautiful, and executed masterfully. While you're a silent protagonist, the journey is conducted through your actions and experiences, not through dialogue.
You may get frustrated at times, or have to backtrack, but I would argue that's apart of the experience. This game wants you to feel and feel everything. The good, the bad, the glad, and the sad.
I could ramble on about this game for hours, it's honestly one of my favorite games and I'm certainly biased towards it, and rightly so because this game has earned it. This game is one of the very few games I can reccommend to anyone of any stripe. I've done multiple playthroughs of the not-Definitive edition, and I listen to the soundtrack all the time. Just drop the 20$ and play it for yourself, you won't regret it.
